A checkout page worked fine in testing b.q: You need the top 10 offers out of a million by discount. What is the most efficient approach the answer recommends?

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: Your product cache is a HashMap with 10 million entries. Why does a get() cost about the same as with 10 entries?
options: It computes the bucket index from the key's hash and jumps straight to that array slot
It keeps keys sorted and runs a binary search, which is nearly constant
It scans entries in parallel threads, so large maps finish just as fast
It caches the most recent lookups, so repeated gets skip the search
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: The hash gives an array index directly, so only the few entries in that bucket are checked: O(1) on average. Binary search would be O(log n) and is what a TreeMap-like structure does.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: Two different SKUs, "pen" and "OD4480", land in bucket 8 of a Java HashMap. What does Java 8+ do with a small number of such collisions?
options: Probes the next free bucket in the array until it finds an empty slot
Immediately converts the bucket into a red-black tree of the two keys
Rejects the second put, since a bucket can hold only one entry at a time
Chains them in a linked list in that bucket and uses equals() to find the right key
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: Java uses chaining: colliding nodes form a short list and lookups compare cached hashes then equals(). Probing other slots is open addressing, which Python's dict uses.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: A bucket in a 1,024-bucket HashMap has grown to 9 colliding entries. What happens in Java 8+?
options: The whole map is rehashed with a new hash function to spread keys
The bucket is converted into a red-black tree, so lookups there become O(log n)
The map doubles to 2,048 buckets, because any long chain forces a resize
Nothing changes; the linked list simply grows and lookups become O(n)
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: Past 8 nodes (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) in a table of at least 64 buckets, the bucket treeifies. Resizing instead only happens when the table has fewer than 64 buckets.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: A long chain of 9 entries builds up in a HashMap that still has only 32 buckets. What does Java do?
options: It treeifies the bucket immediately, exactly as it would in a big table
It throws an exception warning that the hash function is badly designed
It doubles the table instead of treeifying, since the table is below 64 buckets
It moves the extra entries into a separate overflow array for later
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY is 64: in a smaller table a long chain usually just means the table is too small, so the map resizes. Treeification only happens in tables of 64 or more buckets.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: Why does Java convert crowded buckets into trees at all?
options: To cap the damage from bad or hostile hash codes at O(log n) instead of O(n)
To keep the map's iteration order sorted by key for faster printing
To reduce memory, since a tree node is smaller than a linked list node
To make every lookup O(log n), which is faster than O(1) for big maps
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: Strings like "Aa" and "BB" share a hash code, so attackers could craft many colliding keys and turn lookups into long scans. Trees bound that worst case; they do not order the whole map.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: A fresh HashMap with default settings (16 buckets, load factor 0.75) receives products one by one. Which insert triggers the first resize?
options: The 13th insert, because the threshold is 16 x 0.75 = 12
The 16th insert, because the array is full once every bucket is used
The 9th insert, because a bucket treeifies after 8 entries
The 17th insert, because the map resizes only when it overflows
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: Resizing happens when size exceeds capacity x load factor, which is 12, so the 13th insert doubles the table to 32. Waiting until 16 would let chains get longer.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: Why is 0.75 the default load factor in Java's HashMap?
options: It guarantees zero collisions as long as the map stays under 75% full
It matches the CPU cache line size, making each bucket fit in one line
It balances time and memory: fewer collisions than 1.0 without a half-empty array
It is the point at which treeification becomes cheaper than chaining
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: 0.5 wastes memory, 1.0 lengthens chains; 0.75 is the trade-off. No load factor guarantees zero collisions.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: Your service loads 2 million SKUs into an unsized HashMap at startup, and startup is slow. What is the best fix?
options: Lower the load factor to 0.5 so the map resizes less often
Use a TreeMap so inserts never trigger a resize of the array
Pre-size the map (about 2,700,000 capacity, or HashMap.newHashMap) so it allocates once
Insert the SKUs in sorted order so the entries land in fewer buckets
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: An unsized map resizes about 18 times, copying entries each time; sizing it for n / 0.75 avoids that. A lower load factor would make resizes happen sooner, not later.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: Resizing a HashMap copies every entry, which is O(n). Why are inserts still described as O(1)?
options: Because Java resizes in a background thread so callers never wait
Because the table doubles, resizes get rarer, so the cost averages out to amortised O(1)
Because only the colliding buckets are copied, not every entry
Because the resize reuses the old array and copies nothing at all
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: Doubling means each resize is paid for by many cheap inserts, so the average per insert is constant. The unlucky insert that triggers a big resize can still pause for milliseconds.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: During a resize from 16 to 32 buckets, where can an entry currently in bucket 8 end up?
options: In any of the 32 buckets, since hashCode() is called again on resize
Always in bucket 16, since old entries move to the new upper half
Always in bucket 8, since entries keep their index after a resize
Either still in bucket 8 or in bucket 24, decided by one extra bit of its hash
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: Because capacity doubles, (hash & oldCap) decides between the same index and index + old capacity. Java uses the cached hash and never calls hashCode() again.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: Java computes the bucket as `hash & (n - 1)` rather than `hash % n`. Why does this work and help?
options: The AND is more random than modulo, so it removes all collisions
Capacity is a power of two, so the AND keeps the low bits: cheap and never negative
The AND works for any capacity and lets Java pick prime table sizes
The AND spreads high bits into low bits so that keys mix better
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: With n a power of two, n - 1 is all ones in binary, so the AND equals mod for non-negative values and is a single fast operation. Mixing high bits is the separate 'spread' step.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: Before masking, Java does `h ^ (h >>> 16)`. What problem does this solve?
options: It makes the hash code positive so the bucket index is never negative
It encrypts the hash so attackers cannot predict which bucket is used
Keys whose hash codes differ only in high bits would otherwise pile into one bucket
It compresses the 32-bit hash into 16 bits to save space in each node
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: Masking looks only at low bits, so XORing the top 16 bits in lets high bits influence the bucket. It is not security; trees handle hostile keys.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: A developer overrides equals() on an OrderKey class but forgets hashCode(). What happens with a HashMap?
options: Nothing goes wrong, because HashMap only ever calls equals() to compare
The code fails to compile, since Java requires both methods together
Equal keys get different hash codes, land in different buckets, and get() returns null
HashMap detects the mismatch and falls back to a linear scan of entries
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: The contract says equal keys must have equal hash codes; otherwise lookups go to the wrong bucket and duplicates appear. Always override both (records do this for you).

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: You store a CartKey(userId, pincode) in a HashMap, then the user changes address and you set key.pincode = "560001". Why does get(key) now return null even though size() is 1?
options: The map removes an entry automatically whenever its key's fields change
The entry sits in the bucket for the old hash, but get looks in the new hash's bucket
get() uses identity comparison, so the modified key is a new object
The map was resized during the update and the entry was lost in the copy
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: The key's hash changed while it was in the map, so the entry is effectively leaked in its old bucket. Use immutable keys like Strings or records, or remove, change, and re-put.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: A colleague says 'Aa' and 'BB' must be the same key because they have the same hash code (2112). What is right?
options: They are the same key, since HashMap treats equal hashes as equal keys
They cannot both be stored, because the second put overwrites the first
Java changes one of the hash codes on insert so that they never collide
Equal hash codes are only a fast filter; equals() decides whether keys are the same
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: The contract only requires equal keys to have equal hashes, not the reverse. Both keys live in the same bucket and equals() tells them apart.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: Many request threads update a shared SKU cache map. Which choice does the answer recommend?
options: A plain HashMap, since puts to different keys never interfere
Collections.synchronizedMap, since one global lock is the fastest option
A plain HashMap rebuilt from scratch on every request to avoid races
ConcurrentHashMap, with lock-free reads and per-bucket locking on writes
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: Plain HashMap is not thread-safe and can lose updates or corrupt structure. synchronizedMap is correct but makes every thread queue on one lock.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: Using ConcurrentHashMap, you want to increment a per-SKU view counter safely from many threads. What is the best way?
options: Use an atomic method like merge(sku, 1, Integer::sum) instead of get then put
Call get(), add one, then put() the result back, since each call is safe
Store null for new SKUs and replace it with 1 on the first increment
Wrap the ConcurrentHashMap in Collections.synchronizedMap for safety
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: Each call is thread-safe, but get-then-put is a race between threads. ConcurrentHashMap also forbids null values.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: How does Python's dict handle collisions, compared with Java's HashMap?
options: Chaining: it keeps a linked list in each slot, the same as Java
Treeification: each crowded slot becomes a balanced search tree
Rehashing: it picks a new hash function whenever a collision occurs
Open addressing: it probes other slots in the same array until one is free
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: Python's dict probes a pseudo-random sequence of slots instead of chaining. Java chains and later treeifies.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: A report expects a HashMap of order IDs to print in the order they were inserted, but the order looks random. What should you use?
options: HashMap with a load factor of 1.0, which preserves insertion order
LinkedHashMap, since HashMap keeps no order and its order can change after resize
ConcurrentHashMap, which iterates entries in the order they were added
HashMap pre-sized large enough that it never resizes during inserts
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: HashMap gives no ordering guarantee; LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order (TreeMap keeps sorted order). Pre-sizing avoids reordering from resizes but still guarantees no order.

How does a HashMap find a value in const.q: What happens if a key class's hashCode() always returns 1?
options: Every key lands in one bucket: still correct but slow, O(log n) at best as a tree
The map throws an exception since hash codes must be unique per key
Only one entry can ever be stored, since later puts overwrite it
Lookups stay O(1) because equals() still identifies the right key
How does a HashMap find a value in const.why: Correctness holds because equals() decides, but all entries share a bucket. With Comparable keys the tree gives O(log n); otherwise it is near O(n).

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: Your home page needs a 'Top 10 trending' strip from 10 million products, refreshed every few seconds. What is the most efficient core approach?
options: Scan once with a min-heap of size 10, comparing each product to the weakest leader
Fully sort all 10 million products by count and take the first ten
Build a max-heap of all 10 million products and pop the top ten
Keep a sorted array of all products and re-sort it on every refresh
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: A size-k min-heap does about n log k work with only k items in memory. A max-heap of all products also works but must hold all n items.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: Why is a MIN-heap the right choice for keeping a TOP-10 list?
options: A min-heap keeps the strongest product at the root for instant display
Each newcomer is compared with the weakest current leader, which the min-heap keeps at the root
A min-heap sorts all products in ascending order as they arrive
A min-heap uses less memory per node than a max-heap does
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: The question for every arrival is 'is this better than the worst leader?', and the min-heap answers it in O(1) via the root. A max-heap would need all n items to find the top k.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: For n = 10 million and k = 10, roughly how much work does a full sort do compared with a size-k heap?
options: Sort: about 33 million comparisons; heap: about 230 million comparisons
Sort: about 10 million comparisons; heap: about 10 comparisons in total
Sort: about 230 million comparisons; heap: at most about 33 million, often near 10 million
Both about 230 million comparisons, since each must see every product
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: n log2 n is about 230 million; n log2 k is at most about 33 million, and most products fail after one comparison with the root. Seeing every item once is n, not n log n.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: A size-3 min-heap holds [5, 9, 7]. A product with count 6 arrives. What happens?
options: 6 is skipped, because it is smaller than the largest item 9
6 replaces 7, because 7 is the closest value to the newcomer
6 beats the root 5, so 5 is removed and the heap becomes [6, 9, 7]
6 is added and the heap grows to four items [5, 6, 9, 7]
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: The newcomer is compared only with the root (the weakest leader); 6 > 5 so 5 leaves and 6 sits at the root, already smaller than both children. The heap never grows beyond k.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: A heap is stored in a plain array. For the item at index 4, where are its children and parent?
options: Children at 8 and 9, parent at 2
Children at 9 and 10, parent at 1
Children at 5 and 6, parent at 3
Children at 9 and 10, parent at 2
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: Children are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 (9 and 10); the parent is at (i - 1) / 2 with integer division, which is 1. Index 2 would be i / 2, a common slip.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: Your trending list built from all-time view counts keeps showing a phone launched two years ago. What is the fix?
options: Increase k so newer products also have room to appear in the list
Switch to a Count-Min Sketch, which automatically forgets old counts
Add time decay: count only recent buckets (e.g. last 60 minutes) or decay scores by a half-life
Shard the counters by product ID so old products get less weight
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: Trending means recent velocity; without decay old bestsellers win forever. A sketch only approximates counts and does not forget old events by itself.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: You must choose between one-minute sliding-window buckets and exponential decay for trending scores. Which statement is accurate?
options: Windows need one number per product, while decay needs 60 numbers each
Windows are exact and easy to explain but store many counters; decay keeps one smooth score per product
Decay is exact, while windows are always approximate in their counts
Both need the same storage, so the choice only affects ranking order
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: Windows store up to 60 counters per active product and say 'views in the last hour'; decay keeps a single shrinking score and gives smoother lists.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: With exponential decay using a 30-minute half-life, how much does a click from 30 minutes ago count compared with a click now?
options: Half as much
A quarter as much
Nothing at all, since it is outside the window
The same, until a full hour has passed
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: A half-life means the weight halves every 30 minutes. A quarter would be after 60 minutes.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: Memory is tight, so you use a Count-Min Sketch. It reports 1,040 views for product P. Which is possible?
options: The true count could be 1,100, but it could not be 1,000
The true count is exactly 1,040, since sketches are exact
The true count could be 1,000, but it could not be 1,100
The true count could be anything, since sketches have no bounds
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: Collisions only add to counters, so the sketch can overestimate but never underestimates, and the overcount is bounded. Taking the minimum across rows picks the least polluted cell.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: How does a Count-Min Sketch estimate a product's count?
options: Hash it into one counter per row and take the average of those counters
Hash it into one counter per row and take the minimum of those counters
Hash it into one counter per row and take the maximum of those counters
Look up its exact counter in a hash map keyed by the product ID
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: Every collision only inflates a cell, so the minimum across d rows is the least polluted estimate. Averaging would mix in the inflation from collisions.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: Your finance team asks to reuse the trending Count-Min Sketch to compute per-seller billing for product views. What should you say?
options: No; the sketch is approximate and overcounts, fine for trending but not for billing
Yes; the sketch is exact as long as you use enough hash functions
Yes; the sketch undercounts, so sellers would never be overcharged
No; the sketch can only count products, never sellers or other keys
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: Count-Min gives a bounded overestimate with some probability, which is fine for heavy hitters but not for money. For exact counts, partition by product ID with exact counters.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: Three shards each send their local top 10 and the merged list misses the true number 1 product. Events were spread randomly. What is the best fix?
options: Partition events by product ID so each product's full count lives on one shard
Send only the top 5 from each shard so the merge step runs faster
Use a max-heap instead of a min-heap when merging the shard lists
Add more shards so that each product's views are spread more evenly
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: With random splitting a product can be 11th on every shard yet 1st overall. Keying by product ID makes the merge exact; sending much larger lists (like top 1,000) is the other workaround.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: A new phone launch sends 30,000 views a minute, overloading the shard that owns it. What does the answer suggest?
options: Re-partition events randomly so the launch phone spreads across shards
Drop most of its events, since it will obviously be number 1 anyway
Raise k so the heap on that shard has space for more products
Pre-aggregate on each producer for about a second and send one combined increment
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: Producer-side batching cuts per-event load on the hot key while keeping partition-by-product exactness. Random partitioning would break exact merging.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: Which Redis command returns the top 10 products with scores from a sorted set?
options: ZREVRANGE key 0 9 WITHSCORES
ZINCRBY key 10 WITHSCORES
ZUNIONSTORE key 0 9 WITHSCORES
ZRANGE key 0 9 WITHSCORES
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: ZREVRANGE reads highest scores first. ZRANGE returns lowest scores first; ZINCRBY increments and ZUNIONSTORE combines buckets.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: You keep one Redis sorted set per minute and want 'last hour' trending where older minutes count less. Which feature fits?
options: ZINCRBY with a negative value on every key, once per minute
EXPIRE with a shorter TTL on older keys so their scores shrink
ZREVRANGE with a smaller range for keys that are older
ZUNIONSTORE with WEIGHTS across the 60 minute keys
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: ZUNIONSTORE combines the minute buckets and WEIGHTS lets older minutes contribute less, a simple decay. EXPIRE removes old buckets entirely; it does not scale their scores.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: Your trending strip shows 10 items, but out-of-stock items and duplicate colours of one phone must be filtered out. How many candidates should the pipeline keep?
options: Exactly 10, then show fewer items if some are filtered out
All products in the category, so the filters can run on everything
Exactly 10, then re-run the full pipeline whenever a filter removes one
A few more than 10, such as 50, so filters do not leave gaps
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: Keeping k = 50 leaves room for business filters while staying cheap. Keeping everything defeats the point of a size-k heap.

How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.q: Millions of home-page loads need the trending list. What does the read path look like in the worked example?
options: Each page load runs the min-heap over the live counters on demand
Each page load queries all 20 workers and merges their lists itself
Each page load reads the Count-Min Sketch and estimates the top ten
Readers fetch one small, edge-cached key; an aggregator swaps a pointer to a fresh list
How does an app keep a live \"Top 10 tre.why: The aggregator writes the merged list to a fresh Redis key and switches a pointer, so readers never touch counters or see a half-written list.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: A junior asks you to explain dynamic programming in one line. Which is the best plain-words definition?
options: Always pick the locally best choice at each step and never look back
Split the input into independent halves and solve each half separately
Try every possible combination and keep the best one that you find
Solve smaller versions of the same problem and store each answer so it is never recomputed
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: DP is 'remember what you already figured out' for repeated subproblems. Picking the locally best choice is greedy, and independent halves is divide and conquer.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: Which two properties tell you a problem is a good fit for DP?
options: Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Independent subproblems and a provably correct greedy rule
Sorted input and a logarithmic number of choices per step
Optimal substructure and subproblems that never repeat
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: DP pays off when the same smaller questions recur and the best answer is built from best smaller answers. Without repetition, caching saves nothing.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: Your recursive Fibonacci for n = 40 takes seconds. Roughly how many calls does it make, and what does a memo change?
options: About 40 calls; a memo only reduces the memory used by each call
About 1,600 calls; a memo turns quadratic work into linear work
About 331 million calls; a memo halves that to about 165 million
About 331 million calls; with a memo, about 40 to 80 steps, exponential down to linear
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: Each call spawns two more and the same values repeat, so calls grow about 1.6 to the n. With a memo each n is solved once, so work is linear.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: You can climb a 10-step staircase 1 or 2 steps at a time. What recurrence gives the number of ways to reach step n?
options: ways(n) = ways(n-1) x 2, with ways(1) = 1
ways(n) = ways(n-1) + 1, with ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2
ways(n) = ways(n-2) + 2, with ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2
ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), with ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: Your last move came from step n-1 or n-2, so add those counts. This gives 89 ways for 10 steps, the Fibonacci pattern.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: Your memoised recursive solution crashes with a StackOverflowError on large inputs. What is the best change?
options: Make the memo a ConcurrentHashMap so the recursion runs in parallel
Convert it to bottom-up tabulation with a loop that fills the table from base cases
Remove the memo, since caching is what makes the stack grow deep
Switch to a greedy choice at each step to avoid recursion entirely
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: Tabulation has no recursion, so no stack overflow, and loops are fast. Greedy changes the algorithm and may give wrong answers.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: Your bottom-up stair-climbing DP uses an array of size n, but dp[i] only reads dp[i-1] and dp[i-2]. How can you improve memory?
options: Keep just two variables for the previous two values, cutting memory from O(n) to O(1)
Switch to memoisation, which never stores more than two values
Use a HashMap instead of an array, which avoids storing unused entries
Store only every second entry of the array to halve the memory
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: Since only the last two values are needed, rolling variables suffice. Memoisation stores every solved state in its cache.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: A teammate adds a cache to merge sort and calls it 'dynamic programming'. Why is that wrong?
options: Merge sort lacks optimal substructure, so its output would be incorrect
Merge sort's subproblems do not overlap, so caching saves nothing; it is divide and conquer
Merge sort already is DP, so adding a cache just duplicates the work
Caching is never allowed in recursive algorithms, only in loops
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: Each half of merge sort is different data solved once, so there is nothing to reuse. Recursion plus a cache is DP only when subproblems repeat.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: Why can DP solve shortest paths but not the longest simple path (no repeated cities)?
options: Longest paths have no overlapping subproblems, so caching saves nothing
Shortest paths only work on trees, while longest paths need full graphs
Shortest paths have optimal substructure; longest simple paths do not
Longest paths require negative weights, which DP cannot represent
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: If the shortest Chennai-Delhi route goes via Nagpur, its Chennai-Nagpur part must itself be shortest. That property fails for longest simple paths.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: Using vouchers of Rs 1, 3 and 4, you must pay Rs 6 with the fewest vouchers. A greedy 'biggest first' rule picks 4 + 1 + 1. What does this show?
options: Greedy is optimal here, since 3 vouchers is the minimum possible
DP and greedy always agree when the amount is under Rs 10
Greedy is not safe in general; DP finds 3 + 3, which uses 2 vouchers
The coins must be sorted in ascending order for greedy to work
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: Greedy makes one choice and never reconsiders; DP tries each last-coin option per state. Greedy happens to work for some coin systems like 1, 2, 5.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: For fewest-coins coin change, which state and transition are correct?
options: dp[a] = fewest coins for amount a; dp[a] = 1 + min over coins c <= a of dp[a - c]
dp[a] = fewest coins for amount a; dp[a] = dp[a - 1] + dp[a - 2]
dp[a] = number of coin types for amount a; dp[a] = max over c of dp[a - c]
dp[a] = fewest coins for amount a; dp[a] = min over coins of dp[a + c] - 1
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: Think about the last coin used: the rest makes a - c, so add one to the best of those. dp[a-1] + dp[a-2] is the stair-counting recurrence, not coin change.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: Using coins 1, 2 and 5, what is dp[7] for fewest coins, and which coins make it?
options: 3 coins: 5 + 1 + 1
2 coins: 5 + 2
1 coin, since dp[7] simply copies the value of dp[5]
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: dp[7] = 1 + min(dp[6], dp[5], dp[2]) = 1 + min(2, 1, 1) = 2. 5 + 1 + 1 is valid but not minimal.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: Your coin-change table says dp[11] = 3, and the product manager wants to know WHICH vouchers were used. What do you do?
options: Also store the coin that gave the minimum at each amount, then walk back from 11
Re-run the DP with each coin removed to see which ones change the answer
Read the coins directly from dp[11], since it stores the coin list
Use greedy on 11 afterwards, since it always matches the DP's choice
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: Recording the chosen coin per amount lets you trace 11 -> 10 -> 5 -> 0 (1, 5, 5). The dp value itself only stores a count.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: How do you estimate a DP's running time before writing code?
options: Number of states plus work per transition, e.g. O(amount + coins)
Depth of recursion times the size of the memo, e.g. O(amount squared)
Number of states times work per transition, e.g. O(amount x coins) for coin change
Two raised to the number of choices, since DP tries every combination
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: Each state is solved once and each costs one transition's work, so multiply. Two to the n is the brute force DP avoids.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: Which interview problem statement most strongly signals DP?
options: Print every possible permutation of a list of eight product names
Minimum cost to reach the bottom-right of a grid moving only right or down
Find whether a value exists in a sorted array of a million prices
Merge two sorted lists of order IDs into a single sorted list
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: A best value, a choice at each step and natural smaller sub-grids are classic DP signals. Listing every permutation is backtracking, and searching a sorted array is binary search.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: Your checkout wants to pick bank offers and coupons, under rules and a spending cap, to maximise customer savings. With a moderate number of offers, what fits?
options: A knapsack-style DP over (offer index, budget left)
A greedy rule that always takes the single largest discount first
A full sort of offers by discount, then apply them all in that order
A hash map of offers by SKU, looked up once per cart item
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: Each offer is a take-or-skip choice affecting what remains possible, which is knapsack. Greedy can miss better combinations.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: A knapsack DP over a budget W runs very slowly when W is a huge rupee value. Why?
options: Knapsack is exponential in n, so the budget has nothing to do with it
Large budgets cause hash collisions in the memo, slowing every lookup
Its time is O(n x W), pseudo-polynomial: it grows with W's numeric value
DP is always fast, so the slowness must come from recursion overhead
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: The number of states includes every budget value up to W, so a huge W means a huge table. 'DP is always fast' is a misconception.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: When comparing two versions of a config file, a diff tool finds the fewest insertions and deletions. Which DP idea is this?
options: Coin change over the number of lines that differ between the files
Top-k selection of the lines that changed the most between versions
Shortest path over a graph of the file's directory structure
Edit distance / longest common subsequence over (line i of A, line j of B)
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: Diff is a classic LCS/edit-distance DP over pairs of positions in the two files; Git's Myers diff refines that idea.

What is dynamic programming in plain wor.q: Memoisation or tabulation: which statement is a fair trade-off?
options: Memoisation is always asymptotically faster than tabulation for any problem
Memoisation is quick to write and skips unreachable states; tabulation avoids deep recursion
Tabulation solves only the states actually needed, memoisation solves all
Tabulation needs recursion, while memoisation needs explicit loops
What is dynamic programming in plain wor.why: Both usually have the same big-O time. Memo follows the natural recursion and only touches needed states; tabulation needs a correct filling order but avoids stack overflow.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: You are modelling a city's roads for a delivery app's routing engine. What should the edge weight usually be?
options: Physical length of the road segment in kilometres
Number of turns needed to traverse the segment
Speed limit posted on the road segment
Expected travel time on that road segment
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: Apps want the fastest route, so edges carry time (sometimes mixed with tolls or turns). The shortest-distance route can be slower, for example through a jam.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: A teammate uses BFS to find the route from a dark store to a customer. In the example graph it returns W, B, D, H (15 minutes). What is the problem?
options: BFS is correct here; the 13-minute route only exists with negative weights
BFS finds the fastest route, but it is too slow on a city-sized graph
BFS minimises the number of roads, not time; Dijkstra finds W, B, A, C, D, H in 13 minutes
BFS should be run backwards from H to get the fastest route instead
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: BFS explores in rings and is only correct for fastest when every edge has the same weight. More turns can mean less time.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: Running Dijkstra from W, B (distance 2) is settled. It offers a route to A of 2 + 1 = 3 minutes, while A currently shows 4. What happens?
options: A stays at 4, because it was discovered first, directly from W
A is relaxed: its distance becomes 3 and its parent becomes B
A is immediately settled at 3 and removed from further consideration
A is set to 4 + 3 = 7, combining the two routes found so far
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: Relaxing an edge means updating a neighbour when going through this road is quicker, and recording the parent to rebuild the path. A is settled later, when it is the closest unsettled node.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: Why can Dijkstra treat a node as final the moment it is popped from the priority queue?
options: The priority queue sorts all paths, so the first one seen is always best
Each node has only one incoming edge in a road graph, so no other route exists
Dijkstra checks every alternative path before marking a node settled
Weights are non-negative, so any other route must pass a node at least as far and add time
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: With non-negative weights a later route can never undercut a settled distance. This guarantee is exactly what breaks with negative edges.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: Your pricing graph models cashback as negative-cost edges, and you need cheapest paths. What should you use?
options: Dijkstra, since it handles negative weights with a priority queue
A* with an admissible heuristic, which handles negative weights
Bellman-Ford, since Dijkstra breaks when edge weights can be negative
BFS, since negative weights cancel out and make all edges equal
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: A negative edge found later could undercut a 'final' Dijkstra distance. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights at O(V x E).

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: Java's PriorityQueue has no decrease-key operation. How does the standard Dijkstra implementation cope?
options: Lazy deletion: push a new entry when a distance improves and skip stale entries when popped
Remove the old entry with pq.remove() before every update to keep it clean
Never update a distance once a node is in the queue, keeping the first value
Rebuild the whole priority queue each time any distance improves
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: Stale entries are detected with `if (d > dist[u]) continue;`. pq.remove() is O(n), and never updating would give wrong answers.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra with a binary heap on V nodes and E edges?
options: O(V x E)
O(V + E)
O(V squared log E)
O((V + E) log V)
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: Each push and pop on the heap costs O(log V). O(V x E) is Bellman-Ford; O(V + E) is BFS.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: You add A* to your router with h(n) = straight-line distance divided by 100 km/h. Why is this hint safe?
options: It always equals the exact remaining time, so A* explores only the path
It overestimates slightly, which guarantees A* finishes faster
No real road beats a straight line at top speed, so it never overestimates (admissible)
It ignores one-way streets, so it works on any directed graph
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: An admissible heuristic never overestimates the remaining cost, so A* still returns the truly fastest route while exploring fewer nodes.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: To speed up A*, a developer changes the hint to straight-line distance divided by 20 km/h. What could go wrong?
options: Nothing; a slower assumed speed only makes A* explore more nodes
Many roads are faster than 20 km/h, so it overestimates and A* may return a slower route
A* will crash, because heuristics must use the posted speed limit
A* turns into BFS, since every node then gets the same estimate
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: Overestimating breaks admissibility: A* may skip the truly fastest path. With h = 0, A* is exactly Dijkstra.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: What does A* order its priority queue by?
options: f(n) = g(n) + h(n): known time from start plus estimated time to target
h(n) alone: the estimated time from n to the target
g(n) alone: the known time from the start to n
g(n) x h(n): the product of known and estimated times
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: g is Dijkstra's distance and h is the hint; their sum aims the search toward the destination. Using g alone is plain Dijkstra.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: A national maps service gets thousands of route requests per second. Running Dijkstra or A* on the full map per request is too slow. What do production routers do?
options: Run BFS instead, since it is linear time and fast enough at scale
Precompute offline, e.g. contraction hierarchies with shortcut edges, so queries take about a millisecond
Cache every possible origin-destination route ahead of time in memory
Use a larger priority queue so Dijkstra pops nodes in fewer steps
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: CH ranks junctions, adds shortcuts offline, and queries search only upward from both ends, touching hundreds or thousands of nodes. Caching every pair is infeasible.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: Evening traffic makes a main road take 15 minutes instead of 3. Why does this hurt pure contraction hierarchies, and what is the fix?
options: CH ignores weights entirely, so traffic has no effect on it
Shortcuts were built for old weights; customizable variants re-plug new weights in seconds
CH must switch to BFS during rush hour until traffic clears
Shortcuts automatically update, so the only fix is more servers
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: Shortcut times depend on the weights used in preprocessing. Customizable variants split weight-independent work from a fast customisation step.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: How do routing systems usually set road weights for 'right now'?
options: Blend historical speed profiles per road and hour with live GPS pings, updated every few minutes
Use only the posted speed limit, which is stable and predictable
Use only live GPS pings, discarding all historical data each minute
Ask riders to report traffic manually before each delivery starts
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: Historical profiles provide a base and live speeds adjust it; active trips are rerouted when a clearly faster route appears.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: A rider has 12 parcels. A developer proposes trying every possible order of stops. Why is that a bad idea?
options: Dijkstra already gives the best order when run once from the store
There are only 144 orders for 12 stops, but checking each is slow
12! is about 479 million orders and grows factorially; it is the NP-hard TSP, so use heuristics
All orders give the same total time when weights are non-negative
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: Ordering stops is the travelling salesman problem. Dijkstra gives pairwise travel times; it does not choose the order.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: Which approach does the answer suggest for ordering a rider's multi-stop delivery in practice?
options: Nearest neighbour for a quick tour, then 2-opt improvements, on a Dijkstra-built time matrix
Run Dijkstra once from the store and visit stops in order of distance
Sort stops by pincode and visit them in ascending numeric order
Use BFS from each stop and pick the order with the fewest roads
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: Heuristics like nearest neighbour plus 2-opt (or a solver like OR-Tools) give good-enough tours quickly. Visiting in distance order from the store is not the same as optimising the tour.

How does a maps or delivery app find the.q: A road network includes one-way streets. Which graph model fits?
options: An undirected graph stored as a full adjacency matrix
A tree rooted at the dark store with parent pointers only
An unweighted directed graph traversed with plain BFS
A directed, weighted graph stored as an adjacency list
How does a maps or delivery app find the.why: Edge direction captures one-way roads and weights capture travel time. Road graphs are sparse (E is 2 to 3 times V), so an adjacency list is the natural store.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: Your 8 GB laptop runs programs whose virtual sizes add up to over 14 GB, yet everything is fast. How?
options: The OS compresses all programs to half their size the moment they start
The extra 6 GB is always served from swap at RAM speed on an SSD
Only touched pages use RAM (demand paging), so the active working set still fits
Virtual sizes are a display bug; programs never reserve unused memory
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: Allocation is lazy: reserving memory just marks a range valid, and RAM is used only when pages are touched. Swap is about 1,000 times slower than RAM, not equal to it.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: With 4 KB pages, a program reads virtual address 0x5123 and the page table maps page 5 to frame 2. What physical address is read?
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: The low 12 bits (3 hex digits) are the offset 0x123; replace page 5 with frame 2 and keep the offset. Only the page number changes.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: Why must pages (virtual) and frames (physical) be the same size?
options: So that every program gets exactly the same amount of physical RAM
So that the TLB can store whole pages of data rather than translations
Translation swaps only the page number for a frame number and keeps the offset unchanged
So that swap files are the same size as the RAM installed in the machine
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: The offset inside a page is copied as is, which only works if a page fits exactly in a frame.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: Who translates a virtual address into a physical one on every memory load and store?
options: The OS kernel, which intercepts every load and store in software
The MMU, a hardware unit in the CPU, using page tables the OS fills in
The compiler, which rewrites addresses when the program is built
The disk controller, which maps addresses as pages are read in
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: Translation happens on every access, so it must be hardware. The OS only maintains the page tables and handles faults.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: A large JVM heap service shows many TLB misses in profiling. Which change helps most directly?
options: Add more swap space so that the TLB has room for more entries
Switch to 1 KB pages so each translation is cheaper to compute
Use huge pages (2 MB) so each TLB entry covers far more memory
Disable the TLB so the MMU always walks the page table directly
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: Programs roaming big memory overflow the small TLB; 2 MB pages let one entry cover 512 times more. Smaller pages would make TLB misses worse.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: What is the difference between a TLB miss and a page fault?
options: A TLB miss is a hardware table walk; a page fault means the page is not in RAM
They are the same event; both always require reading the page from disk
A TLB miss reads from disk, while a page fault only walks the page table
A page fault is always a bug, while a TLB miss is the normal case
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: A TLB miss is resolved by the MMU walking the page table. A page fault hands control to the OS and may cost a disk read of about 100 microseconds.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: Your monitoring shows thousands of page faults per second on a healthy service. A colleague panics. What is the right reading?
options: Every page fault is an error, so the service has a memory corruption bug
Page faults mean the service has run out of RAM and will be OOM-killed
Most faults are normal minor faults (first touch, cached file pages); watch major faults
Page faults only happen when swap is disabled, so enable swap at once
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: Minor faults just map a frame and are cheap; only major faults hit the disk and are slow. Invalid accesses become segfaults, a different case.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: A program writes to an address that its page table marks read-only. What happens?
options: The OS treats it as an invalid access and sends a segmentation fault
The OS quietly makes the page writable and retries the instruction
The MMU silently ignores the write and continues with the next instruction
The OS swaps the page to disk and then allows the write to succeed
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: Invalid addresses or permission violations are bugs, signalled as segfaults. (Copy-on-write pages are a deliberate special case the OS handles.)

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: Your laptop's disk is at 100% and typing lags by seconds after you start a big load test. What is happening?
options: Thrashing: the combined working set exceeds RAM, so evicted pages are needed again at once
A TLB overflow: the CPU cannot cache translations for so many programs
A memory leak in the OS kernel that slowly fills the page tables
The SSD is failing and needs replacing before the test continues
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: When the active pages don't fit in RAM, the OS spends its time on major faults moving pages. That is thrashing.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: The machine is thrashing. A teammate suggests doubling the swap file. Why won't that help?
options: More swap helps, because pages in swap are accessed at RAM speed
More swap only gives more room to park pages; it does not make RAM bigger, so faults continue
More swap helps, because it shrinks the working set of each program
More swap hurts, because swap files always slow down the TLB
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: Thrashing comes from the working set exceeding RAM; swap just lets it thrash longer. The fix is a smaller working set or more RAM.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: Roughly how much slower is reading a page from an NVMe SSD than from RAM?
options: About 10 times (about 100 ns vs 1 microsecond)
About 1,000 times (about 100 ns vs 50-100 microseconds)
About 100,000 times (about 100 ns vs 10 milliseconds)
About the same, since NVMe sits on the memory bus
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: RAM is around 100 ns and NVMe 50-100 microseconds, about 1,000x. 100,000x is a spinning hard disk.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: A process shows 10 GB 'virtual size' in top. How much RAM is it actually using?
options: 10 GB, since virtual size is the RAM reserved for that process
Look at RSS (resident set size); virtual size counts reserved addresses, not RAM
5 GB, since the OS always keeps half of virtual memory in swap
Nothing, since virtual memory lives entirely on the disk
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: Virtual size includes untouched reserved ranges; RSS shows what is resident. A process can show 10 GB virtual and only 600 MB resident.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: RAM is full and the OS must evict a page. Which page is simply dropped without writing anything?
options: A dirty heap page, since heap data can always be recomputed
Any stack page, since stacks are rebuilt when functions return
A dirty file page, since the file already has an older copy
A clean page from a file, since the file on disk still has the same contents
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: Clean file pages can be re-read from the file. Dirty pages must be written back first, and anonymous heap or stack pages go to swap.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: How does program A get prevented from reading program B's memory?
options: A's page table has no entries pointing at B's frames, so A cannot even form such an address
The OS encrypts every program's memory with a different key
The CPU checks a list of owners before every RAM read and write
Programs are placed in separate RAM chips on the motherboard
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: Separate page tables give isolation by construction; permission bits add protection for kernel, code and data pages. Sharing (libraries, copy-on-write) is deliberate.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: Your search service reads a 20 GB index file with mmap. What happens on the first read of a given 4 KB region?
options: The whole 20 GB file is read into RAM when mmap is called
Every read goes to disk, since mapped files are never cached in RAM
The read fails until the program explicitly calls a load function
A page fault loads that 4 KB from disk; later reads of that page are plain memory reads
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: mmap maps file pages into the address space and loads them lazily via faults. Writes mark pages dirty for later write-back.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: A Java service in a Kubernetes pod with a 2 GB limit is killed with exit code 137, but never throws OutOfMemoryError. What is the likely cause?
options: The JVM heap hit -Xmx, which Kubernetes reports as exit code 137
The node ran out of swap, so Kubernetes restarted every pod on it
A segmentation fault in the JVM, which always exits with code 137
Heap plus off-heap memory exceeded the cgroup limit, so the kernel's OOM killer killed it
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: Metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers count against the cgroup limit; the kernel kills the process before the heap fills. Size the heap with MaxRAMPercentage to leave room.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: Your pod was OOMKilled while the node still had 50 GB free. Why?
options: Kubernetes always kills pods when node swap is disabled
Container limits are per cgroup; its own pages exceeded the limit, regardless of node memory
Containers have their own RAM like VMs, and theirs was full
The node's free memory was all file cache, which cannot be reclaimed
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: Containers share the host kernel; a limit is accounting plus an OOM kill inside the group. File cache is actually reclaimed first.

Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.q: Your free-memory graph shows almost no 'free' RAM on a database server, yet it is fast. What should you watch instead?
options: Free memory only; low free memory always means the server is about to crash
Total virtual size of all processes compared against installed RAM
Swap size, since a large swap file means the server is healthy
'Available' memory and major page faults, since spare RAM is used as file cache
Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM but runs pro.why: The OS fills spare RAM with file cache and drops it instantly when needed. Available memory and major faults show real pressure.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: Objects OldSession and OldToken reference each other, but no local variable or static field points to either. Will Java's GC free them?
options: No; each still has a reference pointing at it, so its count is above zero
Yes; the GC traces from roots, and neither object is reachable from any root
No; reference cycles must be broken manually by setting fields to null
Only if System.gc() is called explicitly after they become unreachable
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: Java uses reachability tracing, not reference counting, so dead cycles are collected. Reference counts would keep the cycle alive, which is CPython's problem, not Java's.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: Which of these is NOT a GC root in Java?
options: An object on the heap that is referenced only by another unreachable object
A local variable in a running thread's stack frame
A static field of a loaded class
An object used as a lock by a running thread
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: Roots are stack locals and parameters, static fields, JNI references and locks held by running threads. Being referenced by garbage does not make an object live.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: Inside placeOrder(), `int qty = 2;` and `Order order = new Order(userId);` run. After the method returns, what happens?
options: qty and the Order object are both freed immediately when the method returns
The Order object stays alive forever because it was created with new
qty and the order reference vanish with the stack frame; the Order object becomes garbage for the GC
The GC must clean up qty and the order reference from the stack later
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: Stack frames are cleaned automatically on return; the GC only manages the heap. With no references left, the Order is unreachable and reclaimed later.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: A heap has 4 GB of garbage and 200 MB of live data. Why is the mark phase relatively cheap?
options: Marking skips the heap entirely and only scans thread stacks
Marking cost is proportional to the number of live objects, not dead ones
Marking cost depends only on heap size, and 4 GB is small
Dead objects are pre-marked when their last reference is dropped
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: The GC walks only what it can reach from roots; it never visits garbage during marking. That is also why copying young collectors are fast when few objects survive.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: Your service has 500 MB free in many 1 KB holes, but allocating a 2 MB array fails. Which GC style prevents this?
options: Mark-sweep, which adds each dead object's space to a free list
Reference counting, which frees each object as soon as it dies
A bigger young generation, which absorbs every large allocation
Mark-compact, which slides live objects together into one big free block
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: Mark-sweep leaves fragmentation; compaction (or copying) creates contiguous free space and makes allocation a cheap pointer bump.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: Why does Java split the heap into young and old generations?
options: Old objects are larger, so they need a separate area with bigger blocks
Young objects are never referenced by old ones, so they can be ignored
Each thread gets its own young generation to avoid lock contention
Most objects die young, so frequent cheap minor GCs of the young space reclaim most garbage
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: The generational hypothesis: request DTOs and strings die in milliseconds, so copying the few survivors is quick. Old objects can point to young ones, which the card table tracks.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: During a minor GC, how does the JVM avoid scanning the whole old generation for references into the young generation?
options: A card table (remembered set) records which old objects point into the young generation
It assumes old objects never reference young objects, so it skips them
It promotes every young object to the old generation before collecting
It stops all threads and scans the full heap on every minor GC
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: The card table lets minor GCs treat only the recorded old-to-young references as extra roots, keeping them fast.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: A static HashMap 'recently viewed offers' cache grows with every unique user. During the sale, a 2.5-second full GC freezes the pod. What is the root cause?
options: The young generation is too small, so minor GCs run too often
Parallel GC cannot collect HashMap entries, only plain objects
The unbounded static map keeps entries reachable, filling the old generation
Traffic jumped 8x, and full GCs always happen at 8x traffic
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: Static fields are GC roots, so every entry stays live and gets promoted. The pause is the symptom; the unbounded cache is the cause.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: What is the best primary fix for the unbounded static cache?
options: Replace it with a bounded cache with maximumSize and expireAfterWrite (e.g. Caffeine), or move it to Redis
Call System.gc() every few minutes so the cache is cleaned regularly
Increase the heap from 6 GB to 24 GB so the cache has more room
Switch to ZGC, which automatically frees entries in unbounded maps
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: No collector can free reachable objects; bounding the cache removes the leak. A bigger heap only delays OutOfMemoryError and can lengthen full GCs.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: How do you tell a memory leak from a heap that is simply too small?
options: Watch old-gen usage right after each full GC: a rising floor means a leak
Count the minor GCs per minute: many minor GCs always means a leak
Check the total heap size: if it is over 4 GB, it must be a leak
Look at CPU usage: high CPU means a leak, low CPU means a small heap
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: If live data after GC keeps climbing, something is holding references. A flat floor with frequent GCs means the heap is just too small for the load.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: Your service's p99 latency spikes every few minutes while the average stays flat. What should you check first?
options: Database indexes, since slow queries always show up at p99 first
Thread stack sizes, since deep stacks slow every request equally
The number of CPU cores, since spikes mean too few cores overall
GC logs for stop-the-world pauses whose timestamps line up with the spikes
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: STW pauses freeze all in-flight requests and mainly hit tail latency. Matching pause times with spike times confirms GC.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: A 2.5-second full GC on one pod leads to p99 of 3 seconds across the whole fleet. How did one pause spread?
options: Full GCs are coordinated across pods, so all pods pause at the same time
The GC on one pod frees memory on other pods through a shared heap
Health checks timed out, the pod was pulled, and its traffic overloaded other pods into their own full GCs
Kubernetes restarts every pod whenever any one pod has a full GC
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: Long pauses can cascade: failed health checks remove capacity, retries pile onto other nodes, and they hit the same problem.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: Your checkout API needs strict tail latency on a 32 GB heap. Which collector fits best?
options: ZGC, which marks and moves objects concurrently with pauses usually under 1 ms
Parallel GC, which uses many threads and so has the shortest pauses
G1 with default settings, which guarantees pauses under 1 ms
Serial collection with System.gc() calls between requests
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: ZGC suits large heaps and strict latency at some CPU and memory cost. Parallel GC is all stop-the-world, best for throughput batch jobs; G1 targets about 200 ms by default.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: A colleague claims 'ZGC and Shenandoah have zero pauses'. What is accurate?
options: They are truly pause-free, because they never stop application threads
They have the same pauses as Parallel GC, only spread over more threads
They are low-pause, not zero-pause: tiny STW phases remain, and barriers cost some CPU and memory
They avoid pauses by skipping compaction, so fragmentation grows over time
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: Both use barriers so the app and GC cooperate while objects move; brief STW phases still exist. ZGC and Shenandoah do compact concurrently.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: How does G1, the default collector since JDK 9, keep pauses near a target?
options: It stops collecting entirely whenever a pause would exceed the target
It uses reference counting for young objects and tracing for old ones
It only ever collects the young generation and never the old
It splits the heap into equal regions and collects the regions with the most garbage first
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: G1 collects incrementally by region, aiming for MaxGCPauseMillis (default 200 ms). It still collects old regions, in mixed collections.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: A teammate says: 'Our heap is under pressure, so let's call System.gc() after each batch.' What is the problem?
options: It is ignored by every JVM, so the call has no effect at all
It often triggers an expensive full GC and still cannot free objects that are reachable
It frees reachable objects too, which can crash the application
It only collects the stack, so the heap pressure stays the same
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: System.gc() can cause a long STW full GC; reachable objects stay alive regardless. Fix the allocations or the leak instead.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: You start tuning a JVM for a sale. Which baseline does the answer recommend?
options: Set the largest heap the machine allows and disable GC logging for speed
Set -Xms equal to -Xmx, enable GC logs and heap dump on OOM, and measure before changing flags
Leave -Xms small so the heap can grow only when the sale traffic arrives
Copy GC flags from another service, since tuning is the same everywhere
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: Equal -Xms/-Xmx avoids resizing; logs and dumps show pauses and who holds memory. In containers, leave headroom below the limit for non-heap memory.

How does Java's garbage collector know w.q: How does CPython's memory management mainly differ from Java's?
options: CPython uses a concurrent mark-sweep collector that never moves objects
CPython uses reference counting plus a cycle collector; Java traces reachability from roots
CPython uses generational copying exactly like Java's young generation
CPython has no automatic memory management and relies on manual frees
How does Java's garbage collector know w.why: CPython frees objects the instant their count hits zero and needs a cycle collector for loops. Concurrent non-moving mark-sweep describes Go.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: Why can a single Node.js thread serve thousands of concurrent users?
options: Node.js runs each request on its own hidden OS thread behind the scenes
JavaScript executes so fast that each request finishes before the next arrives
The event loop runs callbacks in parallel across all available CPU cores
Most of a request's time is spent waiting on I/O, and the thread never idles during that wait
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: Requests are often over 90% waiting; with non-blocking I/O the thread serves others meanwhile. The loop gives concurrency, not parallelism.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: What role does epoll play in an event-loop server on Linux?
options: It runs JavaScript callbacks on a pool of background worker threads
It polls every socket one by one in a tight loop to check for data
It lets the program sleep until any registered socket is ready and reports which ones
It compresses network traffic so that each socket uses less memory
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: epoll is the OS readiness notification: register sockets once, then one call returns the ready ones. Its cost scales with ready sockets, not total sockets.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: Your Node server holds 10,000 mostly idle WebSocket connections. Why is that cheap?
options: epoll's cost depends on the number of ready sockets, and each waiting connection is a small object
Node closes idle connections after a second and reopens them when needed
Each connection gets its own 1 MB thread, which the OS keeps paged out
The kernel merges idle connections into one socket until data arrives
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: Idle sockets cost almost nothing to watch, and waiting state is a few KB of promise or coroutine. 10,000 OS threads would reserve around 10 GB of stack.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: A Python asyncio handler calls `requests.get()` (a blocking library) inside `async def`. What happens under load?
options: Nothing; marking the function async makes requests.get non-blocking
Each call freezes the whole event loop, so throughput collapses to one request at a time
asyncio moves the call to a background thread automatically
Only that one request slows down; other requests continue normally
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: async only helps if what you await is non-blocking. Use httpx or aiohttp with await, or wrap it with asyncio.to_thread.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: Someone adds `time.sleep(1)` inside an asyncio coroutine to wait before retrying. What should it be?
options: `await asyncio.sleep(1)`, which hands control back to the loop while waiting
`time.sleep(1)` is fine, since coroutines pause automatically when sleeping
`asyncio.run(time.sleep(1))`, which runs the sleep on a separate loop
`threading.Event().wait(1)`, which never blocks the event loop
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: time.sleep blocks the single thread and freezes every request. asyncio.sleep registers a timer and yields to the loop.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: A Node endpoint renders a PDF invoice (300 ms of CPU) inside the request handler. Latency for ALL endpoints jumps to seconds. Why?
options: PDF rendering uses too much network bandwidth, starving other requests
The libuv thread pool has only 4 threads, and PDFs exhaust them
Promises time out after 300 ms, so other requests are retried
Callbacks run to completion on one thread, so CPU work blocks every other callback
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: Nothing interrupts a running callback, so the loop cannot serve anyone else while rendering. CPU-heavy work must be offloaded.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: What is the best fix for CPU-heavy PDF rendering in an event-loop service?
options: Wrap the rendering code in async/await so it no longer blocks the loop
Add more await statements inside the rendering loop to speed it up
Increase the server's memory so the PDF renders in less time
Offload it to a worker thread pool, or to a separate invoice service fed by a queue
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: async/await does not make CPU work non-blocking; it still runs on the loop thread. Worker threads (e.g. Piscina) or a separate service move the computation away.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: Your service is 95% CPU-bound math. A teammate proposes rewriting it with async/await to handle more users. What is right?
options: It will help a lot, because async code runs faster than synchronous code
It won't help; async helps I/O waiting, and CPU-bound work needs more cores or processes
It will help, because the event loop spreads work across all cores
It will help only if every function in the codebase is marked async
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: Async lets a machine hold more waiting requests; it does not speed up computation and adds overhead for CPU-bound work.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: Each turn of the loop, after running one I/O callback, Node drains the microtask queue. Which of these runs as a microtask?
options: A setTimeout callback that has just become due
Code after an `await`, a `.then` continuation, or process.nextTick
A socket read callback reported by epoll
An fs.readFile completion from the libuv thread pool
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: Promise continuations and nextTick are microtasks and drain fully after every macrotask. Timers and I/O callbacks are macrotasks.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: A Node service uses an endless chain of promise continuations, and I/O callbacks stop being processed. Why?
options: Promise chains are processed on the libuv pool, which is full
epoll stops reporting readiness while any promise is pending
Microtasks are drained fully before the next macrotask, so an endless chain starves I/O
Timers have higher priority than I/O and block it permanently
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: After each macrotask Node empties the whole microtask queue; if it keeps refilling, the loop never reaches I/O.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: A team says 'Node.js is single-threaded, so it can only use one core'. What is the accurate response?
options: JS runs on one thread per process, but you run one process per core (cluster, PM2, containers)
Node automatically spreads callbacks across all cores, so one process is enough
Node uses only one thread in total, so it cannot use more than one core
Node uses one OS thread per request, so it already uses every core
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: Production Node runs several processes, roughly one per core; libuv also has a small helper thread pool (4 by default) for file, DNS and some crypto work.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: Which operations does Node's hidden libuv thread pool (4 threads by default) handle?
options: All incoming HTTP requests, one thread per request
File system calls, DNS lookups, and some crypto and compression
Promise continuations and process.nextTick callbacks
Network socket reads, which epoll cannot watch
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: The pool covers work the OS cannot do non-blockingly. Network sockets are watched by epoll, and microtasks run on the main thread.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: The delivery-partner API slows from 80 ms to 2 seconds during peak, so in-flight requests jump to about 8,000. What happens to a 200-thread thread-per-request server vs the event-loop service?
options: The thread pool is exhausted and requests time out; the event loop just holds 8,000 small promises
Both cope equally, since each simply waits longer for the partner API
The thread server copes, while the event loop runs out of memory
Both fail, since 8,000 waiting requests exceed any server's limits
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: Threads cost about 1 MB reserved each and pools are finite; promises cost a few KB. Thread-per-request runs out of threads long before CPU when calls are slow.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: What is the clearest metric to alert on when something is blocking a Node event loop?
options: Total number of open sockets on the server at any given time
Average response size in kilobytes over the last minute
The count of promises created per second by the service
Event loop lag: how late a timer fires (e.g. alert above 50 ms)
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: If a timer due now fires 200 ms late, something hogged the thread. Use monitorEventLoopDelay or asyncio debug mode, then profile with a flame graph.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: Your checkout handler reads stock, awaits a pricing call, then writes stock minus one. Two buyers hit it at once. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing; an event loop runs one callback at a time, so races are impossible
A race: state can change between awaits, so both may read the same stock and oversell
The second request is rejected, since a function cannot be awaited twice
The event loop automatically locks shared variables during each await
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: No two callbacks run at the same instant, but another request can run in the gap at an await. Use atomic updates or locks around read-modify-write.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: Your Java team wants event-loop scalability but plain blocking code. What does Java 21 offer?
options: Larger thread pools, since Java 21 shrinks every OS thread stack to 1 KB
A built-in async/await syntax that replaces CompletableFuture
Virtual threads: the JVM parks a blocked virtual thread and runs another on the same carrier
Green threads that run CPU-bound work in parallel on one core
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: Virtual threads keep thread-per-request simplicity with a few KB per thread; a million is realistic. They help I/O-bound work only, and pinning in synchronized blocks was a caveat before Java 24.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: Which statement about concurrency vs parallelism is accurate for an event loop?
options: An event loop gives parallelism, since many requests make progress at once
Concurrency and parallelism are the same, so the loop provides both
An event loop gives concurrency (juggling many tasks), not parallelism (many at the same instant)
An event loop gives neither, since it handles one request at a time
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: One waiter juggling many tables is concurrency; many waiters at once is parallelism. You need processes or threads for parallel CPU work.

How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.q: In Python asyncio, how should you offload CPU-heavy work so it truly runs in parallel?
options: Use loop.run_in_executor with a ProcessPoolExecutor, because the GIL limits threads
Use asyncio.gather, which runs coroutines on separate CPU cores
Use a ThreadPoolExecutor, since Python threads run code in parallel
Mark the CPU function async def so the loop can interleave it
How can Node.js or Python asyncio handle.why: In the standard build the GIL stops threads running Python code in parallel, so processes are needed. asyncio.to_thread suits blocking I/O libraries, not heavy compute.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: You are building a live voice-call feature. On a 4G link with 2% packet loss, testers say calls over TCP keep freezing for a fraction of a second, even though no audio is ever lost. What is the best explanation?
