TCP drops packets on purpose under loss, so the codec has to rebuild missing frames from scratch
Each lost TCP segment holds back all later audio until it is resent, so playback stalls (head-of-line blocking)
TCP sends each audio frame twice for safety, which doubles the bandwidth and causes congestion
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: TCP delivers bytes strictly in order, so one missing segment blocks everything behind it until it is retransmitted, about one round trip or more. TCP does not drop data deliberately; it is the waiting, not loss, that causes the freeze.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: For a live video call, an audio packet arrives 300 ms after its play time. What should a well-designed receiver do with it?
options: Discard it; that slot was already skipped and concealed, so late data has no value
Pause playback, insert the packet in its correct position, then resume the call
Buffer it and play it right after the current frame so no audio is lost
Ask the sender to resend it with higher priority so the next copy is on time
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: For live media, late data is useless: the jitter buffer skipped that frame and packet loss concealment filled the gap. Pausing to insert it is exactly the TCP-style stall the app is trying to avoid.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: Your mobile game sends the player's position 30 times a second over UDP. A teammate wants to add acknowledgements and resends for every position update. What is the best response?
options: Agree, because UDP is unreliable and every game packet must be acknowledged to stay correct
Switch all game traffic to TCP, since adding acks on UDP just rebuilds TCP badly anyway
Send each position update three times so at least one copy usually gets through
Skip resends for positions, since the next update replaces them; ack only one-off events
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: Each world-state update replaces the previous one, so a lost update is fixed by the next one. Important one-off events like a purchase or 'player died' are where a small ack-and-resend layer on UDP belongs.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: A client opens a new HTTPS connection over TCP with TLS 1.3 to a server about 200 ms away (RTT). Roughly how long passes before the first byte of the actual request can be sent?
options: About 400 ms: one round trip for the TCP handshake plus one for TLS 1.3
About 200 ms: TLS 1.3 is folded into the TCP handshake itself
About 100 ms: only the outbound half of the handshake must complete
About 600 ms: three round trips, one for each handshake message
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: The three-way handshake costs one full RTT and TLS 1.3 adds another, so on a 200 ms link about 400 ms is spent before the request. Combining transport and crypto into one RTT is what QUIC does, not TCP.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: A TCP receiver has all bytes up to 2000, is missing 2001-3000, but already holds 3001-5000. Which acknowledgement lets the sender resend only the gap?
options: An ACK 5001, since most of the data has already arrived safely
A cumulative ACK 2001 plus a SACK block saying 3001-5000 has arrived
An ACK 3001, telling the sender the receiver has everything before 3001
A negative ACK listing 2001-3000, which TCP sends instead of normal ACKs

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: A TCP sender receives the same ACK ('still waiting for 2001') three extra times in a row. What does it do?
options: Waits for the retransmission timeout before resending, to avoid wasting bandwidth
Closes the connection, since repeated ACKs mean the receiver is confused
Resends the missing segment immediately (fast retransmit) without waiting for the timer
Ignores the duplicates, because only new ACK numbers carry useful information
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: Three duplicate ACKs signal that later segments arrived but one is missing, so TCP resends at once. Waiting for the RTO (at least about 200 ms on Linux) is the slower fallback path.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: Which statement correctly separates TCP flow control from congestion control?
options: Flow control protects the network; congestion control protects the receiver's buffer
Flow control protects the receiver's buffer; congestion control protects the network
Both protect the receiver, but congestion control also encrypts the data stream
Flow control is used only by UDP, while congestion control is used only by TCP
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: The receiver advertises how much room it has (flow control), while the sender's congestion window limits in-flight data so the network isn't overloaded (congestion control). Swapping them is the common mix-up.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: A product page loads 30 images over one HTTP/2 connection on a lossy mobile link, and a single packet carrying part of one image is lost. What happens, and what would HTTP/3 change?
options: Only the affected image stalls on HTTP/2; HTTP/3 just makes the resend faster
The browser drops that image and shows a placeholder; HTTP/3 resends it automatically
All 30 streams stall until that packet is resent; on HTTP/3 over QUIC only the affected stream waits
All 30 streams stall on both, since HTTP/3 still uses one TCP connection underneath
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over a single TCP byte stream, so TCP's head-of-line blocking stalls every stream. QUIC orders data per stream over UDP, so a loss in one image doesn't block the others.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: Your team asks why HTTP/3 was built on UDP instead of simply fixing TCP's head-of-line blocking. What is the best answer?
options: UDP is inherently faster than TCP on every link, so building on it gives more raw throughput
TCP cannot carry encrypted traffic, so a new protocol was needed to support TLS 1.3
UDP has built-in congestion control that TCP lacks, which QUIC needed for the web
TCP is baked into OS kernels and middleboxes, so it's slow to change; UDP passes through
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: TCP is baked into operating systems and network boxes, so changes take years. QUIC runs over UDP inside apps and browsers, then adds reliability, ordering, congestion control and TLS itself; UDP itself has no congestion control.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: A shopper's phone switches from home Wi-Fi to 4G mid-checkout. With HTTP/3, the connection survives without a fresh handshake. Which QUIC feature makes this possible?

0-RTT resumption, which reopens the connection with no round trip at all
Per-stream ordering, which lets each stream pick its own network path
Built-in TLS 1.3, which keeps the session key valid across networks
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: QUIC identifies a connection by a connection ID, so a change of IP address need not break it. 0-RTT helps when reconnecting to a known server, but it is still a new connection, not migration.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: Why does a DNS lookup for flipkart.com normally go over UDP port 53 rather than TCP?
options: A single tiny query and reply; a handshake would double the time, and clients just retry
DNS answers must be encrypted, and only UDP supports encryption without a handshake
UDP guarantees delivery for messages under 512 bytes, so retries are never needed
TCP cannot carry such small messages efficiently because of its minimum segment size

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: A DNS server's answer is too large to fit in a UDP response. What normally happens next?

The client gets only the first part of the answer and silently uses that
The resolver switches to QUIC, which is the standard fallback for large DNS replies
The response is flagged as truncated and the client retries the query over TCP
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: Oversized answers come back marked truncated, and the client repeats the query over TCP. TCP is also used for zone transfers between DNS servers.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: Your UPI payment API runs over TCP. A developer says idempotency keys are pointless because 'TCP guarantees delivery'. What is the best reply?

If the connection breaks after the server acted, the client retries and may charge twice
Idempotency keys are only needed on UDP, so switching to QUIC would require them
TCP retransmission prevents duplicates, but idempotency keys are needed for encryption

Only a server-side idempotency key prevents the double charge; no transport gives exactly-once processing.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: A colleague claims 'Hotstar-style cricket streaming to lakhs of viewers uses UDP, like video calls'. What is more accurate?
options: Correct; any live video uses UDP because TCP cannot sustain high bitrates
Streaming uses raw UDP multicast across the internet to reach many viewers at once
Streaming uses WebRTC over UDP so every viewer gets sub-second delay
Big streams mostly use buffered HTTP over TCP or QUIC; UDP matters for calls and games
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: A few seconds of delay is fine for viewers and makes CDN caching easy, so HTTP-based streaming over TCP or QUIC is the norm. Low-latency UDP matters mainly for interactive media like calls and games.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: Which set correctly describes what a UDP header (8 bytes) provides?

Source port, destination port, length and checksum, and nothing for ordering or delivery
Ports, an acknowledgement number and a window size, for basic flow control
Ports, a checksum and a connection ID, so sessions survive network changes
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: UDP adds only ports, length and checksum on top of IP, so there is no handshake, ACKs, ordering or congestion control. Sequence numbers are what RTP or the app adds on top.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: Your video-calling app uses UDP and a rising loss rate is reported on a congested network. Since UDP has no congestion control, what should a well-behaved app do?
options: Implement its own: lower bitrate or resolution and add FEC when loss or delay rises
Nothing; UDP traffic is automatically throttled by routers so the app can send freely
Switch every packet to TCP at the first sign of loss, then return to UDP later
Send at a fixed high bitrate so quality stays steady regardless of conditions
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: Real-time apps must behave themselves: WebRTC lowers bitrate or resolution and uses forward error correction when loss rises. Otherwise a UDP app can flood the network.

What is the difference between TCP and U.q: Employees on a corporate network say video calls work but look worse than at home. Logs show UDP is blocked by the firewall. What is most likely happening?
options: The app is still using UDP but at a lower rate imposed by the firewall
The app has switched to HTTP/3, which is slower than UDP for media
The app has fallen back to TCP, for WebRTC via a TURN relay, so losses now cause stalls
The call is going through DNS tunnelling, which limits it to audio quality
What is the difference between TCP and U.why: When UDP is blocked, real-time apps fall back to TCP, often through a TURN relay, and quality usually drops because TCP stalls on loss.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: At home, your phone shows IP 192.168.1.10, but a 'what is my IP' site shows 203.0.113.7. Why are they different?
options: The phone has two network cards, and the site picked the second one
192.168.1.10 is the private home address; sites see the router's public IP
The website is using a cached address from your last visit, not your current one
192.168.1.10 is your IPv6 address and 203.0.113.7 is your IPv4 address
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: Private addresses are only meaningful inside the home and never routed on the internet. The router rewrites outgoing packets to its public IP, so that is all websites ever see.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: Your phone and laptop both open connections from private port 51515 at the same time. How does the router make sure replies don't get mixed up?
options: It refuses the second connection until the first one closes
It forwards replies to both devices and lets each one discard what isn't its own
It gives each one a different public port and maps replies back via its NAT table
It checks the remote server's port, which is always unique per device
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: The router assigns separate public ports and records each mapping, so replies are matched by public port. Matching on the remote port wouldn't work since both may talk to port 443.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: You run a web server on your home laptop. A friend outside tries your public IP and gets nothing. What is the most likely cause?
options: The incoming connection has no NAT table entry, so the router drops it
The laptop's private IP was reused by a neighbour's router on the same ISP
Public IPs can only receive traffic on port 443, and your server uses port 80
The ISP's DNS server has not yet learnt the laptop's private address
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: NAT entries are created only by traffic that starts inside. An unsolicited inbound connection matches nothing and is dropped; port forwarding creates a deliberate mapping.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: You want to expose a home server, but you discover your broadband connection is behind the ISP's CGNAT. Which fix will work?
options: Use a tunnel or cloud relay, or IPv6, because you cannot port-forward through the ISP's NAT box
Set up port forwarding on your home router; that opens the path end to end
Turn on UPnP on your router so it opens the port on the ISP's NAT for you
Change your laptop's private IP to a public-looking address in the 100.64.x.x range
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: With CGNAT, a second NAT you don't control sits in front of you, so home port forwarding only opens half the path. A tunnel, relay or IPv6 avoids that NAT.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: During a big sale, your rate limiter blocks one IP sending 5,000 requests a minute. Within minutes, hundreds of real customers complain. What most likely happened?
options: A single bot was using a botnet, and the customers were part of it unknowingly
The rate limiter has a bug that blocks every IP in the same city
The customers' phones all had the same private IP, so the server merged them
The IP was a mobile operator's carrier-grade NAT address shared by many users
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: Behind CGNAT, hundreds of users share one public IP at once. Rate limiting should be keyed on user account or device, using IP only as one signal.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: As the owner of a shopping API used heavily on mobile data, which logging and limiting policy best fits a world with CGNAT?
options: Rate-limit strictly per IP and ban any IP that exceeds the limit for a day
Rate-limit by account or device token, and log source IP together with source port
Ignore IPs entirely, since they never carry useful information behind NAT
Log only the user's private IP, since that uniquely identifies the device
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: Many users can share one public IP, so limits should key on user or device. Logging the source port with the IP helps identify a user for legal requests; the private IP is never seen by the server.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: A chat app keeps a UDP connection to its server. Users report that after a few idle minutes, messages stop arriving until they reopen the app. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the DHCP lease on the router so the phone keeps its private IP longer
Send small keepalive packets so the router's NAT mapping doesn't expire
Switch the server to a well-known port so the router never forgets it
Ask users to enable port forwarding for the chat app on their routers
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: NAT entries expire when idle, UDP ones after as little as 30 seconds to a few minutes. Without traffic, the server's pushes hit a public port with no mapping. Keepalives refresh it.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: A new smart TV joins your Wi-Fi with no IP address. In what order does DHCP give it one?
options: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge
Request, Offer, Discover, Acknowledge
Discover, Request, Offer, Acknowledge
Offer, Discover, Acknowledge, Request
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: The device broadcasts Discover, the router sends an Offer, the device Requests it, and the router Acknowledges with a lease, gateway and DNS server (DORA).

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: Besides an IP address, what does the router's DHCP Acknowledge typically hand the TV?
options: A public port range and a list of allowed remote servers
A lease time, the gateway address (the router itself) and a DNS server
The router's public IP, so the TV can use it directly on the internet
A MAC address and a NAT table entry for incoming connections
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: The ACK confirms the address with a lease (say 24 hours) plus the default gateway and DNS server. The public IP stays on the router.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: Why can millions of homes all use 192.168.1.x addresses at the same time without conflict?
options: Each ISP adds a hidden suffix that makes every 192.168.1.x address unique
IPv6 automatically translates each private address into a unique global one
Routers coordinate with IANA so no two homes pick the same private address
Private ranges are never routed on the internet, so they never leave the home
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: Ranges like 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255 are reserved as private and never leave the home, so reuse is safe; the router's public IP is what must be unique.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: Which statement best explains why NAT became so widespread?
options: IPv4 has only about 4.3 billion addresses, and the pool ran out around 2011
NAT was designed mainly as a firewall, and saving addresses was a side effect
IPv4 addresses are too long to route efficiently, so NAT shortens them
NAT was needed to let TCP and UDP share the same port numbers
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: NAT stretched IPv4 by letting one public address serve a whole home, or hundreds of customers with CGNAT. Blocking inbound traffic is a side effect, not the purpose.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: A colleague says 'we don't need a firewall on the home router because NAT already protects us'. What is the best response?
options: Correct, NAT inspects every packet for threats, so a firewall would be redundant
Wrong, NAT actually exposes every device, so it must be disabled for safety
NAT blocks inbound only as a side effect; a stateful firewall is the real protection
Correct, as long as UPnP is enabled so NAT can decide which ports are safe
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: NAT exists to save addresses; dropping unknown inbound traffic is incidental. UPnP lets devices open holes themselves, which is convenient but risky.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: Your company is moving to IPv6, and someone worries that 'every home device will now be exposed to the internet'. What is accurate?
options: True, IPv6 removes all filtering, so every device must run its own firewall
False, because IPv6 still requires NAT for every home network
No NAT is needed, but the router's firewall still blocks unsolicited inbound traffic
False, because IPv6 addresses are private and can't be reached from outside
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: IPv6's 128-bit addresses give every device a unique global address, removing the need for NAT, while routers still run a stateful firewall that blocks inbound by default.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: Two friends behind home routers start a video call. How does the media usually end up flowing directly between them?
options: The signalling server forwards all audio and video packets between them throughout the call
Each router automatically port-forwards the call because video apps use well-known ports
Both phones switch to IPv6, which removes the router from the path entirely
They learn public addresses via STUN, swap them, and both send UDP at once (hole punching)
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: Each outgoing packet opens a mapping in its own router, so the other side's packets are accepted. Signalling goes via a server; media usually flows directly, with a TURN relay only as fallback.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: Hole punching fails for a user whose router gives a different public port for every destination. What does the call do?
options: Retries STUN until the router eventually reuses the same port
Falls back to a TURN relay server that forwards all the media
Switches to TCP hole punching, which always works with this kind of NAT
Drops the call, since direct media is required for WebRTC
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: That is symmetric NAT, where the port learnt via STUN doesn't apply to the peer. TURN always works but costs bandwidth; ICE is the procedure that tries options and picks the best working one.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: Your phone on mobile data shows the address 100.64.12.34. What does this tell you?
options: You are behind the operator's carrier-grade NAT; that range is reserved for CGNAT
The phone has a public IPv4 address that websites can reach directly
The phone is using a private home range assigned by your Wi-Fi router
It is an IPv6 address shown in short form by the phone's settings
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: The 100.64.0.0/10 range is set aside for CGNAT, so the operator's NAT box maps you onto a shared public address. Traffic may be translated twice when a home router is also in the path.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: Your cloud application servers sit in a private subnet but must call an external payment gateway. What lets them do this without public IPs?
options: A DHCP server that gives each instance a temporary public address on demand
A DNS resolver that rewrites the private source address in each request
Port forwarding from the payment gateway into the private subnet
A NAT gateway that translates their outbound traffic, like a home router does
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: Cloud servers in private subnets reach out through a NAT gateway, the same idea as home NAT. Inbound traffic to them normally comes through a load balancer with a public address.

Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.q: Which 5 values together identify one connection on the network?
options: Source IP, destination IP, MAC address, port and lease time
Protocol, source IP, destination IP, DNS name and TTL
Protocol, source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port
Source port, destination port, sequence number, checksum and protocol
Your phone, laptop and TV at home all us.why: The 5-tuple is protocol plus source and destination IP and port. Ports are 16-bit (0 to 65535) and let one IP carry many conversations.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: You visited a shopping site 30 seconds ago, and its DNS TTL is 300 seconds. You open it again. What does the DNS step cost this time?
options: Almost nothing, because the browser or OS still holds a valid cached answer
One round trip to the recursive resolver, since browsers never cache DNS
A full walk through root, TLD and authoritative servers, because TTLs reset on each visit
About one TCP round trip, because DNS must reconnect to the resolver each time
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: Answers are cached in the browser, the OS and the resolver for the TTL. With 270 seconds left, no resolver or root/TLD/authoritative lookup happens.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: A resolver has no cached answer for a domain at all. In what order does it walk the DNS hierarchy?
options: Root server, then the .com TLD server, then the authoritative server
Authoritative server, then TLD server, then root server
TLD server, then root server, then the authoritative name server
Root server, then the authoritative server, then the TLD server for confirmation
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: Root says which servers handle .com, the .com TLD says which name servers handle the site, and the authoritative server gives the real answer. This full walk costs about 50-200 ms and happens only on a full miss.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: In an interview, you're asked: 'What is the difference between a recursive resolver and an authoritative name server?' What is the best answer?
options: The resolver looks up and caches answers; the authoritative server holds the true records
The resolver stores the domain's official records; the authoritative server caches them for users
The resolver handles .com names only; the authoritative server handles every other TLD
They are the same server, just named differently depending on whether the cache is warm
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: Your ISP or a public resolver like 8.8.8.8 does the lookup work and caches it. The authoritative server, run for the domain, holds the true records and TTLs.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: A user in Chennai and a user in Delhi both look up the same shopping domain and get different IP addresses. What is the most likely reason?
options: DNS is broken for one of them and is returning a stale or wrong address
A CNAME points to a CDN, whose DNS returns each user's nearest edge
Each ISP assigns its own IP to popular sites using NAT
The site uses load-balancer cookies that change the DNS answer per user
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: Large sites often point to a CDN via a CNAME, and the CDN's DNS answers with a nearby edge's IP. That is how the same name sends different cities to different edges.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: Your API server is in the US with a 200 ms RTT from India. With TCP and TLS 1.3, roughly how long before a new client can even send its HTTP request, and what is the best fix?
options: About 200 ms; upgrading the server's CPU would cut it significantly
About 600 ms; switching to TLS 1.2 would save one round trip
About 400 ms; enabling gzip compression on responses would remove most of it
About 400 ms; a nearby CDN edge at 20-30 ms RTT cuts it to about 40-60 ms
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: TCP costs one RTT and TLS 1.3 another, so about 2 x 200 ms. Handshakes depend on distance, not server speed or compression, which is a big reason CDNs exist.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: What two jobs does the TLS handshake do when you open https://flipkart.com?
options: Turns the domain name into an IP address and checks that the server is reachable
Compresses the page and checks the browser cache for a fresh copy
Proves the server's identity with a certificate and agrees on encryption keys
Picks the nearest CDN edge and balances load across app servers
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: TLS authenticates the server with a certificate signed by a trusted authority and sets up encryption keys. Name-to-IP is DNS's job; reachability is checked by the TCP handshake.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: A colleague argues HTTPS makes pages noticeably slow and suggests serving the homepage over plain HTTP. What is the best reply?
options: He is right; encryption doubles server CPU per request, so plain HTTP is faster
HTTPS costs two extra RTTs on every request, but security outweighs the speed loss
TLS 1.3 adds about one RTT on a new connection and little after; the crypto is cheap
HTTPS is only slow on mobile, so plain HTTP should be used just for app users
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: TLS 1.3 adds one RTT on a new connection (TLS 1.2 took two), session resumption can cut that further, and modern hardware encrypts cheaply. The real costs are round trips, not crypto.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: A product page needs 80 small images. Why does HTTP/2 load them much faster than HTTP/1.1 without keep-alive?
options: HTTP/2 compresses images better, so each file is roughly half the size
HTTP/2 uses UDP instead of TCP, which skips the handshake altogether
HTTP/2 caches every image on the CDN edge, which HTTP/1.1 cannot do
One connection carries all requests at once, so there's one handshake instead of 80
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection with compressed headers. Without keep-alive, each file pays about 2 RTTs of setup; HTTP/2 still runs over TCP (HTTP/3 is the one on QUIC/UDP).

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: Your page's HTML arrives in 300 ms, but the screen stays blank for another second on mid-range phones. Which pair of causes is most likely?
options: Render-blocking CSS or sync scripts, and slow JavaScript execution on the phone
A slow DNS resolver and an expired TLS certificate
Too many database queries on the server and a cold Redis cache
The CDN edge being too far away and the TCP window being too small
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: Once HTML has arrived, network and server steps are mostly done. Browsers won't paint until CSS is ready, plain scripts block parsing, and JS execution on cheap phones can dominate.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: You add a large analytics script in the <head> and notice the page renders later. Which change best fixes this without dropping the script?
options: Move the CSS below the script so styles load after JavaScript
Inline the whole script into the HTML so it needs no extra request
Raise the DNS TTL so the script's domain is resolved faster
Load it with defer or async so it doesn't block HTML parsing
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: A plain <script> blocks parsing while it downloads and runs; defer and async avoid that. Delaying CSS wouldn't help because CSS is needed before paint anyway.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: Which sequence correctly lists how a browser turns HTML into pixels?
options: Paint, layout, DOM, CSSOM, render tree, composite
DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, composite
CSSOM, paint, DOM, render tree, layout, composite
DOM, paint, layout, CSSOM, render tree, composite
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: The browser builds the DOM and CSSOM, combines them into a render tree, works out where boxes go (layout), draws pixels (paint) and combines layers (composite). Paint can't happen before layout.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: A homepage server calls banner, recommendations, cart-count and pincode-offer APIs one after another, each taking about 60 ms. What is the best first fix for server time?
options: Move the app servers onto the CDN edge so the APIs are closer to the user
Call the independent APIs in parallel so the wait is about the slowest one
Increase the HTTP cache TTL for the personalised HTML to a few hours
Switch the browser connection to HTTP/3 to reduce server-side latency
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: Sequential calls add up (about 240 ms here); parallel calls cost roughly the slowest one. Caching personalised HTML is unsafe, and the client protocol doesn't change backend call time.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: Why does a shopping site usually NOT let the CDN cache its homepage HTML for long, while caching the logo, CSS and JS for days?
options: CDNs cannot store HTML files at all, only images, CSS and JavaScript
The HTML is personalised and changes often; static files have versioned names
HTML is always too large for CDN caches, so it must come from the origin
Browsers refuse to use cached HTML for HTTPS sites, but allow cached CSS
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: Cookies, pincode and live offers make the HTML dynamic, so the server says 'don't reuse without checking'. Static assets with versioned names can be cached long and served from the edge.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: The morning after a deploy, origin traffic spikes and the first users see slower pages, even though nothing else changed. What is the most likely reason?
options: The deploy reset every user's DNS cache, forcing full root lookups
The new JS bundle isn't cached at the edge yet, so early requests hit origin
TLS certificates are reissued on every deploy, so all handshakes take longer
The load balancer marks all servers unhealthy until users log in again
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: A fresh bundle has a new name the CDN hasn't seen, so the burst of misses hits origin until the edge warms up. DNS and certificates aren't tied to app deploys.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: A user types flipkart.com, and Chrome goes straight to https:// without trying http:// first. Why?
options: The DNS answer includes a flag telling browsers to use encryption
Every browser upgrades every site to HTTPS before sending any request
The CDN edge redirects the request before the TCP handshake even starts
The site is on Chrome's HSTS list, which marks it as HTTPS-only
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: HSTS records sites that must only be used over HTTPS, so the browser skips plain HTTP. A redirect would need a connection first, so it can't happen before the handshake.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: Your company's DNS provider has a full outage for an hour. What do users experience?
options: Every user is cut off instantly, because each request does a fresh DNS lookup
Nobody is affected, because the CDN keeps serving pages without needing DNS
Users with a cached answer work until the TTL expires; new users can't connect
Users are redirected automatically to the site's IP by their browser
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: Caches at the browser, OS and resolver keep answering until the TTL runs out. That is why large sites use multiple DNS providers and sensible TTLs.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: The team says 'pages are slow, let's buy faster servers'. Profiling shows the server responds in 120 ms. Where should you look first?
options: Database indexes, since server time is always the main bottleneck
Upgrading the load balancer, which usually adds most of the latency
Round trips, heavy images and JS bundles, and JS execution on phones
Lowering the DNS TTL so users get new IPs faster
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: The bottleneck is often on the network and client: handshakes, bytes and heavy JS on weak phones. With 120 ms server time, faster servers won't fix a multi-second page.

What actually happens, step by step, bet.q: Where does a load balancer sit in a typical page request, and what does it commonly do?
options: Between CDN edge and app servers; it spreads load and often terminates TLS
In front of the DNS resolver; it chooses which root server to query
Inside the browser; it splits requests across six parallel connections
Behind the database; it decides which table a query should hit
What actually happens, step by step, bet.why: Dynamic requests or edge misses go to the load balancer, which picks healthy app servers, removes unhealthy ones, and often terminates TLS. App servers then call APIs, caches and databases.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: Two teams encode the exact same URL into QR codes, and the images look slightly different. What is the correct conclusion?
options: They are different drawings of the same payload and decode to the same data
They are different QR codes, because each image is mathematically unique
One of them is corrupted, since the same data must always produce identical pixels
They will scan to different URLs, because the mask pattern changes the payload
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: The same payload can be drawn with different versions, error-correction levels or one of 8 masks. A QR's identity is the decoded data, not the picture.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: Your marketing head worries that 'with crores of coupons, we'll run out of unique QR codes'. What is the best answer?
options: It is a real risk, because QR version 40 supports only about 2,953 distinct codes
It is a real risk, so codes must be retired and reused after each campaign
Not a real risk; collisions only come from short or predictable ID generation
Not a risk, because the QR standard assigns each printer a globally unique range
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: Even a 16-byte random token has 2^128 possibilities, and version 40 holds up to about 2,953 bytes of data, not 2,953 codes. Uniqueness depends on how you generate the ID.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: A team proposes using order numbers (OD1001, OD1002, ...) as the payload of redeemable gift-card QRs. What is the main problem and the better design?
options: Sequential IDs can collide when two orders are placed at once; switch to timestamps
Order numbers are too long for a QR; shorten them to four digits
Order numbers can't be encoded alphanumerically; convert them to pure digits
Sequential IDs are guessable; use a 128-bit random token or a signed payload
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: Sequential IDs are unique by construction but anyone can try the next number. Anything that grants value needs unguessable randomness or a signature, validated on the server.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: You generate 128-bit random tokens for QR tickets. Roughly how many tokens before a random collision becomes likely, and what extra safeguard should you still add?
options: Around 2^61 tokens; still add a unique index and retry on conflict
Around 2^128 tokens; no safeguard is needed because collisions are impossible
Around one million tokens; switch to sequential IDs to avoid collisions
Around 2^32 tokens; prefix each token with the date to reduce collisions
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: By the birthday bound, collisions become likely only around 2^61 (about 2.3 quintillion) IDs. A unique index makes storage enforce uniqueness anyway, retrying on the astronomically rare clash.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: A concert ticket QR is screenshotted and shown at two gates within the same second. How do you guarantee only one entry?
options: Have each gate read the status first, and admit if it says ISSUED, then mark it USED
Sign the ticket with HMAC, so a screenshot no longer passes verification
Make the QR include a timestamp, so a second scan within a second is rejected
One atomic conditional update to USED; only the gate that changes a row admits
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: The check and update happen as one step, so exactly one gate's update affects a row. Read-then-write lets both gates see ISSUED; a signature proves authenticity but a screenshot is still a valid signed copy.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: Government documents and e-invoices embed QR codes that inspectors can verify offline, without calling the issuer. Which technique enables that?
options: An HMAC-SHA256 tag, since the scanner can compute it without any secret
A UUIDv4 in the payload, since random IDs can't be forged
A public-key signature, verified with the issuer's public key
High error-correction level H, which detects any tampering with the data
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: With public-key signatures, only the issuer can sign but anyone with the public key can verify offline. HMAC needs the shared secret, so only your own servers can verify it.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: Your app issues return-pickup QRs that only your own logistics servers ever verify. Which signing approach fits best?
options: A public-key signature, because HMAC can be verified by anyone who scans it
HMAC-SHA256 with a secret held on your servers, since only you need to create and verify
No signature, since the QR's error correction already detects altered data
A hash of the payload alone, which proves it came from your servers
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: HMAC suits the case where only your servers verify. A plain hash can be recomputed by anyone, so it proves nothing about the issuer; error correction repairs damage, it doesn't detect forgery.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: Which statement about QR error correction is accurate?
options: Error correction verifies that the payload was issued by a trusted party
Level H tolerates about 30% damage, which is how a centre logo still scans
Level L allows about 30% damage, while H allows about 7%
Error correction makes each image unique, which is what keeps QR codes distinct
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: Reed-Solomon levels L, M, Q, H recover about 7%, 15%, 25% and 30% damage. It repairs damage; it has nothing to do with authenticity or uniqueness.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: A delivery agent collects Rs 1,299 for order OD4471 by UPI. Why should the app show a dynamic QR rather than the merchant's static counter QR?
options: Its unique reference and pre-filled amount tie the payment to this order
Static QRs can't carry a UPI payee address, so the customer can't pay at all
Dynamic QRs are larger, which makes them faster for phone cameras to scan
Static QRs expire after a day, so they can't be used on delivery runs
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: A dynamic QR carries a unique reference, amount and short expiry, so reconciliation is easy. A static 'pay this account' QR leaves you guessing which payment was for which order.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: The bank retries your payment webhook, delivering the same 'paid' notification for reference R twice. How should the handler behave?
options: Reject the second webhook with an error so the bank stops retrying
Insert a new payment row each time and reconcile duplicates at night
Mark the order paid again and send the customer a second confirmation
Update to PAID only WHERE status='CREATED', so the repeat changes nothing
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: Conditioning the update on the current status makes repeated deliveries harmless. Erroring can cause more retries, and blind inserts create double-confirmed orders.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: A customer scans the delivery QR twice and actually pays Rs 1,299 twice. With a conditional update on status, what happens to the second payment?
options: It overwrites the first payment, so the order shows only the latest one
It finds the order already PAID and is flagged for automatic refund
It is silently ignored and the customer must raise a support ticket
It fails at the bank, because UPI blocks any second payment with the same reference
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: Exactly one payment can move CREATED to PAID. The second sees PAID, affects zero rows and is routed to automatic refund.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: Warehouse bins and packages carry QRs with sequential bin IDs and shipment numbers. Is that a security problem?
options: Yes: every QR must use a 128-bit random token, whatever it's used for
No: these codes grant no value by themselves, so guessable IDs are fine
Yes: sequential IDs will eventually collide as the warehouse grows
No, but only if the QR uses error-correction level H
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: Unguessable tokens matter for things that grant value. For labels that just identify a bin or parcel, sequential business IDs are unique by construction and practical.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: You are designing a document-verification QR where 'same document should always give the same code'. Which ID scheme fits?
options: A content-derived ID, such as a hash of the document
A random 128-bit token generated at each issue
A Snowflake-style ID of time plus machine plus counter
A database sequence number per request
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: Content-derived IDs are unique per content and repeat for identical content, which is the intended behaviour here. Random and sequential IDs give a new value every time.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: A team claims 'our ticket QRs are secure because QR codes are hard to forge'. What is accurate?
options: Correct; QR codes include a built-in checksum that blocks forgery
A QR is plain encoding; security comes from signing and server-side checks
Correct, as long as the QR uses the highest version (177x177)
Incorrect; QR codes are secure only when printed with a logo in the middle
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: Anyone can generate a valid-looking QR with any payload. Forgery is stopped by a signature, and reuse by server-side state.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: A shop owner discovers that a sticker with a fraudster's QR has been pasted over his printed UPI QR. Which measures best reduce this risk?
options: Switch to a higher error-correction level so stickers can't cover the code
Print the QR in colour, since fraudsters usually use black-and-white stickers
Use dynamic QRs, show the payee name before paying, and train merchants
Use sequential IDs for the shop QR so each one is easy to verify by eye
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: Static codes can be covered with another valid QR. Dynamic codes, visible payee confirmation and merchant awareness address the swap; error correction can't tell a fake.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: For a festive campaign you must issue 10 million coupon QRs that stores can verify without a database lookup and still revoke if needed. What design fits best?
options: A signed campaign-plus-serial payload, with a small deny-list for revoking
Plain sequential serial numbers that stores check against a printed list
Random 4-character codes, which are short enough to type at the counter
Store-side hashing of the coupon text, with no signature or server state
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: Signing lets anyone with the key verify without a lookup, and a deny-list handles revocation. Short or sequential codes are guessable; a bare hash proves nothing.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: Ticket scanners at a stadium must work offline because the network is unreliable. How do you still stop a ticket being used twice?
options: Signatures alone are enough; a verified ticket can't be shown twice
Skip the signature offline and just admit any well-formed QR
Encode a one-second expiry into each QR so copies stop working
Verify signatures locally, keep a local used-list, and sync with the server
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: Offline signature checks prove authenticity, but single-use needs state. Scanners track redeemed tokens locally and sync, accepting a small window for cross-gate duplicates.

How does a QR code remain unique?.q: At minimum, how much randomness should a token have if the QR grants value, such as a gift card?
options: About 32 bits, since that already gives over four billion possibilities
About 16 bits, as long as tokens expire within a day
At least 128 bits, which makes guessing and collisions practically impossible
Randomness isn't needed if the token is long enough in characters
How does a QR code remain unique?.why: 128 bits of randomness makes brute-force guessing and accidental collisions practically impossible. 32 bits is guessable at scale, and length without randomness doesn't help.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: OrderService validates the cart, prices offers, reserves stock, charges the card, builds the invoice PDF and sends SMS. The pricing, finance and CRM teams all edit it and keep hitting merge conflicts. Which principle is violated, and what is the fix?
options: SRP: extract pricing, payments and storage, and move invoice and SMS behind an event
OCP: replace the method body with a switch on team name so each team edits its own case
LSP: make OrderService a subclass per team so each overrides only its own part
ISP: give OrderService three interfaces so each team sees only the methods it calls
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: SRP means one reason to change, one actor to answer to; three teams editing one class is the classic god class. After the split, OrderService only orchestrates the flow.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: A teammate splits a cohesive 200-line PriceCalculator into ten 20-line classes 'because SRP says each class should do one thing'. Understanding a price now needs ten files open. What is the best feedback?
options: SRP means one reason to change, not one method per class; this lowers cohesion
Good change; smaller classes always follow SRP better and are easier to test
Good change, but each small class also needs its own interface to satisfy DIP
SRP doesn't apply to calculators; it only applies to service classes
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: A cohesive class serving one concern is fine even with several methods. Scattering one concept over many tiny classes is low cohesion, the opposite of what SRP wants.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: Before every sale, marketing adds new offer types, and each one means editing a switch statement in discount() and re-testing every case. What change best applies Open/Closed?
options: Move the switch into a separate utility class so it is easier to find and edit
Add a default case that handles any new offer type with a generic discount
Freeze the discount method and forbid all edits to it, including bug fixes
Make each offer its own OfferRule class, picked up by an engine that never changes
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: With pluggable rules, a new offer is one new class with its own tests and the engine stays untouched. OCP doesn't forbid bug fixes or refactoring; it makes expected extensions additive.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: Your OfferEngine picks the single best OfferRule. Marketing now asks to stack two offers together. What does this reveal about Open/Closed?
options: OCP was applied wrongly; a correct design never needs the engine edited
OCP only covers changes you predicted; stacking is new, so the engine changes
Stacking can be added as another OfferRule class without touching the engine
OCP forbids changing the engine, so stacking must go in a separate service
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: OCP protects against the variations you anticipated, like new offer types. Changing how rules combine is a different axis. At very high variety, offers often move into configuration or a rules engine.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: GiftCardPayment implements PaymentMethod, but its refund() throws UnsupportedOperationException. RefundService crashes in production for gift-card orders. Which principle is broken and what is a sound fix?
options: Single Responsibility; move refund logic into a separate RefundHelper utility class
Open/Closed; add an instanceof check in RefundService that skips gift cards
Liskov Substitution; split out Refundable, or define a refund every type can honour
Dependency Inversion; inject the gift-card SDK into RefundService directly
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: The subtype can't be used where its parent is expected without breaking callers. An instanceof check papers over the violation and destroys the polymorphism you built.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: A new SubscriptionPayment implements PaymentMethod but throws from charge() unless the amount equals the fixed plan price. What exactly is wrong?
options: It weakens the postcondition, because it promises more than the interface requires
It strengthens the precondition, so it violates Liskov Substitution
Nothing; adding validation in a subclass is always allowed under LSP
It violates ISP, because charge() is a method it does not really need
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: A subtype must not demand more of callers (stronger preconditions), promise less (weaker postconditions), or throw unexpected exceptions. Either make the restriction a documented, handled result in the general contract or keep subscriptions out of that hierarchy.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: 'Pay Later' implements PaymentMethod, and its charge() returns success before the credit check finishes, while callers assume success means the money is secured. What is the right fix?
options: Leave it; returning success early is faster, and callers can recheck later if needed
Make charge() block until the credit check finishes, however long it takes
Add a PENDING result that every caller handles until a webhook confirms
Have callers check if the method is PayLater and treat its success differently
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: Returning success early weakens the postcondition every caller relies on, an LSP violation. An honest PENDING result keeps all implementations substitutable without instanceof checks.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: Your NotificationChannel interface has sendText, sendRich, sendAttachment and track. SmsChannel has to stub out two methods that throw or do nothing. What should you do?
options: Keep one interface and add a supportsAttachments() flag that callers must check
Make SmsChannel extend EmailChannel so it inherits working attachment code
Move all four methods into a NotificationUtils static class
Split it into small capability interfaces and implement only what each supports
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: Interface Segregation says clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use. With capability interfaces, the invoice service depends only on AttachmentSender and can't be routed to SMS by mistake.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: CheckoutService creates new RazorpayClient(KEY) inside itself, and vendor SDK types appear throughout checkout logic. What change best applies Dependency Inversion?
options: Define a domain-owned PaymentGateway interface and inject a Razorpay adapter
Wrap RazorpayClient in a static helper so checkout calls the helper instead
Put the PaymentGateway interface in the Razorpay adapter package so it sits beside the SDK
Mark RazorpayClient as a Spring bean and autowire it directly into checkout
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: With DIP, the high-level module owns the abstraction in business language and the adapter depends on it. Autowiring the concrete client is DI, but checkout is still welded to the vendor.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: A candidate says 'Dependency Inversion is just dependency injection, like Spring autowiring'. What is the most accurate correction?
options: DI passes collaborators in; DIP is about the domain owning the abstraction
They are identical; DIP is simply the older name for dependency injection
DIP means injecting dependencies via setters, while DI means via constructors
DIP is about inverting the call order so low-level code calls high-level code
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: Injection enables DIP but doesn't guarantee it. DIP is about which side owns the interface and which way source-code arrows point; it underlies hexagonal and clean architecture.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: On sale night, the primary gateway's success rate drops from 97% to 80%. How does a DIP-based design help most?
options: Checkout uses a gateway interface, so routing can switch gateways by config
Checkout can catch the vendor's exceptions faster, so customers see clearer error messages
The gateway SDK is loaded once as a singleton, so it can be restarted quickly
All payment logic sits in one class, so a developer can hotfix it in minutes
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: Because the domain owns the abstraction, swapping or routing implementations needs no change to business rules. It also lets tests inject a fake gateway and run in milliseconds.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: A teammate wants interfaces for all 40 service classes 'to follow SOLID and enable mocking'. Most will only ever have one implementation. How do you respond?
options: Agree: every class should have an interface, otherwise unit tests are impossible
Agree, but only for classes over 200 lines, since smaller ones don't need SOLID
Push back: add interfaces only at real seams; concrete classes can be mocked
Disagree, because interfaces break Spring's dependency injection
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: Single-implementation interfaces add a file, an indirection and an IDE jump for no flexibility. Modern mocking libraries can mock concrete classes, so testability alone is rarely enough reason.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: There is one shipping calculator today and no roadmap for another. Someone proposes a plugin framework for calculators. What heuristic should guide you?
options: Build the framework now, since adding it later always needs a full rewrite
Build the framework only if the calculator class has more than five methods
Never abstract shipping, because calculators are stable by nature
YAGNI: stay concrete until a second or third real variant arrives
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: Speculative OCP adds cost with no payoff. A common rule is to abstract on the second or third real variant, at the seams where change actually happens.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: Which code smells most strongly suggest a Liskov Substitution violation?
options: Classes longer than 500 lines and methods with many parameters
Interfaces with only one implementation and many small packages
UnsupportedOperationException in subtypes and instanceof checks in callers
Static helper methods and circular imports between packages
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: These show subtypes that don't honour the parent's behaviour, forcing callers to special-case them. Running one contract test suite against every implementation catches them early.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: Your team mirrors SRP at the service level and asks how to add a new reaction (loyalty points) when an order is placed, without editing the order service. Which approach matches OCP at service scale?
options: Add a loyalty call inside the order service's placeOrder method
Add a new consumer of the OrderPlaced event; the order service is unchanged
Let the loyalty service read the order service's database tables directly
Create a new version of the order API that includes loyalty fields
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: Event-driven extension is OCP at service scale: new behaviour comes from a new subscriber. Reading another service's database breaks DIP's 'depend on published contracts'.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: An architect proposes splitting a small monolith into 12 microservices 'so each follows SRP'. What is the key caution?
options: There is none; smaller services always reduce coupling and are cheaper to change
Service splits are costly to undo; split by business capability and team
Microservices can't follow SRP, because each must handle several actors
SRP only applies to classes, so it gives no guidance on service boundaries
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: A class abstraction is cheap to reverse; a service split is not, and method calls become network calls. Use SOLID inside each service and align boundaries with bounded contexts.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: A mobile app and a seller dashboard both call one huge order API and must track every change to it, even fields they never use. Which principle, applied at service level, suggests the fix?
options: Liskov Substitution: version the API so old clients can substitute new ones
Single Responsibility: merge both clients into one app so there's one consumer
Dependency Inversion: let each client read the order database directly
Interface Segregation: offer client-specific APIs, such as a backend-for-frontend per client
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: ISP at service scale means clients shouldn't depend on endpoints or fields they don't use, so BFFs give each client a focused API. LSP at that scale is about replacements honouring the existing contract.

What are the SOLID principles, and how d.q: The team considers adding an interface for GstCalculator. There's one tax regime and one implementation, and it changes only when the law changes. What is the sensible choice?
options: Add the interface, because tax logic must always be behind an abstraction
Keep it a concrete class, since there's no expected variation
Add an interface plus a factory, so a second regime can be plugged in later
Turn it into a rules engine so finance can edit tax logic without a deploy
What are the SOLID principles, and how d.why: SOLID pays off at real seams of change. A stable single-implementation class gains nothing from an interface; it can be refactored if a real variant ever appears.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: Checkout, refunds and retries each contain the same if/else on payment method that does new UpiGateway(...) or new CardGateway(...). A fifth gateway is coming. What is the best change?
options: Add a gateway interface and a registry-based factory that all callers use
Copy the if/else into a shared base class that checkout, refunds and retries extend
Add the fifth gateway's branch to all three if/else blocks and cover them with tests
Make each gateway a singleton so callers can reach it with getInstance()
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: A factory puts 'which concrete class?' in one place and callers depend only on the interface. A map-based registry beats a growing switch and keeps checkout untouched (open/closed in practice).

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: A team builds RetryingLoggingCachingInventoryClient, then RetryingCachingInventoryClient, and so on for each combination. Which pattern fits better?
options: Singleton: share one fully featured client so combinations aren't needed
Decorator: each concern wraps the client behind the same interface
Factory: create a different subclass for each environment
Observer: have the client publish events that logging and caching subscribe to
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: A decorator implements the same interface, does its extra work and delegates, so layers compose without a subclass per combination. Retries and caching must sit in the call path, which Observer doesn't give.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: A payment client is wrapped as Retry(Metrics(Gateway)). During a gateway outage, the dashboard shows three times more calls than orders. Why?
options: The gateway is double-counting its own calls, which is a vendor bug
Metrics sits inside the retry layer, so every attempt is counted
Retry should never wrap metrics, because decorators can only be stacked one deep
The metrics layer is a singleton shared across pods, so counts are multiplied
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: Decorator order matters: metrics outside retry counts one logical call; inside, it counts each attempt. Both may be wanted deliberately, but the placement must be a conscious choice.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: You add a RetryingGateway decorator around charge(). What else must be true for retrying a payment charge to be safe?
options: The retry must use exponential backoff, which on its own prevents double charges
The gateway must be created by a factory so each retry gets a fresh client
Every attempt must carry the same idempotency key
The decorator must be a singleton so only one retry runs at a time
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: A timeout doesn't tell you whether the charge happened. Backoff spaces out attempts but doesn't prevent duplicates; only an idempotency key lets the gateway recognise the retry.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: A price is computed as Coupon(BankOffer(SellerDiscount(BasePrice))): Rs 2,000 base, 10% seller discount, Rs 150 bank offer, Rs 100 coupon. What is the final price?
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: Rs 2,000 minus 10% is Rs 1,800, minus Rs 150 is Rs 1,650, minus Rs 100 is Rs 1,550. Because percentage rules make order matter, the stack order is fixed in one place and tested.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: Your price rules now have real business precedence: which offers stack, caps, and exclusions. Nested price decorators are getting hard to debug. What is the better approach?
options: Deeper decorator nesting, with one extra layer per exclusion rule
A singleton PriceCache so the decorators run only once per product
An Observer that notifies each rule when the price changes
An explicit pipeline or rules engine with a visible order
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: Decorators work when layers are independent. When layers need each other's state or complex ordering, a visible pipeline is clearer than a deep stack.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: A colleague says 'Decorator and Proxy are the same pattern'. What is the most accurate response?
options: Same shape, different intent: decorator adds behaviour, proxy controls access
They differ in structure: a proxy changes the interface, a decorator keeps it
A proxy can only be used for remote calls, while a decorator works in-process
They are identical; 'proxy' is just the name used in Spring for decorators
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: Both wrap a target behind the same interface. Proxy is for lazy loading, remote calls or security checks and usually hides that it exists. Changing an interface is what Adapter does.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: You must lazily create a ConnectionPool exactly once per JVM, thread-safely, with no locking on reads. Which Java idiom fits best?
options: Double-checked locking with a plain, non-volatile instance field
A public static field initialised to null and set on the first get() call
A synchronized get() that checks and creates the instance on every call
The holder idiom: a nested class whose static field is created on first use
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: The JVM initialises the nested class once, under a lock, only when first used. Double-checked locking needs a volatile field, or another thread may see a half-constructed object; a synchronized getter locks every read.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: A senior engineer insists 'double-checked locking is broken in Java, never use it'. What is accurate today?
options: It is still broken in every Java version, even with volatile
It was broken before Java 5; with a volatile field it's correct today
It works without volatile since Java 8, thanks to the new memory model
It is correct only when the singleton class is declared final
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: Since Java 5, a volatile field makes double-checked locking safe. Enum and holder idioms rely on class initialisation guarantees and are harder to get wrong.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: A developer adds a static singleton OrderCache and says it guarantees one cache for the whole platform. The service runs on 200 pods. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; static singletons are shared across pods by the JVM
Static singletons are lost after each request, so the cache is always empty
A static singleton is per JVM, so 200 pods hold 200 separate caches
It works as long as the singleton uses the holder idiom
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: 'Single' only holds per process. Cluster-wide consistency needs a distributed cache or explicit invalidation; 'one across the cluster' needs tools like leader election or a distributed lock.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: Why are Spring singleton-scoped beans usually preferred over a hand-rolled static ConnectionPool.get()?
options: Spring beans are shared across all pods, while static singletons are not
Spring beans are created fresh per request, which avoids shared state
It's still one instance, but injected, testable and lifecycle-managed
Spring beans skip class initialisation, so they start up faster
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and swappable in tests, and the container creates, configures and closes resources such as a HikariCP pool. A bean is still single per container, not per cluster.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: Which object is a poor candidate for a singleton?
options: A cart object holding the current user's items
The loaded application configuration shared by all services
A database connection pool used by every request
A metrics registry that records counters for the process
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: Singletons suit genuinely shared, process-wide resources. Mutable per-request or per-user state in a singleton leaks between users.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: When an order becomes SHIPPED, OrderService directly calls SMS, push, the search indexer and analytics. A slow SMS provider now slows order updates. Which pattern best addresses the coupling?
options: Observer: listeners register with the order and get notified on change
Factory: create the right notifier for each order status
Decorator: wrap OrderService with SMS, push and search layers
Singleton: share one notifier so calls are made only once
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: Observer decouples the subject from its reactions, so a new reaction is a new listener rather than an edit to order code. To stop slow listeners blocking the publisher, it must also go async, typically via a broker.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: Your in-process OrderEventBus loops over listeners. One listener throws an exception and the remaining listeners never run. What is the right fix?
options: Remove the failing listener from the list permanently the first time it throws
Let the exception propagate so the order update is rolled back
Catch and log each listener's exception so the rest still run
Switch the listener list from CopyOnWriteArrayList to ArrayList
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: Each listener's failure should be isolated. CopyOnWriteArrayList is there so listeners can subscribe during a publish; replacing it doesn't fix failure isolation.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: Notification, warehouse and analytics services, each in its own deployment, must react to OrderConfirmed, and notifications must survive crashes. Why isn't in-process Observer enough?
options: In-process Observer can't support more than two listeners at a time
It's synchronous, not durable and single-process; a broker fixes that
In-process Observer requires every listener to be a singleton
In-process Observer only works with the Factory pattern to create listeners
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: A slow listener blocks the publisher, a crash loses notifications and other services can't subscribe. Moving to a broker gives each service its own consumer group.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: You move order reactions to Kafka. What new responsibilities come with this event-driven design?
options: Idempotent consumers, eventual consistency and a transactional outbox
Nothing new; a broker guarantees exactly-once delivery and strict global ordering
Every consumer must call back the order service to confirm receipt synchronously
Events must be deleted right after publishing to avoid duplicates
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: Brokers bring duplicates, eventual consistency, schema versioning and harder tracing. The outbox writes the event in the same DB transaction as the order, then a relay publishes it.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: Before confirming an order, checkout must check stock and get a yes or no back. Should this be an event published via Observer/pub-sub?
options: Yes: events are always better than direct calls because they reduce coupling
Yes, as long as the stock service replies on a separate topic within 100 ms
No, because stock checks must be done by a singleton in the checkout service
No: the caller needs the result, so it's a request; use a direct call or an explicit workflow
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: Observer suits fire-and-forget reactions. When the caller needs an answer, or the order of steps is strict and business-critical, use a request or a saga/workflow orchestrator.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: An interviewer asks: 'Factory versus Strategy?' What is the best answer?
options: They are the same; Strategy is the GoF name for a simple factory
Factory creates the right object; Strategy swaps an algorithm behind an interface
Factory swaps algorithms at runtime; Strategy decides which class to instantiate
Strategy creates matched families of objects; Factory creates one object at a time
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: They solve different problems and work well together, for example a factory returning the right shipping-cost strategy. Matched families are Abstract Factory's job.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: An OrderRequest has many optional fields (coupons, gift wrap, delivery slot) and cross-field validation. Which creation pattern fits?
options: Abstract Factory: it creates a family of related order objects
Simple factory: it picks which order subclass to create
Builder: it assembles one complex instance step by step
Singleton: it reuses one order request across calls
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: A factory picks among types; a builder assembles one type with many optional parts. Abstract Factory is for matched families such as a gateway, refund client and webhook verifier for one provider.

What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.q: For each payment provider, you need a gateway, a refund client and a webhook verifier that must all match the same provider. Which pattern fits?
options: Factory Method, where one creator method returns a single gateway
Decorator, wrapping the gateway with refund and webhook layers
Builder, assembling the gateway with optional refund and webhook parts
Abstract Factory, which creates a family of related objects that belong together
What are the Factory, Decorator, Singlet.why: Abstract Factory guarantees the created objects come from the same family, so a Razorpay gateway is never paired with another provider's verifier.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: A class has private final List<String> tags assigned straight from the constructor argument, and a getter that returns it. A teammate calls it immutable. What is the best fix?
options: Nothing; the final keyword already stops anyone from changing the list
Wrap the getter's return value in a new ArrayList each time, but keep storing the original
Copy the input with List.copyOf in the constructor and keep the class final
Mark the field volatile so other threads always see the latest tags
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: final only stops the reference being reassigned; the caller's original list and the getter both expose mutation. List.copyOf breaks the link and returns a fixed list.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: A service stores Collections.unmodifiableList(src) and later sees its contents change unexpectedly. Why?
options: It's a read-only view, so changes made through src still show through
unmodifiableList only blocks add, not set, so other code replaced elements
The JVM garbage-collected the wrapper and returned the original list
unmodifiableList is immutable, so the change must come from reflection
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: It wraps the original and reflects its changes. List.copyOf or List.of produce a truly fixed list.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: You build an order summary as List.of(cart1, cart2), where each Cart is a mutable object. Is the summary deeply immutable?
options: Yes: List.of makes every element immutable as well as the list
No: the list itself is fixed, but the Cart elements can still be mutated
Yes, as long as cart1 and cart2 are declared final variables
No: List.of returns a view, so the list itself can grow or shrink
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: List.of fixes the list's structure, but deep immutability also needs immutable elements. Declaring variables final doesn't change the objects they point to.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: You model Money as a Java record holding BigDecimal and Currency. Where should you normalise the scale to 2 decimals and reject negative amounts?
options: In a setter that callers must remember to call after construction
In every service method that uses Money, just before arithmetic
In the record's compact constructor, so every instance is valid
In a static validate() method that runs before the record is serialised
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: The compact constructor runs for every instance, so invalid Money can never exist. Records have no setters, and scattering validation means some paths will skip it.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: A developer writes total.add(itemPrice); in a loop with BigDecimal, and the cart total stays at zero. Why?
options: BigDecimal is immutable; add returns a new value that the code ignores
BigDecimal needs a MathContext for addition, otherwise it returns zero
BigDecimal.add only works on values with the same scale
The loop needs synchronisation because BigDecimal isn't thread-safe
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: Immutable types never change in place, so 'changes' come back as new objects. Assign the result: total = total.add(itemPrice). And never use double for money.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: A team uses a Java record containing an ArrayList of order lines and assumes it is fully immutable. What is the risk?
options: None; records automatically deep-copy all collection components
Records are shallowly immutable, so the list itself can still change
Records can't contain collections at all, so it won't compile
Records make the list immutable but break equals and hashCode
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: Records give private final fields, accessors, equals and hashCode, but a mutable component remains mutable. Copy with List.copyOf in the compact constructor.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: Thousands of request threads read a shared PriceTable, while a background job applies price changes. What is the best lock-free design?
options: An immutable PriceTable behind an AtomicReference, swapped on each change
Use a mutable HashMap and mark the field volatile so readers always see updates
Wrap every read and write in a synchronized block on the table
Give each thread its own copy of the table and update them one by one
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: Readers never see a half-updated table and need no locks; the atomic swap coordinates which version is current. volatile on a mutable map doesn't make compound updates safe.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: A colleague says 'all our domain objects are immutable, so our program is thread-safe'. What is the most accurate response?
options: Correct; immutable objects remove every possible concurrency bug
Wrong; immutable objects are unsafe to share without synchronized getters
Objects are safe to share, but swapping versions still needs atomics or locks
Correct, but only if every field is also marked volatile
