What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: Immutability removes races on the object itself. Swapping in a new version is still a shared update that needs atomic coordination.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: Why can another thread safely read a fully constructed immutable object's final fields without synchronized or volatile?
options: Final fields are stored in a special read-only memory region shared by all threads
The JMM guarantees final fields are visible once the constructor finishes
The JVM automatically wraps every getter of a final field in a lock
Final fields are copied into each thread's stack when the object is created
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: This is the safe-initialisation guarantee for final fields. It breaks if this escapes during construction, for example by registering a listener inside the constructor.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: A HashMap uses a mutable Coupon object as a key. After someone changes the coupon's code field, lookups for it return null. Why?
options: HashMap removes keys automatically when their fields change
The coupon's equals method is broken because it's not final
HashMap copies keys on insertion, so the change didn't reach the map
The key's hash changed, so it now sits in the wrong bucket
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: Map keys must keep a stable hash. That is one reason String is immutable and caches its hash code.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: You need an immutable map with a million SKU entries that changes often. Copying the whole map for each update is too slow. What is the best approach?
options: A persistent structure that copies one path and shares the rest
Use Collections.unmodifiableMap over a HashMap and update the HashMap directly
Make the map's field final, so updates go into the existing structure
Serialise the map to JSON and patch the JSON string for each change
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: With 32-way branching, an update copies about 4 or 5 nodes for a million entries, and both versions stay valid. Alternatively, rebuild a copy-on-write snapshot in batches and swap it atomically.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: A profiler shows heavy GC time in a hot loop that prices a million SKUs using immutable intermediate objects. What is the pragmatic fix?
options: Make every domain class mutable, since immutability is too slow for production
Use confined mutation, like a builder, just in that hot spot
Switch money calculations from BigDecimal to double to reduce allocation
Increase heap size until GC stops appearing in the profile
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: Short-lived allocation is usually cheap, but tight loops can show it. Confined mutation that never escapes the method is safe. double for money trades a GC cost for rounding bugs.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: A customer buys a phone at Rs 17,499. The price later rises to Rs 19,999, and when the customer returns it, the refund comes out at Rs 19,999. What design mistake caused this?
options: The refund service used double instead of BigDecimal for the amount
The price change event was applied twice by the pricing consumer
The order record was immutable, so it couldn't record the new price
The order referenced the live price instead of snapshotting it at purchase
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: Each order line should store a Money snapshot of unit price, discount, tax and price version at checkout, and refunds should use it. Later price changes must not touch existing orders.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: Finance finds a coupon was wrongly applied to a placed order. How should the correction be recorded in an immutable ledger?
options: Update the original order line's discount and total in place
Delete the original order and insert a corrected copy with the same ID
Edit the invoice PDF and keep the order record as it was
Append a compensating adjustment entry and leave the original line as is
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: Corrections are new entries, so the ledger still balances and auditors can see exactly what happened. In-place edits destroy the history that makes audits trustworthy.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: Why do build pipelines reference container images by sha256 digest rather than a tag like latest?
options: Digests are shorter than tags and so speed up image pulls
Tags can't be used in production clusters, only in local builds
A digest always means the same bytes, so tested equals deployed
Digests let the same image be patched in place without a rebuild
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: A tag is mutable and can point to different images over time. Immutable artifacts are built once and promoted unchanged, so rollback is just redeploying the previous digest.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: The sale-banner script is served as sale.9c41e2.js with Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable. Marketing changes the banner at midnight. What happens?
options: The new build gets a new hashed file name, so no CDN purge is needed
The CDN must be purged, or users keep seeing the old banner for a year
Browsers recheck the file every request because 'immutable' forces revalidation
The old file is overwritten in place and every cache picks it up within minutes
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: A content-hashed name never changes content, so it can be cached forever; new content means a new name referenced by the HTML. That avoids purge storms at midnight.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: Your ops team still SSHes into running servers to patch packages, and servers in the same group have drifted apart. What immutable practice addresses this?
options: Schedule a nightly script that re-applies the same patches on every server
Lock down SSH so only senior engineers can patch production servers
Snapshot every server's disk daily so drift can be compared later
Immutable infrastructure: bake a new image and replace the servers
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: Never patching running servers removes configuration drift, and rollback becomes simply running the previous image.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: A privacy request asks you to delete a user's personal data, but it appears in your append-only event store. What is a common approach?
options: Edit the past events in place to blank out the personal fields
Refuse the request, since append-only systems can never delete anything
Move the events to a separate topic with a shorter retention period
Crypto-shredding: encrypt per user and delete that user's key
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: Immutability is about not editing history in place, not keeping everything forever. Deleting the per-user key makes the encrypted data unreadable while the log stays intact.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: Which pairing of system and immutable practice is correct?
options: LSM-tree storage: rows are updated in place to keep writes random-access
Kafka: an append-only log that consumers replay from their own offsets
Event sourcing: only the current state is stored, and history is discarded
CDN content hashing: one file name is reused and purged on each release
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: Kafka appends records and lets each consumer replay from its offset. LSM trees write immutable sorted files and merge later; event sourcing stores the full event sequence.

What is immutability, and why does it ma.q: With event sourcing, a reviewer worries reads will be slow because current state must be rebuilt from every event. What is the standard answer?
options: Delete old events once the current state is computed, to keep the log small
Replay the entire log on every read but cache the HTTP response for a minute
Serve reads from projections and snapshots; the log can rebuild them
Store current state in the events themselves by updating the latest event in place
What is immutability, and why does it ma.why: Projections and snapshots make reads cheap, while the immutable log can rebuild them or create new read models. Deleting or editing events throws away what event sourcing is for.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: A single-core server handles 500 open customer connections, interleaving their work as each waits on I/O. Which description is accurate?
options: It is parallel, because 500 tasks run at once
It is neither, because only one core is available
It is concurrent, but not parallel
It is both, because the OS switches very quickly
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: Concurrency is about structuring overlapping tasks; parallelism needs multiple cores executing at the same instant. One core can be concurrent but not parallel.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: A flash-sale counter is a volatile int left, decremented with if (left > 0) left--. Under load on a single JVM it oversells. Why, and what is the fix?
options: volatile caches the value per thread, so remove volatile to fix it
volatile isn't atomic; use AtomicInteger with compareAndSet, or a lock
The int overflows under load, so switching to a long fixes it
volatile is correct; the oversell must come from a database bug
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: Two threads can both see 1 and both decrement. volatile guarantees visibility and ordering of single reads and writes, not atomicity of read-modify-write.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: A worker thread loops while (running), and another thread sets running = false, but the worker never stops. The field is a plain boolean. What is the fix?
options: Wrap running in an AtomicInteger and increment it to signal stop
Declare running volatile so the worker sees the write
Call Thread.sleep inside the loop so the CPU refreshes its cache
Make the field final so all threads see the same value
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: Without a happens-before edge, the JIT can keep the field in a register and the worker may never see the update. A volatile write happens-before every later read of that field.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: Code does if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, loadValue(k)) on a ConcurrentHashMap shared across threads, and duplicate loads appear. What is the best fix?
options: Use an atomic compound method such as computeIfAbsent
Switch to a plain HashMap, which is faster and has the same behaviour
Mark the map field volatile so all threads see the latest keys
Call containsKey twice, before and after loading, to double-check
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: Another thread can insert between the check and the put, even on a concurrent map. computeIfAbsent, compute, merge and putIfAbsent do it atomically; keep the function short.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: Merging a guest cart into a logged-in cart locks cart A then cart B, while a parallel merge locks B then A. Occasionally both threads hang. What is the best fix?
options: Use a fair ReentrantLock so both threads eventually get their turn
Always acquire cart locks in a global order, such as ascending cart ID
Mark both cart objects volatile so locks are released faster
Increase the thread pool size so more merges can run at once
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: This is a deadlock from circular wait. A global lock order breaks circular wait; fairness only prevents starvation and doesn't stop two threads waiting on each other.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: Two services keep retrying a conflicting operation, each backing off and retrying at exactly the same moment, so neither ever succeeds though neither is blocked. What is this, and the fix?
options: Deadlock; acquire locks in one global order
Starvation; switch to a fair lock instead
Livelock; add randomised backoff to the retries
A race condition; mark the shared field volatile
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: In livelock, threads stay active but keep reacting to each other without progress. Randomised backoff breaks the symmetry.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: A pricing service evaluates CPU-heavy rules on an 8-core machine. A teammate proposes a pool of 200 threads for more throughput. What is the best advice?
options: Agree; more threads always means more throughput on a multi-core machine
Use one virtual thread per rule, since virtual threads speed up CPU work
Use cores x (1 + wait/compute), which gives about 200 here
For CPU-bound work, size the pool near the core count, about 8
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: With no I/O waiting, threads beyond the core count just compete and cause context switches and cache misses. The wait/compute formula is for I/O-bound work.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: An I/O-bound service runs on 8 cores; each task waits about 50 ms on a database and computes for 5 ms. What starting pool size does the common heuristic give?
options: About 88 threads: 8 x (1 + 50/5)
About 8 threads: one per core
About 400 threads: 8 x 50
About 40 threads: 8 x 5
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: threads ≈ cores × (1 + wait/compute) = 8 × 11 = 88. It's a starting point, bounded by downstream capacity and tuned with load tests.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: A service uses Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50). During a downstream slowdown, the JVM runs out of memory. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: 50 threads use too much stack memory; drop to 10 threads
Fixed pools leak threads on exceptions; restart the pool every hour
Its queue is unbounded; use a bounded queue and a rejection policy
The pool lacks fairness; set fair = true to drain tasks evenly
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: Tasks pile up silently in the unbounded queue until memory runs out. A bounded queue gives backpressure, and a per-dependency pool (bulkhead) stops one slow service consuming every thread.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: Checkout on an 8-core machine calls three ~50 ms services using CompletableFuture.supplyAsync with no executor argument. Under load, latency explodes. Why?
options: supplyAsync without an executor runs tasks one at a time on the caller thread
CompletableFuture creates a new platform thread per call, which is too slow
It runs on the shared common pool, which blocking I/O exhausts
The three services must be chained with thenCompose rather than run together
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: The common pool has roughly cores minus one threads and is shared by the whole JVM. Blocking I/O there starves everything; always pass your own executor and add timeouts.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: Checkout needs pricing (40 ms), inventory (25 ms) and offers (60 ms normally, sometimes 2 s on sale night). Offers is optional. What is the best design?
options: Fan out with deadlines, and let only offers fall back on timeout
Call them one after another so failures are easier to trace
Fan out concurrently and wait as long as needed for all three to return
Skip the offers call entirely during the sale to save time
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: Concurrent calls take about the slowest one (about 60 ms) instead of the sum (about 125 ms). completeOnTimeout lets offers degrade gracefully while mandatory calls still fail fast.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: A deal counter was fixed with an AtomicInteger. After scaling checkout to 60 pods, the deal oversells again. Why, and what is the fix?
options: AtomicInteger isn't atomic under high load; replace it with synchronized
Each pod has its own counter; use a conditional database update
The pods' clocks are out of sync; add NTP to every pod
AtomicInteger needs to be volatile when the service runs in containers
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: In-process atomics and locks stop at the JVM boundary. A conditional UPDATE that checks rows affected, an atomic Redis decrement, or partitioning by SKU gives a single authority.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: One very hot deal row in the database becomes a contention bottleneck even with a conditional decrement. What is a sound mitigation?
options: Wrap the update in a Java synchronized block on every pod
Split the stock across several sub-counter rows to spread contention
Remove the WHERE left > 0 condition so updates run faster
Read the row, decrement in Java and write it back without a condition
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: Spreading stock over, say, 10 sub-counters cuts contention on one row. Dropping the condition or doing read-modify-write in app code brings back oversells.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: You use a Redis distributed lock with a lease to guard inventory writes. A holder pauses in a long GC, its lease expires, and another node takes the lock. How do you stop the stale holder's write?
options: Use a fencing token that the storage layer checks and rejects if stale
Make the lease infinite so it never expires during a pause
Check the lock is still held just before writing, which closes the gap
Use synchronized on top of the distributed lock as a second guard
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: A lease can expire while the holder is paused, and a check before writing still races with the pause. Only the storage layer rejecting stale tokens is safe.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: A team moves an I/O-heavy order service to Java 21 virtual threads, creating one per request. Soon the 50-connection database is overwhelmed. What did they miss?
options: Virtual threads must be pooled, like platform threads, to limit their number
Virtual threads don't limit scarce resources; cap DB access with a Semaphore
Virtual threads are only for CPU-bound work, so I/O should stay on platform threads
Virtual threads share one connection, so the pool must be resized to one
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: A million cheap virtual threads can still flood a small database. Don't pool virtual threads; instead limit access to the scarce resource.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: A pricing job that does heavy in-memory computation is moved to virtual threads, expecting a speedup. Throughput doesn't change. Why?
options: The job needs a larger carrier pool, about 200 carriers, to benefit
Virtual threads only run on one core, so the job got slower
Virtual threads help waiting tasks, not CPU-bound work
The job must be rewritten with CompletableFuture for virtual threads to help
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: When a virtual thread blocks on I/O it unmounts and the carrier runs another, which helps I/O-bound work. CPU work has nothing to unmount from.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: On Java 21, a service uses virtual threads but blocks on I/O inside synchronized blocks, and scalability is poor. What explains this, and a fix on that version?
options: Blocking in synchronized pins the carrier; use ReentrantLock on Java 21
synchronized blocks are disabled for virtual threads, so they run single-threaded
Virtual threads can't do I/O at all, so they fall back to platform threads
synchronized makes virtual threads non-daemon, so they never exit
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: In Java 21 to 23, a pinned virtual thread holds its carrier while blocked, so carriers run out. ReentrantLock avoids pinning; JEP 491 in JDK 24 removed most of it.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: A high-traffic metrics counter is incremented by hundreds of threads, and an AtomicLong shows heavy CAS retries. What is the better tool?
options: A volatile long, which avoids CAS and is always atomic
A synchronized long, which never makes threads wait
An AtomicReference<Long>, which uses a different, faster CAS
LongAdder, which spreads increments across per-thread cells
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: Under heavy contention, CAS loops spin and retry on one memory location. LongAdder suits metrics but not logic like 'decrement only if positive'.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: A Spring WebFlux (event-loop) gateway suddenly stalls for all users. A new handler calls a blocking JDBC query. Why does that hurt so much?
options: Event loops run on a few threads; one blocking call stalls every request on that loop
Event loops create a new thread per blocking call, exhausting memory
JDBC calls are automatically retried by the event loop until they time out
Blocking calls are rejected by event loops, so the handler throws errors
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: A few event-loop threads handle huge numbers of connections only if callbacks never block. Blocking or long CPU work on the loop freezes everything scheduled on it.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: Which statement about Java's ReentrantLock compared with synchronized is correct?
options: ReentrantLock gives mutual exclusion but no visibility guarantees
synchronized supports tryLock with a timeout, while ReentrantLock does not
ReentrantLock is released automatically on exceptions, like synchronized
ReentrantLock adds tryLock and fairness but must be unlocked in finally
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: Both give mutual exclusion and visibility. ReentrantLock's extras help with fail-fast behaviour, but unlike synchronized you must unlock in finally.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: A developer holds a lock while calling a partner shipping API that sometimes takes 3 seconds. What is the main problem?
options: Locks expire after one second, so the API call loses mutual exclusion
The lock makes the API call itself slower by blocking its network socket
Nothing, as long as the lock is a ReentrantLock rather than synchronized
Every other thread waits on the slow call; do I/O outside the lock
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: Never do I/O or call another service while holding a lock: it serialises all threads behind a slow external call and invites deadlock if that code takes other locks.

What are multithreading and concurrency,.q: Users rarely edit the same profile at once, but a hot deal counter sees thousands of concurrent decrements. Which locking choice fits each?
options: Pessimistic locking for profiles; optimistic versioning for the hot counter
Optimistic versioning for both, since retries are always cheap
A distributed lock for both, since they run on many pods
Optimistic versioning for profiles; atomic conditional updates for the counter
What are multithreading and concurrency,.why: Optimistic concurrency wins when conflicts are rare. Under heavy contention it causes endless retries, so atomic conditional updates or pessimistic locks fit better.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: You are pairing with a junior developer on a new delivery-fee rule. She wants to write all twenty test cases for the rule first and then write the code in one go. What is the best correction, in TDD terms?
options: Writing all the tests up front is correct TDD as long as none of them pass yet
Write one small failing test, make it pass with minimal code, refactor, then pick the next test
Write all the code first, then add the twenty tests so coverage reaches 100%
Write the twenty tests first but only run them once the whole feature is finished
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: TDD is one small test at a time, interleaved with code in red-green-refactor cycles of a few minutes. Writing every test first is a common misconception; it loses the step-by-step design feedback.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: You write a new test for a coupon rule and it passes immediately, before you have written any production code for it. What should you do?
options: Celebrate and move on, because a passing test means the feature already works
Delete the test, since TDD only allows tests that fail on the first run
Treat it as suspicious: check the test, since a test you never saw fail might be testing nothing
Skip the refactor step for this cycle because the test is already green
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: The Red step means watching the test fail for the right reason. A test that never fails may be asserting nothing or testing the wrong thing, so you fix the test first.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: In the Green step for the discount calculator, the first test only checks that a Rs 999.99 cart gets no discount. A teammate objects that writing 'return 0;' is cheating. What is the best response?
options: He is right; Green should always implement the full rule to avoid rework later
It is allowed only if you also add a TODO comment and skip the refactor step
It is wrong because hard-coded values break the red-green-refactor loop entirely
It is allowed: the simplest passing code is fine, and the next test will force you to generalise
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: Green means the simplest code that passes, even a hard-coded value. The next test (10% at Rs 2,000) forces the generalisation, which keeps you from writing speculative code.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: A team says they 'do TDD', but their code is full of duplication and long methods even though every test is green. Which step are they most likely skipping?
options: The refactor step, where names improve and duplication is removed with tests green
The red step, because they write tests that pass immediately
The green step, because they write more code than the tests need
The end-to-end step, because TDD requires a UI test for every feature
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: Refactor is where design actually happens. Skipping it is the most common way TDD degrades into 'test-first spaghetti'.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: You have been stuck in the red state on one failing test for about 30 minutes. What does TDD practice recommend?
options: Keep going until it passes, since long red phases mean deep design work
Comment out the failing test and continue with the next behaviour
Write the remaining tests for the feature so you can see the full picture
Revert and take a smaller step, since a cycle should take roughly 2-10 minutes
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: Each red-green-refactor cycle should take 2-10 minutes. Being red for 30 minutes signals the step was too big, so you revert and take a smaller one.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: In the worked example, money is passed to discountFor() as a long in paise (for example 99_999 for Rs 999.99) rather than as a double in rupees. Why?
options: Because JUnit 5 assertEquals cannot compare double values at all
To avoid floating-point rounding errors in money calculations
Because paise values make the 10% discount calculation run faster
Because the Rs 500 cap can only be expressed as a whole number of paise
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: The example stores money as paise in a long specifically to avoid floating-point errors. assertEquals can compare doubles with a delta, so that is not the reason.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: All discount-calculator tests pass and line coverage is 100%, but PIT reports that changing 'cartTotalPaise < THRESHOLD_PAISE' to '<=' survives. What is the best next step?
options: Ignore it, because 100% line coverage already proves the threshold is tested
Raise the coverage gate to 100% on all modules so the mutant gets caught
Add a test that exactly 100,000 paise (Rs 1,000) gives a 10,000-paise discount to kill the mutant
Mark the mutant as equivalent, since '<' and '<=' behave the same for money
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: A surviving mutant means no test checks the exact boundary. Coverage only shows the line ran; a boundary test at exactly Rs 1,000 makes the mutant fail.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: Your manager proposes a hard 100% line-coverage target for the whole codebase to improve quality. What is the main risk?
options: Once coverage is a target, people write assertion-free tests to hit it (Goodhart's law)
Coverage tools cannot measure Java code reliably above about 90%
100% coverage forces the team to write too many end-to-end tests
High coverage makes mutation testing impossible to run on the code
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: Coverage shows which lines ran, not whether anything was checked; a test with no assertions gives full coverage. Use it as a signal, with a modest gate (around 70-80%) on new or changed code.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: A team's unit tests mock every collaborator and verify each internal call. Refactors constantly break tests, yet production bugs still slip through. What is the best fix?
options: Add more mocks so every internal call is verified in the exact order it happens
Replace all unit tests with end-to-end tests that drive the full deployed system
Mock only external or nondeterministic boundaries, use fakes for your own repositories, and assert on outcomes
Keep the mocks but raise the coverage gate so more internal paths are exercised
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: Over-mocked tests are coupled to implementation (they break on refactors) and the mocks can lie (they pass when the system is broken). Mock what you don't own, prefer fakes inside, and add integration and contract tests for real wiring.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: Your order service test needs a payment gateway, a system clock, and your own order repository. Following the answer's guidance, which should you mock or stub?
options: All three, so the unit test has no real collaborators at all
The payment gateway and the clock; use an in-memory fake for your own order repository
Only the order repository, since the gateway and clock are simple to call
None of them; a unit test should always use the real gateway and clock
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: Mock what you don't own or what is slow or nondeterministic, like payment gateways and clocks. For your own repositories, a fake (for example a HashMap-backed repository) is preferred.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: Which test double is a working lightweight implementation, such as an order repository backed by an in-memory HashMap?
options: A fake
A stub
A mock
A spy
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: A fake actually works but is simplified, like an in-memory repository. A stub just returns canned answers, and a mock verifies interactions.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: The checkout service depends on the pricing API. Last sale, pricing renamed a response field and checkout broke in production. Which practice best prevents a repeat without a large end-to-end suite?
options: A nightly end-to-end test run of every checkout journey on a shared staging environment
Raising unit-test coverage on the pricing service to at least 90% of changed lines
Mocking the pricing API in checkout's unit tests with the old field names
Pact contract tests: checkout records its expectations in a pact file and pricing's CI verifies against it
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: With Pact, the consumer's expectations are replayed in the provider's CI, so pricing's build fails before deployment if it breaks the contract. This replaces most cross-service E2E tests.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: Your team's tests are mostly manual regression plus slow UI end-to-end scripts, with few unit tests. What shape is this, and what do both the test pyramid and testing trophy agree on?
options: It is the testing trophy, which correctly puts end-to-end tests as the widest layer
It is the 'ice-cream cone'; both shapes say to avoid having most testing manual or end-to-end
It is the test pyramid, which recommends about 70% end-to-end tests at the top
It is a balanced portfolio, as long as the end-to-end suite finishes overnight
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: The pyramid wants many unit tests and few E2E; the trophy makes integration tests widest. Both agree to avoid the ice-cream cone, which is slow and flaky.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: You must change a 4,000-line untested OfferEngine before the festive sale. How do you apply TDD safely?
options: First write characterization tests capturing current behaviour from real inputs, then refactor through seams
Rewrite the engine from scratch with TDD, since legacy code cannot be tested
Write tests describing the correct intended behaviour and fix all failures first
Skip testing for this release and add unit tests after the sale is over
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: Characterization tests record what the code currently does, right or wrong, giving a safety net. Then introduce seams and make each new rule or bug fix start with a failing test.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: A customer reports that the free-shipping threshold is off by one paisa. Under the team's definition of done, what is the first thing you write?
options: The code fix, followed by a regression test once it is deployed
A Given-When-Then scenario in Cucumber, without any unit test
A failing test that reproduces the bug
An end-to-end UI test that places a real order at the threshold
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: Every bug fix starts with a failing test that reproduces the bug; it proves the bug exists and guards against its return.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: A test that checks order-confirmation emails fails about once in twenty runs with no code change. It uses Thread.sleep(2000) to wait for an async job. What is the best fix and team policy?
options: Increase the sleep to 10 seconds and leave the test in the blocking suite
Configure CI to retry every failing test three times before reporting red
Delete the test, because asynchronous behaviour should never be tested
Replace the sleep with polling with a timeout (e.g. Awaitility) and quarantine the test within a day with an owner
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: Fixed sleeps are a classic flakiness cause; polling with timeouts fixes it. Flaky tests should be quarantined fast with a ticket and owner, because flaky suites teach people to ignore red builds.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: You are rolling TDD out to a checkout-pricing team that has never practised it. Which plan best matches the answer's approach?
options: Mandate TDD for every team on day one and track the number of tests written per engineer
Katas and pairing first, then add it to the definition of done and CI gates, and measure escaped defects, change failure rate and lead time
Set a 100% coverage gate in CI and let the team learn TDD from the failing builds
Apply TDD first to the UI layout team, since visual bugs are the most visible to customers
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: Build skill before mandating, apply TDD where logic is dense (pricing rules), then bake it into done and CI. Judge success by business outcomes, not test counts or coverage.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: A senior engineer argues that test-after gives the same coverage as TDD, so TDD is pointless. What is the strongest counter-argument?
options: Test-after loses the design feedback: you bend tests to fit existing code, skip awkward cases, and never see them fail
Test-after can never reach the same line coverage as test-first development
Test-after tests always run slower in CI than tests written before the code
Test-after is not allowed with JUnit 5 parameterized or table-driven tests
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: Coverage can match, but TDD's value is design feedback and tests proven to fail. Test-after is fine for simple glue code; TDD shines for rule-heavy logic.

What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.q: Product, QA and developers agree on this example: 'Given a cart worth Rs 8,000, When the 10 percent festive discount is applied, Then the discount is Rs 500 because of the cap.' What practice is this, and where is its main value?
options: BDD; the main value is replacing all unit tests with Cucumber scenarios
Mutation testing; the main value is killing surviving boundary mutants
Contract testing; the main value is checking request and response shapes
BDD; the main value is the shared conversation that produces the examples
What is Test-Driven Development (TDD), a.why: BDD writes examples in business language as Given-When-Then. Tools like Cucumber can run them, but the real value is the conversation among product, QA and developers.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: A colleague says Git saves space by storing only the changes between versions, like Subversion. What is the more accurate description?
options: Git stores a full copy of every file in every commit, with no sharing
Git stores diffs, and rebuilds each version by replaying them from the first commit
Git stores only the files changed in each commit and nothing about the rest
Git's model is a full snapshot per commit; diffs are computed on demand
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: Each commit records the whole project as a snapshot, with unchanged content shared by hash. Deltas exist only inside packfiles as a storage trick, not as the model.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: In a checkout service of about 5,000 files, Asha edits one file, PaymentClient.java, six folders deep, and commits. Roughly what new objects does Git write?
options: A new blob for every file in the project plus one tree and one commit
One new blob, about one new tree per folder on the path to the root, and one commit
Only a diff object describing the changed lines, plus one commit
One new blob and one commit; trees never change when a file changes
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: Unchanged blobs and trees keep the same hash and are reused. Only the changed blob, the trees on its path up to the root, and the commit itself are new.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: The same README.md appears unchanged in 30 commits and is also copied into two folders. How many blobs does Git store for that content?
options: Thirty, one per commit that contains the file
Two, one for each folder the file appears in
One, because objects are named by the hash of their content
Sixty, one per folder per commit
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: Git is content-addressed: identical content gives an identical hash, so it is stored once no matter how many commits or folders use it.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: Which Git object holds a file's raw bytes but not its name or permissions?
options: A blob
A tree
A commit
A ref
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: A blob is just the content. The file name and mode live in the tree that lists it.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: Which of these is NOT stored inside a commit object?
options: The full contents of each changed file
The hash of the top-level tree
The hash of the parent commit or commits
The author, committer, timestamps and message
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: A commit is a short text record pointing to a top-level tree, its parents, and metadata. File contents live in blobs, reached through the trees.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: Someone quietly edits one byte in a file from a commit made six months ago and rewrites history. What happens to the hashes?
options: Only that blob's hash changes; the commits keep their original hashes
Nothing changes, because commit hashes cover only the message and author
That blob's hash changes, and so do the hashes of its trees, that commit, and every later commit
Only the latest commit's hash changes, because it is the one Git checks
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: A commit hash covers its tree (and thus every blob) and its parent. So any change ripples forward, which is why a commit hash identifies the entire history leading to it.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: You run 'git branch feature/coupons' in a large repository. What does Git actually do?
options: Copies the current working tree into a new hidden folder for the branch
Creates a new commit that records the start of the branch
Duplicates all the blobs so the branch can change them independently
Writes a tiny ref file holding one commit hash; no project files are copied
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: A branch is a 41-byte file (40 hex characters plus a newline) under .git/refs/heads. Creating many branches costs almost nothing.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: You check out an old commit by its hash to debug, make two commits there, then switch back to main. Why might those commits be at risk?
options: Git refuses to save commits made on old hashes, so they were never written
You were in detached HEAD, so the commits are not on any branch and are easy to lose
The commits were automatically merged into main and may cause conflicts
Checking out a hash deletes the branch labels that pointed to later commits
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: When HEAD holds a commit hash directly, new commits belong to no branch. Create a branch for them; otherwise you need git reflog to find them.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: You merge feature into main, and main has not moved since feature branched off. What does Git do?
options: A three-way merge that creates a merge commit with two parents
A rebase that rewrites feature's commits with new hashes onto main
It refuses the merge until you create a merge commit manually
A fast-forward: it slides the main label to feature's latest commit with no new commit
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: If main's tip is an ancestor of feature's tip, main has nothing feature lacks, so Git just moves the label forward.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: Main has commit C and feature has commits D and E, both branching from B. During the merge, CouponService.java changed only on main, PaymentClient.java only on feature, and one line in PaymentConfig.java on both. What happens?
options: Git reports conflicts in all three files because both branches moved
Git takes the one-sided changes automatically and reports a conflict only in PaymentConfig.java
Git fast-forwards main to E and drops commit C's changes
Git takes main's version of every file because main is the target branch
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: A three-way merge compares base B, ours C, and theirs E. Changes made on only one side are taken; only the same lines changed differently on both sides conflict.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: After resolving a merge conflict, what does the resulting merge commit M contain that a normal commit does not?
options: A copy of both versions of every conflicted file
A pointer to the merge base instead of a parent
Two parent hashes, one for each side being merged
A list of diffs showing how the conflict was resolved
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: A merge commit is still a snapshot plus metadata, but with two parents (C and E in the example).

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: Two branches merge cleanly with no conflicts. One renamed a method; the other added a new call to the old method name. Why does CI still need to run?
options: Git merges lines of text, not meaning, so a clean merge can still be logically broken
Clean merges can only happen when both branches changed exactly the same files
Git verifies compilation during a merge, so CI only needs to check style
A clean merge means Git already ran the tests from both branches
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: Git has no idea what code means; it only compares text regions. A conflict-free merge can still fail to compile or behave wrongly, so tests run on the merge commit.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: You run 'git rebase main' on your feature branch with commits D and E. What is true afterwards?
options: D and E keep their hashes but now point to main's latest commit as parent
New commits D' and E' exist with new hashes; the old D and E are abandoned
Git creates a merge commit joining feature and main with two parents
D and E are squashed into a single commit with the hash of main's tip
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: Rebase replays each commit on a new base. Since the parent changes, the hash changes, so these are new commits. Saying rebase 'just moves' commits is a misconception.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: Kiran rebases a shared release branch and force-pushes. Teammates who built on the old commits now see duplicates and conflicts. What is the best set of team rules going forward?
options: Rebase only private branches, use --force-with-lease, and protect key branches against force-push
Always rebase shared branches, since a straight history prevents duplicates
Ban merges and require every developer to force-push after each pull
Delete and recreate the shared branch whenever someone rebases it
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: Rewriting history others have pulled diverges their history from the server. --force-with-lease refuses if the remote moved, and branch protection blocks force-pushes to key branches; git reflog helps recover.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: Your ML team commits 2 GB model weight files to the repository every week and clones are getting huge. What does the answer recommend?
options: Run git gc daily, since packfile deltas shrink model weights like source code
Store the weights as many small text files so Git can deduplicate them
Commit them to a separate branch, since branches store their files separately
Keep them out of normal history with Git LFS or an artifact store, since binaries compress and delta poorly
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: Large binaries are the real exception to Git's efficiency: they compress and delta poorly and bloat every clone. Git LFS or an artifact store is the fix.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: How does a packfile store several successive versions of the same source file?
options: One full copy of the oldest version plus all changes replayed forward
A full uncompressed copy of each version, indexed by commit date
One full copy, usually the newest, plus small deltas for the other versions
Only the newest version; older versions are deleted during git gc
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: During git gc and push or fetch, Git packs objects and delta-compresses similar ones, usually keeping the newest whole because it is read most.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: What does the file .git/refs/heads/main contain, and what happens to it when you commit on main?
options: The list of every commit on main; Git appends the new commit to it
A snapshot of the working files; Git replaces it with the new snapshot
A single commit hash; Git overwrites it with the new commit's hash
The name of the current branch; Git leaves it unchanged after commits
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: A branch is a movable label: one 40-character hash plus a newline. Committing just rewrites it to point to the new commit.

How does Git actually remember every ver.q: What is the role of the index (staging area) when you run 'git add Cart.java'?
options: It stores the diff between Cart.java and its last committed version
It immediately creates a commit containing only Cart.java
It uploads Cart.java to the remote so teammates can see it
It records exactly what the next snapshot will contain, after Git writes the blob if new
How does Git actually remember every ver.why: git add hashes the file, writes a blob if it is new, and records it in the index. git commit then turns the index into trees and a commit.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: The 'My Orders' query runs in 5 ms on your laptop's 1,000-row test database but takes 25 seconds in production on 10 crore orders. What is the most likely reason?
options: Production SSDs are slower, so every query is about 5,000 times slower there
The production optimizer is disabled during peak hours to save CPU
Small tables use a B-tree automatically while large tables never do
Production does a full table scan; on small tables scans are cheap, so the missing index went unnoticed
Why does adding an index make a database.why: With 1,000 rows a full scan reads about 20 pages, well under a millisecond. On 100 million rows (about 20 GB) the same scan takes seconds, which is why a missing index shows up only in production.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: An interviewer asks: binary search on 100 million sorted keys needs about 27 steps, so why does a B-tree index need only 3 or 4 page reads?
options: B-trees use hashing at each level, so lookups take constant time
The database caches all 100 million keys in memory, so no levels are read
Each page holds hundreds to about a thousand keys, so each level multiplies reach by about 1,000
B-trees skip the internal pages and read leaf pages directly by row number
Why does adding an index make a database.why: A 16 KB page fits around 1,000 entries, so 3 levels reach about a billion rows. The root and branch pages are usually in memory, leaving only a few disk reads.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: Your dashboard needs 'all orders from 1 Oct to 10 Oct' and there is a B-tree index on created_at. How does the index serve this range efficiently?
options: It finds 1 Oct in the leaves, then walks sideways along linked leaf pages until 10 Oct
It does a separate root-to-leaf lookup for every second in the range
It cannot serve ranges; B-tree indexes only answer exact equality matches
It reads every leaf page and filters the dates in memory
Why does adding an index make a database.why: Leaf pages are sorted and linked to their neighbours, so a range read is one descent plus a sideways walk. Exact-match-only is a limitation of hash indexes, not B-trees.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: You have an index on (customer_id, created_at). Which query can use it well?
options: WHERE created_at > '2026-10-01'
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND created_at > '2026-10-01'
WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-10-10'
WHERE total > 5000 ORDER BY created_at
Why does adding an index make a database.why: The left-most prefix rule: the index helps only when the query uses its columns from the left. A date range alone skips customer_id, so matching entries are scattered across the whole index.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: You must index for: WHERE seller_id = ? AND status = ? AND created_at BETWEEN ? AND ?. Which column order follows the rule of thumb?
options: (created_at, seller_id, status): the range column first to narrow dates early
(seller_id, status, created_at): equality columns first, then the range column
(status, created_at, seller_id): the lowest-selectivity column first
Any order works, since the optimizer reorders composite index columns
Why does adding an index make a database.why: Put equality columns first and the range or sort column last, so matching entries form one contiguous slice. Column order matters a lot; the optimizer cannot reorder an index.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: A teammate created separate single-column indexes on customer_id and on created_at, and says that is the same as one (customer_id, created_at) index. What is the best response?
options: Correct: the database always merges single-column indexes at no extra cost
Correct: two indexes are better because each can be used independently
Wrong: the database can never use more than one index in any query
Not quite: one composite index serves 'customer 7's latest orders, sorted' far better than combining two
Why does adding an index make a database.why: The composite index already has each customer's entries sorted by date. The database may combine separate indexes, but it is usually slower, and it still has to sort.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: The hottest query is SELECT created_at, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10. With an index on (customer_id, created_at), EXPLAIN shows an Index Scan. What change saves one extra read per returned row?
options: Make the index covering, e.g. (customer_id, created_at, total) or INCLUDE (total)
Add a separate single-column index on total
Change the query to SELECT * so the optimizer fetches whole rows at once
Reverse the index to (created_at, customer_id) to match the ORDER BY
Why does adding an index make a database.why: If the index contains every column the query needs, the database skips the table entirely. In PostgreSQL this appears as an Index Only Scan.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: An orders table during the sale handles thousands of inserts per second and has 6 secondary indexes. Write throughput is dropping. What is the main cost you are seeing?
options: Indexes only slow down reads, so the drop must come from something else
Each insert rebuilds all 6 indexes from scratch, which takes seconds
Each insert updates the table plus all 6 indexes, about 7 B-tree updates, with possible page splits and log writes
Indexes lock the whole table during every insert
Why does adding an index make a database.why: Every index must be maintained on every write. Too many indexes on write-heavy tables directly cut throughput, so each index must earn its place.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: Someone adds an index on status to speed up WHERE status = 'DELIVERED', where DELIVERED is 70% of 10 crore orders. EXPLAIN still shows a full scan. Why?
options: The optimizer has a bug and should be forced to use the index with a hint
Low selectivity: following 70 million pointers as random reads is slower than one sequential scan
Indexes cannot be built on text columns like status
The index only takes effect after the database is restarted
Why does adding an index make a database.why: The optimizer correctly ignores indexes when a big share of rows matches. You still pay the index's write cost, so drop it, or use a partial index if you only query a rare value.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: Your support tool only ever looks up orders WHERE status = 'PENDING', which is about 1% of rows. Which PostgreSQL index fits best?
options: A partial index covering only rows WHERE status = 'PENDING'
A full index on status covering all 5 values
A hash index on status so equality lookups are constant time
No index, since status is always a low-selectivity column
Why does adding an index make a database.why: A partial index indexes only the rare value you query, so it is small and selective, and avoids index overhead for writes of other statuses.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: An ops dashboard runs WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-10-10' and ignores the index on created_at. What is the best rewrite?
options: WHERE DATE(created_at) >= '2026-10-10' AND DATE(created_at) < '2026-10-11'
WHERE CAST(created_at AS DATE) = '2026-10-10'
WHERE created_at LIKE '2026-10-10%'
WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-10' AND created_at < '2026-10-11'
Why does adding an index make a database.why: The index is sorted on the raw value, so wrapping the column in a function forces every row to be computed. A plain range on the column can use the index.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: WHERE LOWER(email) = 'sethu@example.com' is slow even though email is indexed. Which pair of fixes does the answer suggest?
options: Rewrite as WHERE email LIKE '%sethu@example.com' or add a hash index on email
Run ANALYZE to refresh statistics, or increase the buffer pool size
Store emails already lowercased and compare directly, or create an expression index on LOWER(email)
Switch to a covering index on email, or add an index on the id column
Why does adding an index make a database.why: Functions on the column defeat a normal index. Either avoid the function or index the computed value with a functional (expression) index.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: A query on a text column mobile is slow: WHERE mobile = 9876543210 (a number, no quotes). An index on mobile exists. What is the likely cause?
options: The index has too many levels because mobile numbers are 10 digits long
Phone numbers are low-selectivity, so the optimizer skips the index
Numeric literals always force a full table scan in every database
Implicit type conversion: comparing text to a number makes the column effectively wrapped in a conversion
Why does adding an index make a database.why: An implicit cast acts like a function on the column, so the sorted index on the raw text cannot be used. Compare with a string literal of the right type.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: EXPLAIN on a MySQL query shows 'type: ALL', 'rows: 100000000' and 'Extra: Using filesort'. What does this tell you?
options: It is using a covering index and returning rows already sorted
It is using the primary key index and the sort is free
It is doing a full table scan and an extra sort because no index provides the order
It is reading only 100 rows because the result is cached
Why does adding an index make a database.why: type: ALL means a full scan, and Using filesort means an extra sort step. After adding (customer_id, created_at), EXPLAIN showed type: ref, rows: 40, and no filesort.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the optimizer estimated 50 rows but actually read 2 million, and it chose a poor plan. What is the first thing to do?
options: Drop all indexes on the table so the optimizer is forced to scan
Refresh table statistics with ANALYZE, since a big estimate gap points to stale statistics
Add a covering index with every column in the table
Switch the column type to avoid implicit conversion
Why does adding an index make a database.why: A large gap between estimated and actual rows usually means stale statistics. ANALYZE refreshes them so the optimizer can choose a better plan.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: An interviewer asks why databases default to B-tree indexes instead of hash indexes. What is the best answer?
options: Hash indexes only answer exact matches; B-trees also handle ranges, sorting and prefix matches
Hash indexes are always slower than B-trees, even for exact matches
B-trees use less disk space because they store no pointers
Hash indexes cannot be built on integer primary keys
Why does adding an index make a database.why: Most real queries need ranges or ordering, which a sorted B-tree supports. A hash index only helps for equality lookups.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: Write throughput on your orders table dropped after a release. Which checks does the answer recommend first?
options: New indexes on the hot write table, indexed columns now updated on every write, and index usage stats
Raise the isolation level and add more read replicas
Convert all secondary indexes to covering indexes
Increase LIMIT values on read queries to reduce round trips
Why does adding an index make a database.why: Indexes slow every write. Look for newly added ones, for indexed columns that changed often, and drop unused ones using pg_stat_user_indexes or sys.schema_unused_indexes.

Why does adding an index make a database.q: A finance team runs a nightly export that reads 80% of the orders table. A teammate wants to force an index for it. What is the better view?
options: Full table scans are always bad and should be eliminated everywhere
Forcing the index will help because indexes always beat scans
The export should be split into one query per row using the primary key
A full scan is often the fastest plan when a query needs a big share of the table
Why does adding an index make a database.why: For reports and exports touching most rows, a sequential scan beats millions of random index lookups. 'A full table scan is always bad' is a misconception.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: A bank transfer debits Rs 500 from Asha and credits Ravi. The server crashes after the debit. Which ACID property ensures the money does not vanish?
options: Isolation: other transactions cannot see the half-done debit
Durability: committed data survives the crash
Consistency: replicas all return the latest balance
Atomicity: both steps happen or neither does
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: Atomicity is all-or-nothing; the uncommitted debit is rolled back after the crash. Durability only protects changes that were already committed.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: Two users book the last train seat. Each request runs inside a transaction at read committed: SELECT seats_left (both get 1), then UPDATE trains SET seats_left = 0 and insert a booking. What happens?
options: Only one succeeds, because every transaction is atomic
Both get bookings: atomicity does not stop concurrent readers from both seeing 1 seat
Both fail, because the database detects the duplicate booking automatically
The second request gets a dirty read and its booking is rolled back
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: This is a check-then-act race, an isolation problem. At read committed both can read 1 before either writes, so you need FOR UPDATE, a conditional update, or serializable.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: Which single statement most simply fixes the last-seat race for a seat counter?
options: SELECT seats_left FROM trains WHERE train_id = 12635, then UPDATE if the value is above 0
UPDATE trains SET seats_left = 0 WHERE train_id = 12635, then insert the booking
UPDATE trains SET seats_left = seats_left - 1 WHERE train_id = 12635 AND seats_left > 0, then check rows affected
BEGIN; SELECT seats_left FROM trains; COMMIT; then UPDATE outside the transaction
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: The conditional update puts the check inside the write, so the database checks and acts as one step on a locked row. Reading first and then updating leaves a gap for the race.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: Your conditional update '... WHERE seats_left > 0' returns 0 rows affected. What should the app do?
options: Not insert a booking; roll back and report sold out or offer the waitlist
Retry the same update in a loop until it affects 1 row
Insert the booking anyway, since the update itself did not fail
Set seats_left to 1 and try again so the booking can proceed
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: 0 rows affected means someone else took the last seat. The app must not create a booking; it should report sold out or waitlist.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: You use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the train row. Asha's transaction locks it first. What happens to Ravi's FOR UPDATE on the same row?
options: It reads the old value 1 immediately and also books the seat
It fails instantly with a deadlock error
It waits until Asha commits, then reads the fresh value 0 and reports sold out
It skips the locked row and books the next train automatically
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: FOR UPDATE takes a row lock until commit or rollback. The second transaction queues, then sees the updated count. This is pessimistic locking.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: Your booking code runs SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the seat row, then calls the UPI payment gateway (which can take 30 seconds), then commits. During the festive rush, bookings pile up. What is the best redesign?
options: Reserve the seat in a short transaction with a HELD status and expiry, commit, take payment, then confirm or release in another short transaction
Keep the lock but raise the database lock-wait timeout to 60 seconds
Switch to serializable isolation so the payment call is protected automatically
Use optimistic locking so the 30-second payment does not need any lock
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: Never hold a database lock during slow external calls; everyone wanting the row queues behind it. A short reserve transaction plus a separate confirm or release keeps locks to milliseconds.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: A profile-edit screen lets users update their address. Two edits to the same profile at once are very rare, and you don't want reads to block. Which approach fits best?
options: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on every profile read
Serializable isolation for the whole application
A conditional update with WHERE address > 0
Optimistic locking with a version column (@Version in JPA), retrying or failing on a clash
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: Optimistic locking suits rare clashes: no locks on read, and a version check at write time detects conflicts. Hibernate throws OptimisticLockException when the version changed.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: A flash sale has 100 units and 50,000 buyers in one minute. A teammate proposes optimistic locking with a version column on the stock row. What is the best response?
options: Good choice: optimistic locking is always faster because it never waits
Avoid it here: most attempts would clash and retry; a conditional decrement or short pessimistic lock is more efficient
Good choice, as long as each buyer retries up to 1,000 times
Avoid it, because version columns only work at serializable isolation
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: Optimistic locking is only faster when clashes are rare. On a hot row, repeated failed retries waste work, while queueing on a lock or a conditional update is efficient.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: With optimistic locking, you read seats_left = 1 with version 7, then run UPDATE ... SET seats_left = 0, version = 8 WHERE train_id = 12635 AND version = 7. It affects 0 rows. What does that mean?
options: The update succeeded but the row count is not reported for version columns
Someone changed the row since you read it; re-read and retry, or report sold out
The row is locked by another transaction and you must wait
The version column overflowed and must be reset to 0
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: A 0-row result means the version no longer matches, so another transaction got there first. You re-read and decide again.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: In a transaction you read a product's price twice. Between the reads, another transaction commits a price change, and your second read shows the new value. Which anomaly is this?
options: A dirty read
A lost update
A deadlock
A non-repeatable read
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: A non-repeatable read is getting different values for the same row within one transaction because someone committed in between. A dirty read involves uncommitted data.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: Your report reads an order total from another transaction that has not committed yet, and that transaction later rolls back. Which anomaly occurred, and which is the lowest level in the table that prevents it?
options: A dirty read; only serializable prevents it
A non-repeatable read; repeatable read prevents it
A dirty read; read committed prevents it
A lost update; read committed prevents it
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: Reading uncommitted data is a dirty read. All three levels in the answer prevent it, starting with read committed.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: Both a PostgreSQL and a MySQL InnoDB service run at repeatable read and do a plain read-then-write on the same row concurrently. What does the answer say about the lost update?
options: PostgreSQL makes the second updater fail with a serialization error; InnoDB can still lose the update without FOR UPDATE or a conditional update
Both databases prevent it identically, since repeatable read is a SQL standard
Both databases allow it, since only serializable ever catches lost updates
InnoDB raises a serialization error while PostgreSQL silently loses the update
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: Repeatable read behaves differently across databases. Know your database's actual rules rather than assuming the level name means the same thing everywhere.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: Which isolation level is the default in PostgreSQL, and which in MySQL InnoDB?
options: PostgreSQL: serializable; MySQL InnoDB: read committed
PostgreSQL: read committed; MySQL InnoDB: repeatable read
PostgreSQL: repeatable read; MySQL InnoDB: read committed
Both default to serializable
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: Most teams stay at the default (read committed in PostgreSQL) and protect specific hot paths with FOR UPDATE or a conditional update.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: Which isolation level, on its own, always prevents the last-seat race?
options: Read committed
Repeatable read
Serializable
Read uncommitted
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: Serializable guarantees the same result as running transactions one at a time, so it always prevents the race, at the cost of more aborts and retries. Lower levels need an explicit lock or conditional update.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: Transaction 1 locks seat 5 then wants seat 6; transaction 2 locks seat 6 then wants seat 5. What happens, and how do you prevent it?
options: A deadlock; the database aborts one. Lock seats in a consistent order (e.g. ascending ID) and retry the aborted one
Both wait forever; the only fix is restarting the database
A dirty read; raise the isolation level to read committed
A lost update; add a version column to the seat table
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: Databases detect deadlocks and abort one transaction. Locking rows in the same order, keeping transactions short, and retrying on deadlock errors are the standard defences.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: A payment for a held seat fails. The cleanup job marks the booking EXPIRED and adds 1 back to seats_left. Two cleanup workers sometimes run at once. What is the safest design?
options: Mark the booking EXPIRED now and add the seat back in a separate job later
Add the seat back first, then mark the booking EXPIRED if the first step succeeds
Run only one cleanup worker and skip transactions to keep it fast
Do both changes in one transaction, and hand the freed seat on with a conditional update so it is given out only once
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: Atomicity matters: doing only one of the two steps would leak or invent a seat. A conditional update means concurrent workers cannot both hand out the same freed seat.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: Your seats_left column must never go below zero, and you add CHECK (seats_left >= 0). Which ACID property does this rule illustrate?
options: Durability: the rule survives a server restart
Isolation: concurrent transactions cannot read the rule
Consistency: declared data rules hold after every commit
Atomicity: the rule applies to all rows or none
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: ACID consistency means the data moves from one valid state to another. The CHECK constraint is also a useful safety net behind a conditional update.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: In an interview you are asked whether the C in ACID is the same as the C in CAP. What is the best answer?
options: Yes: both mean all replicas return the latest committed value
No: ACID's C means data rules hold; CAP's C means all replicas return the latest value
Yes: both mean declared constraints like CHECK hold after every commit
No: ACID's C means durability, while CAP's C means availability
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: Same word, different ideas. ACID consistency is about valid data; CAP consistency is about replicas agreeing on the latest value.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: Booking a seat now spans two services with separate databases: inventory and payments. How should you keep them consistent?
options: Use a saga or reserve-then-confirm: a chain of local transactions with compensating steps, each idempotent
Wrap both databases in one local BEGIN ... COMMIT transaction
Set both databases to serializable so they behave as one
Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in inventory to lock the payment row too
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: A single local transaction cannot span multiple databases or services. Sagas or reserve-then-confirm patterns, with idempotent steps, handle this.

Two people book the last train seat at t.q: The server crashes seconds after three bookings were committed. On restart, they are still there and a half-done transaction is gone. What mechanism makes this possible?
options: MVCC snapshots that readers keep in application memory
Row locks that stay held on disk across restarts
The repeatable read isolation level's snapshot
A write-ahead log: committed work is replayed and uncommitted work is discarded
Two people book the last train seat at t.why: The write-ahead log is written to disk before data pages, which provides atomicity and durability after a crash. MVCC is for isolation, not recovery.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: Your team is starting a new 'order history' feature and the first meeting turns into a SQL vs NoSQL debate. What should you do first?
options: Pick the database the biggest tech companies use for orders
Pick NoSQL, since it is faster than SQL for any modern feature
Pick whichever database has the most flexible schema
List the top access patterns with their rates, latency targets and atomicity needs
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Start from how the feature reads and writes data, its consistency needs and growth. The database falls out of those answers; copying big tech ignores your own constraints.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: Placing an order must decrement stock, create the order and its items, and record the payment intent, all-or-nothing. Support also runs ad hoc queries like 'orders stuck in PACKED for 2 days'. Which store fits?
options: A key-value store like Redis, since order lookups are by order_id
A wide-column store like Cassandra, since order volume is high
A relational database (MySQL or PostgreSQL) with ACID transactions
A document store like MongoDB, since each order is a self-contained record
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Multi-row atomic changes and unplanned ad hoc queries both point to SQL, which is the safe default for money and stock.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: A food-delivery app stores each user's current cart. Every read and write is by user_id, the target is under 5 ms, and prices are rechecked at checkout. Which store fits best?
options: A key-value store such as Redis or DynamoDB
A graph database such as Neo4j
A relational database with a join across cart and product tables
A wide-column store with one partition per product
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Every access is by one exact key, needs very low latency, and needs no joins or multi-record transactions. A lost cart is annoying, not a financial error.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: A marketplace catalogue holds phones, kurtas and pressure cookers, each with completely different attributes. The product page reads one product by product_id. Which store fits best?
options: A key-value store, since documents cannot be read by ID
A document store like MongoDB, with a variable specs object per product
A graph database, since products are related through categories
A wide-column store, since attributes are appended over time
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Self-contained records with varying shape suit a document store. Search and filters still go to a separate search engine fed by CDC.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: Your catalogue is in MongoDB and product wants full-text search with filters like brand, price range and size. What does the answer recommend?
options: Add MongoDB indexes on every attribute, since a document store is a search engine
Feed a separate search engine (Elasticsearch or OpenSearch) from the catalogue via CDC
Move the catalogue into Redis so filters run in memory
Run the filters as SQL joins against a copy in MySQL on each search
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: A document store is not a search engine. CDC or an outbox publishes changes to an idempotent indexer that keeps search in step.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: An activity feed appends hundreds of millions of events per day ('your order shipped', 'price dropped'), and each user reads their latest 50. A one-second delay is fine. Which store fits best?
options: A relational database with a single events table and a join to users
A graph database linking each event to the user who received it
A wide-column store like Cassandra, partitioned by user_id and sorted newest first
A document store holding one ever-growing document per user
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Massive appends read by one key in time order is the wide-column sweet spot: writes spread across the cluster and each user's events sit in one sorted partition.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: Your Cassandra feed table uses PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), event_ts). Product now asks for 'all users who got a price-drop alert for product P123 yesterday'. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Write a second table keyed by product and date alongside the first, or answer it from an analytics store
Run the query on the existing table with a filter on product; Cassandra handles it
Change the existing partition key to product_id so both queries work
Add a join between the feed table and a products table in Cassandra
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: The table is designed for queries by user, so a product query would scan every partition. In NoSQL you design tables around queries and accept duplicated data.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: A 'friends of friends who bought this brand' feature needs 2-3 hop relationship walks. Which store is the natural fit, and what caveat applies?
options: A document store; embedding all friends in each user document avoids every hop
A key-value store; one GET returns friends of friends directly
A relational database; multi-hop self-joins are always faster than a graph
A graph database; at very large scale teams often store edges in key-value or wide-column stores and walk 1-2 hops in code
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Multi-hop walks are natural in a graph and slow self-joins in SQL. At very large scale, many teams precompute or walk a few hops in code instead.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: A colleague claims 'SQL is consistent and NoSQL is inconsistent', so all money must be in SQL and everything in NoSQL is stale. What is the best correction?
options: He is right: NoSQL databases cannot provide strongly consistent reads at all
Consistency depends on how you use the system: a MySQL replica can be stale, and DynamoDB offers transactions
He is right: SQL databases never return stale data, even from replicas
He is wrong: NoSQL is always more consistent because it keeps three replicas
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Consistency is a requirement you state, not a brand property. Ask what a stale read or lost update would break, then use the system accordingly.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: Which feature can most safely accept eventual consistency, where readers may see data a few seconds old?
options: Stock counts during a flash sale
Payment records for completed orders
Seat counts for the last train seats
Like and view counts on product reviews
