SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Money, stock and seat counts need ACID or strongly consistent conditional writes. Likes, view counts and feeds tolerate staleness, which buys availability and scale.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: A team picks MongoDB because 'it's schemaless, so we never need to think about schema'. A year later the same field has five spellings. What was the mistake?
options: Schemaless moves the schema into application code, which still needs validation and versioning
MongoDB should have been sharded earlier to prevent duplicate fields
They should have used Redis, which enforces field names automatically
Document stores cannot store fields with the same meaning across records
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Without validation and versioning in code you get messy data and painful clean-up. PostgreSQL jsonb is another way to get some flexibility inside SQL.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: Your order database (MySQL) is hitting its limits. A teammate wants to migrate straight to Cassandra. What is the best order of steps?
options: Migrate to Cassandra immediately, since NoSQL is always faster at scale
Move all orders to Redis, since memory is faster than disk
Indexes, query fixes, caching and read replicas first; then shard by a key like user_id or use distributed SQL
Add a graph database to offload relationship queries from MySQL
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Cheap steps come first. Moving to NoSQL means redesigning around queries, so do it only if the access pattern fits; 'SQL doesn't scale' is a misconception.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: A team proposes adding a graph database, a time-series database and a new document store in one quarter. Which costs should you ask them to weigh?
options: Only licence fees, since operational effort is the same for every engine
Backups, upgrades, monitoring and on-call skills per engine; sync lag and drift; and no cross-store transactions
Only query speed, since data sync between stores is instantaneous with CDC
Only storage size, since each new engine halves the load on the others
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Polyglot persistence lets each feature use the right tool, but every extra engine adds operations, skills and data-sync work. Keep one relational system of record and add stores only with a clear trigger.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: In the worked example's cost review, the team had planned five engines. What did they decide about the friend graph?
options: Adopt Neo4j immediately, since friend graphs always need a graph store
Store the graph in Redis, since carts already use Redis
Drop the feature, since no existing store can hold relationships
Start with a friendships table in MySQL, launch without a graph database, and record the trigger for adopting one
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Use the fewest kinds of database you can. The cart reused existing Redis, and the graph could start in MySQL until a clear trigger justifies a new engine.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: A teammate says 'NoSQL is faster than SQL'. What is the most accurate response?
options: Only for the access pattern it was designed for; off-pattern queries can be slow
True for every query, since NoSQL never uses disk
False; SQL is always faster because it uses indexes
True, but only for databases smaller than 1 GB
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: A MySQL primary-key lookup takes about a millisecond, while an off-pattern query in Cassandra may need a full scan.

SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.q: Which store is described as fast at 'get or set by exact key, sub-millisecond' but weak at 'any query not by key'?
options: Document
Wide-column
Key-value
Graph
SQL or NoSQL: how do you actually choose.why: Key-value stores like Redis map a key to a blob. They are extremely fast for exact-key access and poor for anything else.

What are database replication and shardi.q: Your primary database is at 95% CPU and almost all of its load is INSERT and UPDATE. Read replicas sit at 20%. Will adding two more replicas help?
options: Yes: each new replica takes a share of the writes off the primary
Yes: replicas batch writes together before sending them to the primary
No: replicas only serve reads and each one still replays every write
No: replicas only help once the data is sharded across them
What are database replication and shardi.why: Replication scales reads and gives failover, not write capacity. You need to reduce or spread writes: batching, a bigger primary, or eventually sharding.

What are database replication and shardi.q: A user updates their phone number and the profile page immediately shows the old number. What is the most likely cause?
options: The write failed on the primary and was silently rolled back
The shard key changed, so the profile moved to a different shard
The primary served a dirty read of uncommitted data
The read went to a replica that had not yet applied the write (replication lag)
What are database replication and shardi.why: With async replication, replicas can be milliseconds to seconds behind. This is the classic read-your-own-writes problem.

What are database replication and shardi.q: How do you best fix the read-your-own-writes problem for a profile page?
options: Send all reads for all users to the primary permanently
Route that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after they write
Add more replicas so at least one is always up to date
Switch the replicas to serve writes as well as reads
What are database replication and shardi.why: Reading recent writers from the primary, or from a replica caught up to their write position, fixes it without losing the read scaling for everyone else.

What are database replication and shardi.q: Someone accidentally runs DELETE FROM orders on the primary. You have three replicas. What is the situation?
options: The replicas delete the rows too within milliseconds, so you need real backups and point-in-time recovery
The replicas still hold the deleted rows, so you can restore from any of them
The replicas reject the delete because it touches too many rows
Only synchronous replicas copy the delete; async replicas keep the data
What are database replication and shardi.why: Replication copies every change, including mistakes. Replicas are not backups.

What are database replication and shardi.q: With asynchronous replication, the primary crashes and a replica is promoted. What can happen to the last few writes?
options: They are always safe, because async replicas receive writes before the primary
They are replayed from the replica's own write-ahead log automatically
They may be lost, because the primary confirmed them before replicas received them
They are rejected later, causing a deadlock on the new primary
What are database replication and shardi.why: Async replication is fast but can lose the most recent writes on failover. Semi-sync reduces this at the cost of write latency, and idempotent client retries help recover.

What are database replication and shardi.q: Your payments team wants to be sure a confirmed write survives the primary dying, and accepts slower writes. Which replication mode fits?
options: Asynchronous, where the primary confirms before any replica has the write
No replication; a single bigger machine never loses writes
Sharding, since splitting data guarantees no write is ever lost
Synchronous or semi-synchronous, where the primary waits for at least one replica to confirm
What are database replication and shardi.why: Sync or semi-sync makes each write slower but safer on failover. Most systems choose async or semi-sync depending on context.

What are database replication and shardi.q: You are choosing a shard key for an orders database in India. Which is usually the best choice?
options: city: it has many values and city reports become single-shard queries
user_id: it spreads evenly and 'My orders', cancellations and returns hit one shard
order_id: it spreads evenly and 'My orders' becomes a single-shard query
created_at: it spreads evenly and date reports become single-shard queries
What are database replication and shardi.why: A good key spreads load, matches the main queries, and never changes. City creates hot shards for metros; order_id spreads well but scatters a user's history.

What are database replication and shardi.q: Why is city a poor shard key for an orders table in India?
options: Bengaluru, Delhi and Mumbai would be hot shards, and a user's history could span shards
City has too few distinct values to split across any number of shards
City names change too often, forcing rows to move between shards daily
City cannot be hashed, so it only works with range sharding
What are database replication and shardi.why: Many values is not enough; the key must also spread load evenly and match the main queries. City has severe skew.

What are database replication and shardi.q: You use range sharding by user_id: users 1-10 million on shard 1, 10-20 million on shard 2, and so on. What problem will you see?
options: All new users land on the latest shard, making it hot
Range scans become impossible across the shards
Every query must ask all shards, even for one user
Rows move between shards whenever a user places an order
What are database replication and shardi.why: Range sharding makes scans easy but sends new, active keys to the newest range. Hash sharding spreads keys evenly but scatters range queries.

What are database replication and shardi.q: You hash-sharded orders by user_id, but a single mega-seller's flash sale is overwhelming one shard. A teammate says hash sharding should have prevented this. What is the best response?
options: Correct: the hash function is broken and needs replacing with a stronger one
Correct: switching to range sharding would spread the seller's orders evenly
Add read replicas to the hot shard, since they will absorb the extra writes
Hashing spreads different keys evenly but one very hot key still lands on one shard; split that key, cache or queue writes
What are database replication and shardi.why: Hash sharding removes skew between keys, not within one key. Hot keys need targeted fixes like further splitting, caching or queueing.

What are database replication and shardi.q: You sharded with hash(user_id) % 4 and now need 8 servers. Why is this painful, and what would have made it easier?
options: Only new rows need to move, but the hash function must be replaced by a range map
No rows move, but every query must now ask all 8 servers until the next restart
About half the rows must move; starting with many virtual shards (e.g. 1,024 buckets) lets you move whole buckets via a routing map
All rows must move; nothing can help except taking a full maintenance downtime
What are database replication and shardi.why: Changing the modulus remaps about half the keys. Virtual shards (or consistent hashing) mean you only move some buckets, one at a time, with no customer-visible downtime.

What are database replication and shardi.q: Orders are sharded by user_id. Seller dashboards need 'all orders for seller S' on the hot path. What does the answer recommend?
options: Scatter-gather across every shard for each dashboard page load
Publish order events to a stream and build a separate seller-orders store keyed by seller
Re-shard the orders database by seller_id instead of user_id
Join orders and sellers across shards inside the routing layer
What are database replication and shardi.why: Cross-shard queries are the main pain of sharding. A separately keyed store built from events serves the hot path, with seconds of delay acceptable; scatter-gather is for rare queries.

What are database replication and shardi.q: Customer care looks up orders by order ID, but orders are sharded by user_id. How did the worked example route these lookups directly?
options: Customer care queries every shard in parallel for each lookup
Order IDs are sharded separately by order_id range
The order ID encodes the virtual shard number
A nightly batch copies all orders to a single lookup database
What are database replication and shardi.why: Embedding the virtual shard number in the order ID lets the routing layer go straight to the right shard without scatter-gather.

What are database replication and shardi.q: In Year 1, the orders database handles 300 QPS at 15% CPU on one 8-core server. A new engineer wants to shard now to be safe. What is the best response?
options: Shard immediately, since it is far cheaper to shard early than later
Shard by city now so regional growth is handled automatically
Add four read replicas now to scale the future write load
Don't shard yet: it adds permanent complexity; scale up, index, cache and replicate first, but design a clean key like user_id
What are database replication and shardi.why: Shard when measurements, not fear, say so. Designing a clean key early is cheap; actually splitting is not.

What are database replication and shardi.q: Tracking pages push CPU to 85% in the evening and 90% of queries are reads. Which order of fixes matches the worked example?
options: Shard immediately by user_id, then add indexes if CPU is still high
Add the missing index, cache tracking status in Redis, upgrade the machine, and add read replicas
Switch to synchronous replication so reads complete faster
Move orders to a document store, then add a cache in front
What are database replication and shardi.why: Cheap fixes come first: one missing index can cost 10x. Then caching, vertical scaling, and replicas for read load and failover.

What are database replication and shardi.q: Which problem does sharding solve that replication does not?
options: Too much data and too many writes for one machine
Too many reads for one machine
The primary machine dying
Users reading their own writes immediately
What are database replication and shardi.why: Sharding splits data so each server holds and writes only part of it. Replication keeps full copies, scaling reads and giving failover.

What are database replication and shardi.q: Your data is heading past a few TB and backups take hours, though write QPS is fine. What does the symptom table suggest first?
options: Add more read replicas to share the storage
Switch to synchronous replication to speed up backups
Add indexes to compress the data on disk
Archive old data, then shard if it is still needed
What are database replication and shardi.why: Replicas hold everything, so they don't reduce data size. Archiving comes first; sharding follows if size keeps growing.

What are database replication and shardi.q: How does a replica stay in step with the primary in MySQL or PostgreSQL?
options: It streams the primary's change log (binlog or WAL) and replays it
It re-runs every read query that the primary served
It copies the full database from the primary every few seconds
It receives writes directly from the app at the same time as the primary
What are database replication and shardi.why: The primary records every change in a log, and replicas replay that log to reach the same data, usually with some lag.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: A reseller's support tool loads page 5,000 of their orders with LIMIT 20 OFFSET 99980, and it takes 2 seconds while page 1 is instant. Why?
options: Page 5,000 returns 5,000 times more rows than page 1
Deep pages are always read from disk while page 1 is always cached
OFFSET forces the database to rebuild the index for that user
The database walks and throws away all 99,980 earlier rows before returning 20
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: OFFSET means 'skip N rows', and there is no shortcut to a position. The work grows in direct proportion to the page number.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: A query uses LIMIT 20 OFFSET 200000 on a column that already has a B-tree index. A teammate suggests adding another index to fix the slowness. What is the best response?
options: Correct: a second index on the same column halves the number of rows skipped
Correct: a covering index lets the database jump straight to row 200,001
An index finds values fast, not positions; the database still walks 200,000 entries, so switch to keyset pagination
Rebuild the existing index, since deep offsets mean it is fragmented
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: 'Adding an index fixes slow OFFSET' is a misconception. Only a seek on values (keyset) avoids walking the skipped entries.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: A user loads page 1 of a feed with offset pagination, then 3 new posts are added at the top before they load page 2. What do they see?
options: Page 2 skips 3 posts that the user never sees
The last 3 posts of page 1 appear again at the start of page 2
Page 2 shows the 3 new posts first, then continues normally
Page 2 is identical to page 1
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: Offset counts positions, and every item moved down 3 places. With a cursor, page 2 starts after the last seen post, so nothing repeats.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: A customer is scrolling 'My Orders' with offset pagination when one of the orders on page 1 is archived and hidden. What happens on page 2?
options: Everything shifts up one place, so one order is never shown
The archived order appears again on page 2 as a duplicate
Page 2 shows an empty slot where the archived order was
Nothing changes, because deletes do not affect OFFSET
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: A delete moves later items up one position, so OFFSET 20 starts one item later and one order silently vanishes. This led to 'my order is missing' tickets in the worked example.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: Which query correctly fetches the next page of a user's orders after the last seen row (2026-10-14 10:42:07, id 88123), newest first?
options: WHERE user_id = 42 AND (created_at, id) > ('2026-10-14 10:42:07', 88123) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20
WHERE user_id = 42 AND created_at < '2026-10-14 10:42:07' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20
WHERE user_id = 42 AND (created_at, id) < ('2026-10-14 10:42:07', 88123) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20
WHERE user_id = 42 AND id <> 88123 ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: Keyset pagination asks for rows after the last one seen in sort order. For a descending sort that means 'less than' the last (created_at, id).

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: Your keyset query sorts and compares only on created_at. Many orders share the same timestamp to the second. What can go wrong at page edges, and what is the fix?
options: Nothing; keyset pagination is immune to duplicate sort values
The query fails with an error; store timestamps with milliseconds instead
Pages return fewer than 20 rows; increase LIMIT to compensate
Rows with equal timestamps can be skipped or repeated; add the unique id as a tie-breaker
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: Without a unique tie-breaker, the sort is not total, so rows sharing the boundary timestamp may be lost or shown twice. Adding id makes every row's position unique.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: You switched 'My Orders' to keyset pagination, but EXPLAIN shows the database still sorts all of a user's orders on each page. What is the most likely cause?
options: The index does not match the filter plus sort, e.g. it should be (user_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)
Keyset pagination always needs a full sort; only OFFSET avoids it
The cursor token is not signed with an HMAC
The page size is too small for the optimizer to use an index
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: The WHERE filter plus ORDER BY columns, in the same order and direction, must be an index prefix. Otherwise the database sorts everything first and loses the benefit.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: A teammate hears 'cursor pagination' and worries it will hold open a database cursor per user session. What is the correct explanation?
options: Correct: each user holds a server-side database cursor until they stop scrolling
API cursor pagination is stateless: the cursor is just the last row's sort values, sent back by the client
Correct, but the cursor is closed automatically after each page
The cursor is a row number stored in a server-side cache for each user

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: You are designing the orders API response. Why return next_cursor as an opaque, signed token rather than raw created_at and id fields?
options: You can change the sort or storage later without breaking clients, and signing prevents tampering
Opaque tokens make each query run faster on the database
Raw values cannot be compared in SQL, but Base64 strings can
Signed tokens let clients jump directly to any page number
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: Inside, the token is just the sort values Base64-encoded. Keeping it opaque decouples clients from internals, and an HMAC stops them editing it.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: How does the API know whether to return has_more: true without a separate COUNT query?
options: Run COUNT(*) on every request and compare it to the page size
Fetch 21 rows and return 20; a 21st row means another page exists
Return has_more: true always and let the client stop on an empty page
Store the total for each user in the cursor token
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: Fetching limit+1 is a cheap way to detect another page without paying for a total count.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: Product wants 'Page 3 of 612' on the new cursor-based order list. What is the best proposal?
options: Run COUNT(*) on every page load, since counts are cheap with an index
Encode the total count inside every cursor token
Switch back to OFFSET for all pages so the total is free
Drop the exact total: show '1,000+', cache the count, or keep a counter updated on writes
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: COUNT(*) over 100,000 rows still walks 100,000 index entries on every request. Users rarely need an exact total.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: Product wants a 'jump to page 400' box on an infinite-scroll order list. What do you propose?
options: Use keyset pagination and compute page 400's cursor by walking 399 pages server-side
Use OFFSET for every page and add an index on created_at to make it fast
A filter that sets a starting value, like 'orders from March 2024', or offset for the first few pages with a depth cap
Store a precomputed cursor for every page of every user

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: An internal script exports a reseller's 120,000 orders 20 at a time. Using OFFSET it did about 360 million row reads. Roughly how many does keyset pagination need?
options: About 60 million, since keyset halves the average rows walked per page
About 360 million, since keyset only fixes duplicates, not cost
About 6,000, since keyset reads one row per page
About 120,000 row reads, since each of the 6,000 pages reads about 20 entries
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: With keyset every page costs the same (about 20 entries), so 6,000 requests read about 120,000 rows, roughly 3,000 times less work.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: Your marketplace lets users sort a category by price, and prices can change while people browse. Which keyset design and caveat match the answer?
options: Use price alone with an index on price; cursors make the list a perfect snapshot
Use (price, id) with an index on (category_id, price, id); items whose price changes may move, so accept it or use a snapshot of IDs
Use OFFSET only, since keyset cannot sort by any column except time
Use id alone and sort prices in the app after fetching each page
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: Keyset needs a unique, indexed sort key. Cursors fix shifts from inserts and deletes, but a row whose sort value changes can still cross your cursor.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: How do you support a 'previous page' button with keyset pagination?
options: Flip the comparison and sort direction, take 20, reverse them, and return both next_cursor and prev_cursor
Subtract 20 from the OFFSET stored in the cursor
Re-run the first page query and walk forward to the previous cursor
It is impossible; keyset pagination only supports going forward
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: Use '>' with ORDER BY ... ASC from the first row of the current page, then reverse the results so they display newest first.

Why does page 1 of your order history lo.q: An internal admin page lists the 200 sellers in one small region, rarely changes, and needs page numbers. Which approach is reasonable?
options: Keyset is mandatory, since offset is always bad
Load all rows into the browser and paginate with a cursor
Offset pagination is fine for a small, stable list
Use a signed cursor token per page to prevent tampering
Why does page 1 of your order history lo.why: 'Offset is always bad' is a misconception. The problem is deep pages on large or changing data.

OLTP: data minutes behind; OLAP: always live data

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: During a sale, the link between your two data centres drops for 90 seconds. A user on the minority side tries to pay ₹2,000 from a wallet backed by a Raft store (2 replicas in DC-1, 1 in DC-2). What should happen for that user?
options: The payment is accepted locally and reconciled with DC-1 after the link heals
The payment is accepted if the local replica shows enough balance right now
The wallet service stops in both data centres until the partition is over
The payment is refused with a retryable error until the link heals
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: Money is a CP decision: the side without a quorum refuses so the same rupees cannot be spent twice. Accepting locally and reconciling later is the AP choice that allows double spending, and the majority side (DC-1) keeps working normally.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: A teammate says: 'Our network is very reliable, so we chose CA for our replicated order store.' What is the best response?
options: Replicated systems can't opt out of partitions; 'CA' just leaves the split unplanned
CA is fine as long as all replicas sit in one cloud region, where splits can't occur
CA is right for orders, because orders need both consistency and high availability
CA is valid if you also add a cache, since the cache keeps answering during splits
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: P is not optional for a replicated system: switches fail, zones lose connectivity, nodes pause. 'CA' only really describes a single machine; declaring it for replicas means the system will fail in an accidental way when the network does split.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: In the CAP theorem, what does the 'C' precisely mean?
options: The ACID rule that the database enforces constraints like 'balance >= 0'
All replicas eventually converge to the same value once writes stop
Linearizability: every read sees the latest write, as if there were one copy
Every request to a working node gets a correct, non-error answer quickly
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: CAP's C is linearizability, about replicas agreeing on one order of operations. ACID's C is about enforcing rules like constraints, a different idea that only shares the letter.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: A phone deal has 50 units and data is replicated across two data centres. The link between them breaks. If both sides keep reserving stock independently, what is the most likely outcome?
options: Each side may sell up to 50, giving about 100 orders for 50 phones
Both sides sell normally and the counts are summed on heal, so nothing is lost
Last-writer-wins picks the correct stock count, so overselling is prevented
Each side automatically limits itself to 25 units during the partition
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: Scarce stock cannot be merged away: two independent sides can each sell the full 50, leading to cancellations. That is why the reserve step goes through the single owner of the SKU count on the majority side (CP). Adding counts works for likes, not for limited inventory.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: Your like counter shows 1,240 in DC-1 and 1,236 in DC-2 during a 90-second partition. Which design lets both sides keep counting and still end up correct when the link heals?
options: Use last-writer-wins on the total so the newest count overwrites the older
Reject likes on the minority side so only one data centre's count changes
Freeze both counters until the partition ends, then let users like again
Keep a per-replica count and sum them on merge (a CRDT counter)
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: A per-replica counter that is summed (a CRDT) can always be merged without losing anyone's like. Last-writer-wins on a single total would silently drop the other side's increments.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: With N = 3 replicas, W = 2 and R = 2, a partition leaves one replica alone on one side. What does that isolated side do?
options: It serves reads and writes from its one replica, then syncs later
It serves reads but refuses writes, since reads need only one replica
It promotes itself to leader, since the other two look failed to it
It cannot gather 2 replicas, so it must refuse or wait
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: R + W > N makes read and write sets overlap, but a side with one replica cannot reach a quorum of 2, so it refuses. That is the CP lean, while the 2-replica side keeps working.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: There is no outage at all, yet wallet writes take 60 ms longer than likes because each write waits for a replica in Singapore. Which idea best explains this?
options: CAP: the system has chosen consistency over availability for wallets
Replication lag: the Singapore replica is behind and writes must wait
PACELC: with no partition, you still trade latency against consistency
Partition tolerance: the system is preparing for a possible split
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: PACELC's 'Else' part says that in normal operation keeping replicas in sync costs latency. CAP only describes the moment of a partition, so it does not explain everyday slowness.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: Someone says 'Cassandra is AP, so we can never get strong reads from it.' What is the most accurate correction?
options: Cassandra is actually CP, because it runs Paxos on every write by default
It is tunable per query: ONE leans AP, QUORUM on reads and writes leans CP
Cassandra can only be strong on a single node, which then makes it CA
Cassandra is strong only if replication between data centres is turned off
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: Most modern stores let you choose consistency per query. 'Cassandra is AP' describes its low-quorum defaults, not a fixed law.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: A team fears that choosing CP for wallets means the entire wallet service goes down in every partition. What is the best reply?
options: They are right, so make wallets AP and let support fix any overdrafts later
Usually only the minority side refuses; the majority side keeps serving
They are right, but only reads are affected, since writes are always queued
CP never refuses requests; it only adds latency during a partition
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: In a CP system the side holding a majority continues normally. Good design also narrows CP to the few operations that need it (the debit or reserve step) and returns clear retryable errors.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: A review posted in DC-2 shows up in DC-1 about 90 seconds later. The author refreshes and does not see their own review, and complains. What is the targeted fix?
options: Make reviews CP so nobody sees a review until every replica has it
Read-your-own-writes: serve the author from the replica they wrote to
Use last-writer-wins so the newest review version is always shown
Add more replicas so the review spreads to DC-1 more quickly
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: Reviews are fine to be eventually consistent for others. The only real pain is the author not seeing their own write, which read-your-own-writes fixes without paying strong-consistency cost for everyone.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: Why does an AP store work well for a shopping cart but badly for 'only 1 unit left'?
options: Carts merge safely by union; two sides selling the last unit cannot
Carts live on one node only, while stock is replicated to many nodes
Carts change rarely so conflicts are rare, while stock changes constantly
AP stores can hold sets but not numbers, so stock counts aren't supported
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: AP needs a conflict-resolution plan. Cart contents merge naturally by union; two independent sales of the last unit become an order you cannot fulfil.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: In a design review you must decide CP vs AP for many kinds of data. What question should you ask for each piece?
options: What does a stale or conflicting value of this data cost us?
Which database does the rest of the company already use for it?
How many reads per second does this data get compared with writes?
Is this data stored in more than one region, or in only one?
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: The answer recommends deciding per piece of data based on the harm of a stale or conflicting value: money and scarce stock lean CP, likes and views lean AP. Read/write ratio matters for scaling, not for this choice.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: Your CP payment path returns errors for the minority side during a partition, and users retry several times. What else is needed so retries don't double-charge anyone?
options: Switch payments to AP during partitions so retries are never needed
Use last-writer-wins on the balance so duplicate debits overwrite
Idempotency keys, so a repeated payment request is applied only once
Put a cache in front of the wallet so retries are answered from it
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: The answer pairs retryable CP errors with idempotency keys so a retry cannot apply the same debit twice. Last-writer-wins would hide conflicts rather than prevent double charges.

What does the CAP theorem really say, in.q: What is the main weakness of last-writer-wins as a conflict-resolution rule in an AP system?
options: It needs a quorum of replicas to agree, so it fails during a partition
It silently drops one write, and drifting clocks can pick the wrong one
It keeps every conflicting version forever, so storage keeps growing
It only works for counters, not for other data such as user profiles
What does the CAP theorem really say, in.why: LWW is simple but loses data: one write is discarded, and timestamps from drifting clocks may not reflect the real order. CRDTs or app-level merges avoid that loss.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: Sethu updates his pincode, the app says 'saved', he refreshes and sees the old pincode. The write went to the primary. What most likely happened?
options: The write was lost because the primary replied before saving it
Optimistic UI rolled the change back because the server rejected it
The load balancer sent her write to a replica that ignores writes
Her refresh hit a read replica that had not yet applied the change
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: With asynchronous replication the primary says 'saved' before followers copy the change (replication lag). A read landing on a lagging replica returns the old value; the data is late, not lost.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: A user edits their profile name, refreshes and sees the new name, refreshes again and sees the old name. Which guarantee is broken?
options: Read-your-own-writes: the write never reached the primary
Eventual consistency: the replicas will never agree on it
Quorum overlap: R + W was not greater than N for this read
Monotonic reads: the data appeared to go back in time
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: The two refreshes hit different replicas, one caught up and one lagging. Monotonic reads means once you see a version you never see an older one; fixes are pinning the user to one replica or carrying the highest version seen.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: Your app writes an address and gets back log position 88,412. On the next read, the chosen replica is at 88,390. With version-token routing, what should the service do?
options: Serve from the replica, since 22 changes is normal lag
Wait briefly or forward the read to the primary
Return an error and ask the user to refresh later
Push the address to the replica, then answer from it
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: A version token says 'give me data at version 88,412 or newer'. A replica behind that must wait or hand the read to the primary, so the user always sees their own write.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: Why is version-token routing usually better than 'always read from the primary for 30 seconds after a write'?
options: It checks the replica's real position, so it uses the primary only when needed
It removes replication lag entirely by making replication synchronous
It sends all of that user's reads to the primary, the freshest copy
It works without storing anything in the session or on the server
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: A fixed window guesses at lag: it fails if lag exceeds 30 seconds and sends needless traffic to the primary when replicas are already fine. The token checks the actual replica position.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: A team pins every user to one read replica by hashing user ID, but writes still go to the primary. Users still sometimes don't see their own edits. Why?
options: Hashing user IDs spreads one user across many replicas, so pinning does nothing
Pinned replicas stop receiving changes from the primary until the session ends
Pinning stops going back in time, but a lagging pinned replica still lacks the write
Pinning only works with synchronous replication, which they have not enabled
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: Stickiness gives monotonic reads but not freshness. It must be paired with primary-after-write or version tokens for read-your-own-writes.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: With N = 5 replicas and W = 3, what is the smallest R that guarantees a read overlaps the latest completed write?
options: R = 3, because R + W must be greater than 5
R = 2, because 2 + 3 equals N, which is enough
R = 1, because three replicas already hold it
R = 5, because a safe read must ask every replica
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: Overlap needs R + W > N. With R = 2 the sum is exactly 5, so read and write sets could miss each other; R = 3 gives 6 > 5.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: Which N = 3 setting gives fast reads but makes writes fail whenever any one node is down?
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: W = 3 needs every replica to confirm a write, so one dead node blocks writes, while R = 1 keeps reads fast. W = 2, R = 2 survives one node down.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: In a flash sale, the product page reads stock from a replica and shows '5 left', while the true count is 3. What is the right design stance?
options: Read the product page from the primary too, so the shown count is always exact
Hide the stock count entirely during sales, since replicas cannot be trusted
Use optimistic UI on the order button so the purchase feels instant to users
Showing stale stock is fine; the order step decrements conditionally on the primary
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: 'Show stale, decide fresh': the display can lag, but the final decrement uses something like UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty > 0 on the primary, so the last unit is never sold twice.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: A developer proposes reading everything from the primary so no one ever sees stale data. What is the main problem?
options: Primaries can only serve writes, not reads, in most databases
Reading from the primary breaks monotonic reads for most users
Replicas sit idle and the primary becomes the read bottleneck
Writes slow down because replication is forced to be synchronous
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: Reads outnumber writes by hundreds to one; replicas exist to serve them. Use the primary only where freshness matters: the writer's own recent data and money or stock decisions.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: Your app shows 'Payment successful' instantly using optimistic UI, before the server responds. Why is this a bad idea?
options: Optimistic UI cannot roll back once shown, so errors are never displayed
A false 'success' on a payment is harmful; it is only for low-risk actions
Optimistic UI only works for reads, not for writes such as payments
It makes the payment write go to a lagging replica, not the primary
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: Optimistic UI makes the screen look consistent, not the data. For likes or cart quantity a rollback is fine; telling someone a payment succeeded when it might fail is not.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: Which statement best describes eventual consistency?
options: All copies are guaranteed to agree within one second of any write
Every read returns the most recent completed write on any replica
If writes stop, all copies eventually agree, with no promise of when
Replicas may disagree permanently unless an operator steps in
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: The definition only promises convergence once writes stop; it gives no time bound. Lag is usually milliseconds but can be minutes under load, so measure it.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: A user saves a new address on their phone, then opens the app on their laptop and sees the old one. The phone app stores a version token in its local session. What would fix the laptop case?
options: Keep the user's last write version server-side, keyed by user ID
Store the version token in a longer-lived cookie on the phone
Pin the laptop to the same read replica the phone was using
Extend the phone's read-from-primary window to five minutes
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: A token held on one device doesn't help another. Keeping the last write version server-side (for example in a cache keyed by user ID), or reading the user's own data from the primary, makes read-your-own-writes work across devices.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: Someone claims R + W > N makes a Cassandra-style store fully strongly consistent. What is the most accurate response?
options: It helps a lot, but failures, retries and timestamp ties can still break it
It is correct; quorum overlap gives exactly the same guarantee as Raft
It is wrong; R + W > N gives no benefit at all over W = 1, R = 1
It is correct, but only when N is an odd number such as 3 or 5
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: Quorum overlap means you normally see the latest completed write, but half-failed writes, timestamp ties and sloppy quorums break it. True single-copy behaviour needs a consensus protocol like Raft or Paxos.

You update your address, refresh, and th.q: Why do most databases replicate asynchronously by default?
options: Asynchronous replication removes replication lag between primary and replicas
The primary can confirm a write without waiting for followers, keeping writes fast
Synchronous replication is not supported by any of the mainstream databases
Asynchronous replication guarantees read-your-own-writes for every single user
You update your address, refresh, and th.why: Async means the primary doesn't wait for followers, which keeps writes fast at the cost of lag. Synchronous replication removes lag but slows every write.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: Your order service runs 300 pods writing to 64 database shards, and each shard uses AUTO_INCREMENT for order IDs. What goes wrong?
options: Auto-increment IDs turn random, so they no longer sort by time
Each shard quickly runs out of IDs because counters are 32-bit
The shards coordinate their counters, making every insert slow
Each shard's counter starts at 1, so shards produce the same IDs
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: Per-shard counters are independent, so shard 1 and shard 2 both create order 1. A single shared counter avoids that but becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: Your team switched order primary keys from auto-increment to UUID v4 and inserts slowed down noticeably. What is the most likely cause?
options: UUID v4 values often collide, so the database retries many inserts
Each UUID v4 needs a network call to a central ID-issuing service
Random keys scatter inserts across the B-tree, causing page splits
UUID v4 keys sort by time, so every insert fights for one page
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: Collisions are negligible; the costs are random insert positions (page splits, poor caching) and 16-byte keys that enlarge every index. A time-ordered ID (UUID v7, ULID or Snowflake) inserts near the end of the B-tree.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: You want IDs generated without any coordination but still inserting cheaply into a B-tree index. Which choice fits best?
options: UUID v4, because 122 random bits make collisions effectively impossible
A central counter service, since it hands out strictly sequential numbers
Snowflake with the same machine ID on every pod to keep config simple
UUID v7 or ULID: a millisecond timestamp first, then random bits
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: Time-first IDs sort by creation time, so new rows go near the end of the index, and the random bits keep servers apart without coordination. UUID v4 needs no coordination but scatters inserts.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: In the standard Snowflake layout, how many bits go to time, machine ID and sequence?
options: 32 bits of time, 16 bits of machine ID, 16 bits of sequence
41 bits of time, 10 bits of machine ID, 12 bits of sequence
48 bits of time, 8 bits of machine ID, 8 bits of sequence
41 bits of time, 12 bits of machine ID, 10 bits of sequence
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: Snowflake uses 1 sign bit plus 41 bits of milliseconds (about 69.7 years), 10 machine bits (1,024 machines) and 12 sequence bits (4,096 IDs per ms per machine).

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: A Snowflake generator on one pod needs a 4,097th ID within the same millisecond. What does it do?
options: Borrows a sequence number from another machine ID for that ms
Wraps the sequence back to 0 in the same millisecond and goes on
Waits for the next millisecond and resets the sequence to 0
Switches to a UUID v4 for any overflow IDs in that millisecond
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: 12 sequence bits allow 4,096 IDs per ms. Wrapping to 0 in the same millisecond would repeat an ID, so the generator spins until the clock moves on.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: Two pods accidentally start with the same Snowflake machine ID. What is the risk and the best protection?
options: No risk, since their clocks differ by a few ms and keep the IDs apart
Only ordering suffers; enable NTP slewing so the two clocks line up
Silent duplicates; lease machine IDs from etcd, add a unique constraint
None needed, as the generator detects the clash at start-up and exits
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: The machine bits are what separate servers; with equal machine IDs and the same time and sequence, IDs repeat. Leased assignments prevent it and a unique constraint catches any slip.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: At 00:07, NTP steps one pod's clock back by 30 ms. What should a well-written Snowflake generator do?
options: See now < lastMs and wait until the clock passes it
Carry on, since the machine ID alone keeps IDs unique
Reset the sequence to 0 and reuse the earlier timestamps
Pick a new random machine ID until the clock catches up
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: Reusing past timestamps with the same machine ID and a reset sequence can repeat an ID. Small backward jumps are handled by waiting; large ones by refusing and alerting, with NTP configured to slew.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: Across different servers, a clock that is 20 ms ahead affects Snowflake IDs how?
options: It causes duplicates with servers that reach that time 20 ms later
Only ordering: its IDs look newer, but machine IDs keep them unique
It has no effect at all, because Snowflake ignores wall-clock time
It makes the sequence counter overflow early on the faster server
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: Across machines, the machine bits guarantee uniqueness; skew only makes cross-machine order approximate. Snowflake IDs strictly increase only within one machine.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: Customer order URLs look like /orders/10452 today and /orders/10987 tomorrow. What two problems does this create?
options: IDs collide across shards, and URLs are too long for SMS
IDs sort badly in indexes and can't be idempotency keys
IDs reveal the buyer's city and expire after a fixed time
Rivals can estimate volume, and users can try nearby IDs
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: Sequential public IDs leak volume (the German tank problem) and invite enumeration, which becomes an IDOR breach if an ownership check is missing.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: You replace public order IDs with random tokens like OD-7KX29QPM4R. A teammate suggests removing the ownership check on /orders/{id} since IDs are now unguessable. Your response?
options: Agree, because random tokens can't be guessed, so orders are private
Keep the check; unguessable IDs reduce risk but aren't access control
Agree, but only if the token is at least 20 characters in length
Disagree, and go back to sequential IDs so logs are easier to read
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: IDs leak through links, logs and screenshots. Every request must still verify the logged-in user owns the order.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: With block allocation, each server takes 1,000 IDs from a central table. One server restarts halfway through its block. What happens?
options: The central table reissues the unused IDs to another server
The rest of its block is skipped, leaving a harmless gap
The server must reuse its old block after restart to avoid gaps
All servers pause until the central table is reconciled
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: Unused IDs from a block are simply abandoned. IDs stay unique and mostly increasing; gaps are expected. If you truly need gap-free numbers (like legal invoice numbers), use a separate serialized sequence.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: Why is it useful that a Snowflake order ID exists before the database insert?
options: It can go into the payment request and serve as the idempotency key
It lets the database skip the unique constraint check on insert
It means the order can go to any shard without a routing rule
It guarantees the order commits, so no transaction is needed
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: With auto-increment you only learn the ID after inserting. A pre-generated ID can be sent to payment and used to deduplicate retries.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: Roughly how many UUID v4s would you need to generate for a 50% chance of a single collision?
options: About 2.7 x 10^18 (a billion per second for 85 years)
About 1 billion, because of the birthday paradox
About 5.3 x 10^36, the total number of possible values
About 4 million, the same as Snowflake's per-second limit
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: The birthday paradox makes odds grow with the square of the count, but even so a 50% chance needs about 2.7 x 10^18 IDs. With 1 billion the chance is around 10^-19.

How do hundreds of servers each create o.q: What does Snowflake's 41-bit timestamp give you if you choose a custom epoch of 1 Jan 2025?
options: About 69.7 years of millisecond timestamps
About 41 years of second-level timestamps
About 136 years of millisecond timestamps
Exactly 1,024 days before a reset is needed
How do hundreds of servers each create o.why: 2^41 milliseconds is about 69.7 years, counted from the epoch you choose, which is why a recent custom epoch is used.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: A database replies 'committed' for an order and the power fails 2 ms later, before any data page is written. What happens on restart?
options: The order is lost, since the table file on disk never contained it
The order survives only if a checkpoint ran in those 2 milliseconds
The order is half-saved and must be repaired from the replica by hand
The order survives: its fsynced WAL records are redone on restart
If the power goes off right after a data.why: 'Saved' means the log is on disk, not the table file. Recovery reads the WAL from the last checkpoint and redoes committed changes that were only in memory.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: Your code calls write() on a log file and immediately tells the user 'saved'. Why is this not durable?
options: write() goes to disk, but the disk may reorder the sectors later
write() may only reach the OS cache; fsync forces it to the device
write() is durable, but recovery will not read that file back
write() is durable only for files smaller than one 8 KB page
If the power goes off right after a data.why: A normal write lands in the operating system's page cache, which vanishes on power loss. fsync waits until the device has it, and the disk must honour fsync.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: Saving one order touches about six pages across tables and indexes. Why do databases log the change first instead of writing those pages before replying?
options: One sequential log append is fast and all-or-nothing
The log is kept in memory, so it never touches disk
Data pages cannot be written while a transaction is open
Writing pages directly is durable but uses more memory
If the power goes off right after a data.why: Scattered random page writes are slow, and a crash halfway would leave some pages new and some old. A single sequential append ending in a commit record is fast and atomic.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: Which statement captures both parts of the write-ahead rule?
options: Log first: before acknowledging the commit and before writing the page
Pages first: data pages are written, then the log at each checkpoint
Ack first: the commit is confirmed, then the log is flushed shortly after
Undo only: log records are written only for transactions that abort
If the power goes off right after a data.why: Part (a) means a commit is acknowledged only after its log records are durable; part (b) means a dirty page is never written before the log describing it. Pages carry an LSN to enforce this.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: Your WAL already records every change. Why does the database still need checkpoints?
options: To bound recovery replay and let older WAL be recycled
Because the WAL is wiped after each commit and must be rebuilt
Because checkpoints are what make each commit durable
Because replicas can only read data files, not the WAL
If the power goes off right after a data.why: A checkpoint records that changes up to some LSN are in the data files. Without it the log grows forever and recovery replays all of it. Frequent checkpoints mean faster recovery but more disk writes.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: A product manager wants synchronous_commit = off on the whole order database to speed up a festive sale. What is your advice?
options: Fine, because it only affects replicas and the primary stays durable
Keep it on for orders; off can lose the last moments of acked commits
Fine, as long as fsync is turned off too so the gains are consistent
Not allowed, because it can corrupt the database after any crash
If the power goes off right after a data.why: synchronous_commit = off replies before fsync, risking a short tail of lost commits but not corruption. That is unacceptable for orders and payments; clickstream can use it. Group commit and fast disks give throughput safely.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: What is the real difference in risk between PostgreSQL synchronous_commit = off and fsync = off?
options: Both only lose the last few commits; neither corrupts the database
The first can corrupt the database; the second loses recent commits
The first loses recent commits; the second can corrupt the database
Both can corrupt the database, but fsync = off is the faster one
If the power goes off right after a data.why: Losing a short tail of commits leaves a consistent database. Turning off fsync breaks the write-ahead rule itself, so pages and log can disagree after a crash.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: On a spinning disk, each fsync takes around 5-10 ms. How do databases still achieve thousands of durable commits per second?
options: They skip fsync for most commits and fsync once a second
They write commits into data pages, which need no fsync
They keep the WAL in RAM and flush it at checkpoints only
Group commit: many waiting commits share a single fsync
If the power goes off right after a data.why: One fsync per commit would cap a spinning disk at roughly 100-200 commits per second. Group commit lets each commit still wait for a real fsync while sharing it.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: After a crash, why can redo safely be run twice on the same page?
options: Redo only applies aborted transactions, which are harmless
Redo overwrites the whole data file from a backup each time
The database deletes WAL records as soon as they are replayed
Each page stores its last LSN, so applied records are skipped
If the power goes off right after a data.why: Comparing the page LSN with the record LSN makes replay idempotent; already-applied changes are not reapplied.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: How does PostgreSQL deal with changes from transactions that never committed after a crash, given it does only redo?
options: It runs a separate undo pass using undo logs, just like InnoDB
MVCC hides row versions whose transaction has no commit record
It deletes the data file and restores from the latest backup
It treats them as committed, because they are in the WAL
If the power goes off right after a data.why: PostgreSQL relies on MVCC visibility instead of undo. InnoDB uses undo logs, and the classic ARIES design uses analysis, redo and undo passes.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: A power cut hits while an 8 KB page is half written to disk. How does PostgreSQL protect against this torn page?
options: It uses a doublewrite buffer, exactly like MySQL InnoDB
It marks the page read-only until the next checkpoint ends
full_page_writes logs a full page image after each checkpoint
It relies on the SSD never writing half of a page
If the power goes off right after a data.why: Redo can't fix a garbage page, so PostgreSQL logs a full copy of each page the first time it changes after a checkpoint and restores from it. InnoDB solves the same problem with a doublewrite buffer.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: A disk in your database server dies completely, and separately someone runs a bad DELETE. What protects you here?
options: Replicas and backups; the WAL only covers single-machine crashes
The WAL, because it records every change and can replay all data
Checkpoints, because they keep a full copy of every data page
synchronous_commit = on, because it guarantees no data loss ever
If the power goes off right after a data.why: The WAL lives on the same machine and also faithfully records the bad DELETE. Disk loss and human mistakes need copies elsewhere and point-in-time backups.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: Your Kafka cluster has replication factor 3. Where does Kafka's durability for a produced message usually come from?
options: An fsync on every message, just like a database commit
The consumer offset, which records the message was read
Replication: acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2
The producer buffer, which retries until brokers restart
If the power goes off right after a data.why: A Kafka partition is a write-ahead log, but by default Kafka doesn't fsync each message; it relies on copies on at least two brokers before acknowledging, so one machine losing power loses nothing.

If the power goes off right after a data.q: With PostgreSQL synchronous replication configured, what does 'committed' mean for an order?
options: The data pages are written on both servers first
The WAL is flushed on the primary and on a standby
The order is in memory and queued for the standby
The standby has run a checkpoint covering the order
If the power goes off right after a data.why: Synchronous replication waits for the standby to have the WAL, typically adding about a millisecond, so the order survives losing the whole primary server and failover loses nothing.

Yes: promote the cross-region replica, since region copies are kept apart
Yes: replicas ignore DDL such as DROP and only copy row-level changes
Yes, if the replica is synchronous, since it holds every committed write

Promote a replica, then replay the binlog backwards to undo the DROP
On a new server, restore full + incrementals, replay log to just before the DROP

Someone accidentally deletes the orders.q: Why should a point-in-time restore usually go to a separate server instead of over production?
options: Restoring over production is not supported by Postgres or MySQL
Production kept taking other writes; restoring over it would wipe them
A separate server restores faster because it has no replicas attached
Production disks are too full to hold both the backup and the log
Someone accidentally deletes the orders.why: Restore the old state on the side, check it, and copy back only what was lost. Overwriting production loses every later valid write.

Someone accidentally deletes the orders.q: You back up every night at 2 AM and do not keep the transaction log. The database is lost at 11 PM. What is your actual RPO for this incident?
options: About 3 hours: the time until the next backup
Zero, since the nightly backup is a full copy
About 21 hours: every write since 2 AM
24 hours, since RPO always equals the interval
Someone accidentally deletes the orders.why: RPO is how much data you lose, measured in time since the last copy left the building. Shipping the log every few minutes would cut it to minutes.

Someone accidentally deletes the orders.q: Which pair correctly defines RPO and RTO?
options: RPO: how much data you can lose; RTO: how long you can be down
RPO: how long you can be down; RTO: how much data you can lose
RPO: how often backups run; RTO: how long a backup takes to make
RPO: how many replicas you keep; RTO: how many regions you use
Someone accidentally deletes the orders.why: RPO is about data (how far back you may lose, measured in time); RTO is about downtime. You can have a tiny RPO with a long RTO, or the reverse.

Someone accidentally deletes the orders.q: Your plan restores 2 TB from object storage (about 70 minutes) then replays logs (about 40 minutes). The business now wants an RTO of 30 minutes. What gets you closer?
options: Ship the log every minute instead of every five minutes
A delayed replica or warm standby, plus fast storage snapshots
Add a third live replica in the same region as the primary
Take full backups every night instead of once a week
Someone accidentally deletes the orders.why: RTO is set by restore speed and practice, so copy from a standby instead of restoring and rehearse the runbook. Shipping logs more often improves RPO, not RTO; extra live replicas copy the mistake too.

Someone accidentally deletes the orders.q: Which setup gives the lowest RPO for a whole-site hardware loss?
options: Hourly storage snapshots in the same region
Log shipped every 5 minutes to object storage
Nightly full backups copied to another region
A synchronous replica in a second site
Someone accidentally deletes the orders.why: A synchronous replica has every committed write, so RPO is close to zero for hardware loss. It does not help against human mistakes, which it copies instantly.

Someone accidentally deletes the orders.q: Ransomware gets your cloud admin password and deletes every backup in the same account before encrypting production. What would have protected you?

Immutable backups (e.g. S3 Object Lock) in a separate account
A cross-region replica, since attackers reach only one region
Encrypting backups with the same admin keys as production

Someone accidentally deletes the orders.q: Your backup dashboard has been green for months but no one has ever restored a backup. What is the most important gap?

Backups should run more often to reduce the RPO

Incrementals end up larger than full backups over time
Incrementals restore only onto the original server
The restore chain grows long and one bad link breaks it

Someone accidentally deletes the orders.q: What is a delayed replica and when does it help?
options: A replica kept, say, 1 hour behind; it lets you undo recent mistakes
A far-away replica that lags from latency; it stops ransomware
A replica that applies changes only at checkpoints to save disk I/O
A replica kept powered off until needed, to cut cloud costs
Someone accidentally deletes the orders.why: A deliberate delay gives a window where the mistake has not yet been applied, so you can copy the data from it, cutting RTO for human errors compared with a full restore.

Someone accidentally deletes the orders.q: During the incident, the team switches checkout off with a feature flag before starting the restore. Why?
options: To stop the bleeding, so failed half-written orders don't pile up
Because a restore cannot start while customers are browsing
Because the feature flag automatically starts point-in-time recovery
Because switching off checkout brings the RPO down to zero

options: A third replica so the delete is spread over more copies
Hourly backups instead of nightly ones for the database
Least privilege: no account can DROP production tables
A multi-region active-active setup for the order database

Someone accidentally deletes the orders.q: What is the difference between high availability (HA) and disaster recovery (DR)?

HA fails over small faults in seconds; DR recovers from big losses
HA and DR are the same idea, both measured using RPO only
HA is about backups; DR is about replicas in the same rack

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: A 5-node Raft cluster loses 2 nodes. Can it still accept writes? What if it loses 3?
options: With 2 lost, writes stop if the leader was hit; with 3 lost, reads stop
It accepts writes in both cases, as the survivors form a new cluster
With 2 lost, 3 remain, a majority, so yes; with 3 lost, writes stop
With 2 lost it serves reads only; with 3 lost it goes single-leader
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: A 5-node cluster needs 3 for a majority, so it tolerates 2 failures. With only 2 nodes left no majority is possible, so it stops accepting writes until nodes return.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: Your team wants to grow a 3-node etcd cluster to 4 nodes 'for more fault tolerance'. What do you advise?
options: Good idea: 4 nodes survive 2 failures, half of them
Don't: 4 nodes still survive only 1 failure, like 3
Good idea, but only if the 4th is a dedicated leader
Don't: Raft requires exactly 3 nodes, never 4
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: 4 nodes need 3 for a majority, so they survive only 1 failure while adding latency and another machine that can fail. Use odd sizes: 3 survives 1, 5 survives 2.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: Why can two leaders never both win elections in the same Raft term?
options: The node with the higher IP address always wins ties
Elections wait until every node confirms the leader died
Only the node with the longest uptime may stand
Nodes vote once per term and any two majorities overlap
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: Winning needs a majority; two majorities share at least one node; that node can't vote twice in one term. So a second leader in that term is impossible.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: Why does Raft pick each follower's election timeout randomly, for example between 150 and 300 ms?
options: So one follower usually times out first and wins cleanly
So slower nodes get more time to finish garbage collection
So the leader's heartbeat interval can be random as well
So elections happen at random even when the leader is healthy
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: If all followers timed out together they would all become candidates and split the vote repeatedly. Randomness staggers them so elections usually settle in a round or two.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: A follower receives a RequestVote from a candidate whose log is missing entries it already has. What does the follower do?
options: Votes yes, then sends its missing entries to the candidate
Votes no: the candidate's log must be at least as up to date
Votes yes if it hasn't voted this term, whatever the logs say
Ignores the request and starts its own election immediately
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: The up-to-date check (last entry's term, then length) ensures the winner holds every committed entry, since each committed entry lives on a majority of voters.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: In a 5-node cluster, the leader appends an entry and E2 and E3 acknowledge it. E4 and E5 have not yet. Is the entry committed?
options: No: every node must store the entry first
No: at least 4 of 5 nodes must acknowledge
Yes: with the leader that is 3 of 5, a majority
Yes, but only once E4 and E5 have applied it
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: Commit needs a majority counting the leader. Lagging followers catch up later; only a majority must have each committed entry.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: A leader appends 'price list 43' to its own log, then crashes before sending it to anyone. What happens to that entry?
options: The new leader recovers it from the old node's disk and commits it
It is committed automatically as soon as the old leader restarts
It was never committed, so it is overwritten when the node returns
It stays in the log forever as an orphan but is never applied
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: When the old node returns it sees the higher term, steps down, and the uncommitted entry is overwritten. It was never acknowledged, so the client timed out and retries, ideally with a unique request ID.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: A 5-node cluster splits into a 3-node side and a 2-node side, and the old leader is on the 2-node side. Why is there no split brain?
options: The old leader can't get a majority, so none of its writes commit
The 2-node side keeps leading while the 3-node side waits it out
Both sides elect leaders, and their writes merge when the link heals
The old leader detects the split and shuts down every node at once
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: Only a majority can elect or commit. The 3-node side elects a leader in a higher term, and when the network heals the old leader sees that term and steps down.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: A node that has been offline returns and receives a message carrying term 8 while its own term is 7 and it believes it is leader. What does it do?
options: Rejects the message, as it still leads its own term
Starts an election in term 9 to win leadership back
Keeps leading but forwards writes to the term-8 leader
Updates its term to 8 and steps down to follower
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: Terms only go up. Seeing a higher term means someone newer is in charge, so the node becomes a follower. Messages with an older term are rejected.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: A follower's heartbeat timeout fires, but the leader was only paused for garbage collection. What is the consequence in Raft?
options: Two leaders run at once and accept conflicting writes
A needless election may cost a little time, but safety holds
The paused leader's committed entries are lost for good
The cluster halts until an operator picks a leader by hand
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: Raft accepts that 'slow' and 'dead' look the same. A wrong guess triggers an extra election; the term rules make the old leader step down, so no split brain.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: Your team runs one Raft group and finds that write throughput doesn't grow when you add followers. Why, and how do systems like CockroachDB scale?
options: Followers need faster disks; with NVMe one group scales linearly
One leader takes all writes; scale by splitting data into many groups
Raft has a fixed cap of 1,000 writes per second on any hardware
Followers should accept writes too; enable Raft's multi-leader mode
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: Raft is for correctness, not speed: every write goes through one leader and waits for a majority. Databases run one Raft group per data range to spread load.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: A follower in your Raft cluster serves a read and returns a value older than one the leader just committed. Why?
options: The leader's commit isn't real until all followers apply it
Raft followers deliberately serve values one term behind
Followers can lag; fresh reads go through the confirmed leader
Followers apply entries only at checkpoints, not continuously
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: Only a majority must hold each committed entry, so any single follower can be behind. Up-to-date reads go through a leader that confirms it is still leader.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: Which kind of data is typically put through consensus such as etcd or Kafka KRaft?
options: Small critical facts: leader, config, lock holder, shard owner
High-volume event streams such as every product-page click
Large media files such as product images and videos
Analytics tables that are rebuilt from scratch every night
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: Each consensus write costs a majority round trip and a disk flush, so it is reserved for small metadata where correctness matters most.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: What is a realistic latency cost for each write in a Raft group spread across regions, compared with a single data centre?
options: About 20-50 ms across regions vs about 1-10 ms in one DC
Under 1 ms in both cases, since only the leader writes disk
About 500 ms across regions vs about 100 ms in one DC
The same in both, since followers acknowledge asynchronously
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: Each write needs a round trip to a majority plus an fsync, so distance between nodes directly sets write latency.

How do a group of servers agree on one l.q: What does a Raft follower check when it receives AppendEntries, and why?
options: That the leader's term is lower than its own, to keep out stale leaders
That no other follower has applied the new entry yet, to avoid repeats
That the client who sent the write is allowed to change that data
That its log matches at the previous index and term, keeping logs identical
How do a group of servers agree on one l.why: If the previous index and term don't match, the follower rejects; the leader backs up until they agree and overwrites the follower's wrong entries. This consistency check keeps every log the same.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: Ten app servers each wrap the 6 AM invoice job in a Java ReentrantLock. Customers receive ten invoice emails. Why?
options: ReentrantLock allows re-entry, so one server took the lock ten times
The cron expression is wrong and fires ten times on every server
Each server's lock is in its own memory, so all ten take one and run
The lock was released too early inside the finally block each time
How do you make sure only one server run.why: An in-process lock only coordinates threads in one JVM. Across servers the lock must live in shared storage such as Redis, etcd or the database.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: Which Redis command correctly acquires a lock for the invoice job?
options: SETNX lock:invoice 1, then EXPIRE lock:invoice 300
SET lock:invoice <unique-id> NX PX 300000
SET lock:invoice <unique-id> PX 300000 (no NX flag)
GET lock:invoice, and if empty, SET it to the hostname
How do you make sure only one server run.why: One atomic command: NX means only one server can create the key, PX gives auto-expiry, and the unique value enables safe release. SETNX then EXPIRE can leave a never-expiring lock if the process crashes between them.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: Server A's Redis lock expired while its job was still running, and server B took the lock. Server A finishes and runs a plain DEL on the key. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: Redis refuses DEL on another client's key
A deletes B's lock, so a third server can grab it
A's DEL fails, so the lock stays until its TTL ends
B's job is cancelled the moment its key disappears
How do you make sure only one server run.why: Release must be compare-and-delete: a Lua script deletes the key only if it still holds your unique value. A plain DEL removes whoever currently holds the lock.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: Why is the Redis lock release written as a Lua script rather than a GET followed by DEL from the client?
options: Lua is faster than two network calls, and that is the main reason
Redis runs it atomically, so nothing slips in between check and delete
Clients may not call DEL directly on a key that was set with NX
Lua scripts automatically extend the TTL before deleting the key
How do you make sure only one server run.why: With separate GET and DEL, the lock could expire and be taken by another server between them, and you'd delete their lock. The Lua script makes check-and-delete one indivisible step.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: Server A holds the lock with a 30 s TTL, then freezes in a 40 s GC pause. Server B takes the lock and writes. A wakes and writes too. Why can't A simply check 'do I still hold the lock?' before writing?
options: The check works but adds too much latency per write
Redis won't let a client read a key it set earlier
The pause can strike between the check and the write
A can't reach Redis after a pause until it reconnects
How do you make sure only one server run.why: A process cannot reliably know it was paused. Only the protected resource rejecting stale holders (fencing) or idempotent writes fix this.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: Server A has fencing token 33, freezes in a GC pause, and B gets token 34 and writes. A wakes and writes with 33. What stops A?
options: Redis revokes token 33, so A's write is never sent
A's watchdog spots the pause and cancels the write
The lock service deletes all writes made with 33
Storage has seen 34 and rejects any lower token
