How do you make sure only one server run.why: Fencing moves the check to the resource: each write carries the token and anything lower than the highest seen is rejected, for example UPDATE ... WHERE fence < 34.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: For fencing tokens to work, what must be true of the system being protected?
options: It must run on the same server as the lock service
It must accept writes from only one IP at a time
It must use Redis as its storage so tokens compare
It must track the highest token and reject lower ones
How do you make sure only one server run.why: Fencing only works when the resource checks the token. For outside side effects like an email provider or payment gateway, which can't, you still need idempotency keys.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: How do you pick the TTL for a lease-based lock on a job that normally takes 4 minutes?
options: Exactly 4 minutes, so the lock frees the moment the job should end
As long as possible, such as 24 hours, so it can never expire
Above runtime plus worst pause, or shorter with a renewing watchdog
Very short, like 1 second, so a crashed holder never blocks anyone
How do you make sure only one server run.why: Too short and it expires mid-job; too long and a crashed holder blocks recovery. A watchdog (as in Redisson) extends the TTL while the job is alive.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: Your single Redis primary fails over to a replica that had not yet received the lock key. What can happen?
options: The new primary has no lock, so a second server can take it
The lock survives, since Redis replicates keys synchronously
All servers block until the old primary comes back online
The replica rejects lock requests until an operator clears it
How do you make sure only one server run.why: Single-node Redis is a single point of failure for the lock. Redlock tries to address this but is debated; etcd/ZooKeeper use consensus. For 'send email once', idempotency covers this gap.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: Your team uses etcd for a strict leader election. A colleague says consensus makes the lock perfectly safe, so fencing is unnecessary. What is the flaw?
options: Consensus guards the lock record, not a paused client acting late
etcd does not use consensus, so the lock record itself can vanish
etcd leases never expire, so a crashed client holds the lock forever
etcd revision numbers can go down, so they can't serve as tokens
How do you make sure only one server run.why: etcd and ZooKeeper survive node failures, but the GC-pause problem is on the client side: its lease can expire while it keeps acting. etcd revisions and ZooKeeper sequence numbers are natural fencing tokens.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: Your scheduled jobs already write to PostgreSQL and run a few times a day. What is often the simplest good locking choice?
options: A new 5-node ZooKeeper cluster just for these jobs
Redlock spread across 5 independent Redis nodes
Java synchronized blocks, with jobs pinned to one server
The database itself: a row lock, advisory lock or claim row
How do you make sure only one server run.why: The database can be the lock with no new infrastructure (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, pg_try_advisory_lock, or a unique claim row); libraries like ShedLock or Quartz cluster mode do this. A consensus cluster for one cron job is usually overkill.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: How does INSERT INTO job_runs (job, run_date, owner) with a unique constraint on (job, run_date) act as a lock?
options: The insert blocks every other table write until the job is done
The constraint makes the job run on whichever server inserts last
Only one insert per job and day succeeds; the rest fail and skip
It works only if all servers insert in exactly the same millisecond
How do you make sure only one server run.why: A unique key turns 'claim this run' into a race only one can win, and the row doubles as an audit record that today's run started.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: Why is a unique key on (customer_id, invoice_date) more important than the lock for the invoice job?
options: If the lock ever fails, a second send still gets rejected
The unique key makes the job run faster than the lock
It stops the job from being scheduled on many servers
It removes the need for a TTL on the Redis lock key
How do you make sure only one server run.why: Expiry during a pause, failover or a manual re-run can let the job run twice. Idempotency makes that harmless: the lock saves work, the unique key guarantees correctness.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: The invoice job crashes after processing 1,20,000 of 2 lakh sellers. What should happen next in a well-designed setup?
options: Another server takes the expired lock and resumes, skipping sent rows
An operator must restart the job by hand from the very beginning
The whole batch is rolled back and every seller is emailed again
Nothing runs again until the next day's 6 AM scheduled trigger
How do you make sure only one server run.why: Recording progress with unique keys lets any new holder resume safely. The job_runs row shows the run started but did not finish.

How do you make sure only one server run.q: Someone says 'with a distributed lock, our job is executed exactly once.' What is the accurate correction?
options: Correct, as long as the lock is taken with both NX and a TTL
A lock gives 'usually once'; idempotency gives exactly-once effect
Correct, but only if the lock lives in etcd rather than Redis
Correct, but only for jobs that finish well within the TTL
How do you make sure only one server run.why: Expiry, failover and re-runs mean a lock cannot guarantee single execution. Designing the job so a second run does nothing is what makes the outcome correct.

options: One copy takes writes and read-only copies follow it synchronously
Each copy holds a different subset of data and never replicates
All copies must win a majority vote before any write can commit
Several copies all accept writes and sync with each other later
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: In multi-master every DC writes locally and syncs asynchronously, so conflicts are possible by design. Single-leader has one writer; the majority vote describes consensus stores.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: Every user is pinned to a home DC, so a teammate says the SuperCoins wallet can never diverge. What is the best response?
options: Pinning helps, but moves, jobs, failover and retries can bypass it
Correct: pinning removes every possible conflict, nothing else needed
Wrong: pinning makes it worse, since users then write in both DCs
Correct, as long as both DCs run NTP so their clocks agree exactly
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: Pinning makes each user single-writer only for writes that obey it. Migrations with lag, batch jobs, mirrored Kafka consumers, failovers and retries bypass it unless deliberately routed and fenced.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: Shreya has 100 coins. DC1 credits +50 and DC2 approves a spend of 80 before seeing the credit. With last-write-wins on a balance field, what can the result be?
options: Always 70, since LWW applies both changes in time order
Always 20, because spends carry later timestamps than credits
20 or 150, depending on timestamps, though 70 is correct
Always 150, because credits win over spends during a merge
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: LWW keeps one balance and drops the other real change; which one survives depends on timestamps and clock skew. A ledger union gives 100 + 50 - 80 = 70.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: A CashbackEarned Kafka topic is mirrored to both DCs, and a consumer in each DC credits wallets. What happens and what is the fix?
options: Nothing, because Kafka mirroring removes duplicate messages
Double credits; only the owner DC applies, with a unique entry key
Lost events; add a third DC so a majority always receives them
Delayed credits; add more consumer threads in both DCs
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: Mirrored consumers in both DCs apply each event twice. Route credits via the directory to the owner DC and make the ledger entry key unique (such as the cashback ID) so a second apply is rejected.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: Why store a wallet as an append-only ledger of entries with unique keys instead of a single balance field?
options: Merging becomes a union by key, and the balance is the sum
A ledger uses less storage than one balance row per user
A ledger by itself stops the balance from going negative
A ledger removes the need for replication between DCs
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: Entries like +50 cashback and -80 spend merge regardless of arrival order: nothing is lost and duplicates collapse. A ledger alone does not stop overdrafts; that needs single ownership and conditional spends.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: Shreya has 100 coins. DC1 writes a coin-expiry entry of -60 while DC2, unaware, approves an 80-coin spend. Both ledgers are unioned. What is the result and what does it show?
options: 40: the union discards the later of the two debit entries
20: expiry entries are ignored when ledgers are merged
An error: the union hits a key clash and drops both debits
-40: a ledger alone can't stop overdrafts without one owner
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: Union gives 100 - 60 - 80 = -40. Each DC approved using only what it saw. A 'spend only if enough' rule needs one owner checking the full balance.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: Why can't a PN-counter CRDT alone keep a wallet from going negative?
options: PN-counters drop some decrements when merging per-DC counts
PN-counters only support increments, so spends can't be stored
PN-counters need synchronised clocks, which two DCs never have
Each DC approves spends alone, and the merge just adds them up
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: A PN-counter guarantees no lost updates, but two spends approved separately can together exceed the balance. Overdraft checks need coordination: one owner or a consensus store.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: How should a spend be written in the owner DC to prevent overdrafts and repeats?
options: Read the balance, compute the new value in app code, write it
Write the spend to both DCs and let replication sort it out
Unique ledger key plus UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= amount
Check a per-DC cached balance and approve if it is enough
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: The unique key blocks repeats; the conditional update (also checking version and owner epoch) affects 0 rows if funds are short, so the transaction rolls back. Read-modify-write in app code and cached balances allow races.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: While moving Shreya from DC1 to DC2, why does the protocol bump an ownership epoch from 7 to 8 instead of only updating the directory?
options: So DC2 knows how many coins Shreya held at the time of the move
So replication speeds up and DC2 catches up with DC1 faster
Only for the audit log; the epoch plays no part in writes
So DC1 can reject late writes still tagged with the old epoch
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: Slow jobs, retries or cached routes may still send writes to DC1 after the flip. Fencing with an epoch means any write carrying the stale epoch is rejected by the old owner.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: In the fenced migration protocol, how do you know DC2 has caught up before flipping ownership?
options: DC2 has applied DC1's latest per-user sequence number
A fixed 2-second wait, since lag is normally milliseconds
The last-write wall-clock timestamps match in both DCs
DC2's balance row for the user is non-zero
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: Lag can grow to seconds or minutes during sales. Measuring catch-up by sequence numbers (or the TiCDC checkpoint ts) avoids guessing and clock skew.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: DC1 suddenly goes down and some of its last writes never replicated to DC2. What is the recommended approach?
options: Copy DC2's data over DC1 when it returns so both match at once
Let DC2 allow unlimited spends for DC1's users to avoid complaints
Apply a pre-agreed policy: pause or cap spends, then union on fail-back
Delete DC1's unreplicated writes so they can't conflict later
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: Decide before the outage: pause spends for affected users, or allow a capped amount (for example 200 coins) with a known worst-case loss. Queue credits. On fail-back, merge ledgers by union, never overwrite one DC with the other.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: Your continuous reconciliation job finds a user whose ledger totals differ between DCs. How should the mismatch be fixed?
options: Add a compensating entry, keeping the history intact
Edit or delete the wrong historical entry directly
Copy the larger DC's balance over the smaller one
Reset the balance to zero in both DCs and notify
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: Corrections are new entries, never edits to history, so the audit trail stays complete.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: The coin wallet runs on one TiDB cluster stretched across both DCs. Can the database itself diverge between DCs?
options: Yes: each DC's copy accepts writes independently
No, Raft majority commits; app-level risks still remain
Yes, unless TiCDC is set to run in both directions
No, so idempotency keys and conditional updates are moot
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: A stretched cluster has one committed version per row. App risks remain: retries creating duplicate credits, stale or cached reads for spend decisions, and read-modify-write in app code.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: The wallet instead runs on two TiDB clusters linked by TiCDC in both directions. What happens if both sides write the same row?
options: The later-applied change just overwrites; there is no merge
Raft resolves it by a majority vote across both clusters
TiCDC rejects the second write and alerts an operator
TiCDC merges both changes by adding the numeric deltas
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: Two TiCDC-linked clusters are asynchronous multi-master. You need single writer, a ledger with unique keys, checkpoint-gated moves, epoch fencing, AUTO_RANDOM or disjoint ID ranges, and reconciliation.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: On a stretched TiDB setup, a developer wants to approve spends using follower reads (AS OF TIMESTAMP) to cut latency. Your response?
options: Fine, because Raft makes follower reads always current
Fine for showing a balance, never for approving a spend
Fine, provided the spend is below 200 coins
Not possible, because TiDB has no follower reads
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: Approving a spend must use the current balance via a conditional update or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. Stale reads can approve a spend the balance can't cover.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: If the business needs the wallet to never be wrong, what is the trade-off of a synchronously replicated consensus store such as Spanner or CockroachDB?
options: Writes get faster, but reads may return stale coin balances
It allows conflicts, which are merged by last-write-wins
Each spend waits on a cross-DC round trip; a third site is needed
It requires users to be pinned to one DC permanently
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: Consensus means there is never a second version, but each write waits for a majority across sites, and a third location keeps a majority when one DC fails. Many teams accept that latency for money.

What is multi-master replication? If an.q: A team says 'we have idempotency keys on every wallet operation, so two DCs can never overdraw a wallet.' What is wrong?
options: Idempotency keys only work for credits, never for debits
Keys stop repeats of one operation, not two different spends
Idempotency keys must be timestamps, which drift across DCs
Nothing is wrong; idempotency keys fully prevent overdrafts
What is multi-master replication? If an.why: Two distinct spends have different keys, so both pass. Preventing overdraft needs a single owner doing conditional writes.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: Your product service checks Redis first; on a miss it reads MySQL and then stores the result in Redis with a TTL. Which read pattern is this?
options: Read-through, where the cache itself loads data on a miss
Refresh-ahead, where entries are reloaded before they expire
Cache-aside (lazy loading), where the application owns the miss logic
Write-through, where cache and database are written together
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: The application checks the cache and fills it on a miss, which is cache-aside. Read-through looks similar but the loading happens inside the cache library via a loader function; plain Redis does not do that by itself.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: A team is designing a read-heavy product-details service for a festive sale. Which combination should be their default starting point?
options: Cache-aside, delete the key on write, and a TTL with random jitter
Write-through for every write, with no TTL since writes keep it fresh
Write-behind with Redis as the source of truth and long TTLs
Cache-aside, update the cache value on write, and a fixed identical TTL
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: The answer's default for read-heavy data is cache-aside plus delete-on-write plus a jittered TTL. Updating the cache on write risks out-of-order updates, and identical TTLs invite an avalanche.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: Two admins change product 123's price within milliseconds. After each DB write, the code SETs the new price in Redis. Later the cache shows the older price even though the DB has the newer one. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the TTL so the correct value stays in the cache longer
Wrap both cache updates in a Redis transaction so they apply together
Switch the price cache to write-behind so writes are batched in order
Delete the cache key after the DB commit instead of updating it, and keep a TTL
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: Concurrent cache updates can land in the opposite order to the DB commits, leaving the old value cached. Deletes are idempotent and order-independent, so the next read loads the committed value; a longer TTL only makes the wrong value live longer.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: Your service already deletes cache keys after every write and also consumes CDC events. A developer proposes removing TTLs since invalidation 'covers everything'. What is the best response?
options: Agree: with CDC in place, a TTL only lowers the hit ratio for no benefit
Keep the TTL: invalidations can be lost, and the TTL bounds how long any mistake lives
Agree, but only if the eviction policy is set to allkeys-lru
Keep the TTL only for keys that use write-behind, and drop it elsewhere
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: Invalidations get lost through crashed consumers, scripts writing the DB directly, or the delete-vs-read race. The TTL is the upper bound on staleness; eviction policy does not replace it because eviction only happens under memory pressure.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: A reader misses on product 123, reads price 500 from the DB, and before it sets the cache a writer updates the price to 450 and deletes the key. The reader then sets 500. Which mitigation does the answer NOT list for this race?
options: A delayed second delete one to two seconds after the write
Switching from deleting the key to updating it with the new price
Versioned values where a set succeeds only if its version is newer
Always keeping a TTL as the safety net on the key
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: Delayed second delete, version-checked sets (a small Lua script), CDC-driven deletes and a TTL are the listed mitigations. Updating instead of deleting reintroduces the out-of-order writer problem rather than fixing this race.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: Users add items to their cart and immediately open the cart page, expecting to see the change. Which write pattern fits this data best?
options: Write-around, so the cart write only goes to the database
Write-behind, flushing cart changes to the database every 30 seconds
Cache-aside with a 10-minute TTL and no invalidation on write
Write-through to Redis and the cart database, so the read right after is fresh
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: Write-through fits data that is read right after it is written, like a cart. Write-behind would risk losing cart changes if Redis fails before the flush, and write-around makes the first read after a write miss.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: You need to count product page views at very high rates, and losing about 30 seconds of counts during a failover is acceptable. Which strategy fits?
options: Write-behind: INCR in Redis and flush to the analytics DB periodically
Write-through: update Redis and the analytics DB on every single view
Write-around: write each view straight to the database only
Refresh-ahead: reload the counter from the DB before it expires
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: Write-behind suits high-rate, loss-tolerant writes like view counters. Write-through would push every view synchronously to the database, defeating the purpose at that write rate.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: A colleague says 'write-behind is just a faster write-through, so let's use it everywhere'. What is the key flaw in this view?
options: Write-behind is actually slower because it writes the database twice
Write-behind cannot be used with Redis, only with in-process caches
Write-behind changes durability: until the flush, the only copy lives in the cache
Write-behind makes reads stale, but its durability matches write-through
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: With write-behind the cache is the temporary source of truth, so a crash before the flush loses data. It needs a durable buffer such as Redis AOF or a Kafka topic, batching, retries and idempotent DB writes.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: Your Redis cache fills up during load testing and writes start failing with errors instead of old keys being removed. What is the most likely cause?
options: Redis LRU is exact and refuses to evict keys accessed in the last second
The keys have TTLs, and Redis never evicts keys that have a TTL
allkeys-lru is set, which only evicts keys that have no TTL
maxmemory-policy is still the default noeviction, so Redis rejects writes when full
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: Redis does not evict automatically: the default policy is noeviction, so writes fail when memory is full. You must set maxmemory and a policy such as allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for a pure cache.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: One Redis cluster holds both product cache entries and user sessions. During a sale, memory pressure starts evicting sessions and users get logged out. What is the best fix?
options: Switch the shared cluster to allkeys-lfu so sessions count as popular
Move sessions to a separate cluster with noeviction or volatile-* and replication
Remove TTLs from product keys so they are never evicted before sessions
Raise maxmemory-samples so Redis evicts sessions more accurately
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: Sessions are Redis used as a store, not a cache, so they should not share an evictable cluster. allkeys-* policies can evict any key, including sessions; separate clusters (or volatile-* with TTLs only on cache keys) protect must-keep data.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: For a catalog where the same bestseller products stay popular for weeks, which Redis eviction policy does the answer recommend?
options: allkeys-lru, since one scan cannot affect recency-based eviction
volatile-ttl, which removes keys with the longest TTL first
allkeys-lfu, which evicts the least frequently used keys
noeviction, so popular products are never dropped
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: LFU suits stable popularity like bestsellers, and Redis LFU uses a decaying counter so old popularity fades. LRU suits recency-driven data and is vulnerable to a big scan pushing out popular keys.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: At 00:00 the hero phone's cache key expires and thousands of requests miss together, sending product DB CPU to 100%. What is happening and what is one direct fix?
options: A cache stampede; use single-flight or a lock so only one request rebuilds the key
Cache penetration; add a Bloom filter of valid product IDs
A cache avalanche; spread TTLs with jitter across all keys
A hot-key problem; switch the eviction policy to allkeys-lfu
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: Many concurrent misses rebuilding one key is a stampede (thundering herd). Single-flight, a distributed lock or probabilistic early expiration fix it; a Bloom filter addresses lookups for IDs that don't exist.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: During a sale the hero phone gets about 200,000 reads per second, more than one Redis shard can serve. What is the best fix?
options: Add an in-process L1 cache with a 1-5 s TTL, or replicate the key with suffixes
Increase the key's TTL so it never expires during the sale
Add negative caching so missing products are cached for 60 s
Move the key to write-behind so reads come from the buffer
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: This is a hot-key problem: one shard cannot serve the load no matter the TTL. A short-lived local L1 cache or key replicas such as product:123#0 to #9 spread the reads.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: Bots are scraping random, non-existent product IDs. Every request misses Redis and hits MySQL. Which pair of fixes targets this?
options: Jittered TTLs plus staggered warm-up of the top products
Single-flight plus a distributed lock on each product key
Negative caching of 'not found' for 30-60 s plus a Bloom filter of valid IDs
Write-through plus a longer TTL on existing product keys
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: This is cache penetration. Negative caching stops repeat DB hits for the same missing ID, and a Bloom filter rejects IDs that are definitely absent; it can say 'maybe present' wrongly but never 'absent' wrongly.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: A warm-up job loads 50,000 products at 23:30, all with a TTL of exactly 30 minutes. What risk does this create and how do you avoid it?
options: A stampede on one key; add a distributed lock per product
An avalanche when all expire together; spread TTLs (for example over 20-40 minutes)
Penetration from bots; add negative caching for missing IDs
Hot keys on one shard; replicate each key ten times
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: Keys loaded at the same moment with the same TTL expire at the same moment, hitting the DB all at once. Jittered TTLs and staggered warm-up avoid the cliff; the worked example spreads them over 20-40 minutes.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: A team proposes caching inventory counts with write-behind to speed up the checkout reservation. What is the best response?
options: Accept it, as long as the inventory keys use a 5-10 second TTL
Accept it, but switch to write-through so the cache is always exact
Accept it, and add a Bloom filter so out-of-stock SKUs are rejected
Reject it: reserve stock with a conditional DB update; cache counts only for display
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: Any cached count can be stale and write-behind can lose decrements, which causes overselling. The cache can show 'Only 3 left' as a hint, but the sale decision is UPDATE ... WHERE qty > 0 against the source of truth.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: Your product cache hit ratio drops from 95% to 90% after a change. How much does load on the product database change?
options: It rises by about 5%, matching the hit-ratio drop
It rises by about 50%, from 5% to 7.5% of reads
It roughly doubles, from 1 in 20 reads to 1 in 10
It stays similar, since 90% is still a healthy hit ratio
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: At 95% the DB sees 5% of reads; at 90% it sees 10%, which is double. This is why small hit-ratio changes matter, and why hit ratio should be tracked per key type.

What are the main caching strategies, an.q: Which of these is the answer's example of data you should NOT serve from a cache at decision time?
options: A wallet balance used to approve a payment
Product titles and specifications on a listing page
Ratings and recommendations shown on a product page
Product images served on a catalog grid
What are the main caching strategies, an.why: Data that must be exactly right at decision time, such as balances, stock for reservation, coupon limits and payment state, should be read from the source of truth. Descriptions, ratings and images tolerate staleness.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: A user in Coimbatore opens a phone's product page and the image comes from a nearby CDN edge instead of the company's image service. How did that edge decide to hold this image?
options: The CDN copied the whole catalog to every edge before the sale began
The origin pushed every new image to all edges as soon as it was uploaded
It fetched it on demand when someone nearby first requested it, and kept it
The edge predicted local demand from the user's past shopping history
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: CDN edges fill on demand: a file is stored only after someone nearby asks for it, and popular files stay while unpopular ones are evicted. Pre-warming exists but is rare.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: An origin sends Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, s-maxage=3600. How long may the browser and the CDN each treat the response as fresh?
options: Browser 5 minutes; CDN 1 hour
Browser 1 hour; CDN 5 minutes
Both 5 minutes, since max-age applies to every cache
Both 1 hour, since s-maxage overrides max-age everywhere
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: s-maxage applies only to shared caches like the CDN and overrides max-age there, so the CDN uses 3,600 s while the browser uses 300 s. It does not affect browsers.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: A developer adds Cache-Control: no-cache to an API, expecting the CDN to never store it. What actually happens?
options: The CDN never stores the response, same as no-store
The CDN stores it but only the user's browser may serve it
The CDN stores it for its default TTL and ignores the header
The CDN may store it but must revalidate with the origin before each use
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: no-cache allows storing but requires revalidation every time. The directive that forbids storing is no-store; private limits storage to the user's own browser.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: A CDN copy of front.jpg with ETag "9f2e1d" has gone stale, and the image has not changed at the origin. What happens on the next request?
options: The edge deletes its copy and downloads the full 150 KB image again
The edge sends If-None-Match: "9f2e1d", gets 304 with no body, and serves its copy
The edge keeps serving the stale copy forever until someone purges it
The edge sends the ETag and the origin replies 200 with the same file
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: Stale copies are revalidated with a conditional request. If unchanged, the origin answers 304 Not Modified with no body (a few hundred bytes), and the edge resets the copy's age.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: A popular image has max-age=86400, yet a rarely viewed seller image with the same header disappears from the Patna edge after a few hours. Why?
options: The CDN halves max-age for files that are requested less often
max-age is a freshness limit, not a guarantee; unpopular files can be evicted early
max-age only applies to browsers, so the CDN ignores it entirely
The origin must have purged that image by tag in the meantime
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: Edges have limited space and evict least recently used items. A TTL is a maximum time a copy counts as fresh, not a promise to keep it.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: After a release, the image CDN's hit ratio falls from 95% to 70%. Marketing has started appending ?utm_source=whatsapp to shared links. What is the most likely cause?
options: The origin shield was removed, so every edge now misses on first request
Browsers began sending If-None-Match, which bypasses the edge cache
max-age was raised, making the CDN revalidate more often
The tracking parameter is part of the cache key, splitting one file into many copies
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: The cache key is usually host plus path plus query string, so junk parameters create many copies of the same file. Good setups ignore such parameters; also check new cookies, Vary headers, shorter TTLs and Set-Cookie.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: Your image service serves WebP to newer phones and JPEG to older ones from the same URL. Which approach keeps the CDN correct without killing the hit rate?
options: Send Vary: Accept so the image format becomes part of the cache key
Send Vary: User-Agent so each phone model gets its own cached copy
Send Cache-Control: private so only browsers cache each format
Send no Vary header and let the CDN pick a format per edge
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: When a response differs by format, that must be in the key, and Vary: Accept does that with few variants. Vary: User-Agent creates thousands of variants and destroys the hit rate.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: You deployed a fix to app.js and purged the CDN, but some users still run the old JavaScript. What is the better approach?
options: Purge the CDN again by prefix, which also clears browser copies
Set max-age=0 on app.js so every cache refetches it on each load
Use content-hashed names like app.81bd07.js, cached immutable for a year, with short-TTL HTML
Send Vary: Cookie on app.js so each user gets a fresh copy
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: A purge clears CDN copies but cannot reach browsers. Versioned names mean the new HTML points to a URL no cache has seen, so the old file is simply never requested again.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: Why can a file named app.3f9a2c.js safely be served with max-age=31536000, immutable?
options: Browsers automatically revalidate immutable files once a day
The CDN purges all immutable files after every deploy
JavaScript files are too small for staleness to matter
Its content never changes under that name; a new build gets a new name
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: The hash in the name is derived from content, so a given URL always means the same bytes. immutable tells caches never to revalidate, and a deploy just points the HTML to a new URL.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: The CDN has 200 edges. A new sale banner goes live and a million phones request it in the same second. What does an origin shield change?
options: Edges skip their own cache and stream the banner directly from the origin
Edges ask the shield first, which collapses misses into about one origin request
The shield pushes the banner to all 200 edges before the sale starts
The shield lowers the TTL so edges revalidate the banner more often
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: Without a shield the origin could see one miss per edge, about 200 or more. The shield is an extra cache layer that all edges ask before the origin, and it merges simultaneous requests (request collapsing).

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: A seller replaces the main photo of product 4471, and every size of that product's images must update within seconds at the CDN. What is the best tool?
options: Wait for the 30-day s-maxage to expire on each copy
Send Vary: Accept so the CDN fetches the new photo
Purge by tag (surrogate key) product-4471
Change max-age on the origin to zero for all images
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: Tagging responses with a surrogate key lets one purge drop every cached size of that product's images in seconds. Browsers may still show the old photo for up to their max-age, which is acceptable for a photo.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: A team wants to cache the logged-in 'My Orders' page at the CDN for just 1 second to cut origin load. What is the right response?
options: Reject it: personal pages must be private or no-store; even 1 second can leak data
Accept it, since a 1-second TTL is too short for anyone else to see it
Accept it if the response also sends Vary: Accept
Accept it, but use no-cache so the CDN revalidates each time
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: Any shared cache of a personal page can serve one user's data to another, regardless of TTL. Personal responses and responses that set cookies should send private, no-store.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: You want the product page to load fast from the CDN but show an accurate price and 'only 3 left' badge during a flash sale. Which design fits?
options: Cache the shared page shell briefly; load price and stock from a small uncached API
Cache the full page including price for 30 days and purge on every change
Mark the whole page no-store so nothing is ever served from the edge
Cache the full page with stale-if-error so prices stay available
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: The common pattern is to cache the shared shell and fetch personal or fast-changing parts separately. Caching everything long forces constant purges, and no-store throws away the CDN's benefit.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: Which header lets the edge keep serving a cached image for a day if the origin goes down?
options: stale-while-revalidate=86400
s-maxage=86400
stale-if-error=86400
no-cache with an ETag
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: stale-if-error lets a cache serve a stale copy when the origin errors. stale-while-revalidate serves stale briefly while checking in the background; it is not about origin failure.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: On sale day, 50 million image requests arrive per hour at a 97% hit ratio. Roughly how many requests miss at the edges?
options: About 48.5 million, which all go to the origin
About 1.5 million, which the origin shield mostly absorbs
About 3 million, since each miss is retried once
About 150,000, since only 0.3% of requests miss
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: 3% of 50 million is 1.5 million misses; the other 48.5 million are served at the edges. Most misses then hit at the shield rather than the origin.

How does a CDN decide what to keep close.q: Why does a user in Chennai get faster responses from a CDN edge than from a distant origin?
options: The CDN compresses every file to a tenth of its original size
The edge renders pages faster because it has more CPU than the origin
The phone caches all files permanently after the first visit
DNS or anycast routes them to a nearby edge, cutting round trips to a few ms
How does a CDN decide what to keep close.why: DNS or anycast sends users to the closest edge, so a round trip might take about 5 ms instead of 40-80 ms. A product page loads dozens of files, so this saving adds up.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: A junior engineer says Redis is fast 'because it is single-threaded'. What is the main reason, according to the answer?
options: One thread is faster than many threads on any multi-core machine
Redis compresses all values so less data crosses the network
All data lives in RAM, which is about 1,000 times faster than SSD for random reads
Redis writes every command to disk sequentially, which is very fast
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: In-memory storage is the main reason: RAM reads take about 100 ns versus tens to hundreds of microseconds for SSD. Single-threading keeps Redis simple and lock-free without losing speed, but it is not the source of the speed.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: Two app servers send INCR stock:sku9 to the same Redis at the same moment. Why can the increments never interleave or be half-done?
options: Commands run one at a time on the main thread, so each command is atomic
Redis takes a row-level lock on the key for the duration of INCR
I/O threads queue the commands and merge them before execution
Replication to a replica confirms each INCR before the next runs
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: The main thread runs each command to completion before the next, so there are no locks and every command is atomic. I/O threads only read and write network bytes; they never execute commands.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: How does a single Redis thread serve 10,000 open client connections without stalling on a slow client?
options: It spawns one lightweight thread per connection and runs them in parallel
It forks a child process for every 1,000 connections
It processes connections round-robin and waits for each reply
I/O multiplexing: epoll reports which sockets are ready, and only those are handled
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: Redis asks the OS (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS) which sockets have data ready and handles only those, so it never blocks waiting on one client.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: On a many-core server with thousands of clients, profiling shows Redis CPU spent mostly on reading and writing socket bytes, not executing commands. Which setting is designed for this?
options: appendfsync always, so writes are spread over more disk threads
io-threads, so helper threads do network reads and writes while commands stay single-threaded
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru, so fewer keys need to be scanned
Enable multi-threaded command execution so commands run in parallel
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: Redis 6 added I/O threads to parallelise reading, parsing and writing replies; the main thread still executes every command in order. There is no setting to run commands in parallel on one instance.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: An engineer runs KEYS cart:* on a shard with 15 million keys and every client times out for several seconds. What should the team do?
options: Switch to UNLINK, which deletes matching keys in the background
Disable KEYS in production and iterate with SCAN using a cursor in small batches
Add I/O threads so KEYS runs in parallel with other commands
Add more shards so the KEYS command finishes faster
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: KEYS is O(N) and runs on the single command thread, blocking everyone. SCAN walks the keyspace in small batches with a cursor; I/O threads do not parallelise command execution.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: You need to delete a hash with 5 million fields without freezing Redis. What is the best approach?
options: Use DEL inside a MULTI/EXEC transaction so it runs atomically
Use DEL, then run BGREWRITEAOF to reclaim the memory later
Use HGETALL first to load the fields, then DEL in one call
Use UNLINK, which removes the key now and frees memory in a background thread
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: DEL frees all fields on the main thread, blocking all clients. UNLINK frees big values in the background; and better still, avoid creating such big keys.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: Your session Redis uses AOF with appendfsync everysec. The machine loses power. About how much data can be lost?
options: Up to about one second of writes, since the log is forced to disk once per second
Nothing, because AOF writes every command to disk before replying
Everything since the last RDB snapshot, which may be hours
Everything, because Redis keeps all data in RAM only
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: everysec fsyncs the AOF once a second, so writes since the last fsync may still be in memory or OS buffers. always is safest but slowest; RDB alone loses everything since the last snapshot.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: A pure product cache, where MySQL is the source of truth, needs fast warm restarts but can tolerate losing recent writes. Which persistence setup does the worked example use?
options: AOF with appendfsync always
AOF with appendfsync everysec plus RDB
RDB snapshots only
No persistence and synchronous replication
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: The cache shards run RDB only for compact files and faster warm restarts, since the database holds the real data. AOF everysec is used for the separate session store where losing more than a second is not acceptable.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: During a midnight deal, 40% of reads hit product:SKU9. The team adds 4 more shards, but one shard stays at 100% CPU. What is happening and what fixes it?
options: Slots are unbalanced; rebalancing hash slots evenly will spread the key
The shard is single-threaded; enable io-threads to run commands in parallel
The key's TTL is too short; a longer TTL will cut the shard's CPU
A hot key lives on one shard; add a short local app cache or split the key into copies
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: One key maps to one slot on one shard, so adding shards cannot spread its load. A 1-second in-process cache, read replicas, or copies like price:sku9:1 to :8 spread the reads.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: In the worked example, 200 app servers each keep a 1-second local cache of the hot product. About how many reads per second does Redis now see for that key?
options: About 40,000, a quarter of the original load
At most about 200, down from about 160,000
About 16,000, a tenth of the original load
About 2,000, since each server refreshes ten times per second
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: Each app server refreshes the key at most once a second, so 200 servers send about 200 reads per second instead of 160,000. The stock count stays in Redis using atomic DECR.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: A team wants to keep payment and order records only in Redis, with replicas for safety. What is the best objection?
options: Redis cannot persist data to disk, so a restart loses everything
Redis replicas cannot serve reads, so failover is impossible
Replication is asynchronous, so acknowledged writes can be lost, and data must fit in RAM
Redis commands are not atomic, so concurrent writes can corrupt records
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: A write acknowledged by the primary can be lost if it crashes before the replica receives it; WAIT reduces but does not remove this risk. For money or orders, keep the source of truth in a database built for it.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: In Redis Cluster, you need MGET on a user's cart and wishlist in one call, but it fails because the keys are on different slots. What fixes it?
options: Use hash tags like {user42}:cart and {user42}:wishlist so both map to one slot
Increase the number of hash slots beyond 16,384
Use KEYS user42* to fetch both values in one call
Send the commands to a replica, which holds all slots
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: Multi-key commands work only when all keys share a slot. Hash tags make Redis hash only the part in braces, forcing related keys into the same slot.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: How does Redis Cluster decide which node owns a key?
options: CRC16(key) mod 16384 gives a hash slot, and each primary owns a range of slots
hash(key) mod N, where N is the current number of primaries
A consistent-hashing ring where each node has 150 virtual nodes
The client sends each key to a random primary, which forwards it
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: Redis Cluster uses 16,384 fixed hash slots and assigns slot ranges to primaries. This spreads memory and CPU across machines, which is how Redis uses many cores: many single-threaded processes.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: App servers call GET for 50 product keys one by one, each waiting for its reply. Latency is high even though Redis CPU is low. What is the best fix?
options: Add I/O threads, since Redis is spending its time parsing commands
Move the keys into one big hash so lookups use fewer CPU cycles
Use MGET or pipelining, since the network round trip costs more than Redis's work
Enable AOF everysec so reads are served from disk in parallel
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: A data-centre round trip of 0.2-0.5 ms dwarfs a few microseconds of Redis work. Pipelining and batch commands like MGET avoid paying that round trip 50 times.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: Which statement about Redis's threading is accurate?
options: Redis is purely single-threaded; nothing else ever runs in parallel
Commands run on one thread, but background threads and a forked child do other work
Since Redis 6, commands execute in parallel across io-threads
Redis uses one thread per CPU core to run commands on different keys
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: Background threads free big values and flush the AOF, and RDB snapshots use a forked child process. Commands still run on a single main thread; I/O threads only handle network bytes.

Why is Redis so fast even though it most.q: During an RDB snapshot on a busy 60 GB instance, memory use rises noticeably and there is a brief pause. Why?
options: RDB writes every command to a log, doubling memory until the rewrite
The snapshot runs on the main thread and blocks until the file is written
Snapshots disable eviction, so new keys accumulate during the save
Forking a huge process can pause briefly, and copy-on-write copies pages that change
Why is Redis so fast even though it most.why: RDB forks a child that writes the dataset while the parent serves traffic. Copy-on-write only copies pages that change, so a busy instance uses extra memory, and forking a huge instance can pause it briefly.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: Your 4 cache servers use server = hash(key) % 4. You add a 5th server and switch to % 5. Roughly what share of keys now points to a different server?
options: About 20%
About 25%
About 80%
About 50%
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: A key stays only if hash % 4 equals hash % 5, which is 4 of every 20 values, so 20% stay and 80% move. 20% is what consistent hashing achieves, not modulo.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: You run 10 cache servers with hash % 10 and add an 11th. Roughly what share of keys moves?
options: About 91%, since only about 1 in 11 keys stays
About 9%, since the new server takes 1/11 of the keys
About 10%, since one server's worth of keys moves
About 50%, since half the remainders change
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: Going from N to N + 1 servers, only about 1/(N + 1) of keys stay, so about 10 in 11 move. With modulo, the bigger the cluster, the worse it gets.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: The product cache serves 200,000 reads/s at a 95% hit ratio across 4 servers. The team adds a 5th using key % N. What happens to database load?
options: It rises from about 10,000 to about 48,000 reads/s for a few minutes
It stays near 10,000 reads/s since the new server only adds capacity
It doubles to about 20,000 reads/s while the 5th server warms up
It jumps from about 10,000 to about 160,000 reads/s as the hit ratio falls to about 19%
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: With modulo, 80% of keys move, so only the 20% that stayed still hit: about 19% hit ratio and 160,000 DB reads/s, a self-inflicted outage. About 48,000 is the consistent-hashing outcome.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: On a consistent-hashing ring, how is a key's server chosen?
options: Hash the key and take the remainder mod the number of servers
Hash the key onto the ring and walk clockwise to the first server
Pick the server whose hash value is numerically closest in either direction
Ask a coordinator which server has the most free memory
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: Servers and keys are both hashed onto a ring of values; each key belongs to the first server clockwise, wrapping past the top back to 0. N never appears in the formula.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: A 5th server E joins a consistent-hashing ring (no virtual nodes) and lands between A and B. Which keys move?
options: All keys whose hash is greater than E's position move to E
Only keys in the arc from A to E, which move from B to E
About a fifth of each server's keys move to E
All of A's keys move to E, since E is just after A
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: Keys in the arc just before E used to walk on to B and now stop at E. Only B loses keys and only E gains them; without vnodes it does not take a little from every server.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: Without virtual nodes, server C on a ring A, B, C, D crashes. What is the operational risk?
options: All keys on the ring are remapped, causing a full miss storm
C's keys are lost permanently, even with replication
C's keys are split evenly across A, B and D
All of C's keys land on D, doubling D's load and risking a cascading failure
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: Only C's keys move, and they all go to the next server clockwise. Spreading them across many neighbours is exactly what virtual nodes provide.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: Your ring places each real server at only one point, and monitoring shows one server owns about 40% of keys while another owns 10%. What is the standard fix?
options: Give each server many virtual nodes, for example 100-256 points
Switch the hash function to SHA-256 for better security
Go back to key % N, which always splits keys evenly
Increase the replication factor to 3 on every key
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: With few points, random placement is lumpy; hundreds of vnodes per server even each share out to close to 1/N. The hash needs good spread, not cryptographic security.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: You add a new cache machine with twice the RAM of the others to a ring that uses 150 vnodes per server. How do you make it take a bigger share?
options: Place it at the top of the ring so it receives wrapped keys
Give it a lower replication factor than the others
Give it more virtual nodes, for example 300 instead of 150
Hash its name twice so it appears at a larger position
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: Weighting is done by vnode count: a server with more points owns proportionally more of the ring.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: A phone's product page gets 50,000 reads/s at midnight. The team already uses 200 vnodes per server, but one server is overloaded. Why, and what helps?
options: 200 vnodes is too few; raising it to 1,000 will spread that key
The ring is uneven; rehashing with xxHash will move the key
Replication factor is too low; RF 3 automatically spreads reads
Vnodes balance key ranges, not one key's popularity; use a local cache or key copies
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: One key still maps to exactly one server however many vnodes exist. A hot key needs an in-process cache or copies such as phone:1#1 and phone:1#2 read at random.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: With replication factor 3 on a ring with virtual nodes, why must you skip some vnodes when choosing replicas?
options: Skipping vnodes reduces the ring size and speeds up lookups
Consecutive vnodes may belong to the same physical server, so two copies could share a machine
Adjacent vnodes always sit in the same availability zone
The owner's vnode must be skipped so the primary copy is elsewhere
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: Replicas should be the next R distinct physical servers clockwise, ideally in different racks or zones. Otherwise one machine failure could take out two copies.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: An interviewer asks whether 'consistent' in consistent hashing refers to the C in CAP. What is correct?
options: Yes; it guarantees read-after-write consistency across replicas
Yes; it ensures all replicas agree before a write is acknowledged
No; it means keys map consistently to the same server as the cluster changes
Partly; it gives strong consistency only when vnodes are used
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: The term is about stable key-to-server mapping during membership changes. It says nothing about read-after-write correctness.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: A colleague says consistent hashing means adding a server moves zero data. What is accurate?
options: Some movement is unavoidable; it moves the minimum, about 1/(N + 1) of keys
It is true when every server has at least 100 virtual nodes
It is true for removals, but additions move about half the keys
Movement is zero for caches but not for replicated databases
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: The new server must own something, so roughly 1/(N + 1) of keys move to it, and only from the affected servers. Removing a server moves only its own keys, about 1/N.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: Which system does NOT use a hash ring, but still avoids remapping most keys when a node joins?
options: Redis Cluster, using 16,384 fixed hash slots assigned to nodes
Apache Cassandra, using a token ring with vnodes
Memcached clients using Ketama-style hashing
Amazon Dynamo-style stores using preference lists
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: Redis Cluster maps keys with CRC16(key) % 16384 and moves slot ranges between nodes. N never appears in the formula, so only some slots move when a node joins.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: In a Java ring implementation backed by a TreeMap, what does serverFor(key) do when ceilingEntry(hash(key)) returns null?
options: Throws an exception because the key is outside the ring
Returns the last entry, the server just before the key
Wraps around and returns the first entry in the map
Adds a new virtual node at the key's position
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: A null ceiling means the key's position is past the last server, so the lookup wraps to the start of the ring, just like walking clockwise past the top.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: A ring has 10 servers with 200 vnodes each. Roughly how many comparisons does a TreeMap lookup take?
options: About 200, one per vnode of the target server
About 11, since lookup is O(log V) over 2,000 entries
About 2,000, one per entry on the ring
About 10, one per real server
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: V = 10 x 200 = 2,000 entries, and log2 of 2,000 is about 11. More vnodes give smoother balance at the cost of a bigger ring table.

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.q: On sale night one of 5 cache servers (150 vnodes each) crashes. How does its load spread?
options: All of its keys go to the single next server, doubling that server
Every key on the ring is remapped, causing an 80% miss storm
Its keys stay unavailable until the server restarts
Its ~20% of keys spread across the other 4, about 5% extra each
If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5t.why: With vnodes, the failed server's many small arcs are owned by many different neighbours. Without vnodes, everything would land on one unlucky neighbour.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: A signup page checks a Bloom filter of taken usernames. For 'sethu_k' the filter answers 'definitely not'. How reliable is that answer?
options: About 99% correct, since the false positive rate is 1%
Reliable only if the filter was rebuilt in the last 24 hours
Always correct: a Bloom filter never gives false negatives
Unreliable: it must always be confirmed with the database
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: Any added name sets all its k bits, and bits are never switched off, so finding a 0 bit proves the name was never added. The 1% error applies only to 'maybe yes' answers.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: A 10-bit filter has bits 1, 2, 4, 7 and 9 set. A name hashes to positions 2, 5 and 9. What does the filter say?
options: Definitely not added, because bit 5 is 0
Maybe yes, because two of its three bits are 1
Maybe yes, because bits 2 and 9 match an existing name
Definitely added, because most of its bits are set
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: If any of an item's bits is 0, the item was never added. All three bits must be 1 for a 'maybe yes'.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: 'kiran' was never added to the filter, yet all three of its bits are 1 because 'ravi' and 'meena' set them. What is this called, and what should the signup page do?
options: A false negative; rebuild the filter immediately
A hash collision; tell the user the name is taken
A false positive; tell the user the name is taken to stay safe
A false positive; confirm 'maybe taken' with a database check
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: Other items switching on the same bits causes a wrong 'maybe yes'. 'Maybe' means 'go and check'; otherwise about 1 in 100 users would be wrongly told a free name is taken.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: About how much memory does a Bloom filter need for 10 crore usernames at a 1% false positive rate?
options: About 1.2 GB, the size of the raw username text
About 120 MB, at roughly 9.6 bits per item with k = 7
About 6-10 GB, similar to a Java HashSet
About 12 MB, at roughly 1 bit per item
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: m = -n ln(p) / (ln 2)^2 gives about 9.6 bits per item for 1%, so 10 crore items need about 120 MB. A HashSet<String> would take 6-10 GB because it stores every name.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: You need a filter for 5 crore product IDs at 1% false positives. Roughly how much memory and how many hash functions?
options: About 120 MB with k = 7
About 60 MB with k = 7
About 60 MB with k = 3
About 30 MB with k = 10
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: 5 crore times 9.6 bits is about 480 million bits, which is about 60 MB, and the best k for 1% is about 7. k = 3 is the best count for a 10% target.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: Your filter at 1% false positives (9.6 bits/item) is too noisy, and you want 0.1%. Roughly how many bits per item do you need?
options: About 96, since 10x fewer errors needs 10x more bits
About 19.2, since you need twice the bits for each 10x
About 9.6, but with k raised from 7 to 20
About 14.4, since each extra 4.8 bits per item cuts errors 10 times
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: Every extra 4.8 bits per item cuts false positives tenfold: 9.6 for 1%, 14.4 for 0.1%, 19.2 for 0.01%. Raising k beyond the best value fills the array faster and increases errors.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: A developer says 'more hash functions always make a Bloom filter more accurate', and wants k = 30 instead of 7 for a 1% filter. What is the issue?
options: Past the best k, extra hashes fill the array faster and raise false positives
More hashes are always more accurate, but lookups become too slow
k must equal the number of bytes per item, so 30 is invalid
More hashes cause false negatives when bits overlap
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: The best k leaves about half the bits at 1 when full; going higher sets more bits per item and makes coincidental matches more likely. Bloom filters never produce false negatives regardless of k.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: You sized a filter for 10 crore names at 1%, but the platform grew to 20 crore names. What happens to the false positive rate?
options: It doubles to about 2%, in proportion to the item count
It stays at 1%, since the error rate is set at creation
It jumps to about 16%, since bits per item halve while k stays 7
It becomes 0%, since more bits are set to 1
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: Overfilling is the real danger: at double the planned load, 1% becomes about 16%. Size for growth, watch the fraction of bits set, and rebuild bigger when needed.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: A user deletes their account, and a developer switches off that username's k bits in the plain Bloom filter. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing; the name is simply removed and lookups stay correct
The deleted name will still show 'maybe yes' until the next rebuild
The false positive rate rises because fewer bits are set
Shared bits are cleared, so other existing names may be reported 'definitely not' wrongly
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: Bits can be shared by several items, so clearing them causes false negatives, breaking the filter's one promise. Use a counting Bloom filter, a cuckoo filter, or periodic rebuilds instead.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: You need deletes in a membership filter and can afford extra memory. Which option does the answer describe, and at what cost?
options: A plain Bloom filter with a second bit array for deleted items, at 2x memory
A counting Bloom filter with small per-position counters, at about 4x the memory
A Java HashSet of deleted names, with no extra memory for the filter
A counting Bloom filter, at the same memory as a plain filter
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: Each position holds a small counter (often 4 bits): add increments, delete decrements. Cuckoo filters support deletes at near-Bloom memory; periodic rebuilds are the simplest fix.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: Two users both see 'sethu_k' as available and click Sign Up at the same moment. What ensures only one gets it?
options: The Bloom filter's add() is atomic, so the second check fails
The second user's filter lookup now returns 'definitely not'
The database's unique constraint lets one insert win; the filter never decides
A counting Bloom filter tracks pending signups to prevent duplicates
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: The filter is only a cheap pre-check. The source of truth, the unique constraint, decides races; the losing user sees 'just taken'.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: Bots hammer a Zomato-like app with random restaurant IDs that don't exist. The cache always misses and the database is overloaded. How does a Bloom filter help?
options: A filter of valid IDs rejects 'definitely not real' IDs before cache and DB
A filter of recently requested IDs tells the cache to store them longer
A filter of invalid IDs blocks bots after their first request
A filter of cached IDs lets the DB skip writing new restaurants
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: This is cache penetration: missing keys never get cached, so every request falls to the DB. A Bloom filter of valid IDs stops fake IDs up front, letting only about 1% slip through.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: Why do RocksDB, Cassandra and HBase keep a Bloom filter per on-disk file?
options: To skip reading any sorted file that definitely does not contain the key
To store the keys compactly so the files can be deleted
To detect corrupted files by checking their bit patterns
To decide which file to compact first in the LSM tree
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: In an LSM tree a key may be in any of many files. An in-memory Bloom filter per file lets a lookup skip files that definitely lack the key, saving many disk reads.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: A news feed uses a per-user Bloom filter of articles already shown. What happens on a false positive?
options: A previously seen article is shown again to the user
The user's feed fails to load until the filter is rebuilt
One fresh article is skipped, which is a harmless cost
All articles from that source are hidden from the user
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: A false 'maybe seen' just skips one unseen item. The filter never wrongly says 'not seen' for an article that was shown, so repeats do not happen.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: What does the memory needed by a Bloom filter depend on?
options: The number of items and the average length of each item
Only the number of items and the target false positive rate
The total bytes of all items stored in the filter
The number of servers that will query the filter
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: The filter never stores items, so memory depends only on n and p. That is why 10 crore usernames fit in about 120 MB versus 1.2 GB of raw text.

How can a system answer \"is this userna.q: Many signup servers must share one up-to-date filter of usernames. What does the answer suggest for production?
options: Write a custom filter with SHA-256 hashes on each server
Store every username in a Redis set and call it a Bloom filter
Keep a separate filter per server and never synchronise them
Use a tested library or RedisBloom (BF.ADD, BF.EXISTS) shared by all servers
How can a system answer \"is this userna.why: Guava's BloomFilter is a tested in-process option, and RedisBloom lets many servers share one filter. A Redis set would store every name and lose the memory advantage.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: An interviewer asks, 'Explain L1, L2 and L3 caches with an e-commerce example.' What is the best way to start?
options: Assume CPU caches, since L1/L2/L3 always refers to hardware
Assume app tiers, since CPU caches are irrelevant to engineers
Clarify it can mean CPU caches or app cache tiers, then cover both briefly
Say L1, L2 and L3 are Redis replication levels
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: The terms are used for both hardware caches and application tiers, and interviewers mean either. Covering both shows you understand the shared idea: keep the hot part close.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: Roughly what latencies do CPU L1, L2, L3 and RAM have on a modern server?
options: About 1 ns, 3-5 ns, 10-20 ns and 80-100 ns
About 1 µs, 5 µs, 20 µs and 100 µs
About 1 ns, 2 ns, 3 ns and 4 ns
About 10 ns, 1 ns, 100 ns and 1 ms
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: Each level is bigger and slower: L1 ~1 ns per core, L2 ~3-5 ns per core, L3 ~10-20 ns shared, RAM ~80-100 ns. The gap to RAM is the memory wall.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: Which CPU cache level is shared by all cores on the chip?
options: L1, because it holds instructions for all cores
L2, because it sits between L1 and RAM
None; every level is private to one core
L3, the last-level cache
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: L1 and L2 are per core; L3 (8-100+ MB) is shared across cores. Coherence protocols like MESI keep each core's copies consistent.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: A hot pricing loop walks a linked list of rules and is several times slower than an array version, though both are O(n). Why?
options: Linked lists use more CPU instructions per element than arrays
Array elements share 64-byte cache lines and prefetch well; list hops miss and wait on RAM
Arrays are stored in L3 while linked lists are always stored in RAM
The JVM cannot JIT-compile loops over linked lists
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: Contiguous arrays exploit spatial locality and the prefetcher streams them. Pointer-chasing jumps to scattered addresses, so most steps miss L1/L2 and wait about 100 ns for RAM.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: Two threads each increment their own counter, but the parallel version is slower than one thread. The counters are adjacent fields in one object. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: Lock contention; replace the counters with a synchronized block
False sharing on one 64-byte line; pad the counters onto separate cache lines
L3 is too small; move the counters into a larger heap object
Prefetching failure; convert the counters into a linked list
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: Different variables in the same cache line make the line bounce between cores on every write. Padding hot per-thread counters onto separate lines removes the contention.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: In application cache tiers, what are L1, L2 and L3 typically?
options: Redis, the database buffer pool, and the CDN
The CDN, Redis, and in-process memory
Browser cache, in-process memory, and Redis
In-process memory, a distributed cache like Redis, and the CDN/edge
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: L1 is inside each app server (microseconds), L2 is a shared cluster (~0.3-1 ms), and L3 is the edge near users. Some write-ups call the database buffer pool L3; the principle is the same.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: With a 90% hit ratio at L1 and 90% of the remainder hit at L2, what share of reads reaches the database?
options: About 1%
About 10%
About 19%
About 0.1%
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: 10% miss L1, and 10% of those miss L2, so 0.1 x 0.1 = 1% reach the database. Multiplied hit ratios are why tiers shed so much load.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: A sale SKU is read 120,000 times per second from 300 app servers, overloading one Redis shard. What single change helps most?
options: Add more Redis shards so the key is spread across them
Raise the Redis TTL to 1 hour so the key never expires
A 1-second in-process L1 entry per server, leaving about 300 Redis reads/s
Move the SKU to the CDN with a 1-year versioned URL
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: One key lives on one shard, so more shards do not help. With a 1-second L1 TTL, each server reads Redis for that key at most once per second, about 300 reads/s.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: Which data is the best fit for an L1 in-process cache?
options: Per-user carts that must look the same on every server
Large search facets too big to fit in one server's memory
The final inventory count used to accept an order
Small, very hot, read-mostly data like pricing rules or feature flags
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: L1 suits tiny, hot data where a few seconds of staleness is fine. Carts and sessions belong in shared L2, and inventory decisions must use the source of truth.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: Which data belongs in the L3/CDN tier rather than L1 or L2?
options: A user's session and cart contents
Images, JS/CSS and logged-out listing pages, identical for many users
The wallet balance shown before payment
Expensive per-user recommendation results
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: The CDN serves everyone the same thing: static assets, logged-out pages, even short-lived API responses. Personalised data mostly cannot live there.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: At 12:00:05 a deal price drops. 400 app servers hold the old price in a 2-second L1 cache. How does the worked example keep them in sync?
options: Each server polls the database every 100 ms for price changes
The CDN purges the price and app servers reload from it
A Kafka PriceChanged event updates Redis and a pub/sub broadcast drops every L1 entry
L1 entries are write-through, so Redis updates them directly
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: The consumer writes v58 into Redis and sends a pub/sub invalidation; servers drop L1 within about 100 ms. The short TTL caps worst-case staleness at 2 seconds on the page.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: A late invalidation message arrives after newer data was already cached. Which technique stops it overwriting the newer value?
options: Versioned keys like product:123:v42, so old versions are simply not read
A longer L1 TTL so the newer value stays cached
Write-behind so the newer value is flushed first
Request coalescing so only one request rebuilds the key
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: When data changes the version bumps, so stale entries and late messages refer to an old key. Coalescing addresses stampedes, not ordering.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: Your 10-minute Redis TTL for 50,000 popular products expires at the same moment, and the catalogue database falls over. Which pair of fixes is best?
options: Jitter TTLs and use single-flight or stale-while-revalidate on misses
Remove TTLs entirely and rely on manual invalidation
Add more L1 tiers so misses take longer to reach the database
Shorten the TTL to 1 minute so each expiry is smaller
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: Jitter spreads expiries; coalescing or serving stale lets one request rebuild each key while others wait. Pre-warming before the sale also helps.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: A team says 'our hit ratio is 99%, so the database is safe on sale day'. What is the flaw?
options: A 99% hit ratio means the cache is too large and wasting memory
Hit ratio is irrelevant; only cache latency matters for the database
If the 1% of misses arrive together (mass expiry, cold start), you still get a stampede
99% is impossible across tiers, so the metric must be wrong
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: Average hit ratio hides bursts. Stagger TTLs, warm caches before the sale, and coalesce misses so simultaneous misses do not all hit the database.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: A product manager proposes adding a fourth cache layer 'to be extra fast'. What is the best response?
options: Agree; more layers always reduce latency and database load
Every layer adds staleness and invalidation work; add one only for a named problem
Agree, as long as each layer uses the same TTL
Disagree; three is the maximum supported by Redis
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: Each tier must be justified by a specific problem such as latency, hot keys or load. Otherwise it only adds consistency complexity.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: During a 30-second Redis failover on sale day, what keeps the product page up in the worked example?
options: The CDN automatically caches all API responses during failover
Checkout switches to reading prices from L1 instead of the source
The database scales up instantly to absorb all Redis traffic
L1 entries and stale-while-revalidate keep serving; misses go through a circuit breaker
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: L1 keeps serving hot keys and stale entries are served where allowed, while misses go to the database through a circuit breaker and rate limiter. Checkout never trusts cached prices.

What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.q: On the product page, the 'only 3 left' badge comes from cache. Where must the decision to sell the unit come from?
options: The L1 cache, since it is refreshed every 2 seconds
Redis L2, since it is invalidated by Kafka events
An atomic reservation against the inventory source of truth
The CDN's cached API response for the product
What are L1, L2 and L3 caches, what prob.why: Cache the display count if you like, but the decision to sell must use the atomic source of truth, or a stale value causes overselling. The same goes for the price charged at payment.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: Two clients each GET stock:PHONE-128 (value 1) and then DECR it in separate calls. Stock ends at -1. What is the best fix in Redis?
options: Use DECR instead of DECRBY, since DECR is atomic
Pipeline the GET and DECR so they travel in one packet
A Lua script that reads, checks and decrements as one atomic step
Wrap GET and DECR in MULTI/EXEC and branch on the GET result
