What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: Each command is atomic, but a sequence from one client is not. MULTI/EXEC cannot branch on a value read inside it because reads return only at EXEC; pipelining just batches network traffic.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: Why is a Redis Lua script atomic?
options: It runs start to finish on Redis's single main thread, so nothing interleaves
Redis takes a global lock that other threads must wait on
Redis copies the data, runs the script, then swaps the copy in
Lua scripts run on a dedicated thread that has priority over clients
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: Redis executes commands one at a time on one thread, and a script is executed as one unit there. That is also why a slow script blocks every other client.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: A script decrements a coupon counter, then calls SADD on a key that turns out to hold a string, raising an error. What state is Redis left in?
options: Both writes are undone, since scripts are all-or-nothing
The decrement is undone, but the error is logged for retry
Redis refuses the whole script before running any command
The decrement stays; Redis does not roll back scripts on error
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: Scripts are atomic in the sense of no interleaving, not all-or-nothing. That is why you validate everything first and write last.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: You are writing a script that checks stock, validates the quantity and then writes. What ordering does the answer recommend?
options: Write first, then check, and undo the write if the check fails
Do all checks and input validation first, then all writes
Interleave each check with its write to keep the script short
Use redis.pcall for every write so errors roll back automatically
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: Because there is no rollback, a failure after the first write leaves partial changes. Checks first, writes last; pcall only returns errors as values, it does not undo anything.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: A developer writes a Lua script that loops over 1 million keys to recompute totals. During peak, other clients start getting BUSY errors. What is the lesson?
options: Lua runs in parallel, so the BUSY error means too many I/O threads
Scripts block the whole server; keep them O(1) or small-N, usually under 1 ms
BUSY means the script was rolled back; just retry it
Raise busy-reply-threshold so other clients wait without errors
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: While a script runs, every other client waits; after busy-reply-threshold (default 5 s) Redis answers BUSY. A long script is an outage for everyone, so keep scripts tiny and bounded.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: A script that has already written data is stuck running past the busy threshold. How can you stop it?
options: With SCRIPT KILL, which also rolls back its writes
With FUNCTION DELETE, which aborts the running function
With CLIENT KILL on the calling client, which stops the script
Only with SHUTDOWN NOSAVE, since SCRIPT KILL works only for read-only scripts
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: SCRIPT KILL can stop a script that has not written. Once it has written, stopping it would leave data half-changed, so Redis only allows SHUTDOWN NOSAVE.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: In Redis Cluster, a script using stock:PHONE-128 and holds:PHONE-128 fails with CROSSSLOT. What is the fix?
options: Use hash tags like stock:{PHONE-128} and holds:{PHONE-128} so both land in one slot
Build the key names inside the script instead of passing them in KEYS
Run the script with EVALSHA instead of EVAL
Split the script into two MULTI/EXEC transactions on each node
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: A script runs on one node, so all keys must share a hash slot. Hash tags hash only the braced part; keys should always be passed via KEYS so the cluster can route and check them.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: In EVAL "<script>" 1 stock:PHONE-128 1, what does the first 1 after the script mean?
options: The script should be run once and then cached
The quantity to reserve is 1
One of the following arguments is a key, so stock:PHONE-128 is KEYS[1]
The script uses Redis database number 1
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: numkeys tells Redis how many following arguments are KEYS; the rest go to ARGV. Here ARGV[1] = 1 is the quantity wanted.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: Your order service sends the same 2 KB Lua script on every checkout call. How do you save bandwidth, and what happens after a Redis restart?
options: Use EVALSHA; after a restart Redis replays scripts from the AOF
Use MULTI/EXEC to send the script once per transaction
Compress the script with gzip before sending it with EVAL
SCRIPT LOAD then EVALSHA by hash; on NOSCRIPT, clients fall back to EVAL
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: SCRIPT LOAD returns a SHA1 you call with EVALSHA. If Redis forgot the script, you get NOSCRIPT and libraries like redis-py's register_script fall back to EVAL automatically.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: You want named, versioned server-side logic that persists with the dataset and replicates, so apps don't keep reloading scripts. What does Redis 7 offer?
options: SCRIPT LOAD with a persistent flag set to yes
Functions, loaded with FUNCTION LOAD and called with FCALL
EVALSHA with the script's SHA1 stored in the AOF
Modules written in Lua and loaded at startup
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: Redis 7 Functions are named libraries that persist with the dataset and replicate to replicas. Scripts loaded via SCRIPT LOAD can be lost on restart.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: On sale day, a hot SKU uses WATCH plus MULTI/EXEC for reservations, and most transactions abort and retry. Why is Lua the better tool here?
options: Lua runs on multiple threads, so contention disappears
Lua takes a lock on the key, while WATCH does not
Lua reads, decides and writes in one pass with no retries under contention
Lua rolls back on conflict, while MULTI/EXEC does not
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: WATCH is optimistic locking: if the key changes before EXEC, the transaction aborts and retries, which is constant on a hot key. A Lua script is atomic by construction, so it never needs to retry.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: Your service releases a lock with GET lock in the app, then DEL lock if the value matches its token. Occasionally it deletes another worker's lock. What fixes it?
options: A script that compares the value to the token and deletes in one atomic step
Use UNLINK instead of DEL so deletion happens in the background
Add a longer TTL to the lock so it never expires early
Use SET NX on release so only the owner can delete
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: Between your GET and DEL, your lock could expire and be taken by someone else. 'if GET == token then DEL' in a script removes the lock only if it is still yours.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: A coupon script returns {1, 9312} and the order service applies the discount. Where should the durable record of the redemption live?
options: In the database as the source of truth, reconciled with the Redis counter
Only in Redis, since the script made the decision atomically
In the script's return value, cached in the app for an hour
In a Redis replica, which is guaranteed to have every write
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: Redis is the fast gate; orders and money belong in the database. Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose the last few writes, which is why a reconciliation job compares counts.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: Payment fails after a customer's coupon was redeemed in Redis. What does the worked example do?
options: Do nothing; the counter self-corrects at the next reconciliation
Call DEL on the coupon keys and reload them from the database
Run a release script that INCRs the counter and SREMs the user, atomically
Run INCR from the app, then SREM in a separate call
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: A small release script reverses both changes as one step, so no other request sees a half-reverted state. Separate calls would reintroduce the race the script avoids.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: Which task is a natural fit for a Redis Lua script?
options: Calling an external payment gateway and storing its response
A per-user token-bucket rate limiter that refills and takes a token in one call
Reading a CSV file from disk and loading it into a hash
Running a nightly report that scans every key in the database
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: Rate limiting is check-then-act on Redis data and O(1) per call. Scripts cannot make network calls or touch files, and a full keyspace scan would block the server.

What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.q: A script uses the current time and a random number. Is this safe with replication in Redis 7?
options: No; replicas re-run the script and would get different results
Only if the script is called with EVALSHA instead of EVAL
Only if every replica's clock is synchronised to the primary
Yes; replicas receive the script's effects (the writes), not the script itself
What is Redis Lua scripting, and when sh.why: Since Redis 5, and as the only mode in Redis 7, effects replication sends the actual writes. So non-deterministic inputs like time or randomness are safe.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: Which description of Apache Kafka is most accurate?
options: A task queue where each message is processed once and then deleted
A distributed database for querying the latest state of each order
A distributed, durable, replicated log that many consumers read and can replay
An API gateway that routes synchronous requests between services
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: Producers publish events once; independent consumers read them in order at their own pace, and events are retained for replay. A task queue deletes messages after consumption.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: Ten systems produce data and fifteen consume it, each integrated directly. How does a Kafka backbone change the number of connections?
options: From up to about 150 point-to-point links to about 25 connections to Kafka
From 150 links to 10, since only producers connect to Kafka
From 25 links to 150, since every consumer needs every topic
It stays at 150, but each link becomes asynchronous
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: N x M direct integrations become N + M connections to one backbone, with one format discipline and one place to monitor.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: Checkout synchronously calls six services, each 99.9% available. Roughly what is checkout's availability from those calls alone?
options: 99.9%, since each service is 99.9% available
About 94%, since each call removes one percent
About 99.99%, since retries mask most failures
About 99.4%, around 4 hours of failures a month
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: 0.999^6 is about 99.4%. With Kafka, checkout depends only on Kafka accepting the event, and downstream outages show up as lag, not failed checkouts.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: At midnight on sale day, orders hit 20x normal and the SMS provider cannot keep up. With Kafka between checkout and SMS, what happens?
options: Kafka drops excess SMS events once the partition is full
Events build up as consumer lag and are worked off later; checkout is unaffected
Checkout slows down until SMS catches up, since Kafka applies backpressure
Kafka redirects excess events to the email consumer instead
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: Kafka absorbs the spike: SMS falls behind (in the example by 2 million messages) and confirmations arrive minutes late, but nothing is lost and checkout keeps returning in about 200 ms.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: A new fraud team wants to train on the last 7 days of orders and then score live orders without asking other teams to change anything. Which Kafka property enables this?
options: Exactly-once delivery, so the fraud team never sees duplicates
Retention plus independent consumer groups; replay from the earliest retained offset
Global ordering across partitions, so the history is consistent
Per-message acks, so old messages are re-sent to the new team
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: Kafka keeps events for a retention period, and each consumer group tracks its own offsets. The fraud team creates a group, replays the week, then continues live while producers and others are unaffected.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: Invoice PDFs must be generated once per order, with per-message retry and priority for B2B orders. What is the best choice?
options: A Kafka topic with one consumer group per priority level
Kafka with a long retention so failed PDFs can be replayed
Redis Streams, since invoice generation must be memory-bound
A RabbitMQ or SQS work queue, optionally fed by a Kafka consumer
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: Queues are for work done once, with per-message acks, retry and priority built in. Kafka is for facts read by many; it can still feed the queue from order events.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: A colleague says 'Kafka is just a faster RabbitMQ'. What is the key difference?
options: Their retention and consumption models: a replayable log for many readers vs a task broker
Kafka uses AMQP while RabbitMQ uses a custom binary protocol
RabbitMQ is distributed while Kafka runs on a single broker
Kafka supports routing via exchanges while RabbitMQ does not
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: Throughput is not the main difference. Kafka keeps events for many independent readers and replay; RabbitMQ routes tasks to workers and usually deletes them once consumed, with flexible exchanges and priorities.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: You need every event for a given order (placed, paid, shipped) to be processed in order. How do you achieve this in Kafka?
options: Use a single partition for the whole topic, since Kafka orders globally
Rely on Kafka's global ordering across all partitions
Use order_id as the message key so all its events go to one partition
Use a random key so events spread evenly and stay ordered
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: Kafka guarantees order only within a partition. Keying by the entity ID keeps each entity's events together and in order while still allowing parallelism across entities.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: A team assumes Kafka's exactly-once feature means their consumer that sends SMS will never send duplicates. What is the gap?
options: Exactly-once only works if replication factor is 1
Exactly-once covers SMS only if the consumer uses acks=all
There is no gap; transactions extend to all downstream systems
Exactly-once applies within Kafka; external side effects still need idempotent handlers
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: The idempotent producer and transactions give exactly-once inside Kafka. Calling an SMS provider is outside Kafka, so the handler must be idempotent to avoid duplicates on retry.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: A product manager wants the coupon-validation check ('is this coupon valid?') to go through Kafka. What is the best response?
options: Agree; Kafka can return a response faster than any API
Keep it a synchronous API call; Kafka is for events others react to
Agree, but use a single partition so the answer is ordered
Agree, and set retention to zero so the request is not stored
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: A request that needs an immediate answer is still request-response. Kafka is for things that happened and that other systems react to asynchronously.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: Search shows old prices for 30 minutes after a midnight price drop because it polls the catalogue database. How does the worked example fix this with Kafka?
options: Search polls Kafka every 30 minutes instead of the database
Checkout publishes prices to search through a direct API call
Debezium CDC streams price changes into Kafka, and a Connect sink updates search in seconds
A nightly ETL job copies prices from Kafka into the search index
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: Change data capture turns every catalogue and price change into an event, and a Connect sink applies it to search within seconds. Batch and polling are exactly the latency Kafka removes.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: Which combination of settings does the answer give for not losing data in Kafka?
options: RF 3, acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2, idempotent producer, commit offsets after processing
RF 1, acks=0, and committing offsets before processing
RF 3, acks=1, and auto-committing offsets every 5 seconds
RF 2, acks=all, and min.insync.replicas=3
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: Replication plus acks=all with min ISR 2 means a write is on at least two brokers before it is acknowledged. Committing offsets only after processing prevents a crash from skipping events.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: Only the notification service needs order events, and no one needs replay. Kafka or SQS?
options: SQS is simpler here; choose Kafka when several teams need the same events and replay
Kafka, since SQS cannot deliver order events reliably
Kafka, since any event-driven design should use a log
SQS, but only if the events are larger than 1 MB
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: For one consumer with simple decoupling, a managed queue has zero ops. Kafka's value grows when many independent consumers share the same stream and need replay.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: A team wants Kafka semantics and the same Kafka clients, but with fewer servers and no JVM or ZooKeeper. Which option fits?
options: RabbitMQ, which supports the Kafka protocol via exchanges
AWS SQS, which accepts Kafka clients through FIFO queues
Redpanda, a Kafka-API-compatible engine written in C++
Redis Streams, which is the Kafka protocol inside Redis
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: Redpanda keeps the Kafka API with simpler operations and lower latency. Azure Event Hubs also speaks the Kafka protocol, but RabbitMQ, SQS and Redis Streams do not.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: Which technology does the answer recommend for a multi-tenant platform with heavy, built-in geo-replication?
options: NATS JetStream
Apache Pulsar
AWS SQS
Redis Streams
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: Pulsar separates compute and storage (BookKeeper) and has multi-tenancy and geo-replication built in. NATS suits lightweight low-latency messaging, and Redis Streams is memory-bound.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: A bug in the loyalty service mis-credited points for 3 hours. How does Kafka help fix the damage?
options: Ask checkout to republish the last 3 hours of orders
Restore the loyalty database from last night's backup only
Delete the affected partitions so the events are sent again
Fix the bug, rewind the loyalty consumer group to the incident start, and reprocess
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: Events are retained, so a consumer group can be rewound to an earlier offset and recompute. No producer or other consumer needs to change.

What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.q: Why can a modest Kafka cluster handle millions of events per second on ordinary disks?
options: Every event is stored in RAM only and never written to disk
Consumers delete events after reading, keeping logs very small
Sequential appends, batching and compression, page cache, zero-copy, partition parallelism
Each event is indexed by a B-tree for fast random access
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: Writes are sequential appends and reads are sequential scans served largely from the OS page cache, often with zero-copy transfer. Partitions spread work across brokers and consumers.

options: At LinkedIn around 2010, to move activity data and metrics in real time
At Google around 2004, as the storage layer for Bigtable
At Amazon around 2007, as part of the Dynamo paper
At Netflix around 2015, to stream video between data centres
What is Kafka, what problem does it solv.why: LinkedIn built Kafka for page views, searches and metrics at volumes older brokers could not handle. It was open-sourced in 2011 and its creators founded Confluent.

What are the different terminologies in.q: Your team publishes OrderPlaced, PaymentCaptured and OrderShipped for each order and needs consumers to see one order's events in sequence. What should the Kafka key be?
options: order_id, so all events of one order land in the same partition and stay in order
A random UUID per event, so load spreads evenly across all partitions
No key at all, because Kafka keeps strict order across the entire topic
The event timestamp, so Kafka sorts events by time across the whole topic
What are the different terminologies in.why: The key decides the partition and is the unit of ordering, and order is guaranteed only inside a partition. Timestamps are not an ordering guarantee across producers, and Kafka never orders a whole multi-partition topic.

What are the different terminologies in.q: The search team wants every new search node to boot with the current price of every SKU, without replaying years of price changes. Which Kafka feature fits best?
options: A log-compacted product-prices topic keyed by sku_id, read from the beginning
A dead-letter topic that collects only the most recent price per SKU
Tiered storage so years of price history can be replayed cheaply from S3
A product-prices topic with 7-day time-based retention, read from latest
What are the different terminologies in.why: Log compaction keeps only the latest event per key, so reading from the start yields exactly the current price per SKU. Tiered storage keeps more history cheaply but still forces a full replay of every change.

What are the different terminologies in.q: order-events has 12 partitions and the fulfilment consumer group runs 20 instances on sale day. What actually happens?
options: Only 12 instances get partitions; the other 8 sit idle
Each of the 20 instances reads all 12 partitions in parallel
Kafka automatically splits the topic into 20 partitions to match
All 20 share the load, each taking about 60% of a partition
What are the different terminologies in.why: Within a group each partition goes to exactly one consumer, so parallelism is capped at the partition count. Partitions are never split between members of the same group, and Kafka does not repartition automatically.

What are the different terminologies in.q: Payments are produced with acks=all, yet a broker failure still lost a captured-payment event. What setting was most likely missing?
options: The producer was not idempotent, so the retry overwrote the event
min.insync.replicas was 1; it should be 2 with replication factor 3
linger.ms was too high, so the batch was dropped during failover
auto.offset.reset was set to latest instead of earliest on the producer
What are the different terminologies in.why: acks=all only waits for the current in-sync replicas; if min.insync.replicas is 1 and only the leader was in sync, the write lived in one copy. Idempotence prevents duplicates and reordering on retry, not loss on broker failure.

What are the different terminologies in.q: At midnight on a sale day, lag on the order-notifications consumer group jumps from 0 to 2 million. What does this mean and what is the right response?
options: The topic is full; delete old segments manually so new orders can be written
Kafka has started dropping events; immediately raise retention.ms so nothing more is lost
The producer is broken; switch checkout to acks=0 so it stops waiting on the brokers
Confirmations are minutes late but not lost; scale consumers up to the partition count or shed non-critical work
What are the different terminologies in.why: Consumer lag means the group is behind, while events wait safely in Kafka; you catch up by adding consumers (up to the partition count) or deferring non-critical work. Lag does not mean data loss, and dropping to acks=0 would make durability worse.

What are the different terminologies in.q: The legacy catalogue lives in MySQL, and the catalogue team has no bandwidth to build APIs. Search and recommendations need every product change. What is the cleanest Kafka-based approach?
options: Use MirrorMaker 2 to copy the MySQL database into a Kafka cluster
Have search poll the MySQL tables every minute and diff the results
Write a Kafka Streams KTable directly on top of the MySQL tables
Use a Debezium CDC source connector in Kafka Connect to turn each row change into an event
What are the different terminologies in.why: Debezium CDC is a Connect source connector that publishes every row change as an event without the owning team writing code. MirrorMaker replicates Kafka topics between clusters, not databases.

What are the different terminologies in.q: A stream job reads order-events and writes both invoice-events and loyalty-points-events. A crash must never produce an invoice without points, or points twice. What Kafka feature guarantees this?
options: acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 on both output topics
An idempotent producer, which makes retries unable to create duplicates
Log compaction on both output topics keyed by order_id
A Kafka transaction that writes both topics and commits the input offset atomically
What are the different terminologies in.why: Transactions make writes to several topics plus the consumer offset commit all-or-nothing. An idempotent producer only removes retry duplicates within a partition; it does not tie two topics and an offset together.

What are the different terminologies in.q: A team says: 'We use Kafka exactly-once, so our database insert and SMS will each happen exactly once.' What is the best correction?
options: Kafka transactions cover Kafka-to-Kafka only; external side effects still need idempotent handlers or an outbox
Exactly-once is impossible in Kafka, so they should switch to a queue
That is correct only if the consumer commits offsets before processing
That is correct as long as the producer uses acks=all and RF 3
What are the different terminologies in.why: Exactly-once in Kafka is about reads, writes and offsets inside Kafka; a database write or SMS can still be repeated after a crash. Durability settings like acks=all prevent loss, not duplicate side effects.

What are the different terminologies in.q: A producer team wants to rename a field in order-events. Thirty consumer teams depend on the topic. Which component should stop a breaking change from being deployed?
options: Kafka Connect, which validates every message against a sink
Consumer group rebalancing, which pauses incompatible consumers
The controller (KRaft), which rejects malformed records
Schema Registry with compatibility rules on the topic's schema
What are the different terminologies in.why: Schema Registry stores each topic's schemas and enforces compatibility rules (for example new fields need defaults), so a producer cannot ship a change that breaks consumers. The controller manages partition leadership, not payload formats.

What are the different terminologies in.q: One order event in the notifications consumer keeps failing because the customer's phone number is malformed, and it is blocking the partition. What is the standard fix?
options: Delete the partition's segment that contains the bad event
Keep retrying it in place; the partition must stay strictly ordered
Move it to a retry or dead-letter topic, alert, and replay it later after fixing
Reset the group's offset to latest so the bad event is skipped forever
What are the different terminologies in.why: A retry or dead-letter topic moves the poison event aside so the partition keeps flowing, while the event is preserved for inspection and replay. Resetting to latest skips every unprocessed event, not just the bad one.

What are the different terminologies in.q: Which statement best describes how a Kafka consumer group shares a topic?
options: Each event is pushed to every consumer in the group, like a broadcast
Consumers in a group take turns reading the same partition round-robin
Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group; different groups each get every event
Only one consumer per group is active; the rest are hot standbys
What are the different terminologies in.why: Inside a group, partitions are divided so each event is processed once, in parallel; separate groups are fully independent copies. A group can have many active consumers, up to the partition count.

What are the different terminologies in.q: A team says 'acks=all' alone makes their payment-events topic safe. Which configuration actually makes acknowledged writes durable?
options: Replication factor 3 with acks=1 and lz4 compression enabled
Replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2 and acks=all together
Replication factor 1 with acks=all and an idempotent producer
Replication factor 3, acks=all and min.insync.replicas=1
What are the different terminologies in.why: acks=all is only meaningful when at least two in-sync copies are required; RF 3 with min ISR 2 tolerates one broker loss. With min.insync.replicas=1, acks=all can succeed with just the leader's copy.

What are the different terminologies in.q: A new fraud-model team joins next month and wants to train on last week's orders. Why is Kafka a better fit than a traditional queue here?
options: Kafka sends past events to new consumers automatically as a welcome batch
A queue would work equally well, since queues also keep read messages
Kafka keeps events after they are read, so a new group can replay anything still within retention
Kafka stores events forever by default, so any history is always available
What are the different terminologies in.why: Kafka is a replicated log: reading does not delete events, and a new group with auto.offset.reset=earliest can replay within retention. Retention is finite (for example 7 days) unless compaction or tiered storage is used, and queues delete messages after acknowledgement.

What are the different terminologies in.q: You are sizing partitions for a new topic and someone suggests 'just use 2,000 partitions so we never run out.' What is the best response?
options: Agree, since extra partitions are free and can be removed later without impact
Use exactly one partition per expected consumer, with no headroom at all
Size from target throughput and largest group's parallelism with 2-3x headroom; partitions have real costs
Use one partition, since Kafka only orders events within a single partition
What are the different terminologies in.why: Each partition adds files, memory, failover and rebalance work, and changing the count later remaps keys and breaks per-key ordering, so plan with headroom from throughput (roughly 10-50 MB/s per partition) and parallelism. One partition would cap throughput and consumer parallelism.

What are the different terminologies in.q: Your company wants consumers to resume in a second region if the primary data centre fails. Which Kafka tool is designed for this?
options: A log-compacted topic that keeps the latest event per key
MirrorMaker 2 (or cluster linking) replicating critical topics across regions
Tiered storage that moves old segments to S3 in the primary region
Increasing replication factor to 5 within the same cluster
What are the different terminologies in.why: MirrorMaker 2 replicates topics between clusters or regions and translates offsets so consumers can resume elsewhere. A higher RF only protects against broker failures within one cluster, not a whole data-centre outage.

What are the different terminologies in.q: To delete a SKU permanently from a log-compacted product-prices topic, what should the producer send?
options: A request to the controller to remove the key from the partition
A tombstone: an event with that sku_id key and a null value
Nothing; compaction deletes keys automatically after 7 days
An event with an empty string value so compaction overwrites it
What are the different terminologies in.why: Compaction keeps the latest value per key, so to remove a key you write a tombstone (null value). Compaction does not delete by age, and an empty string is still a value that would be kept.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: Your email service runs 4 workers and each order-confirmation email must be sent once. Should the workers read one queue or each subscribe to a topic?
options: Each worker subscribes to the topic, so every worker gets a backup copy
Each worker subscribes to the topic with a different group ID for speed
One queue (or one Kafka consumer group), so each email job goes to only one worker
Either works, since topics and queues both deliver each message once
What is the difference between a queue a.why: A queue is point-to-point, so competing consumers split the work. If each worker subscribed separately to a topic, every customer would get 4 emails.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: An 'Order placed' event must reach inventory, payments and notifications, and each team reacts independently. Which messaging pattern fits?
options: One queue shared by all three services as competing consumers
A dead-letter queue that all three services read from
Three services sharing one Kafka consumer group ID
A topic (publish-subscribe), with each service as its own subscriber or consumer group
What is the difference between a queue a.why: A topic gives every subscriber its own copy, which is what broadcast to independent teams needs. A shared queue or shared group would give each event to only one of the three services.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: A Kafka topic has 6 partitions. Group X has 1 consumer and group Y has 8 consumers. What happens?
options: Both groups see every message, and all 8 consumers in Y share the 6 partitions evenly
Both groups see every message; X's consumer reads all 6 partitions, Y has 6 busy consumers and 2 idle
Group X sees 1/9 of messages and group Y sees 8/9, split by consumer count
Group Y sees every message but group X sees nothing until Y commits
What is the difference between a queue a.why: Different groups are independent and each sees everything; within a group a partition goes to one consumer, so extra consumers beyond the partition count are idle. Partitions cannot be split within a group.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: A notification service runs 5 instances with group.id=notification-service. You start one more instance with group.id=inventory-service. What does the new instance receive?
options: Nothing, because only one group may read a topic at a time
Only messages the notification group failed to process
About one-sixth of the messages, as a sixth member of the shared pool
Every message in the topic, independently of the notification group
What is the difference between a queue a.why: The group.id is the switch: same ID shares partitions, a different ID is a new subscriber that gets every message. Kafka allows any number of independent groups on one topic.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: A message in your SQS queue keeps failing because its data is malformed. There is no DLQ configured. What happens?
options: It reappears after every visibility timeout and is retried forever
The queue stops delivering all other messages until it is fixed
SQS moves it to the end of the queue and processes it last, once
SQS deletes it after the first failure since the worker never acked
What is the difference between a queue a.why: Without an ack the message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout, so a poison message loops forever. A DLQ with a redrive policy moves it aside after N receives (say 5) so the main queue keeps flowing.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: A worker sends the confirmation SMS for order 9812 but crashes before acking the queue message. What happens and what is the right defence?
options: The message is redelivered to another worker, so the handler must be idempotent (check 'already sent?')
The broker detects the SMS was sent and silently deletes the message
The message moves straight to the DLQ, so no duplicate can occur
The message is lost, so the worker should ack before sending the SMS
What is the difference between a queue a.why: Queues are typically at-least-once: no ack means redelivery, so a duplicate is possible and consumers must be idempotent. Acking before doing the work risks losing the job if the crash happens mid-way.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: Why might a team put an SQS queue between an SNS topic and their service instead of subscribing the service's HTTP endpoint directly?
options: SQS guarantees exactly-once processing, which SNS cannot provide
SNS cannot deliver to HTTP endpoints, only to queues
The queue buffers messages while the service is slow or down, and gives it its own retries, DLQ and scaling
The queue lets SNS keep messages for 7 days for replay like Kafka
What is the difference between a queue a.why: SNS does not keep messages, so a down HTTP subscriber can miss them once retries run out; an SQS queue holds them and isolates the service's retries and DLQ. SQS standard is still at-least-once, not exactly-once.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: Which statement about deletion is correct?
options: Both Kafka and queues delete a message as soon as any consumer reads it
Kafka deletes a message once every group has read it; queues never delete
Kafka deletes by retention, not on read; a queue deletes a message after the consumer's ack
Queues delete on read; Kafka deletes when the producer sends a tombstone
What is the difference between a queue a.why: In Kafka, reading changes only the reader's offset and retention removes data; queues delete after the ack, not merely on read. Kafka does not track whether all groups have read a message.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: Order events for one order must be processed in sequence. Your team uses AWS. Which option gives per-order ordering?
options: A standard queue with more competing consumers
An SQS standard queue, which keeps strict global order
An SNS topic with many HTTP subscribers
An SQS FIFO queue with the order ID as the message group ID
What is the difference between a queue a.why: SQS FIFO gives strict order within a message group ID (and de-duplication) at lower throughput. SQS standard offers only best-effort ordering, and more competing consumers make processing order even less predictable.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: A live price-ticker widget only cares about the latest price while the user's page is open. What kind of subscription suits it?
options: A non-durable subscription that receives only while connected
A competing-consumer queue shared with other users' widgets
A dead-letter queue that collects missed price updates
A durable subscription that queues every missed price for later
What is the difference between a queue a.why: Non-durable subscriptions suit live data where only the latest value matters; business events like orders need durable ones. Replaying stale prices to a reconnected ticker would be wasted work.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: In the festive-sale example, orders has 12 partitions and the notification group scales from 5 to 13 instances. What happens to the 13th instance?
options: It receives a full copy of every message as a backup
It gets no partition and sits idle, since 12 partitions cap the group at 12 active consumers
It takes half of a busy partition, speeding that partition up
Kafka adds a 13th partition automatically to keep it busy
What is the difference between a queue a.why: Partitions are a group's ceiling on parallelism; a partition cannot be split within a group. Kafka does not auto-add partitions.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: Notification instance 3 owns partition 7 and crashes after sending an SMS but before committing the offset. What happens next?
options: Kafka rebalances partition 7 to another instance, which resumes from the last committed offset and may resend
All 12 partitions are reprocessed from offset 0 by every instance
The SMS is guaranteed not to repeat because Kafka tracks side effects
Partition 7 is paused until instance 3 comes back online
What is the difference between a queue a.why: On rebalance, the new owner resumes from the last committed offset, so uncommitted work may repeat; the service records 'SMS sent for order 9812' to skip duplicates. Kafka knows nothing about external side effects.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: A colleague says 'a topic is just a queue with many readers.' What is the best correction?
options: Correct; topics and queues differ only in which vendor provides them
Queue readers split the messages between them; topic subscribers each get all of them
Topic subscribers split messages; queue readers each get all of them
Correct; the only difference is that topics are faster than queues
What is the difference between a queue a.why: The core difference is who gets each message: one consumer (queue) versus every subscriber (topic). The reversed version swaps the two definitions.

What is the difference between a queue a.q: On AWS without Kafka, a new fraud-check service wants every 'Order placed' event without changing checkout. In the SNS-to-SQS design, what do you do?
options: Ask checkout to also publish directly to a new fraud HTTP endpoint
Add a fourth SQS queue subscribed to the existing SNS topic for the fraud service
Make the fraud service a competing consumer on the inventory queue
Read from the notification service's DLQ, which holds every order
What is the difference between a queue a.why: SNS fans out to each subscribed queue, so adding a subscription extends the system without touching the producer. Competing on another service's queue would steal that service's messages.

What is the difference between streaming.q: Orders are published only to an SQS queue consumed by billing. A new recommendations team wants the last 5 days of orders and then live orders. What is the best change?
options: Let recommendations read the same SQS queue as a second competing consumer
Ask billing to stop acking messages so they stay in the queue longer
Publish OrderPlaced to a stream with enough retention; each team uses its own consumer group, recommendations starting 5 days back
Increase the SQS visibility timeout to 5 days so old messages come back
What is the difference between streaming.why: Acked SQS messages are deleted, and a second worker on the same queue would compete with billing rather than get its own copy. A stream retains events regardless of reads, so a new group can replay from an earlier offset.

What is the difference between streaming.q: Your Kafka invoice consumer sometimes hits a job that takes 3 minutes or fails repeatedly, and lag on that partition explodes. Why?
options: Stream acks are positional, so a slow or failing message blocks everything behind it in the partition
Kafka deletes slow messages, so the consumer re-reads the whole partition
The partition count is too high, which slows down every consumer
The producer is not idempotent, so each failure creates new copies
What is the difference between streaming.why: Committing an offset means 'everything before it is done', so you cannot skip one message and return later: this is head-of-line blocking. The fixes are moving the work to a real job queue, or sending failures to a retry/DLQ topic and committing.

What is the difference between streaming.q: A fraud job counts payment attempts per card in 5-minute windows by processing time and misses bursts from phones that reconnected late. What should change?
options: Switch to processing-time session windows so late events start new sessions
Shrink the window to 1 minute so the late events fall into the next one
Use event-time windows with watermarks that allow bounded lateness, plus a grace period or side output
Add more partitions so late events are processed faster by more consumers
What is the difference between streaming.why: Event time places each attempt in the window when it actually happened, and watermarks decide when a window can close despite late arrivals. Smaller or processing-time windows still assign late events to the wrong time.

What is the difference between streaming.q: Each order needs an invoice PDF rendered; each render is one unit of work that may need individual retries, delay and a DLQ. What fits best?
options: A Flink job with 5-minute tumbling windows over orders
A job queue such as SQS, with competing workers and a dead-letter queue
A log-compacted topic keyed by order ID
A Kafka topic read by one consumer group with the PDF logic inline
What is the difference between streaming.why: Queues give per-message ack, visibility timeout, DLQ and delay, so one bad invoice is retried on its own. On a stream, a failing invoice would block its partition.

What is the difference between streaming.q: Which rule of thumb best separates a queue from a stream?
options: 'Do this work once' means a queue; 'this happened, and anyone may care, now or later' means a stream
'Small messages' means a queue; 'large messages' means a stream
'Must be durable' means a stream; 'can be lost' means a queue
'Needs ordering' means a queue; 'no ordering needed' means a stream
What is the difference between streaming.why: A queue models tasks consumed once and deleted, a stream models retained facts read by many. Both queues and streams store messages durably, so durability is not the deciding factor.

What is the difference between streaming.q: A worker deletes an SQS message before rendering the invoice, and crashes mid-render. Which delivery semantic did it implement?
options: Effectively-once: SQS de-duplicates the deleted message automatically
At-most-once: acking before processing means a crash loses the job
Exactly-once: deleting first prevents any duplicate rendering
At-least-once: the job will be redelivered after the visibility timeout
What is the difference between streaming.why: Ack or commit before processing gives at-most-once, so a crash loses the message. At-least-once needs the delete after the work, which is why the SQS sample deletes only after renderAndStore.

What is the difference between streaming.q: Your team claims Flink's exactly-once guarantee means customers will never get two OTP SMS messages. What is the most accurate response?
options: Correct, because checkpoints record which SMS messages were sent
Correct, as long as the Kafka producer has idempotence enabled
Wrong, because Flink offers only at-most-once delivery
Exactly-once holds inside Flink's boundary; an external SMS still needs an idempotency key at the receiver
What is the difference between streaming.why: Checkpoints and two-phase-commit sinks make state and output effectively-once inside the system, not side effects like SMS or card charges. The idempotent producer only removes duplicates from producer retries.

What is the difference between streaming.q: A new analytics service is added after some events were sent. In which setup can it read those past events?
options: A RabbitMQ fanout exchange copying to each bound queue
An SNS topic fanning out to one SQS queue per subscriber
An SQS FIFO queue with message group IDs
A Kafka topic within retention, where the new consumer group starts from an earlier offset
What is the difference between streaming.why: Queue-style pub/sub copies messages only to subscribers that existed when the message was sent; a stream lets a new subscriber start from the beginning of retention. Both queue designs can do pub/sub, but not for the past.

What is the difference between streaming.q: At 00:00 orders spike 15x and the invoice queue depth climbs to 400,000. Checkout is not slowed. What is the correct reading of this?
options: Producers are blocked, so the order service must switch to a stream
The DLQ is full, so the 400,000 invoices have failed and must be replayed
The queue is a pull-based buffer absorbing backpressure; scale workers on queue depth and age of oldest message
The queue is about to drop messages, so checkout should be throttled immediately
What is the difference between streaming.why: Both queues and streams buffer, so a slow consumer grows the backlog instead of crashing the producer; queue depth and oldest-message age are the signals, and autoscaling drains it. Depth alone does not indicate failures.

What is the difference between streaming.q: A loyalty-service bug miscredited points for 3 hours. After the fix, how does a stream help recovery?
options: Read the DLQ, which automatically contains every event processed by the buggy code
Nothing can be done, since consumed events are deleted from the stream
Ask the producer to resend 3 hours of events from its own database
Reset the consumer group's offsets to before the bug and reprocess with idempotent upserts by order ID
What is the difference between streaming.why: Streams retain events regardless of reads, so a group can rewind offsets and replay; idempotent upserts keep reprocessing safe. With a queue, the acked messages would already be gone.

What is the difference between streaming.q: Someone proposes using Kafka as the job queue for long-running, sometimes-failing tasks with per-task delays and priorities. What is the most accurate concern?
options: Kafka cannot be read by more than one consumer at a time
Kafka lacks per-message ack, delay and priority, and slow jobs block their partition
Kafka cannot store messages durably, so jobs would be lost
Kafka deletes each message as soon as it is read, so retries fail
What is the difference between streaming.why: Kafka is a retained, partitioned log with positional commits, so it lacks queue features out of the box (share groups are only starting to add per-message acks). It is durable and supports many consumers, so those are not the issue.

What is the difference between streaming.q: You need a dashboard of payment attempts per card where windows are fixed 1-minute, non-overlapping buckets. Which window type is this?
options: Session window
Tumbling window
Sliding (hopping) window
Watermark window
What is the difference between streaming.why: Tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping. Sliding windows overlap (5 minutes every 1 minute), session windows are defined by inactivity gaps, and a watermark is a progress estimate, not a window type.

What is the difference between streaming.q: What does a watermark do in a stream processor?
options: It estimates that events older than time T have probably all arrived, so event-time windows can close
It marks the highest offset the consumer group has committed
It caps how many unacked messages a worker can hold at once
It records the processing time when each event reached the server
What is the difference between streaming.why: A watermark is a moving timestamp that lets the processor close windows despite out-of-order arrival. The committed offset is a bookmark, and the prefetch cap is a queue feature.

What is the difference between streaming.q: Your AWS-native team of four needs background jobs with retries and a DLQ, and does not want to run Kafka. What should they lean towards?
options: SQS (with SNS for fan-out), and Kinesis if they later need a managed stream
A Flink cluster with checkpointing
Apache Pulsar with geo-replication
A self-hosted Kafka cluster with share groups
What is the difference between streaming.why: SQS and SNS are managed with near-zero ops and cover jobs, retries and DLQ; Kinesis gives a stream without running Kafka. Self-hosting Kafka or Pulsar adds operational load a small team doesn't need here.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: A topic has 8 partitions and you send all events for order 42 with no key. Will a consumer see them in order?
options: Yes, because Kafka orders the whole topic by offset
Yes, because each message's timestamp keeps them in order
Not necessarily; keyless messages spread across partitions with no order between them
Yes, as long as only one consumer group reads the topic
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: Without a key, messages go round-robin or sticky across partitions, and there is no ordering between partitions. Using order_id as the key puts them in one partition.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: Your producer has retries on, enable.idempotence=false and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5. Can two same-key messages be stored out of order?
options: No: the same key always lands in the same partition, which is ordered
No: Kafka holds later batches until earlier ones are acknowledged
Only if the partition leader changes during the send
Yes: if an earlier batch fails and is retried after a later batch succeeds, the later one is written first
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: A retried batch can land after a batch that was sent later, flipping their order. Turning on idempotence (default since 3.0) or setting max in-flight to 1 lets the broker enforce sequence numbers.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: You grow order-events from 12 to 24 partitions during peak traffic. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, because Kafka moves existing messages to their new partitions
hash(key) mod 24 maps keys to new partitions, so an order's old and new events are read by different consumers in no defined order
All consumers restart from offset 0 and reprocess the whole topic
The producer rejects keyed messages until the topic is rebuilt
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: Changing the partition count changes hash mod N, so ord-17 may move mid-stream while its old events remain in the old partition. Kafka does not move existing data, which is why you size up front or migrate in a quiet window.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: Why does Kafka not offer ordering across all partitions of a topic?
options: Global order needs a single sequencer or consensus on every write, plus one consumer, which destroys parallelism
Partitions live on different disks, so offsets cannot be compared
ZooKeeper could not store a global order, and KRaft has not added it yet
Global order is supported, but only when timestamps are enabled
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: A partition has one leader assigning offsets in sequence, so per-partition order is free; a total order would funnel everything through one point. Timestamps drift and interleave, so they cannot give a guarantee.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: Your consumer pulls messages from one partition and hands them to a pool of 20 threads. SHIPPED sometimes gets processed before PAID for the same order. Best fix?
options: Route by key, e.g. hash(order_id) mod N to a fixed worker, so each order is processed serially
Switch the topic to a single partition so all orders are serial
Increase the pool to 100 threads so every message finishes faster
Commit offsets before processing to lock the order in place
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: Kafka delivers a partition in order, but parallel threads can finish out of order; hashing the key to one worker keeps per-key order while different keys still run in parallel. A single partition would throw away all parallelism.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: The payment service and order service both emit events for ord-17 from different producers. PAYMENT_CAPTURED lands after CANCELLED even though payment happened first. What is the robust fix?
options: Sort events by the producer timestamp before applying them
Give each service its own partition so they don't interfere
Enable the idempotent producer on both services
Add a per-order version set by the owning service; consumers apply only the next expected version
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: Kafka orders by arrival at the leader, not real-world time, so a version from the owner of the order's state is needed. Producer timestamps drift, and idempotence only orders one producer's own retries.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: A fulfilment instance crashes after handling PACKED for ord-17 but before committing. What happens and how should the handler cope?
options: Another instance re-reads PACKED; the handler ignores it if stored.version >= event.version
Kafka skips PACKED automatically since it was already processed
The partition stays locked until the crashed instance restarts
PACKED is lost because the crashed instance held it in memory
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: On rebalance, the new owner resumes from the last committed offset, so uncommitted work is redelivered in order but duplicated; idempotent version checks prevent a double-pack. Ordered does not mean exactly once.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: In Kafka, what is the 'unit of ordering' that application designers control?
options: The broker ID, since each broker keeps its own global order
The consumer group ID, which decides which events are ordered
The message key, since the same key always goes to the same partition
The topic name, since each topic is totally ordered
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: The default partitioner computes murmur2(key) mod partitions, so equal keys share a partition and its order. Topics with several partitions have no total order.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: One seller produces 30% of events and seller_id is the key; that partition is the bottleneck. Their events only need order per product. Best move?
options: Remove the key entirely so events spread round-robin
Key by seller_id plus product_id so the seller's load spreads while per-product order holds
Add more partitions, since that spreads a single hot key automatically
Add more consumers to the group to split that partition
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: A single key always lives in one partition, so more partitions or consumers can't spread it; a finer key matching the real ordering need does. Removing the key would lose per-product ordering too.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: An admin audit trail must be read in one total order and has low volume. What is a reasonable design?
options: Use many partitions with no key so events spread evenly
Use a single partition, accepting one partition's throughput and one consumer
Use 96 partitions and sort events by timestamp in the consumer
Use 12 partitions keyed by admin user ID
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: One partition gives total order at the cost of throughput and parallelism, which is fine for low volume. Timestamp sorting across partitions is not a guarantee, and per-admin keys give only per-admin order.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: A consumer fails on PAID for ord-17, skips it, and continues. What is the risk and better approach?
options: No risk, since Kafka redelivers skipped messages at the end of the partition
Later events for ord-17 overtake PAID; use a per-key retry topic or pause the partition instead of skipping
PAID is deleted forever, so the producer must resend it
The rest of the partition is blocked until PAID is processed
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: Skipping lets SHIPPED for the same order be applied before PAID, breaking per-key order. Kafka does not redeliver skipped messages on its own.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: Your team uses order_id as the key and says ordering is now fully guaranteed end to end. Which extra condition is NOT required for that to be true?
options: Using more than one consumer group on the topic
The producer must be idempotent so retries can't reorder
The consumer must not process one key's messages in parallel
The partition count must not change while orders are in flight
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: Same key is enough only with an idempotent producer, a stable partition count and serial per-key consumption. The number of consumer groups doesn't affect ordering within each group.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: Roughly how should you choose the partition count for a new topic?
options: As many as possible, since more partitions has no downside
One per consumer group reading the topic
Exactly the number of brokers, so each broker owns one partition
max(target throughput / per-partition throughput, desired consumer parallelism), with 2-3x headroom
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: A partition handles roughly 10-50 MB/s and caps consumer parallelism in a group, so size for both with growth room to avoid repartitioning under load. More partitions cost files, elections and rebalance time.

Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.q: With the idempotent producer enabled (default since Kafka 3.0), how many in-flight requests per connection can you keep while preserving order?
options: Exactly 3, matching the replication factor
Unlimited, because idempotence removes all ordering risk
Up to 5, because the leader rejects out-of-sequence batches and drops duplicates
Only 1; anything more always risks reordering
Why does Kafka guarantee ordering only w.why: Idempotence numbers batches per partition so the broker enforces sequence with up to 5 in flight. Without idempotence, the old safe rule was max.in.flight=1.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: A consumer finishes processing a message and commits its offset. A colleague expects the message to be gone from Kafka. What actually happened?
options: Only the group's position was saved in __consumer_offsets; the message stays until retention or compaction removes it
The broker marked the message acked and will delete it at the next cleanup
The message was deleted from that group's view but kept for other groups
The message was moved to a dead-letter topic for audit purposes
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: Consuming is a read; committing just writes a small record of the group's position. The broker keeps no per-message ack state, so nothing triggers a delete; only retention (time/size) or compaction does.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: Your analytics consumer group has been down for 9 days on a topic with default settings. What happens when it restarts?
options: Data older than ~7 days is gone, and expired offsets plus auto.offset.reset=latest make it silently skip even the remaining backlog
It resumes from its last offset, and Kafka restores deleted data from replicas
It resumes exactly from its last committed offset and reads all 9 days
It fails to start until an admin manually recreates the group
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: Retention (7 days) has deleted part of the backlog, and offsets of an inactive group expire after offsets.retention.minutes (7 days), so the default reset to latest jumps to the end. Replicas follow the same retention, so they can't restore it.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: A points consumer credited Plus members 1% instead of 5% for two days. You reset offsets to the deploy time and replay. What must be true of the consumer?
options: It must run as a single instance so replay preserves order
It must use auto.offset.reset=latest so only new events are replayed
It must be idempotent: upsert the correct points per order_id rather than increment, and suppress external side effects
It must commit offsets before processing to avoid double counting
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: Replay redelivers events already processed; an upsert like 'points for OD4471 = 250' makes reprocessing safe, while 'add 250' would double-credit. Commit-before-processing gives at-most-once and could skip records.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: Why can Kafka serve many consumer groups at high throughput when a classic queue struggles with heavy fan-out?
options: Kafka compresses each message separately for every consumer group
The broker keeps no per-message state; groups read the same bytes sequentially, often from page cache via zero-copy
Kafka copies each message into a separate queue per group, in parallel
Kafka deletes messages as soon as the fastest group reads them
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: With only one offset per group per partition, there are no acks, timers or per-copy bookkeeping, and sequential reads from page cache are cheap. A queue must copy each message per subscriber and track acks for each copy.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: A topic has retention.ms of 7 days, but you find records 7 days and 20 hours old still on disk. Is something broken?
options: Yes; it means a consumer group still holds those records unacked
No; deletion removes whole closed segments, so records live until their segment's newest record ages out
No; Kafka doubles retention automatically when consumers lag
Yes; retention should delete each record at exactly 7 days
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: Kafka deletes per closed segment, checked every few minutes, so data often outlives the limit, and the active segment is never deleted. Consumer progress plays no part in deletion.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: An order_events topic must keep 90 days of history for new ML teams, but keeping that on broker SSDs is too expensive. What is the best fit?
options: Raise retention.bytes to unlimited and add more SSD brokers
Lower the replication factor to 1 to save disk
Log compaction, so 90 days of orders fit in a smaller space
Tiered storage: short local retention on brokers and long total retention in object storage like S3
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: Tiered storage moves closed segments to object storage (local.retention.ms short, retention.ms long), and consumers read old data transparently. Compaction keeps only the latest per key, losing the history the ML teams need.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: A customer requests deletion of their personal data under DPDP. It sits in a 90-day, time-retained Kafka topic. Which approach actually works?
options: Lower retention.ms to 1 day for that customer's records only
Commit the group offset past the customer's records
Delete the specific record from the partition with an admin command
Crypto-shredding: encrypt per customer and delete that customer's key (or keep PII in compacted topics and write a tombstone)
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: You cannot delete one record from a time-retained topic; crypto-shredding, short retention, or compacted topics with tombstones are the options. Committing offsets never removes data.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: Your consumer has enable.auto.commit=false and calls commitSync() after handling each poll batch. What delivery guarantee is this?
options: At-least-once: a crash before the commit means reprocessing, so handlers must be idempotent
At-most-once: a crash may skip records that were already fetched
No guarantee: without auto-commit, offsets are never saved
Exactly-once: manual commits prevent all duplicates
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: Committing after processing means some records may be handled twice after a crash, but none are lost. At-most-once is commit-before-processing; exactly-once needs transactions for Kafka-to-Kafka.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: Analytics falls 40 minutes behind at the midnight sale launch. What is the impact on inventory, fraud and notifications groups?
options: They pause until analytics catches up, to keep groups in sync
They slow down too, because the broker must hold messages for analytics
None; lag is just analytics' bookmark further back on disk, and it catches up later
Their messages are delayed because Kafka throttles all groups equally
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: Groups are independent: each has its own offsets, and a slow one simply builds lag. Kafka does not hold or throttle other groups for it.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: A poison message keeps failing in your Kafka consumer. Unlike SQS, there's no built-in DLQ. What is the standard approach?
options: Publish it to a retry topic with an attempt count, commit past it, and after N tries send it to a dead-letter topic and alert
Lower retention so the message is deleted sooner
Keep retrying in place, since skipping breaks the commit log
Reset the group to latest to jump over the bad record
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: Kafka has no per-message retry, so you build retry and dead-letter topics to stop one record blocking a partition forever. Resetting to latest would skip every unprocessed record, not just the bad one.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: In week two, the recommendations team wants 90 days of order history from tiered storage and then live orders. What do they need to do?
options: Join the existing analytics group so they share its offsets
Create a new consumer group with auto.offset.reset=earliest; the order team changes nothing
Use auto.offset.reset=latest and request a backfill file
Ask the order service to republish 90 days of events to a new topic
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: A brand-new group with earliest reads all retained history, then keeps consuming live, at no cost to the producer. Joining the analytics group would split partitions with analytics instead of getting every event.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: Which is the best way to estimate broker disk for retention?
options: Average throughput x retention period, ignoring compression and replication
Peak throughput x record size / compression x retention period x replication factor, plus headroom
Number of partitions x segment.bytes, regardless of throughput
Number of consumer groups x average lag x record size
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: Storage is paid for retention times the replication factor, after compression, with headroom (keep disks under 60-70%). The example: about 215 GB/day compressed x 7 days x RF 3 is roughly 4.5 TB.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: Using the example's numbers, 10,000 events/s at 1 KB with about 4x zstd compression, how much broker disk do 7 days of retention at RF 3 need?
options: About 860 GB
About 1.5 TB
About 18 TB
About 4.5 TB
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: 10 MB/s is about 860 GB/day raw, about 215 GB/day compressed, about 1.5 TB for 7 days, and about 4.5 TB with RF 3. 1.5 TB forgets replication; 18 TB forgets compression.

A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.q: A config topic uses cleanup.policy=compact. A slow consumer must still learn that key SKU-9 was deleted. What makes that possible?
options: The broker pushes a delete notification to every group
Deleted keys are written to __consumer_offsets for consumers to check
The tombstone (null value) is kept for delete.retention.ms (default 1 day) before it is removed
Compaction keeps every old value for a key forever
A Kafka consumer reads a message, proces.why: A tombstone marks a key deleted and lingers for delete.retention.ms so slow consumers see it. Compaction keeps only the latest record per key, not the history.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: Your order service commits the order and then calls kafka.send(). A deploy kills the pod right between the two. What happens, and how does the outbox fix it?
options: Nothing is lost, since Kafka retries the send after the pod restarts
The order is saved but OrderPlaced is never sent; with an outbox the event row commits with the order and the relay publishes it later
The database rolls back the order because the send failed
The order is saved and the event is buffered in the Kafka client's disk cache
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: This is the dual-write problem: the database and the broker can't share a transaction, so a crash between them leaves them inconsistent. The outbox makes the intent to publish durable in the same local transaction.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: The relay publishes an outbox row to Kafka and then crashes before marking it published. What happens and what must consumers do?
options: The row is lost, so consumers must poll the outbox table directly
The row is published again on restart, so consumers must be idempotent, e.g. an inbox table with a unique message_id
The relay rolls back the Kafka message before restarting
Kafka rejects the duplicate automatically because of the outbox UUID
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: The outbox gives at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once. Kafka doesn't know the outbox ID is a business de-dup key, so the consumer's inbox (unique constraint, same transaction as the work) skips the duplicate.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: OrderCancelled for order 4471 is being processed before OrderPlaced. Which two outbox settings prevent this?
options: Use a random UUID as the key, and run many unordered relay workers
Increase the poll interval, and delete published rows sooner
Use the order ID as the Kafka key, and publish outbox rows in commit order per aggregate
Use Kafka transactions, and add an index on published_at
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: Keying by aggregate ID puts both events in one partition, and a single ordered relay (or CDC following the commit log) keeps commit order. Parallel relay workers must partition work by aggregate to preserve this.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: A teammate says: 'Just publish right after the commit, and retry if the publish fails.' What is the flaw?
options: The retry would publish the event before the commit is visible
If the process dies between commit and publish, the retry never runs; the intent to publish is not durable
Kafka does not allow retries for events tied to a database commit
Retries are fine, but they add too much latency to the API call
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: In-memory retries vanish with a crash, OOM kill or deploy; the outbox stores the event in the same transaction so it survives. Latency is not the core problem here.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: Why does the outbox write the event into a table in the service's own database rather than publishing to Kafka inside the transaction?
options: Database tables guarantee exactly-once delivery to consumers
The outbox table compresses events better than Kafka does
A local transaction makes the order row and event row atomic; Kafka can't join a database transaction
Kafka is too slow to call during a request, so it must be deferred
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: The point is atomicity: both commit or neither does, using only a local transaction. The outbox still delivers at-least-once, not exactly-once.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: Your team proposes 2PC/XA across MySQL and Kafka instead of an outbox. What is the strongest objection?
options: 2PC requires Debezium, which adds infrastructure
2PC is fine, but it only works with PostgreSQL, not MySQL
2PC guarantees at-most-once, so events could be lost
2PC is slow, fragile, and widely unsupported by brokers and managed databases; the outbox gets the same practical guarantee locally
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: XA is poorly supported by brokers and cloud databases, adds latency, and a failed coordinator can leave locks held. Debezium is unrelated to 2PC.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: Someone argues Kafka transactions make the outbox unnecessary. What is the correct response?
options: Kafka transactions cover Kafka writes and offsets but not your database, so the DB-plus-event problem remains
Correct, as long as the producer uses acks=all
Wrong, because Kafka transactions only work with a single partition
Correct, because Kafka transactions include any JDBC database in the same commit
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: Kafka transactions are atomic across Kafka topics and consumer offsets only, which suits Kafka-to-Kafka processing. acks=all is about durability, not atomicity with a database.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: You run a polling relay with three workers. How do they share unsent outbox rows without blocking or double-publishing each other's batches?
options: SELECT * FROM outbox with no filter, deduplicating in Kafka afterwards
LOCK TABLE outbox for each worker in turn, every 100-500 ms
Each worker reads every row and publishes only rows with an even hash
SELECT ... WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 500 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: SKIP LOCKED lets workers grab different batches concurrently, and the partial index on unsent rows keeps the query cheap. Locking the whole table serialises workers; for strict per-aggregate order, partition work by aggregate.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: You're choosing between a polling relay and Debezium CDC. Which statement is accurate?
options: Polling is simple and works anywhere; CDC gives tens-of-ms latency and no polling load but means running Debezium and Connect
Polling cannot scale beyond a few events per second, so CDC is mandatory
CDC requires a published_at column; polling does not
CDC gives exactly-once delivery while polling gives at-least-once
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: Start with a poller and move to CDC for lower latency or less DB load; with an index, batching and SKIP LOCKED, polling handles thousands per second. Both are at-least-once, and CDC rows can even be deleted right after insert.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: On sale night, Kafka has a 2-minute broker issue. What happens with a CDC-based outbox?
options: Checkout fails for 2 minutes because the API cannot reach Kafka
Orders keep committing, Debezium pauses, outbox lag rises and alerts, and the backlog publishes in order afterwards with nothing lost
Orders commit, but their outbox rows are dropped since Kafka was down
Debezium writes events to a local file and the order service replays them
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: The API never talks to Kafka, so checkout is unaffected; events wait as outbox rows or in the database log. Outbox lag (age of the oldest unpublished row) is the health signal to alert on.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: What is the difference between an outbox and an inbox?
options: Outbox is producer-side reliable publishing; inbox is consumer-side de-duplication of processed message IDs
Outbox is for Kafka and inbox is for RabbitMQ
They are the same table, used by both producer and consumer
Outbox de-duplicates consumers; inbox publishes producer events
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: The outbox makes publishing reliable; the inbox, written in the same transaction as the side effect, makes processing idempotent. You usually want both.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: Why use an outbox table instead of running CDC directly on the orders business tables?
options: The outbox provides a deliberate, versioned public event contract instead of coupling consumers to internal schema
The outbox delivers events exactly once while table CDC does not
CDC cannot read business tables, only tables named outbox
Business-table CDC is not atomic with the order write
