What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: CDC on business tables works and is simpler, but any internal schema change can break consumers. The outbox events are designed as a contract with versioned payloads.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: Which metric is the key health signal for an outbox relay?
options: The total number of rows ever written to the outbox
The size of the inventory consumer's inbox table
The API's p99 latency for placing orders
Outbox lag: the age of the oldest unpublished row
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: A growing age of the oldest unsent row means the relay or broker is in trouble and downstream is falling behind. Total rows only grows with traffic and housekeeping should purge published rows anyway.

What is the transactional outbox pattern.q: The inventory consumer handles OrderPlaced. How should it apply the inbox pattern to avoid reserving stock twice?
options: Check Kafka's offset to see whether the message was processed before
Reserve stock first, then insert the message_id in a separate later transaction
Insert the message_id into an inbox table with a unique constraint in the same DB transaction as the stock reservation
Keep processed message IDs in an in-memory set per consumer instance
What is the transactional outbox pattern.why: Doing both in one transaction makes the duplicate hit the unique constraint and roll back cleanly. A separate transaction or in-memory set fails after crashes or rebalances, which is when duplicates happen.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: A nightly job appends yesterday's orders to a sales table. It fails halfway and the on-call engineer reruns it. What goes wrong and what is the right design?
options: The rerun skips the half already written, so data is lost; switch to streaming
Rows are double counted; fix it by running the job twice a day instead of once
Nothing goes wrong, since the warehouse de-duplicates appended rows automatically
Rows written before the failure are written again, double counting sales; overwrite the date partition so reruns are idempotent
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: Blind appends make reruns and backfills unsafe. Overwriting one date partition gives the same result no matter how many times the job runs.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: Orders arrive at 10:00:10, 10:00:40 and 10:01:20. Using 3-minute windows sliding every minute, how many windows contain the 10:00:40 order?
options: One, because each event falls in exactly one window
Three: the windows starting at 9:58, 9:59 and 10:00
Two: the windows starting at 9:59 and 10:00
Six: one window per 30 seconds of the 3-minute size
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: With size 3 minutes and step 1 minute, an event belongs to size/step = 3 overlapping windows. 'Exactly one window' describes tumbling windows.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: A phone records an order at 10:00:50, but the event reaches the stream job at 10:03:10 after the 10:00-10:01 window closed. Which is NOT a valid way to handle it?
options: Drop it and count the number of dropped late events
Send it to a side output for a batch job to fix later
Allow extra lateness and emit a corrected result for 10:00-10:01
Reassign the order to the 10:03 window based on its processing time
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: Late events can be allowed (corrected result), side-output for a batch fix, or dropped and counted. Moving it to the processing-time window puts the order in the wrong minute and makes replays inconsistent.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: A team says their Flink job is exactly-once, yet customers sometimes get two 'sale is live' SMS messages from it. How is that possible?
options: Exactly-once covers the engine's state; after a crash and replay the job calls the SMS service again unless the sink de-duplicates
Flink's exactly-once is broken whenever more than one worker runs
The SMS gateway duplicates messages; Flink cannot have caused it
The watermark was too small, so the window fired twice
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: After restoring from a checkpoint, events are reprocessed, so external side effects repeat; end-to-end needs a replayable source and idempotent or transactional sinks. The engine guarantee is about state, not the outside world.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: Finance needs daily sales per category by the next morning, and the numbers must be exactly reconcilable. What processing model fits?
options: A streaming job with 1-second tumbling windows
A streaming job with in-memory state and millisecond latency
A micro-batch every 30 seconds writing directly to the dashboard
A nightly batch job over yesterday's bounded data, gated by quality checks
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: If nobody acts on the number within minutes, batch is simpler, cheaper and easy to rerun. The batch number is the number of record; streaming adds complexity without a decision that needs it.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: Your team moves from ETL to ELT on a cloud warehouse. What is the main benefit they gain?
options: Transformations happen in a separate tool, which reduces warehouse cost
Only clean data ever reaches the warehouse, so nobody can query messy tables
Raw data is kept in the warehouse, so when a rule changes they can recompute history with SQL
Data no longer needs extracting, because the warehouse reads sources live
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: ELT loads raw first and transforms inside the warehouse, so history can be recomputed. 'Only clean data reaches the warehouse' describes classic ETL, and ELT's cost is the discipline needed to avoid reporting off raw tables.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: Orders arrive at 10:00:20 (Rs 100), 10:00:50 (Rs 200) and 10:01:30 (Rs 300). What is the total for the 1-minute tumbling window 10:00-10:01?
options: Rs 600
Rs 300
Rs 100
Rs 500
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: The first two orders (Rs 100 + Rs 200) fall in 10:00-10:01; the Rs 300 order is in the next tumbling window. Rs 600 is the 2-minute sliding window 10:00-10:02.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: A stream worker dies at 9:12 PM, restores from the 9:11 PM checkpoint and replays from saved Kafka offsets. Why is there no double counting on the live dashboard?
options: The engine skips the replayed events because it remembers them from before the crash
State and offsets are restored together, and the sink upserts by city + window so replayed results overwrite the same rows
Kafka deletes events after the first read, so they cannot be replayed
The watermark discards every event older than the checkpoint
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: Checkpoints save state and offsets atomically, giving exactly-once state, and an idempotent upsert sink keeps output correct. The replayed events really are reprocessed, which is why the sink design matters.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: The live war-room GMV is 0.4% below the finance batch number the next morning. Which should the company treat as the number of record?
options: Neither until the streaming job is rebuilt with a longer watermark
The live number, since it was computed from events as they happened
The batch number; the live number is for fast decisions and misses very late events and later cancellations
The average of both, to balance freshness and accuracy
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: Batch sees complete, bounded data and is how you correct streaming results. A watermark is a guess, so very late events can slip past it.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: Your company runs a nightly Spark job for accurate history and a separate Flink job for today's numbers, and the two keep drifting apart. Which architecture is this, and what is its key drawback?
options: Lambda architecture; the same logic is written twice and the copies drift
Lambda architecture; it cannot recompute history at all
Kappa architecture; it cannot produce fresh numbers
Kappa architecture; it needs very long event retention
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: Lambda runs a batch layer and a speed layer merged at query time, duplicating logic. Kappa uses only streaming and recomputes by replaying the log.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: Before refreshing the finance dashboard, a quality check finds yesterday's row count is 45% below the same day last week. What should the pipeline do?
options: Stop before publishing, so the dashboard keeps the last good numbers, and alert
Switch the dashboard to the streaming job's numbers automatically
Append yesterday's rows a second time to make up the shortfall
Publish anyway and add a footnote that the data may be incomplete
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: A pipeline that quietly publishes wrong numbers is worse than one that fails loudly; checks like volume, nulls and reconciliation gate publishing. Appending again would double count.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: A marketing campaign report needs data no older than about an hour. What is a sensible choice?
options: A streaming job with in-memory state and millisecond latency
Micro-batch every 15-60 minutes
A weekly backfill of the whole campaign
A daily batch job at 2 AM
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: Micro-batch is the middle ground for within-an-hour freshness without the complexity of streaming. A daily job is too stale, while millisecond streaming is overkill.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: A week later, orders paid with a new wallet are found to have a null city. The team fixes the transform. What makes the 7-day backfill safe?
options: Each run is parameterised by date and overwrites its own date partition
Each run appends to the table, and duplicates are removed by the dashboard
The streaming job automatically replays the week
The warehouse locks the table so only one run can append at a time
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: Idempotent, date-parameterised jobs make 'rerun 1-14 Oct' one safe command. Appending would double count anything already loaded.

A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.q: Why should a sale-day GMV stream job window by event time rather than processing time?
options: Processing time cannot be used with tumbling windows
Event time guarantees no late events will ever arrive
Processing time puts delayed events in the wrong minute and makes replays give different answers
Event time is cheaper to compute because no timestamp parsing is needed
A sales dashboard can update once a nigh.why: Event time places each order in the minute it actually happened, so results are correct and repeatable. Late events still occur, which is why watermarks and lateness policies exist.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: Your consumer processes 800 messages/s and the producer sends 1,000/s for 15 minutes. How many messages are waiting at the end, and how long would a new one wait?
options: 180,000 waiting; a new message waits about 180 seconds
180,000 waiting; a new message waits about 225 seconds
15,000 waiting; a new message waits about 19 seconds
900,000 waiting; a new message waits about 15 minutes
What happens when one part of a system p.why: The queue grows by 200/s for 900 s, giving 180,000; wait = items waiting / finish rate = 180,000 / 800 = 225 s. Dividing by the arrival rate (1,000/s) gives the wrong 180 s.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: A teammate proposes raising an in-memory queue from 10,000 to 1,000,000 items to stop 'queue full' errors. What is wrong with this?
options: It only fails if consumers are also scaled up at the same time
Nothing; a larger queue absorbs the overload until traffic drops
It is fine as long as the queue is in memory rather than on disk
It adds no capacity; under sustained overload it still fills, items wait far longer, and the failure becomes an out-of-memory crash
What happens when one part of a system p.why: By Little's law a longer queue is higher latency; it only delays noticing the overload. A bounded queue with a clean rejection is safer than an eventual OutOfMemoryError.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: A Kafka consumer group shows lag of 600,000 messages and processes 2,000 messages/s. The topic has 8 partitions and 8 consumers. How far behind is it, and will a 9th consumer help?
options: About 5 minutes behind; a 9th consumer sits idle, so add partitions, speed up processing or batch
About 300 minutes behind; a 9th consumer would halve the lag
About 5 minutes behind; a 9th consumer adds about 12% more throughput
About 30 seconds behind; no action is needed
What happens when one part of a system p.why: Lag / consume rate = 600,000 / 2,000 = 300 s. A partition is read by only one consumer per group, so with 8 partitions the 9th is idle.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: On sale day checkout is overloaded. Why return HTTP 429 with Retry-After instead of letting requests wait, and what should the client do?
options: Fast rejection keeps accepted requests fast; the client waits Retry-After plus jitter and reuses its idempotency key
429 tells the client the order succeeded later, so it should not retry
The client should retry at exactly Retry-After so all users return together
Rejection is a failure; the client should retry immediately in a tight loop
What happens when one part of a system p.why: A quick 'no' frees resources, and jitter stops millions of phones retrying in the same second; an idempotency key prevents duplicate orders. Retrying at the exact same moment would cause a retry storm.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: Your service handles 1,000 requests/s and each spends 0.2 s inside it. Using Little's law, about how many requests are in flight at once?
options: About 5,000
About 20
About 1,000
About 200
What happens when one part of a system p.why: L = lambda x W = 1,000 x 0.2 = 200, which helps size threads or connections. 5,000 comes from dividing instead of multiplying.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: You can accept at most 2 seconds of queueing and your workers process 500 items/s. How large should the bounded queue be?
options: About 1,000,000 items
About 1,000 items
Unbounded, with autoscaling as protection
About 250 items
What happens when one part of a system p.why: Size from the latency budget: 500 items/s x 2 s = 1,000. A million-item queue just hides overload as latency and memory growth.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: An inventory service is overloaded, so the team adds 50 more consumer workers, but things get worse. What is the most likely reason?
options: Workers need at least 10 minutes to warm up their JVM caches
Adding workers always reduces throughput due to rebalancing
The real bottleneck is the shared database, so more workers just move the queue into the database
50 workers exceed the rate limiter, so all requests are rejected
What happens when one part of a system p.why: Scaling consumers helps only if the bottleneck can scale; otherwise extra workers pile pressure onto the database. Scaling also takes minutes, so limits and shedding are still needed.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: Under overload, which work should a marketplace shed first?
options: The oldest paying customers' requests, to favour new users
Requests in arrival order, regardless of type, to be fair
'Recommended for you' widgets and analytics events, before checkout and payment
Payment and order placement, since they are the most expensive calls
What happens when one part of a system p.why: Drop low-priority and stale work first and protect revenue-critical paths like payment. Shedding checkout first sacrifices the most important work.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: A web server thread blocks indefinitely on a full queue when submitting work. What is the better pattern for a user-facing path?
options: Switch to an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue so offer never blocks
Keep blocking forever, since all user requests must eventually succeed
Offer with a short timeout (e.g. 50 ms), then fail fast with 503 'busy, retry later'
Drop the request silently without telling the client
What happens when one part of a system p.why: Blocking forever in a web server piles up threads too; a timed offer followed by a clean rejection keeps the server responsive. An unbounded queue just hides the overload until memory runs out.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: What does ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy do when the pool's bounded queue is full?
options: The pool grows extra threads beyond its maximum
The oldest task in the queue is dropped to make room
The task is silently discarded with no error
The submitting thread runs the task itself, so it stops submitting new work for a while
What happens when one part of a system p.why: CallerRunsPolicy pushes the cost back onto the caller, a simple form of backpressure. Silently discarding or dropping the oldest are different rejection policies.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: How do Reactive Streams (Java Flow, Reactor, RxJava) prevent overload by design?
options: The framework autoscales subscribers whenever lag grows
The publisher pushes as fast as it can and the subscriber buffers without limit
The subscriber calls request(n), and the publisher may not send more than requested
Each element is sent twice so slow subscribers can skip duplicates
What happens when one part of a system p.why: Reactive Streams turn push into pull, so demand flows backwards through every stage. The source still needs an explicit policy (bounded buffer, drop or slow down) when nobody is requesting.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: A team says 'we use Kafka, so we don't need to think about backpressure.' What is the best correction?
options: Kafka decouples producers, but lag still means stale data, and data beyond retention is deleted; monitor lag in time and scale consumers
Correct; Kafka stores everything forever, so lag never matters
Correct; Kafka automatically slows producers when consumers lag
Wrong; Kafka blocks producers whenever any consumer group falls behind
What happens when one part of a system p.why: Kafka is a large durable buffer bounded by retention, and producers never wait for consumers. Alert on lag in seconds, watch whether it keeps rising, and autoscale up to the partition count.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: During overload, clients retry failed calls immediately and indefinitely, and load triples. What is this and how do you stop it?
options: Normal recovery; retries always improve reliability under load
A retry storm; use exponential backoff with jitter, capped attempts, Retry-After, and a retry budget
Kafka lag; add more partitions to the topic
A rate-limit bug; remove the rate limiter so requests succeed
What happens when one part of a system p.why: Under overload, uncapped retries multiply load. Backoff with jitter, attempt caps, honouring Retry-After and limiting retries to about 10% of traffic keep them from making it worse.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: At the gateway, what is a token bucket rate limiter doing?
options: Each request needs a token, and tokens refill at a fixed rate, so only a set amount of work gets in
It gives each request a priority token used by load shedding
It batches requests into groups of 100 before forwarding them
It queues all excess requests in memory until tokens are free
What happens when one part of a system p.why: A token bucket stops excess work at the front door, protecting everything behind it, and can be per user, per key or global. Queuing everything in memory is the unbounded-queue trap.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: Your batch job writes each record to the database in its own round trip and can't keep up. What is a good fix that limits added latency?
options: Retry each failed write immediately without backoff
Batch writes with no cap, flushing only when 1 million items arrive
Add a larger in-memory queue in front of the database writer
Batch writes, capped by size and time, e.g. '100 items or 20 ms'
What happens when one part of a system p.why: Batching shares the fixed per-trip cost and often multiplies throughput; capping by size and time bounds the extra latency. An uncapped batch adds unbounded delay.

What happens when one part of a system p.q: Email consumer lag reaches 400,000 messages at 2,000/s during the sale. Is this a problem?
options: No; lag in Kafka never matters because data is kept forever
Not necessarily; it is about 3 minutes behind, fine for confirmations, as long as the lag drains rather than keeps rising
Yes; any lag above 100,000 means messages are being lost
Yes; it means 400,000 customers will never get their email
What happens when one part of a system p.why: Lag / rate = 400,000 / 2,000 = 200 s, about 3 minutes, acceptable for email. Steady or draining lag is fine; lag that keeps rising signals sustained overload, and data past retention would be lost.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: Your order-tracking screen sometimes shows PACKED before PAID for the same order. Events are produced with a random key. What is the best first fix?
options: Switch the consumer group to read from all partitions with one shared thread pool
Increase the topic's partition count so each event gets its own partition faster
Sort events by their producer timestamp in the consumer before applying them
Produce every event for an order with key order_id so they all land in one partition
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Kafka only orders messages within one partition, so all events for an order must share the key that maps them to the same partition. Sorting by timestamp is unreliable because clocks skew and retries can stamp later times on earlier changes.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: A team disabled producer idempotence but kept max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5. Batch A fails and is retried after batch B succeeds. What happens, and what is a correct fix?
options: B can land before A, reordering a key's events; turn idempotence on or set max in flight to 1
A is dropped permanently; raising retries to the maximum value fixes the problem
Nothing goes wrong, because acks=all alone guarantees batches land in send order
B is rejected by the broker; lowering delivery.timeout.ms makes A arrive first
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Without idempotence, a retried batch can land after a later batch that already succeeded. Idempotence lets the broker enforce sequence numbers with up to 5 in flight; otherwise you need 1 in flight. acks=all is about durability, not ordering of retries.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: With enable.idempotence=true, how does the broker stop retries from reordering or duplicating batches?
options: It stores a hash of every message ever sent and drops any repeated payloads
It forces the producer to wait for each batch's reply before sending the next one
It tracks a producer ID and a per-partition sequence number and rejects duplicate or out-of-order batches
It stamps every message with the broker's clock and sorts batches by that time
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: The idempotent producer gets a producer ID, and each batch carries a sequence number per partition that the broker checks. That is why up to 5 requests can stay in flight safely rather than having to drop to 1.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: Which broker setting combination ensures an acknowledged message cannot silently vanish when a partition leader dies?
options: replication.factor=1, min.insync.replicas=1 and unclean leader election enabled
replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2 and unclean leader election disabled
replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=1 and unclean leader election enabled
replication.factor=2, min.insync.replicas=2 and acks=1 on every producer
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: With RF 3 and min ISR 2, an acks=all write sits on at least two brokers, and with unclean election off only an in-sync copy can become leader. Allowing unclean election lets a lagging copy take over and drop the tail.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: During the Big Billion Days prep, someone proposes growing the keyed `orders` topic from 12 to 16 partitions mid-sale for more throughput. What is the main ordering risk?
options: Consumers stop reading until every producer is restarted with the new partition list
Existing messages are deleted when partitions are added, losing the order history
The idempotent producer resets its sequence numbers and starts rejecting all batches
hash(key) % partitionCount changes, so an order's new events go to a different partition and may be read out of order
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Keys map to partitions with hash(key) modulo the partition count, so changing the count moves a key's future events to a new partition while its old events remain on the old one. That is why the answer says to size partitions up front.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: Your consumer hands records to a 16-thread pool to speed up processing. Customers now get the 'shipped' SMS before 'packed'. What is the best fix?
options: Switch the consumer to read_committed isolation so threads see events in order
Route records to workers by key so the same order always goes to the same worker sequentially
Add more partitions so each thread gets its own partition and its own keys
Keep round-robin dispatch but add a short sleep before each SHIPPED event is handled
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: A consumer group preserves partition order only if each partition or key is processed sequentially. Routing by key keeps per-order order while still allowing parallelism across orders; read_committed only hides uncommitted transactional writes.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: Processing PAID for order 4471 fails, so the consumer pushes it to a retry topic and moves on to PACKED. What should it do instead?
options: Pause that key until PAID succeeds, or send every later event for that key to the retry path behind PAID
Commit the offset for PAID first so the retry topic can reorder events afterwards
Process PACKED immediately and let the retry topic apply PAID whenever it gets to it
Drop PAID after one failed attempt because PACKED implies the payment went through
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Retries must not let later events overtake earlier ones for the same key. Either hold the key or keep its later events queued behind the failed one; processing PACKED first breaks per-order order.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: A team says: 'We use Kafka transactions, so our order DB update and the cross-DC copy are exactly-once.' What is wrong with this?
options: Transactions only work when acks=1, so they cannot be combined with acks=all
Transactions cover the database but stop working once consumers commit offsets
Transactions are atomic only within one Kafka cluster; they don't cover your database or a second DC
Transactions are atomic across clusters but only when MirrorMaker 2 runs in sync mode
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Kafka transactions atomically write outputs and consumer offsets inside one cluster, giving exactly-once for Kafka-to-Kafka processing. The database needs something like the outbox pattern, and nothing stretches a transaction across two clusters.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: DC1 loses power one second after SHIPPED v4 was acknowledged with acks=all. MirrorMaker 2 copies to DC2. What should you expect in DC2?
options: v4 may be missing, because cross-DC copying is asynchronous and the newest tail may not have arrived
v4 is in DC2 but with the same offset, because MirrorMaker 2 preserves offsets
All of DC1's data for that partition is discarded and must be rebuilt from scratch
v4 is guaranteed to be in DC2, because acks=all waits for the DC2 copy too
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: MM2, Replicator and Cluster Linking are asynchronous: the producer's acks=all is satisfied by DC1 brokers, and the copy happens later. So a lost tail (RPO > 0) is normal and must be recovered, e.g. by outbox replay.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: After failing over to DC2 using MM2's translated offsets, a consumer re-reads PACKED v3 that it had already applied. Is this a bug?
options: Yes; it means unclean leader election happened in DC2 and data was rewritten
No; but the consumer must apply v3 again because DC2's copy is the new truth
Yes; MM2 should translate offsets exactly, so the checkpoint topic is corrupted
No; offset translation is conservative so consumers resume slightly early, and the version check drops v3
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: MM2 checkpoints map offsets approximately and conservatively, so you get re-delivery rather than skips. A consumer that remembers last applied version 3 drops v3 as a duplicate.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: Which statement about cross-DC copy tools matches the answer?
options: MM2 is synchronous so it avoids a lost tail, while Cluster Linking is asynchronous
MM2 usually changes offsets on the target; Cluster Linking keeps the same offsets but still has a lost tail
Cluster Linking changes offsets on the target; MM2 keeps them byte-for-byte
Both MM2 and Cluster Linking keep identical offsets and never lose the tail
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: MM2 writes into new partitions (e.g. dc1.orders) where offsets differ, so it uses checkpoints for translation. Cluster Linking makes byte-for-byte mirror topics with the same offsets, but all these tools are asynchronous.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: Your company wants zero acknowledged-data loss if a whole site fails. You have three data centres in one metro, 2 ms apart. Which pattern fits best?
options: One cluster in a single site with replication.factor=3 and nightly backups
Two separate clusters with MirrorMaker 2 running active-active for every key
A stretch cluster over the three sites with broker.rack set, acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2
A stretch cluster over two distant regions 40 ms apart with acks=all
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: A stretch cluster places each partition's three replicas in three sites, so every acknowledged write is in at least two sites and offsets don't change on failover. It needs close sites and three of them so the KRaft quorum keeps a majority.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: An architect proposes a stretch cluster across Mumbai and Delhi only (about 35 ms apart). What are the two main problems?
options: Producers would lose idempotence, and transactions would need read_uncommitted
Kafka forbids racks in different cities, and replication factor can't exceed two
Offsets would differ between the two sites, and MirrorMaker 2 can't run on top
Every acks=all write pays the cross-region round trip, and with two sites you can't keep a majority if one fails
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Stretch clusters only make sense with single-digit millisecond latency between sites; 30-40 ms hurts producer latency and throughput. Losing one of two sites leaves no majority for the KRaft controllers or min ISR.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: DC1 fails and you run an active-passive failover. What should be the FIRST step?
options: Fence DC1 producers (DNS, config, ACLs) so there can never be two writers
Switch DC1 back on immediately once power returns to recover the lost tail
Replay the outbox into DC2 before anything else is changed
Start DC2 consumers from offset zero so nothing at all can be missed
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Fencing first prevents split-brain if DC1 flickers back. The runbook order is fence, drain lag if possible, translate offsets, start DC2 consumers, switch producers, replay the lost tail, then fail back carefully later.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: After failover, SHIPPED v4 for order 4471 never reached DC2. How does the answer recover it?
options: Raise MM2's replication speed so lost-tail events are copied faster next time
Ask the customer to refresh the app so the client resends the shipping event
Republish recent rows from the shipping service's outbox table into DC2; the version check removes duplicates
Wait for DC1 to come back and let MM2 copy v4 across automatically on restart
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Outbox replay republishes a time window of rows from the source of truth, deliberately creating duplicates that the per-key version check drops. It only works if that database itself survived in DC2, so the database's RPO matters too.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: Weeks after the outage, DC1 is repaired. An engineer wants to just switch it back on and resume. What is the correct approach?
options: Delete DC2's topics so DC1 is the only copy and there is no confusion
Do a planned failback: copy DC2's data back, fence DC2, then switch traffic
Switch DC1 on and let both DCs take writes until MM2 catches them up
Switch DC1 on with its stale tail because it was the original primary
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Failback is a planned move; turning DC1 back on with its stale tail risks two histories and lost DC2 writes. Letting both write is split-brain.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: You run active-active across DC-South and DC-North. What rule keeps per-order ordering well defined?
options: Each order has one home region that alone writes its events; the other region only reads mirrored copies
Both regions write every event and consumers keep whichever copy arrives first
The region with lower latency to the customer writes each individual event
Both regions may write any order as long as their clocks are NTP-synchronised
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: One writer per key gives a single well-defined order; failed regions' keys are re-homed via the failover runbook. Letting both regions write the same key is split-brain, and no tool can fix the interleaving afterwards.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: A consumer's last applied version for order 4471 is 2 and it receives v4. What should it do?
options: Drop v4 as a duplicate because it is not exactly equal to the last version
Treat it as a gap: wait briefly for v3 or fetch current state from the source of truth and record that version
Apply v4 on top of v2 because newer always wins for order status
Rewind the partition to offset zero and reprocess every event for all orders
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Version greater than last + 1 means a gap; the consumer waits or fetches the current state (e.g. SHIPPED, version 4) and overwrites. Only versions less than or equal to last are dropped as duplicates.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: Where should a consumer store its 'last applied version per key' for the version check to be safe?
options: In an in-memory map that is rebuilt from scratch on every restart
In a separate cache updated after the projection change is committed
In the same transaction as its own update to its projection or database
In the Kafka message headers so the next consumer can read it
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Saving the version in the same transaction as the update ensures the two never disagree after a crash. The producer's version should likewise come from the DB row, ideally written with the outbox row.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: A developer suggests ordering cross-DC events by event timestamp instead of a version number. Why is that unsafe?
options: Timestamps are fine across DCs but cost more storage than version numbers
Kafka strips timestamps from messages when MirrorMaker 2 copies them
Timestamps only work when idempotence is off and max in flight is 1
Clock skew between DCs and retries that stamp later times on earlier changes can reverse close events
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Machine clocks in two DCs drift by milliseconds or more, so events 5 ms apart can appear reversed. A version from the single owner of the key is the only reliable order.

How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.q: A teammate says: 'Idempotent producer is on, so we have exactly-once end to end and consumers don't need dedup.' What is the best response?
options: Correct, as long as acks=all is also set on every producer in both DCs
Idempotence prevents duplicates only if max in flight is set above five
Correct, idempotence covers consumers, databases and second clusters as well
Idempotence only stops duplicates and reordering from producer retries into one partition; consumers still need dedup
How do you make sure Kafka messages stay.why: Consumers can reprocess after a crash or failover, and nothing covers the database or a second cluster. Idempotent consumers with a per-key version check are still required.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: A 6-person startup building a grocery delivery app wants to begin with 12 microservices 'so we can scale later'. What is the best advice?
options: Build one unstructured monolith now and plan a full rewrite into services next year
Start with a modular monolith with strict modules, and split services out later when real pain appears
Use 12 services but let them share one database to keep the operations simple
Go ahead with 12 services, since splitting later is always far harder than starting split
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Six people can't run 12 services well, boundaries are still changing, and network and data costs slow them down. A modular monolith keeps the seams so splitting later is easy; a shared database would create a distributed monolith.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: According to the answer, microservices mainly solve which kind of problem?
options: An organisational scaling problem, such as many teams blocking each other
A database problem, since each service can finally use joins across tables
A code quality problem, since services force developers to write cleaner code
A raw performance problem, since network calls are faster than function calls
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: The main payoff is teams deploying and owning parts independently. The technical cost (network calls, distributed data, operations) is real and paid every day; network calls are slower than function calls, not faster.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: Your weekly release has 300 changes and a coupons bug keeps rolling back everyone's work. Which benefit of splitting directly addresses this?
options: Network calls, so the coupons bug turns into a timeout instead of a crash
Technology freedom, so the coupons team can rewrite its code in a new language
Distributed data, so coupons can be eventually consistent with the orders table
Independent deploys, so each team ships on its own schedule without one shared release train
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Deploy queue pain is a classic signal to split: separate services let one team ship without waiting for or being rolled back by another. Changing languages doesn't fix the shared release train.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: During a festive sale, product search needs 40x normal capacity while seller onboarding needs almost none. Why does this favour extracting search?
options: A monolith cannot run behind a load balancer, so it cannot scale out at all
Extracting search removes the need for any caching during the sale period
As its own service, search scales alone instead of running hundreds of copies of the whole app
Search must be split because read-heavy code is not allowed inside a monolith
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Scaling mismatch is a strong reason to split: in a monolith you'd pay for 400 copies of everything, including admin screens. Monoliths can scale horizontally fine; the issue is scaling unequal parts.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: The reviews feature has a memory leak. In the monolith, it occasionally takes down checkout. Which microservices benefit addresses this, and how should the product page behave?
options: Technology freedom; rewrite reviews in Python so it can never leak memory
Independent scaling; add more checkout instances so the leak is spread out
Team ownership; assign checkout's team to also be on-call for reviews
Fault isolation; the page shows 'reviews unavailable' and still lets people buy
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: In one process, a leak in reviews can crash checkout. As a separate service with a timeout and fallback, a slow or failing reviews service degrades only its own part of the page.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: One product page calls 6 services in a chain, each 99.9% available. Roughly how available is the chain?
options: About 94%, because each hop removes one percent
About 99.99%, because more services add redundancy
About 99.4%
About 99.9%, the same as each service
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Availabilities multiply: 0.999^6 is about 0.994. Chained network calls reduce overall availability, which is why timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and idempotency become necessary.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: Checkout needs to 'place order and reserve stock' across the Orders and Inventory services, each with its own database. What does the answer recommend?
options: A saga of local transactions with compensating steps, publishing events via an outbox
Retry the whole flow until both succeed, without any compensating actions
A single SQL transaction spanning both services' databases with a shared join
Let Orders write directly into Inventory's stock table to keep it atomic
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Each service does a local transaction and publishes an event; on failure earlier steps run compensations like refund or release stock. The outbox ensures events aren't lost; writing into another service's tables creates a distributed monolith.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: A user complains checkout took 9 seconds. The request touched 8 services. What is most needed to find the slow hop quickly?
options: A weekly load test that replays production traffic against staging
Distributed tracing with a request ID carried through every call, plus central logs
Merging the 8 services into one database so queries can be compared
Larger instances for all 8 services so no hop can ever be slow again
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Without a trace ID flowing through every call (viewed in a tool like Jaeger) and central logs, finding the slow hop is guesswork. In the worked example a trace ID found the slow hop in two minutes.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: Which sentence best summarises the trade microservices make?
options: They trade operational complexity for simpler code and fewer deployments
They remove complexity entirely by making every service small and simple
They trade code complexity for operational and distributed-systems complexity
They trade network latency for faster in-process function calls
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Splitting moves complexity into network failures, distributed data, debugging and per-service operations. The trade is worth it only when organisational gains are larger.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: In a modular monolith, the Cart module imports an internal class from Payments. What should catch this?
options: An architecture test such as ArchUnit that fails the build when module boundaries are broken
Nothing; in a monolith any module may freely use any other module's classes
The production load balancer, which rejects calls that cross module boundaries
A nightly database job that checks which module wrote each table row
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: A modular monolith enforces public interfaces between modules and module-owned tables, with build tools like ArchUnit checking the rules. That keeps the seams clean for a later extraction.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: Orders calls Payments through a PaymentsApi interface inside the monolith. Later, Payments is extracted as a service. What changes?
options: Nothing changes, because the interface automatically becomes a network call
Only the PaymentsApi implementation changes to an HTTP or gRPC client; callers stay the same
Every caller of PaymentsApi must be rewritten to build HTTP requests itself
Orders must move into the Payments service so the interface still works
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Coding against an interface means extraction only swaps the implementation behind it. That's why a modular monolith gives most of the clarity of microservices and ready-made seams.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: Which of these is a WEAK reason to split a module into a microservice?
options: A full build and test run takes 45 minutes, so people batch changes
A heavy batch job regularly slows down user-facing traffic
A crash in a low-priority feature keeps hurting the critical path
The code is messy and microservices are seen as the modern approach
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: A messy monolith becomes messy microservices plus network calls; 'it's modern' or 'Netflix does it' are weak reasons. Long builds, scaling mismatches and reliability conflicts are real signals.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: A team splits the system into a 'database service', a 'validation service' and a 'UI service'. What is the problem?
options: They split by technical layer, so every feature has to touch every service
Layer services are fine as long as each runs in its own Docker container
Nothing; splitting by layer is the recommended way to draw service boundaries
They have too few services; layers should be split into even smaller pieces
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Boundaries should follow business capabilities (Catalogue, Cart, Payments, Delivery). Layer-based splits force each feature across all services. A good boundary means most features change only one service.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: Orders and Inventory are separate services, but both read and write the same `stock` table. What have they built?
options: A healthy design, since sharing a table avoids eventual consistency
A distributed monolith: microservice costs with no independent changes
A modular monolith, which is the recommended starting point
A strangler fig, because the shared table is gradually migrated
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Neither team can change the table safely without the other and they often must deploy together. Inventory should own the table; Orders should use its API or events.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: One team split Order into Order-Create, Order-Update and Order-Read services sharing a database; every change needed three lockstep deploys. What is the lesson?
options: Add a fourth Order-Delete service so each verb has its own owner
Give each verb service a copy of the database so they can deploy separately
Split by business capability, not by verb or layer; merge them back into one Orders service
Keep the split but add a shared release train for the three services
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Services that must deploy together and share data are a distributed monolith. The fix in the worked example was to merge them into one Orders service owning its data.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: You want to move Payments out of a large monolith safely. Which plan follows the strangler fig pattern?
options: Build Payments, then switch 100% of traffic over in one night with no comparison
Freeze all features for a year and rebuild the whole system as microservices at once
Keep Payments code in the monolith and let the new service share its database
Put a router in front, build Payments with its own data, shift traffic 1% to 10% to 100%, then delete the old path
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Strangler fig migrates one capability at a time behind a router, moves data, shifts traffic gradually while comparing results, and removes the old code. Big-bang rewrites usually run late while the old system keeps changing.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: A mid-size e-commerce company asks which service to extract first. Which is the best candidate?
options: The admin screens, because they get the least traffic and nobody will notice
A read-heavy part with clear edges and real pain, like search, fed by catalogue events
Whichever module has the most lines of code, to shrink the monolith quickly
The most tangled core module, since it causes the most merge conflicts
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: First extractions should have clear edges, real pain and few dependencies, often search or payments. Starting with the most tangled core is risky because its boundaries are unclear.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: A team claims 'Microservices are always more scalable than a monolith.' What is the best correction?
options: Wrong; microservices can never scale beyond the size of their database
Correct; a monolith can only run as one instance on one machine
A monolith scales horizontally behind a load balancer; services help when parts need different scaling
Correct; network calls between services add capacity to the system
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Monoliths scale out fine. Microservices help when parts have different scaling needs or when teams are the bottleneck.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: Your company now has 120 services and each team builds its own CI, dashboards and alerting. What does the answer suggest?
options: Letting each team keep reinventing tooling for maximum technology freedom
Merging all 120 services back into one monolith immediately
Removing monitoring from low-traffic services to save operational cost
A platform team providing a standard service template, CI/CD, tracing, dashboards and on-call tooling
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Every service needs pipelines, deploys, dashboards, alerts and on-call; 50 or 120 services means that many of each. Platform basics should exist before you have many services.

Monolith or microservices: when is split.q: How can you tell you've drawn a service boundary in the wrong place?
options: Features keep needing changes in several services at once, or services must deploy together
Services talk to each other mostly through published events
Most new features change only one service and its database
Each service can do its main job even when a neighbour is briefly down
Monolith or microservices: when is split.why: Lockstep changes, joint deploys and long chatty call chains suggest merging or redrawing. The other options describe signs of a good boundary.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: Your shopping app's product page calls GET /products/42 (60 fields, uses 8), then seller, reviews and delivery-estimate endpoints one after another. Which two problems is it showing?
options: HTTP/2 head-of-line blocking and a missing protobuf contract
Over-fetching from the 60-field response and under-fetching from needing four round trips
The N+1 query problem and a missing idempotency key on GET
Over-caching from the CDN and under-caching in the browser
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: Getting 60 fields to use 8 is over-fetching; needing four sequential calls is under-fetching (around 200 ms each on mobile). N+1 is a GraphQL server-side problem, not this client pattern.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: Your team must keep REST but wants the product page to load in one call with exactly its data. What is the standard REST-side fix?
options: Switch every endpoint to POST so the client can send a list of wanted fields
Move the four calls into a gRPC bidirectional stream from the phone
Add Cache-Control: max-age=60 to all four existing endpoints
Add a Backend for Frontend endpoint like GET /app/product-page/42 that combines everything
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: A BFF combines the data a screen needs into one tailored response. It works, but you maintain one per screen and client type. Caching alone doesn't remove the four round trips.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: Android needs 3 images and a short title, web needs 8 images and the full description, and a lite app needs title, price and one thumbnail. Which API style fits best for these apps?
options: GraphQL, where each client writes a query naming exactly the fields it wants
Plain REST with one fixed response shape that includes every field
gRPC, because browsers and phones call protobuf services natively
A REST API with a new version number for each client type
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: GraphQL lets each front-end ask for its own shape in one round trip from one endpoint. gRPC is meant for service-to-service traffic and browsers need a proxy.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: A GraphQL query lists 50 orders with each order's customer name, and the database log shows 51 queries. What is happening and what is the fix?
options: Under-fetching; split the query into 50 separate REST calls
Over-fetching; remove the customer name field from the schema
The N+1 problem; use a DataLoader to batch all customer IDs into one de-duplicated call
A cache miss; add Cache-Control headers to the /graphql endpoint
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: A naive resolver runs one query for orders and one per order for the customer. DataLoader collects the IDs requested in the same tick and makes one batched call, de-duplicating repeats.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: Why can't a CDN cache GraphQL responses as easily as REST GETs, and what is a common fix?
options: GraphQL responses are binary protobuf, so a JSON gateway must decode them first
Every GraphQL response is personalised, so caching is never possible at all
GraphQL forbids Cache-Control headers; the only fix is to switch to REST
Requests usually go as POSTs with different bodies to one URL; persisted queries let apps send a hash via GET
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: CDNs cache by URL; one endpoint receiving varied POST bodies defeats that. Persisted queries register queries ahead of time, so the app sends a short hash, allowing GET and CDN caching.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: Your monitoring shows 100% HTTP 200 for the /graphql endpoint, yet users report broken pages. What is the likely cause?
options: GraphQL errors usually come back as HTTP 200 with an errors array, so monitoring must read the body
The CDN is caching error pages and rewriting their status codes to 200
gRPC deadlines are silently converting timeouts into successful responses
The REST BFF is swallowing 404s before they reach the GraphQL layer
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: Unlike REST, GraphQL typically signals errors inside the response body. Monitoring based only on status codes will miss them.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: A public GraphQL endpoint gets a query nested ten levels deep that hammers the database. Which set of protections does the answer suggest?
options: Converting each nested level into a separate versioned REST endpoint
Depth and cost limits, capped page sizes, resolver timeouts, rate limits, and persisted-only queries in production
Switching the endpoint to HTTP/2 and adding protobuf encoding for responses
Adding an ETag header so repeated deep queries return 304 Not Modified
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: Expensive queries are a known GraphQL risk, so you bound depth and cost, cap pages, time out resolvers, rate limit per client, and allow only pre-approved queries in production.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: Pricing and Inventory are internal Java and Go services exchanging thousands of small calls per second. Which API style best fits?
options: REST with CDN caching so repeated internal calls are served from the edge
GraphQL with a single endpoint so each service picks its own fields
gRPC with protobuf over HTTP/2, a code-generated contract and per-call deadlines
Server-Sent Events so Inventory can push stock changes to Pricing
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: gRPC's compact binary messages, multiplexed HTTP/2 connections, deadlines and compile-time contracts suit internal service-to-service traffic where you control both sides.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: What makes a gRPC call cheap compared with opening a fresh HTTP/1.1 request each time?
options: gRPC skips TLS entirely, so no encryption overhead is ever paid
gRPC sends JSON field names, which compress better than protobuf numbers
HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests on one long-lived connection with compressed headers
gRPC caches every response at the CDN, so most calls never hit the server
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: HTTP/2 carries many concurrent calls over one connection, avoiding a new TCP and TLS handshake per call. Protobuf identifies fields by number, not name, which keeps messages small.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: A product-page resolver calls the delivery service over gRPC with a 100 ms deadline, and the delivery service is slow. What should happen?
options: The whole GraphQL response fails with a 503 so the client retries the page
The gateway converts the call to REST and retries it without a deadline
The resolver waits indefinitely because gRPC calls cannot be cancelled
The call times out and only that field is null; the page renders with 'Delivery date shown at checkout'
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: Deadlines give each call a time budget so a slow service doesn't hold everyone up. In GraphQL a failed field can be null while the rest of the page still renders.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: Your pricing service must push live price drops continuously to an internal aggregator. Which gRPC feature fits?
options: Unary calls polled every second, since gRPC has no streaming support
Server streaming, where one request receives a stream of PriceReply messages
An ETag on each reply so the aggregator gets 304 Not Modified when unchanged
Persisted queries, so the aggregator sends a hash and gets cached prices
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: gRPC supports unary, server streaming, client streaming and bidirectional streaming. A rpc that returns stream PriceReply fits continuous price updates; the aggregator then fans out to apps over WebSockets.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: A partner seller in Coimbatore with a small PHP shop wants to update stock and prices in your marketplace. Which API is easiest for them?
options: A public REST API with JSON and clear status codes such as 429 for rate limits
A bidirectional gRPC stream that keeps one connection open per seller
An internal GraphQL layer shared with your mobile apps and their resolvers
A gRPC API, since its generated contracts work in every browser without a proxy
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: Partners use many languages and tools, expect readable JSON and easy debugging, and may call from browsers. REST with clear status codes is simplest; gRPC needs gRPC-Web or a gateway for browsers.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: A teammate exposes POST /getProduct that returns 200 for everything, including 'not found'. They call it a REST API. What is wrong?
options: REST means resources, correct verbs and meaningful status codes; this loses caching and error signalling
Nothing; REST simply means sending JSON over HTTP in any form
REST APIs must use GraphQL-style error arrays instead of status codes
It should return 304 Not Modified instead of 200 for missing products
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: A REST read should be GET /products/{id} returning 404 when missing; GET is cacheable and status codes tell clients what happened. A POST returning 200 for everything is not REST.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: A mobile app retries POST /orders after a timeout and the customer gets two orders. What does the answer recommend?
options: Return 409 Conflict on every second POST from the same phone
Change the endpoint to GET /orders so the request becomes idempotent
Send an Idempotency-Key header so the server recognises the retry as the same order
Add Cache-Control: max-age=60 so the retry is served from cache
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: GET, PUT and DELETE should be idempotent but POST is not, so payment-like POSTs carry an idempotency key. Turning a create into a GET violates HTTP semantics and risks caching writes.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: A browser has product 42 cached with ETag "v17". It sends If-None-Match: "v17" and nothing changed. What does the server return?
options: 409 Conflict because the ETag already exists
200 OK with the full product body again
204 No Content with a new ETag
304 Not Modified with no body
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: Conditional requests with ETags let the server confirm the cached copy is still valid without resending it. This is part of REST's caching strength.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: You must make a breaking change to a REST product response. Old app versions stay on phones for months. What is the usual approach?
options: Reuse the old field names with new types so URLs don't need to change
Add a new version like /v2/products/42 and keep /v1 alive while clients migrate
Rename fields in place, since REST clients fail loudly on unknown names
Change /products/42 in place and force all users to update the app the same day
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: Adding is safe and removing or renaming breaks clients, so breaking changes get a new version kept alongside the old one. REST clients ignore unknown fields, so adding optional fields is safe.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: How does GraphQL usually handle API evolution compared with REST?
options: It deletes unused fields automatically when no query has used them for a day
It renames fields freely because clients receive the schema at runtime
No versions: add fields, mark old ones @deprecated, and measure which clients still use them before removing
It requires a new /graphql/v2 endpoint for every field added to the schema
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: Because every client lists the fields it uses, you can measure exact usage of a deprecated field before removing it. That lets GraphQL avoid versioned endpoints.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: A teammate deletes field 3 from a protobuf message and later adds a new field reusing number 3 with a different type. What is the risk and the rule?
options: The new field will be rejected at compile time by every old service binary
Old services read field 3 with the old meaning and silently corrupt data; mark it reserved and use fresh numbers
No risk; protobuf identifies fields by name, so the number doesn't matter
Only performance suffers, since reused numbers cause larger message sizes
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: Protobuf identifies fields by number on the wire, so reusing a number with a new type makes old and new services misread data. Use `reserved 3;` and always assign new numbers.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: Mid-sale, the pricing team adds bank_offer_paise = 7 to PriceReply. Older consumers haven't been redeployed. What happens?
options: Old consumers skip unknown field 7, so no coordinated deploy is needed
All services must redeploy together or the gRPC connection will refuse calls
Old consumers crash because protobuf rejects any unknown field number
Old consumers read field 7 as price_paise and show wrong prices
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: Adding a field with a new number is backward compatible: old readers ignore unknown fields, so services can talk during a rolling deploy.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: A teammate argues 'gRPC is always faster, so let's use it for the public product page too.' What is the best counterpoint?
options: gRPC is actually slower than JSON because protobuf messages are larger
gRPC cannot carry product data because it only supports streaming calls
gRPC requires one TCP connection per request, which overloads phones
Browsers need gRPC-Web or a gateway, and a CDN-cached REST response at 10 ms beats any uncached call
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: gRPC is faster on the wire but has no HTTP caching and needs a proxy for browsers. Cacheable public reads are often best as REST GETs served from the CDN.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: Which statement about GraphQL is a misconception the answer warns about?
options: GraphQL lets each client choose exactly which fields it receives
GraphQL automatically makes the backend efficient because clients ask for less
GraphQL usually exposes one endpoint backed by a typed schema
GraphQL resolvers are functions that fetch individual fields
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: Clients ask for less, but a naive server can make many more database calls (N+1), so batching and cost limits are still needed. The other statements are accurate descriptions.

REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.q: For a large e-commerce platform, which combination does the answer describe as typical?
options: REST for public and partner APIs, GraphQL or a BFF for your own apps, gRPC between internal services
REST everywhere, since GraphQL and gRPC cannot coexist in one system
GraphQL everywhere, since it fully replaces both REST and gRPC
gRPC for public APIs, REST between internal services, GraphQL only for admin tools
REST, GraphQL or gRPC: what is the diffe.why: Choose by the caller: partners, your own UIs, or your own services. Most large systems use two or all three styles.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: Servers A, B and C use round robin. Every third request is a slow 3-second report and it always lands on C. What goes wrong and what fixes it?
options: C is removed by health checks; consistent hashing on user ID fixes it
C builds a queue while A and B idle; least connections sends new requests to the least busy server
Nothing goes wrong, because round robin always spreads work evenly
A crashes from overload; weighted round robin with weight 0 for A fixes it
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Round robin counts requests, not work, so uneven request costs pile up on one server. Least connections (or power of two choices) adapts to how busy each server actually is.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: Server A has 8 CPUs; B and C have 4 each. Which algorithm and weights fit?
options: Weighted round robin with weights 2, 1, 1
Consistent hashing with 2 virtual nodes for A and 1 for others
Plain round robin, since all three are in the same pool
Least connections with A's limit set to half of B and C
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Weighted round robin gives bigger servers more turns: out of every 4 requests A gets 2, B and C get 1 each.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: You want 1% of traffic to try a new release of the checkout service before rolling out fully. Which load-balancing feature helps?
options: Consistent hashing so the newest servers get the most keys
Connection draining on the old version so traffic shifts gradually
Weighted round robin with weight 1 for the new version and 99 for the old
Sticky sessions so the first 1% of users always get the new code
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Weights are also used for canary releases: a small weight sends a small share of traffic to the new code. Draining is for removing servers, not splitting traffic.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: Least connections tracking is expensive at your scale. What cheap approximation does the answer mention?
options: Round robin with a random sleep before each request
Hash the request URL modulo the number of servers
Pick the server with the lowest IP address on each request
Power of two choices: pick 2 servers at random and send to the less busy one
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Power of two choices gives most of the benefit of least connections while only checking two servers per request.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: You have 4 cache servers and route with hash(userId) % 4. You add a 5th server. What happens?
options: No keys move until the old servers are restarted
Only the new server's keys change, so hit rate is unaffected
About 20% of keys move, and the rest keep their warm caches
About 80% of keys move, most caches go cold and the database gets hammered
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: With modulo hashing, changing N remaps almost every key. Consistent hashing would move only about 1/5 of keys, keeping most caches warm.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: Why do consistent hashing rings place each server at many points ('virtual nodes')?
options: To spread each server around the ring so keys are shared out more evenly
To encrypt the key so clients can't guess which server they hit
To make every request visit several servers for redundancy
To let a dead server keep receiving traffic until draining ends
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Virtual nodes (e.g. 100 per server) smooth the distribution of keys across servers. Each key still goes to the next server clockwise on the ring.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: When is key-based stickiness via consistent hashing actually worth using?
options: When servers store logged-in sessions only in their own memory
When you want the load balancer to retry POST requests safely
When a server keeps a local cache per key, so routing the same key keeps it warm
When all requests cost the same and servers are identical
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Hashing helps performance by keeping per-key caches warm. Stickiness should be a performance hint, never needed for correctness; sessions belong in a shared store like Redis.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: You need /search to go to the search pool and /cart to the cart pool. Which load balancer type is required?
options: A Layer 4 load balancer that routes by IP and port, such as AWS NLB
A Layer 7 load balancer that reads the HTTP path, such as NGINX, Envoy or AWS ALB
A DNS round-robin setup returning several IPs for the domain
An anycast IP announced from several sites using BGP
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Only L7 reads the full HTTP request (path, host, headers, cookies). L4 sees just IP and port, so it can't route by URL path; it's faster but less smart.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: A large site places L4 load balancers at the edge in front of a fleet of L7 proxies. Why combine them?
options: Combining them removes the need for health checks on servers
L4 cheaply spreads connections across many L7 proxies, which do the smart path-based routing
L4 terminates TLS while L7 only forwards raw TCP bytes
L7 is faster than L4, so it must be the outermost layer
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: L4 is fast; L7 is smart. A common setup uses L4 to distribute load across L7 proxies, which route by path or header and usually terminate TLS.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: Health checks run every 5s with timeout 2s, unhealthy threshold 3 and healthy threshold 2. Roughly how long before a dead server is removed?
options: Instantly, on the first failed check
About 2 seconds, one timeout
About 10 to 15 seconds
About 1 minute, to avoid flapping
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Three consecutive failures at 5-second intervals take roughly 10-15 seconds. Passive checks on real traffic can eject a failing server faster, in a second or two.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: Server C answers /health with 200 but returns errors on many real requests. How does the load balancer catch this?
options: Passive health checks (outlier detection) eject it after several consecutive errors on real traffic
Sticky sessions move its users elsewhere after the first error
It can't; a 200 from /health always keeps the server in the pool
Active checks catch it by retrying /health with a longer timeout
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: A 200 from /health only proves the process is up. Passive checks watch real traffic and can eject a server (say for 30 seconds) even before the next active check.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: Your /health endpoint checks the shared database. During a brief DB slowdown, every server fails health checks. What is the lesson?
options: Make /health check even more dependencies so failures are detected sooner
Lower the unhealthy threshold to 1 so bad servers leave faster
Use sticky sessions so users stay on servers that still pass
Keep /health shallow so a shared dependency doesn't remove the whole pool at once
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: A deep health check that fails on shared dependencies removes all servers together. Many load balancers fail open in that case; the fix is a shallow check plus separate alerting on dependencies.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: A server crashes while handling a 'place order' POST. Should the load balancer automatically retry it on another server?
options: Not blindly; the order may already exist, so retry only with an idempotency key the order service checks
No, and the client must never retry a failed POST under any circumstance
Yes, but only if the request is retried within 2 seconds
Yes, always; load balancers make every request safe to retry
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Only idempotent requests like GET can be retried automatically. A POST may have partly succeeded, so a retry could duplicate the order; an idempotency key lets the server recognise the repeat.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: Every deploy of your product service causes a short burst of 502 errors. What is the missing practice?
options: Using weighted round robin with weight 0 for every server at once
Connection draining: stop sending new requests, let in-flight ones finish, then stop the server
Consistent hashing so requests stick to servers that aren't being deployed
Increasing the health check interval so servers aren't marked down
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: With draining, the server gets no new requests and in-flight work completes (e.g. 30-60 s timeout). The app should fail /health on SIGTERM, finish work, then exit.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: Your app keeps carts in each server's memory and uses sticky-session cookies. What problems does this cause?
options: Carts become slower because Redis is never involved in the request
The load balancer can't do health checks on sticky servers
TLS termination fails because cookies are encrypted per server
If that server dies the cart is lost, and load is uneven since new servers only get new users
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Sticky sessions tie correctness to one server. Stateless servers with sessions in Redis or a signed token let any server serve any request.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: You run 50 healthy app servers behind a single load balancer machine, which then fails. What happens and what prevents it?
options: The servers automatically elect one of themselves as the new load balancer
Nothing much; the 50 servers keep receiving traffic directly from users
The whole site goes down; use an HA pair with a virtual IP, several LBs behind DNS, anycast, or a managed multi-zone LB
Only a quarter of users are affected, because DNS caches the server IPs
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: A single load balancer is a single point of failure. Redundancy options include an active-passive pair sharing a virtual IP, multiple IPs in DNS, or anycast.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: Why is relying only on DNS with multiple load balancer IPs slow to recover when one IP dies?
options: DNS requires BGP route changes that take hours to propagate
DNS only ever returns one IP, so other load balancers are never used
Clients and resolvers cache DNS answers, so removing a dead IP can take minutes depending on TTL
DNS sends health checks only once a day to each IP
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: DNS answers are cached for their TTL, so removing a dead IP isn't instant. Anycast instead shifts traffic via routing to the next healthy site.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: The product service normally runs on 40 servers. A midnight sale is expected to need 200. What should the team do?
options: Switch to round robin so 40 servers can handle 5x the load
Turn off health checks during the sale to avoid removing busy servers
Rely on autoscaling at midnight, since it adds servers within seconds
Pre-scale to 200 an hour early, because autoscaling takes minutes and can't add 160 servers in 30 seconds
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Scaling takes minutes while failures and spikes take seconds. For known spikes, pre-scale.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: An autoscaled server just booted with an empty cache. What should the load balancer do?
options: Keep it out of the pool until the next deploy completes
Send traffic only after it passes health checks, and ramp it up with a slow-start warm-up
Give it the full share of traffic immediately to warm its cache faster
Route all sticky users to it so its cache fills quickly
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: New servers join after passing health checks; slow start (e.g. 60 seconds) avoids flooding a cold server. On scale-in, servers are drained before termination.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: At 00:03 in a sale, one of 200 servers crashes. The pool has 30% headroom. What is the expected user impact?
options: Minimal: in-flight GETs are retried elsewhere, the server is ejected in seconds, and 199 servers absorb 0.5% more each
None at all: even in-flight POSTs are always retried safely by the proxy
Severe: the load balancer stops routing until an engineer removes the server
Severe: all users on that server lose carts stored in Redis
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Passive detection ejects it in about 2 seconds and active checks confirm. In-flight POSTs are not auto-retried by the proxy; the app retries with an idempotency key.

How does a load balancer decide which se.q: If all servers in a pool suddenly fail health checks, what does the answer say it usually indicates?
options: That the load balancer's algorithm should switch to round robin
A shared dependency or a bad health check, rather than every server truly being dead
A hardware fault that has hit every server at the exact same moment
That sticky sessions have been disabled by a recent deploy
How does a load balancer decide which se.why: Simultaneous failure points to something common like the database or an overly deep /health. Many load balancers fail open and keep sending traffic to all servers.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: A fresher says 'a Docker container is just a lightweight VM.' What is the most accurate correction?
options: It is a compressed disk image that the host OS emulates instruction by instruction
