It is a normal process fenced by namespaces and limited by cgroups, sharing the host kernel
It is a hypervisor slice with its own virtual CPUs and virtual disks
It is a VM with a smaller guest kernel that boots in under a second
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: A container has no second kernel; it is an isolated, budgeted process on the host kernel. That is exactly why it is fast and why its isolation is weaker than a VM's.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: What does a virtual machine have that a container does not?
options: Its own complete guest operating system, kernel included, running on virtual hardware from a hypervisor
Its own cgroup limits on CPU and memory usage
Its own image registry that stores every version of the app
Its own copy-on-write writable layer on top of the image
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: A hypervisor (KVM, ESXi, Hyper-V) gives each VM virtual CPUs, memory and disks, and the VM boots a full OS. cgroups and writable layers are container features.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: Two containers on the same host both show their app as process ID 1. How is that possible?
options: Docker restarts the host's init process inside every container
cgroups renumber processes so each container's budget starts at 1
Each container runs its own kernel, which numbers processes from 1
Each has its own PID namespace, so the kernel shows each a separate process list starting at 1
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Namespaces control what a process can see. On the host, both apps appear with ordinary, different PIDs; there is no separate kernel.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: You run `docker run --memory=512m` and the app tries to use 600 MB. What happens?
options: The namespace hides the extra memory so the app sees only 512 MB free
The whole host swaps heavily and every container slows down equally
The kernel's cgroup limit kills that container; other containers on the host are unaffected
The container is moved to a host with more free memory automatically
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: cgroups set the budget (CPU, memory, I/O, process count). Exceeding the memory limit gets that container killed, which is why a leaking release only took down its own containers.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: Which pair of Linux kernel features is 'the whole trick' behind containers?
options: Namespaces for what a process can see, and cgroups for how much it can use
Virtual CPUs for compute, and virtual disks for storage
OverlayFS for storage, and DNS for container name resolution
Hypervisors for hardware emulation, and BIOS for booting the guest
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Docker didn't invent namespaces or cgroups; it made them easy with a Dockerfile, a build command, a run command and a standard way to ship images.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: You change one line of Java code and rebuild. Your Dockerfile copies pom.xml, runs dependency:go-offline, then copies src. Why aren't dependencies re-downloaded?
options: Maven dependencies are stored in the host kernel and shared automatically
The dependency layer depends only on pom.xml, which didn't change, so Docker reuses that cached layer
The registry skips downloads because the image tag stayed the same
Docker always caches every layer regardless of which files changed
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Docker reuses a layer if that step and everything before it are unchanged; the first changed step and everything after it rebuild. Copying the manifest before the source keeps rebuilds to seconds.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: A teammate's Dockerfile does `COPY . .` first and then `RUN mvn dependency:go-offline`. Every build takes 8 minutes. What is the best fix?
options: Push the image to the registry before building so layers are pre-cached
Add more RUN steps at the top so caching has more layers to use
Copy pom.xml and download dependencies before copying the source code
Switch the base image from Ubuntu to Alpine to make downloads faster
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Copying all source first means any code change invalidates the dependency layer. Order steps from least to most frequently changing.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: Why does the example Dockerfile use a multi-stage build?
options: So the image can run on both Windows and Linux hosts unchanged
So each stage gets its own cgroup memory limit at runtime
So the container can boot two kernels, one for building and one for running
The build stage has the full Maven toolchain; the final stage carries only a JRE and the jar
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Multi-stage builds keep build tools out of the final image, making it smaller and reducing attack surface. They have nothing to do with kernels or OS portability.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: Twenty containers on a server all run from the same cart-service image. How does disk and memory usage scale?
options: Each container boots its own guest OS, so usage grows by GBs per container
They share one writable layer, so a file edited in one appears in all
They share the image's read-only layers; each adds only its own thin writable layer
Each container stores a full copy of every image layer on disk
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Images are stacks of read-only layers merged by a union file system like OverlayFS. Each container gets its own writable layer with copy-on-write.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: An app inside a container edits a config file that came from a lower image layer. What happens?
options: The change is pushed back to the registry as a new image tag
The change is written into the shared read-only layer for all containers
The edit fails because all image files are permanently read-only
The file is copied up into the container's writable layer first, then changed there (copy-on-write)
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Lower layers stay read-only and shared; modifications go to the container's own writable layer, which is deleted when the container is removed.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: A developer stores uploaded invoices inside the container's file system. After a redeploy they're gone. Why, and what is the fix?
options: The writable layer is deleted with the container; keep data in volumes or a database
cgroups wiped the files for exceeding the disk budget; raise the limit
The registry garbage-collected the files; increase the registry retention
The namespace hid the files from the new container; share the PID namespace
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Containers are disposable and their writable layer goes with them. Persistent data belongs in volumes or external storage.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: Your Spring Boot service runs in a container that starts 'in under a second', yet it takes 15 seconds before serving requests. Why?
options: The registry is re-downloading the image on every start
Containers remove the OS boot, not the app's own start-up; the JVM still needs to warm up
The container is secretly booting a full Linux kernel first
Namespaces take about 15 seconds to set up for a Java process
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: The runtime starts in under a second, but a heavy Java app may still need 5-20 seconds. That's why sale-time scaling still pre-warms a buffer.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: Roughly how do VMs and containers compare according to the answer?
options: VMs: several GB and 30 s to minutes to boot; containers: MBs of overhead and under 1 s to start
Both take about the same time to start, but VMs use less memory
Containers need hundreds of MB of guest OS each; VMs share one kernel
VMs: a few MB and under 1 s; containers: several GB and minutes to start
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: A full guest OS costs GBs and boot time; containers add only a few MB beyond the app. Density goes from tens of VMs to hundreds of containers per server.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: A developer tested a fix on Java 21, but three production VMs still ran Java 17 and crashed. How did containerising fix this?
options: The registry blocks deploys to servers with an older Java version
Docker automatically upgrades the host's Java to match the laptop
Containers translate Java 21 bytecode so it runs on Java 17
The Java version became part of the image, and every environment pulls the same tested image
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Docker turned the environment into code (Dockerfile) and a versioned artifact (image), so servers can't drift. Build once, deploy that same image everywhere.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: Someone re-pushed a different build under the tag cart-service:1.42.0. How do you guarantee production runs exactly what was tested?
options: Use a larger base image so the tag can't be overwritten
Deploy by tag but restart containers twice to refresh the cache
Deploy by image digest (sha256 hash of content) rather than by tag
Rebuild the image separately in each environment from the same Dockerfile
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: A digest identifies exact bytes; tags can be reused. Rebuilding per environment defeats 'build once, deploy everywhere'.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: After containerising, which of these can STILL differ between your laptop and production?
options: The Java runtime version included in the image
Configuration, secrets, external services, CPU architecture and the host kernel
The app's library versions packed into the image
The files in the image's read-only layers
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Docker fixes files and versions. Config, secrets, databases, ARM vs x86 and the kernel can still differ, which is why the problem shrank rather than vanished.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: Why is container isolation considered weaker than VM isolation?
options: Containers have no memory limits, so one can read another's RAM directly
Containers use a hypervisor that is larger and easier to attack than a kernel
Containers always run as root on the host with no way to change it
All containers share one host kernel, so a kernel escape could expose every container on that host
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Sharing the kernel gives speed but is the weak spot. With VMs, an attacker must break the hypervisor, a much smaller and harder target.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: Your marketplace lets thousands of unknown sellers upload scripts that run on your platform. Are plain containers enough?
options: No; add a stronger boundary like gVisor or Firecracker micro-VMs, plus non-root users and strict limits
Yes; namespaces fully prevent any kernel-level escape between tenants
No; you must give each seller a dedicated physical server instead
Yes, as long as each seller's script uses a different base image
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Untrusted multi-tenant code needs a VM-like boundary. gVisor provides a user-space kernel and Firecracker micro-VMs boot in a fraction of a second.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: Your team needs to run a Windows-only legacy app on Linux hosts. What should you use?
options: A multi-stage Dockerfile with a Windows build stage and a Linux run stage
A VM, because containers share the host's Linux kernel and can't run a Windows kernel
A container with a user namespace mapped to a Windows administrator
A Windows container image, since Docker translates Windows calls to Linux
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Containers bring no kernel of their own, so different OSes need VMs. Docker Desktop on Mac and Windows itself runs a small Linux VM.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: Which hardening step from the answer addresses the risk of root inside a container?
options: Tagging every image with a semantic version number
Exposing port 8080 instead of port 80 in the Dockerfile
Running the app as a non-root user (e.g. USER 1001) in the Dockerfile
Using a larger base image with more security tools installed
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Without user namespaces, root inside can be root on the host for many purposes. Other hardening: minimal images, scanning, deploy by digest, read-only root FS, resource limits.

What is a Docker container really, how i.q: What is the normal production setup described in the answer?
options: Containers on bare metal only, since VMs are obsolete
One VM per container to get both speed and strong isolation
Containers running on top of VMs, with sandboxes for untrusted code
VMs only, since containers are too insecure for production
What is a Docker container really, how i.why: Clouds run your containers on VMs anyway; Kubernetes nodes are often cloud VMs. Sandboxes like gVisor are added where code is untrusted.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: What is the core idea behind how Kubernetes keeps apps running?
options: You script each step, such as 'start container on node 3', and it runs them once
It runs every container on every node so one is always available
It snapshots each container's memory and restores it after a crash
You declare desired state, and control loops keep reconciling actual state toward it
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Like a thermostat, controllers repeatedly check, compare and fix the gap between what you asked for and what is running.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: You run `kubectl apply` on a Deployment YAML. What has happened at that moment?
options: The kubelet on every node has already started all the containers
The API server stored the desired state in etcd; controllers then act to make it real
The HPA has calculated replicas and booked new machines in the cloud
The scheduler has permanently assigned each pod to a fixed node
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Applying YAML records a wish. A chain follows: Deployment controller creates pod records, the scheduler picks nodes, kubelets start containers and report back.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: A Deployment wants 6 replicas. The node running 2 of them loses power. What happens?
options: After the node is marked unreachable, the ReplicaSet sees 4, creates 2 pods, and the scheduler places them on healthy nodes
The 2 pods are restarted on the same node by its kubelet once power returns
The HPA immediately doubles replicas to 12 to compensate for the loss
Nothing changes until an engineer manually re-applies the Deployment YAML
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Pods on a dead node are treated as lost after a timeout (about 5 minutes by default, tunable). The ReplicaSet notices the gap and recreates them elsewhere; once ready, the Service sends them traffic.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: A pod requests 500m CPU. Node A has 300m unrequested, node B has 2 cores free. Where does the scheduler place it?
options: Either node, because the scheduler places pods using limits, not requests
Neither; the pod stays Pending until node A frees enough CPU
Node B, because node A is filtered out for not fitting the request
Node A, because the scheduler prefers the most tightly packed node
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Scheduling filters out nodes that can't fit the request, then scores the rest. The scheduler uses requests, not limits.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: A new pod stays Pending because no node has enough requested capacity. What usually resolves it?
options: The readiness probe marks it ready so the scheduler retries it
The HPA reduces the pod's CPU request until it fits
The kubelet throttles other pods to make room for it
A cluster autoscaler sees the Pending pod and adds a new node
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Pending due to no fit is the signal for a cluster autoscaler (if configured) to add machines; new nodes take 1-3 minutes or more.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: A team says 'Our scheduler places pods based on their limits, so we set high limits.' What is wrong?
options: Limits are used for placement, but only for memory, not CPU
Nothing; limits are exactly what the scheduler reserves on a node
The scheduler reserves and places by requests; limits only cap usage at runtime
The scheduler ignores both and places pods randomly across nodes
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Request is the guaranteed booking used for scheduling; limit is the ceiling. Requests set too high waste money; too low and pods fight for CPU at peak.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: A container exceeds its CPU limit during a sale. What happens?
options: Its readiness probe is disabled until load falls
It is throttled (slowed down), not killed
It is OOMKilled and restarted by the kubelet
It is evicted to another node with more CPU
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Over the CPU limit the container is throttled; over the memory limit it is OOMKilled. Many teams skip CPU limits to avoid needless throttling.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: A container keeps restarting with reason OOMKilled. What does it mean and what should you check?
options: It exceeded its memory limit; check for a leak, whether the limit is realistic, and that the JVM heap fits inside it
It exceeded its CPU limit; remove the CPU limit so it is no longer killed
The node ran out of disk; add a larger volume to the pod
Its liveness probe timed out; increase the probe interval to fix it
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: OOMKilled means the memory limit was crossed. For Java, a heap sized larger than the container limit is a common cause.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: A pod shows CrashLoopBackOff, with restarts waiting 10 s, 20 s, 40 s and growing. What does this tell you?
options: The readiness probe failed, so the pod was removed from the Service
Kubernetes has fixed the bug and is slowly ramping up traffic to it
The container keeps crashing on start; Kubernetes is retrying with backoff but a human must fix the bug
The node is out of memory, so the scheduler is waiting for a new one
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: The kubelet restarts the process with growing waits up to 5 minutes. Kubernetes restarts processes; it does not fix a bug that crashes on every start.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: Your pod's readiness probe fails while its liveness probe passes. What does Kubernetes do?
options: Kills and restarts the container immediately
Removes the pod from the Service so it gets no traffic, without restarting it
Deletes the pod and creates a new one on another node
Keeps sending traffic but logs a warning event
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Readiness controls traffic; liveness controls restarts. When readiness passes again, the pod rejoins the Service.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: Your liveness probe calls the database. The DB slows down for a minute and every cart pod restarts at once. What is the fix?
options: Make liveness check only the process itself; dependency trouble shouldn't trigger restarts
Make liveness check even more dependencies so problems are caught sooner
Remove probes entirely and rely on the HPA to replace bad pods
Replace the readiness probe with the liveness probe on all pods
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: A liveness check tied to a shared dependency causes restart storms. Liveness should answer 'is this process stuck?' only.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: A large Java service takes 90 seconds to boot and keeps getting killed by its liveness probe during start-up. What should you add?
options: A readiness probe with a shorter interval than the liveness probe
A larger maxSurge value in the Deployment's rolling update
A higher CPU limit, so the JVM is throttled less during boot
A startup probe, which gives slow apps time to boot before liveness checks begin
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Startup probes hold off liveness checks until the app has started, preventing premature restarts of slow-starting services.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: You update the cart image from 2.3.1 to 2.4.0 with 4 replicas, maxSurge 25% and maxUnavailable 25%. How does the rollout proceed?
options: It deletes all 4 old pods, then starts 4 new pods together
It starts 4 new pods alongside the old ones and switches traffic at once
It adds 1 new pod, waits until it's ready, removes 1 old pod, and repeats
It updates the image inside the running containers without restarting
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: A rolling update creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts pods gradually, gated by readiness. 25% of 4 is 1 pod at a time.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: During a hotfix rollout, new pods fail readiness because of a bad config. What happens?
options: Kubernetes kills the old pods anyway to finish the rollout on time
The rollout stalls while old pods keep serving; you can run kubectl rollout undo
The Service sends traffic to new pods regardless of readiness
The HPA scales the new version up until readiness eventually passes
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Rollouts only proceed when new pods are ready, so a bad version stalls instead of replacing healthy pods. Readiness probes are what make this safe.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: For a midnight hotfix on a busy cart service, you want capacity to never drop during the rollout. Which settings fit?
options: maxSurge 100% and maxUnavailable 100%
maxSurge 0 and maxUnavailable 100%
maxSurge 0 and maxUnavailable 25%
maxSurge 25% and maxUnavailable 0
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: maxUnavailable 0 means no pod may be missing; maxSurge lets extra new pods come up first. This was the hotfix setting in the worked example.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: An HPA targets 60% CPU. 8 pods average 75%. How many replicas will it ask for?
options: 10 pods
12 pods
9 pods
8 pods
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentValue / targetValue) = ceil(8 x 75 / 60) = ceil(10) = 10, within maxReplicas.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: An HPA with a 50% CPU target sees 6 pods averaging 90%. How many replicas will it request?
options: 9 pods
11 pods
12 pods
10 pods
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: ceil(6 x 90 / 50) = ceil(10.8) = 11, as long as that is within maxReplicas. The formula always rounds up.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: Traffic falls and the HPA computes fewer replicas, but pods don't drop for a few minutes. Why?
options: The cluster autoscaler must first remove nodes before pods are removed
The HPA can only scale up; scaling down must be done manually
Pods cannot be removed until their liveness probes fail
Scale-down waits for a stabilization window (5 minutes by default) to avoid flapping
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: The stabilization window stops a short dip from causing repeated scale-down and scale-up.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: A cricket final is expected to send a 4x spike within seconds of the toss. Why shouldn't you rely only on the HPA?
options: Metric checks, pod readiness (30-90 s) and new nodes (1-3 min) add up; pre-scale by raising minReplicas
The HPA scales down during spikes to protect the database
The HPA can only react to memory, not CPU, so it won't notice the spike
The HPA reacts instantly, but Services can't route to more than 10 pods
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: The HPA checks about every 15 seconds and handles gradual doubling well, not a 2-second spike. For known peaks, teams pre-scale ahead of time.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: You scale the order service from 10 to 60 pods but latency doesn't improve; the shared MySQL is at 100% CPU. What does the answer say?
options: Kubernetes should automatically scale MySQL too once pods are added
You need to raise maxSurge so new pods share the database load
Kubernetes scales copies; if the database is the bottleneck, more pods add load. Protect it with caching or rate limits
Set CPU limits on pods so the database gets more CPU on the node
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Adding pods helps only if the app is stateless and the bottleneck is the app tier. A saturated database needs caching, rate limits or its own scaling.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: What does a Kubernetes Service give you?
options: A physical machine that runs containers and reports their state
A database that stores the cluster's desired state
A stable name and IP in front of a changing set of pods, spreading requests across ready ones
A guaranteed number of running pods for a given image version
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Pods come and go with new IPs; the Service name like `cart` stays fixed. Deployments keep N pods; nodes are machines; etcd stores state.

What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.q: A 3-person team runs two small services with steady traffic. They ask if they should adopt Kubernetes. What is the best advice?
options: Yes, but run their own self-managed control plane to learn it fully
It's likely overkill; a managed PaaS or a couple of VMs behind a load balancer is simpler
Yes, Kubernetes is mandatory for any production deployment today
No, they should run their services as plain processes on one laptop
What does Kubernetes actually do? How do.why: Kubernetes has a steep learning curve and many moving parts. It shines with many services, teams and frequent deploys, and even then most companies use a managed version (EKS, GKE, AKS).

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: Your food app shows order status, which changes about five times in 40 minutes. A junior insists on WebSockets. What is a reasonable view?
options: Polling every 15-30 seconds can be perfectly fine; WebSockets add stateful servers and reconnect logic
Long polling is unusable here because it needs a WebSocket upgrade first
WebSockets are always better than polling, so they are the only correct choice
Short polling every 100 ms is best because it gives near-instant updates cheaply
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: For rare updates, polling is the simplest thing that works. WebSockets bring heartbeats, reconnection and stateful connection servers, which may not be worth it.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: 1 million fans poll a live score API every 5 seconds. How many requests per second is that?
options: 20,000 requests per second
12,000 requests per second
200,000 requests per second
5,000,000 requests per second
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: 1,000,000 / 5 = 200,000 per second. If the score changes once every 30 seconds, about 5 of every 6 requests return nothing new.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: 500,000 users poll an order-status API every 10 seconds. What is the load and the average extra delay?
options: 50,000 requests per second, with no extra delay at all
500,000 requests per second, with about 1 second average delay
5,000 requests per second, with about 10 seconds average delay
50,000 requests per second, with about 5 seconds average delay (up to 10 s)
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: 500,000 / 10 = 50,000 per second. Average delay is half the polling interval, worst case the full interval.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: Your delivery app must poll but wants fresher updates near the end without multiplying load. What helper does the answer suggest?
options: Disable CDN caching so each poll reaches the origin server
Adaptive intervals, e.g. poll faster once the order is 'out for delivery'
Remove ETags so every response always includes the full body
Poll every 100 ms for the whole order to remove all delay
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: Polling faster cuts delay but multiplies load; adaptive intervals spend requests where freshness matters. ETags (304 Not Modified) and short CDN caching also help.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: How does long polling differ from short polling?
options: The server holds the request open until there's news or a timeout (say 25-30 s), then the client asks again
The server keeps one response open forever and streams text events into it
The connection is upgraded with a 101 response to a two-way channel
The client polls less often, such as every 5 minutes instead of every 5 seconds
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: Long polling gives near-instant latency over plain HTTP with at most one empty reply per timeout. It needs async I/O on the server so waiting requests don't each hold a thread.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: With long polling, an update arrives just after the server replied and before the browser's next request. How do you avoid losing it?
options: The server retries sending the update until the browser's next request lands
The client asks for 'everything after version 57' so the server returns anything it missed
The browser polls twice per cycle so there's never a gap between requests
The load balancer buffers responses and merges them into the next reply
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: Updates can slip into the gap between reply and next request, so clients send the last version seen and the server replies with anything newer.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: For a live cricket score page where the browser rarely sends anything, which approach does the answer recommend?
options: Short polling every second, because SSE can't carry JSON data
WebSockets, because SSE is an obsolete technology replaced by them
Push notifications to the browser tab for every ball bowled
Server-Sent Events, with one-way push, automatic reconnect and Last-Event-ID resume
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: Scores flow server to client, exactly what SSE does. SSE is a current standard, simpler than WebSockets for one-way updates, and carries text such as JSON.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: What does an SSE response look like on the wire?
options: A series of separate HTTP responses, each closed after one score update
A protobuf stream over HTTP/2 that browsers need a proxy to read
An HTTP response with Content-Type text/event-stream that never finishes, carrying id/event/data lines separated by blank lines
A 101 Switching Protocols reply followed by binary frames with 2-14 byte headers
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: SSE keeps one HTTP response open and writes small text messages into it. The browser uses EventSource to listen for named events.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: Riya's SSE stream drops in a lift after event 9. When it reconnects, how does she get events 10 and 11?
options: The load balancer stored the events in a sticky session cookie
The order service resends every event from the start of the order
The browser sends Last-Event-ID: 9 and the server replays later events from a short buffer
She can't; SSE has no reconnect, so the app must reload the page
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: EventSource reconnects automatically and sends Last-Event-ID; any connection server subscribed to the topic can replay from its buffer. Which server she lands on doesn't matter.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: Why might many open tabs using SSE run out of connections on an older browser?
options: Servers reject more than 6 Last-Event-ID headers from the same IP
Over HTTP/1.1 browsers allow only about 6 connections per domain; HTTP/2 removes this limit in practice
Each SSE stream needs its own WebSocket upgrade, capped at 6 per browser
SSE allows only one connection per user account across all devices
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: The 6-per-domain limit is an HTTP/1.1 browser constraint, not an SSE rule. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one connection.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: Your team is building a live auction where buyers place bids constantly and see others' bids instantly. Which approach fits best?
options: Short polling every 30 seconds, because bids rarely change
Push notifications, because sockets are killed when the app is open
SSE, because it allows the browser to send bids up the same stream
WebSockets, because both sides send often with low latency on one two-way channel
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: Chat, bidding, games and shared documents need frequent client-to-server messages, which WebSockets handle on the same connection. SSE is one-way.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: What does the server reply to a WebSocket upgrade request, and what changes after that?
options: 101 Switching Protocols with Sec-WebSocket-Accept; the TCP connection then carries WebSocket frames, not HTTP
202 Accepted; the browser then polls the server every few seconds
200 OK with text/event-stream; the server then streams one-way text events
304 Not Modified; the browser then reuses its cached copy of the page
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: The server hashes the client's Sec-WebSocket-Key into Sec-WebSocket-Accept. After the 101, both sides send small frames in either direction at any time.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: Your WebSocket users on mobile keep getting silently disconnected after about a minute of no score changes. What is the likely fix?
options: Switch the connection to short polling every 60 seconds instead
Increase the WebSocket frame header from 2 bytes to 14 bytes
Disable TLS so the connection isn't inspected by proxies
Send ping/pong heartbeats every 20-30 seconds, under the load balancer's ~60 s idle timeout
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: Load balancers and mobile networks close idle connections; many LBs time out around 60 seconds. Heartbeats keep the connection alive and detect dead peers.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: Which of these must you build yourself with raw WebSockets but get for free with SSE?
options: An HTTP-based opening handshake
Two-way messaging from browser to server
Automatic reconnection and resume after a gap
Binary frame support for compact payloads
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: SSE's EventSource reconnects and resumes with Last-Event-ID. With WebSockets you build reconnection, resume, heartbeats and auth yourself, or use a library like Socket.IO.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: A score service produces one update; 10 million fans are connected across 300 connection servers. How should the update reach them?
options: Publish once to a pub/sub topic like match-123; each connection server subscribed to it forwards to its own users
The database trigger pushes the change straight to every open socket
Each fan's browser polls the score service directly to fetch the update
The score service opens a connection to each fan and writes the update directly
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: Push is stateful, so updates must find the server holding each connection. Pub/sub (Redis Pub/Sub, Kafka, NATS) lets one publish fan out without the producer knowing who is connected.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: Planning capacity for 2 million mostly idle SSE connections, what usually limits how many one connection server can hold?
options: The database, which must hold a row lock per open connection
Memory per connection and file-descriptor limits, not CPU
The CDN, which can only cache 6 connections per domain
CPU, because each idle connection consumes a full core
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: With async I/O (Netty, Node.js, Go), one machine holds tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand idle connections. Load-test with realistic message rates rather than trusting a number.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: A connection server holding 100,000 users crashes. What prevents it from knocking over the next server?
options: Clients switch permanently to short polling every 100 ms after a crash
The load balancer blocks all reconnections until the crashed server returns
Clients reconnect immediately at the same instant to minimise downtime
Clients reconnect with exponential backoff plus random jitter, so they don't all arrive at once
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: Without jitter, 100,000 clients reconnecting simultaneously form a thundering herd. Backoff like 1, 2, 4, 8 s capped around 30 s, plus randomness, spreads them out.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: A client reconnects after 20 minutes offline, and the server's replay buffer only holds 2 minutes. What should happen?
options: Reject the reconnect and ask the user to reinstall the app
Fall back to fetching the current full state with a normal API call, then continue live updates
Keep the client disconnected until the buffer is enlarged
Replay the 2 minutes available and assume nothing else happened
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: Snapshot fallback handles gaps too big to replay. For a score or order status, the latest state matters more than every step in between.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: Riya taps 'Call rider' on an order screen that uses SSE. How is that action sent?
options: As a normal HTTP POST, separate from the one-way SSE stream
By waiting for the next SSE event and attaching the request to it
Through a WebSocket upgrade of the existing SSE connection
Up the SSE stream, since SSE is two-way after the first event
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: SSE is server-to-client only; occasional client actions go through ordinary requests. That's why SSE is enough for order tracking.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: Your food app wants to tell users their order arrived while the app is in the background. What should it use?
options: SSE with a longer retry interval so it reconnects later
A WebSocket with heartbeats every 5 seconds to keep it alive
A push notification, since sockets are killed when the app sleeps
Long polling with a 30-minute timeout per request
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: Mobile operating systems kill background sockets, so live channels only work while the app is active. Push notifications cover the background case.

How does a live cricket score or order-t.q: A developer says 'once my client reconnects, it is up to date.' Why is this wrong?
options: Reconnects are rare on mobile, so missed updates don't matter
The server pauses publishing until all clients reconnect
Updates sent while it was offline are lost unless you use sequence numbers, replay or a snapshot
Reconnecting always replays every missed update automatically in any protocol
How does a live cricket score or order-t.why: Design for disconnects as the normal case: give each update a per-topic sequence number, resume from the last seen, and fall back to a snapshot.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: During a sale, the cart service scales from 4 to 40 instances, but the new ones get no traffic. What is the likely cause?
options: Callers use a fixed list of IPs instead of discovering instances by name
The service mesh sidecars haven't encrypted traffic with mutual TLS yet
The new instances are failing liveness probes and being restarted
The API gateway's rate limit is blocking traffic to new instances
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Hard-coded IPs never learn about new instances. A registry or Kubernetes Service adds them automatically once they pass health checks. Addresses are temporary; names are stable.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: After a rolling deploy, the order service keeps calling payment IPs that no longer exist. What principle did it violate?
options: Route all internal calls through the public API gateway
Always deploy every service at the same time as its callers
Use long DNS TTLs so callers cache addresses for hours
Depend on stable service names, not temporary IP addresses
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: In containers each new instance usually gets a fresh IP. Calling by name via a registry or Kubernetes Service avoids dead addresses; long DNS caching makes it worse.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: A payment instance registers itself with Eureka at startup and sends heartbeats. It hangs and heartbeats stop. What happens?
options: The API gateway restarts it using its liveness probe
Its callers keep using it because registries never remove entries
After heartbeats are missed for a while (say 30-90 s), the registry drops it from the healthy list
It stays registered until an engineer removes it manually
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Self-registration with heartbeats (TTL) is the classic Eureka style. Missing heartbeats lead to removal so callers stop getting that instance.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: Which is an example of third-party registration?
options: An instance calling the registry on startup and sending heartbeats
Kubernetes or a Consul agent registering instances because it knows which ones it started
A developer adding instance IPs to a shared config file
A client caching the registry's list and picking round-robin
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: In third-party registration a separate agent or the platform registers instances. Self-registration is the instance doing it itself, as in Eureka.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: Your team's service registry runs on a single node and crashes during a sale. What does the answer recommend?
options: Route all service-to-service calls through the API gateway instead
Run the registry as a 3- or 5-node cluster, and let clients keep using their cached instance lists
Increase heartbeat frequency so the registry recovers faster
Switch to hard-coded IPs as a backup so callers never need the registry
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Consul and etcd run as 3- or 5-node clusters so losing a node is harmless. Clients also cache their last known lists and keep working briefly.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: In client-side discovery, who picks which payment instance to call?
options: A load balancer reads the registry and forwards the request
The API gateway picks the instance for every internal call
The payment service picks which caller to accept requests from
The caller fetches the healthy instance list from the registry and picks one itself
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Client-side discovery (Eureka plus a client library) avoids an extra hop and allows smart choices like same-zone first, but needs a library in every language.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: Your company has services in Java, Go, Python and Node.js on Kubernetes. Which discovery style does the answer suggest by default?
options: Routing every internal call through the API gateway
Client-side discovery, so each language maintains its own registry library
Server-side discovery, since callers stay simple and language-neutral
Hard-coded IPs per language, refreshed during each deploy
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Server-side discovery (Kubernetes Services, AWS load balancers) keeps callers simple. Client-side makes sense when you need zone-aware or custom balancing and can maintain libraries everywhere.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: What is a trade-off of server-side discovery compared with client-side?
options: One extra network hop, and the load balancer must itself be reliable
Callers must cache the instance list and choose an instance themselves
Every programming language needs its own discovery library
It can't remove unhealthy instances from rotation
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Server-side adds a hop through a load balancer or proxy that must be highly available. Needing a library per language is the cost of client-side discovery.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: The order service calls http://payment-service/pay inside Kubernetes. What turns that name into a working pod address?
options: Cluster DNS resolves it to the Service's stable virtual IP, and kube-proxy forwards to a ready pod
The API gateway looks up the pod IP and rewrites the request
The order pod reads the payment pod IPs from a mounted config file
The payment pod announces its IP to callers via Server-Sent Events
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: CoreDNS maps the name to the ClusterIP, which stays stable; kube-proxy (or an eBPF replacement) forwards to one of the ready pods in the EndpointSlices.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: A new pod is running but still loading its cache. Should it get traffic, and which check controls this?
options: Yes; the API gateway decides which pods are ready, not Kubernetes
Yes; once the liveness probe passes it must receive traffic
No; its readiness probe should fail, keeping it out of the Service's endpoints
No; its liveness probe should fail so it gets restarted until ready
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Readiness decides traffic; liveness decides restarts. A warming pod is alive but not ready, so failing liveness would restart it needlessly.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: Outside Kubernetes, your services use plain DNS records pointing directly at instance IPs. Some clients cache answers for hours. What is the problem?
options: DNS requires every service to run a sidecar proxy to resolve names
Plain DNS has caching/TTL issues and no health awareness, so clients keep calling dead instances
DNS answers are encrypted, so callers can't read instance addresses
DNS can only store one IP per name, so load can't be spread
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: DNS works well when it points to a stable virtual IP or load balancer, or with short TTLs backed by health checks. Long-cached instance IPs go stale.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: A team says the API gateway and the service registry are the same thing. What is the correct distinction?
options: The gateway stores instance addresses; the registry handles TLS and auth
Both are the same component, just named differently by different vendors
The registry rate-limits users; the gateway runs health checks on instances
The registry knows where healthy instances are; the gateway is an edge proxy that uses it to route outside traffic
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: The registry is a live phone book. The gateway is the front door that routes, terminates TLS, authenticates and rate-limits, using discovery to find instances.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: A bot sends 5,000 order requests per minute during a midnight sale. Where should it be stopped, and how?
options: At the database, which locks the order table for that user
At the API gateway's rate limit, which returns HTTP 429 before requests reach the order service
At the payment service, which rejects charges after the first 100
At the service registry, which deregisters the bot's IP address
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Rate limiting is a shared edge job of the gateway, so bots and runaway clients can't flood internal services.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: Your mobile app's home screen needs banners, recommendations and cart count. The team wants one call from the app. Which gateway role helps?
options: Mutual TLS: encrypting calls between internal services
Service registration: adding banner instances to the registry
Aggregation: one /home call fans out to several services and returns one combined response
TLS termination: decrypting HTTPS once at the edge
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Gateways can aggregate several backend calls into one response; when built per app this is often called a BFF (backend for frontend).

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: Why does the gateway authenticate the login token once at the edge?
options: So rate limiting is no longer needed for logged-in users
So the registry can store each user's token next to instance IPs
So internal services can skip TLS between each other permanently
So internal services receive a verified user ID and don't each repeat token checks
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Centralising auth, TLS termination and rate limiting in the gateway avoids every service re-implementing them.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: An architect proposes routing all service-to-service calls through the API gateway for consistency. What is the issue?
options: It adds a hop and a choke point; internal east-west calls should go service to service
Nothing; all traffic should pass through the gateway for safety
Gateways can only handle HTTPS, and internal calls use plain HTTP
Gateways cannot route by path, so internal routing would break
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: The gateway handles north-south traffic from outside. East-west internal traffic goes directly between services, or through a service mesh.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: A company with 300 services needs mutual TLS, retries and metrics on all internal calls without changing app code. What fits?
options: A bigger API gateway that every internal call must pass through
Plain DNS with very short TTLs for each service
Client-side discovery libraries rewritten in every language
A service mesh such as Istio or Linkerd, with sidecar proxies managed by a control plane
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: A mesh handles east-west traffic: discovery, load balancing, retries, timeouts, mTLS and metrics via proxies like Envoy. It adds moving parts, so it's overkill for about ten services.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: Someone claims 'a service mesh replaces the API gateway.' What is the best response?
options: They overlap but serve different traffic; the mesh manages internal calls, the gateway is the public front door
Correct; the gateway only exists to run sidecar proxies
Correct; once you have a mesh, the gateway should be removed
Wrong; a mesh handles only outside traffic and never internal calls
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: The gateway handles user auth, API keys and rate limits for outside callers; the mesh secures and manages internal calls. Many systems run both.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: The gateway's /home aggregation calls recommendations with no timeout. Recommendations slows down, and checkout slows too. What is the fix?
options: Remove rate limiting so more gateway threads are available
Increase the recommendations DNS TTL so lookups are faster
A per-route timeout (e.g. 200 ms) with a fallback like 'show popular items'
Move checkout's business logic into the gateway for speed
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Without timeouts a slow backend ties up shared gateway threads and hurts unrelated routes. Per-route timeouts and circuit breakers isolate the damage.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: Which practice best keeps the API gateway from becoming a bottleneck or single point of failure?
options: Putting shared business rules into the gateway so services stay small
Many stateless instances across zones, no business logic inside, and separate gateways per audience
Sending partner, app and web traffic through one shared gateway pool
One large gateway instance with session state stored in its memory
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Keep it thin and stateless, replicate across zones behind a load balancer, split by audience so a partner surge doesn't hurt shoppers, and load-test with headroom.

In a microservices app, how does one ser.q: A payment pod's node fails mid-sale and some in-flight requests fail. The order service retries once on another instance. Why is that safe?
options: Readiness probes roll back any charge made by the failed pod
The registry guarantees the failed request never reached the payment pod
Payment calls carry an idempotency key, so a retry cannot charge the customer twice
The gateway deduplicates all internal calls between services
In a microservices app, how does one ser.why: Retries on non-idempotent operations need an idempotency key. The failed pod is removed from endpoints within seconds as its readiness stops passing.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: Your company runs 300 microservices in Java, Go and Python, and each language library has different retry and timeout defaults. Security also cannot prove every internal call is encrypted. What does a service mesh like Istio offer here?
options: It moves mTLS, retries, timeouts and telemetry out of app code into platform configuration applied uniformly to all services
It provides one shared Java library that all teams must import to get consistent network behaviour
It routes all internal calls through a single central API gateway that applies the policies
It replaces Kubernetes scheduling so every service runs with identical runtime settings and libraries
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: A mesh puts proxies beside every service and configures them centrally, so behaviour is language-agnostic and changed by config. A shared library still needs 300 upgrades and only works for one language.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: The istiod pods in your cluster crash and stay down for five minutes during normal traffic. What happens to live service-to-service calls?
options: Calls continue but silently drop to plain text because mTLS needs istiod for each handshake
Proxies fall back to random routing until istiod returns and resends the routing tables
Traffic keeps flowing on the proxies' last known config; only config changes and new certificate issuance pause
All calls fail immediately because every request must be authorised by istiod first
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: istiod is the control plane and is not in the request path. Envoy proxies (the data plane) keep using their last config; mTLS handshakes use certificates they already hold.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: In Istio terms, which statement correctly maps the parts of the mesh?
options: The ingress gateway is the control plane; sidecars are optional data stores for routing rules
Kiali is the control plane that configures proxies; Prometheus is the data plane that carries requests
istiod is the data plane that carries traffic; Envoy proxies are the control plane that store config
Envoy proxies are the data plane that carry traffic; istiod is the control plane that pushes config and certificates
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: Data plane = the proxies on the request path; control plane = istiod, which watches Kubernetes, issues certificates and pushes config over xDS. Kiali and Prometheus are observability tools.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: Your platform team complains that sidecars cost memory in every one of 3,000 pods and every Istio upgrade needs pod restarts. Most services only need encryption and identity. What should they evaluate?
options: Running one Envoy sidecar per namespace instead of per pod, shared by all pods through iptables
Ambient mode: a per-node ztunnel handles L4 and mTLS, with optional waypoint proxies only where L7 features are needed
Turning off mTLS so that the sidecars need far fewer CPU cycles and memory for each request
Moving istiod into every pod so that config no longer has to be pushed over the network
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: Ambient mode removes per-pod sidecars: ztunnel (one per node) gives mTLS and identity, and waypoint proxies add HTTP-level features only where required. Dropping mTLS would defeat the security goal.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: In Istio ambient mode, a team needs header-based HTTP routing and retries for one service. Which component provides that?
options: istiod itself, which proxies HTTP requests that need header checks
The ztunnel on each node, which handles all L7 routing by default
A waypoint proxy (Envoy) deployed for that namespace or service
The Kubernetes kube-proxy, which Istio extends with HTTP rules
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: ztunnel handles only L4 and mTLS; L7 features like HTTP routing, retries and header policies need an optional waypoint proxy.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: A security audit requires that only the checkout service may call POST /charge on the payments service, and that this is enforced by identity, not IP. Which Istio feature fits?
options: A firewall rule allowing only the pod IP range of checkout to reach the payments service
A DestinationRule with outlier detection that ejects any caller that is not checkout
A VirtualService that routes only checkout's traffic to the payments subset named charge
An AuthorizationPolicy using workload identities (SPIFFE IDs from service accounts) issued by istiod
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: AuthorizationPolicy says who may call whom based on certificate identity (e.g. spiffe://cluster.local/ns/checkout/sa/checkout-api). IP-based rules break when pods move and are not zero trust.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: You must enable mTLS across 300 services without causing an outage, while some old batch jobs and a VM-based service still send plain text. What is the right first step?
options: Set PeerAuthentication to PERMISSIVE, enrol services gradually, and switch to STRICT namespace by namespace once traffic is nearly all mTLS
Set STRICT mode mesh-wide immediately so any plain-text caller is found quickly by its errors
Leave mTLS off until every service is enrolled, then enable STRICT for the whole mesh in one change
Use STRICT for new services only and allow old callers to bypass the mesh permanently
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: PERMISSIVE accepts both plain text and mTLS, so unenrolled callers keep working while dashboards show progress. Going STRICT at once would break the stragglers, possibly during peak traffic.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: You want to send 5% of checkout traffic to a new version v2, and let internal testers with header x-canary: true always hit v2. Which Istio objects do you configure?
options: A Gateway listing v1 and v2 as hosts, and a PeerAuthentication that weights calls 95/5
A DestinationRule defining subsets v1 and v2, and a VirtualService with a header match plus 95/5 weights
An AuthorizationPolicy allowing testers to call v2, and a Kubernetes Service per version
A DestinationRule with 95/5 weights, and a VirtualService that defines subsets v1 and v2
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: The DestinationRule defines named subsets (and load balancing, outlier detection); the VirtualService holds routing rules such as header matches and weights. The last option swaps their roles.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: Your team says, "We added Istio, so tracing should just work," but Jaeger shows each service as a separate one-span trace. What is the most likely cause?
options: Jaeger cannot read Envoy spans and needs Kiali to merge them into one trace per request
mTLS encrypts the trace headers, so the next proxy cannot read and join the spans
The Envoy sidecars do not create spans unless ambient mode is turned on for the namespace
The applications are not forwarding trace headers like traceparent or B3 from incoming to outgoing requests
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: Proxies create spans, but only the app knows which outgoing call belongs to which incoming request, so it must propagate trace headers (usually via an OpenTelemetry library).

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: Before the sale, you want to check whether the product page degrades gracefully when the inventory service is slow, without changing any code. What can Istio do?
options: Use outlier detection to permanently eject the inventory service from the load-balancing pool
Use fault injection to add a 3-second delay to 10% of calls to inventory, or return 503 for a small share
Set mTLS to STRICT on inventory so that some callers fail and the page shows its fallback
Lower the inventory service's CPU limit through istiod until it responds slowly to every call
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: Fault injection is mesh-level chaos testing: delays or error codes are injected by config. Outlier detection is a circuit-breaking mechanism, not a test tool.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: An engineer edits the checkout DestinationRule and renames a subset that the VirtualService still points to. During peak traffic, every call to checkout returns 503 from Envoy, not the app. Which prevention best addresses this?
options: Run istioctl analyze in CI, review mesh config as code, and order changes: add subsets first, shift traffic, remove old subsets last
Increase retries on the checkout route so transient 503s from Envoy are retried until they pass
Turn off mTLS while editing DestinationRules so that a mismatch cannot cause connection failures
Scale checkout pods up before every config change so there is spare capacity for 503 bursts
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: The 503s come from a routing/config mismatch, so validation, careful ordering and progressive rollout with fast rollback prevent it. Retries just repeat a call that has no valid route.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: An on-call engineer sees 503 errors on a service in the mesh, but the app's own logs show no failed requests. Where should they look first?
options: The application's garbage-collection logs, since Envoy never generates HTTP status codes itself
istiod's request log, because every request in the mesh passes through istiod
Envoy access logs and their response flags, such as no healthy upstream or no route
The Kubernetes scheduler events, since 503s always mean pods failed to schedule
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: With a mesh, a 503 can come from Envoy rather than the app; response flags in access logs explain why. istiod is not in the request path.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: A team argues: "Istio is our API gateway, so we don't need anything else for service-to-service traffic." Which statement best corrects the confusion?
options: A mesh handles only north-south traffic from clients; an API gateway handles east-west traffic
A mesh replaces Kubernetes networking, so gateways are no longer needed in any architecture
A gateway mainly handles north-south traffic from clients; a mesh mainly handles east-west service-to-service traffic
A gateway and a mesh are the same thing; Istio just adds Kubernetes support to a gateway
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: Istio includes an ingress gateway, but most of its value is east-west (service to service). The two concepts overlap but are not identical.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: After adopting Istio, a developer proposes deleting the payment service's idempotency logic because "mesh retries already make us resilient". What is the best response?
options: Delete it, but set retries to 10 attempts so payments eventually succeed for every customer
Keep it: retries are only safe for idempotent operations, and retrying a non-idempotent charge can bill the customer twice
Delete it: Envoy retries automatically de-duplicate requests, so double charges cannot happen
Keep it only until ambient mode is enabled, since ztunnel guarantees exactly-once delivery
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: The mesh does not know business semantics; the app still owns correctness. Mesh retries on a non-idempotent call can duplicate the charge.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: A startup has 12 services, all in Go with a good shared resilience library, no platform team, and a very tight latency budget. Should it adopt Istio now?
options: Probably not yet: libraries plus an API gateway are often enough, and the mesh's complexity and latency cost would outweigh its benefits
Yes: Istio is effectively free and every Kubernetes system should run it from day one
Yes: ambient mode removes all learning and operational cost, so size does not matter
No: Istio only works with Java services, so a Go-only company cannot use it at all
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: The answer's checklist says to avoid or wait if under about 20 services, one language with a good library, no platform team, or tight unmeasured latency budgets. Ambient lowers machine cost, not the learning cost.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: Which of these is the best reason Istio became popular, according to the answer?
options: It guarantees exactly-once delivery for all service-to-service calls in the cluster
It removes the need for Kubernetes and runs services directly on bare-metal machines
It adds no CPU, memory or latency overhead because proxies run inside the Linux kernel
It is language-agnostic, enables zero-trust mTLS without code changes, fits Kubernetes, and is a CNCF graduated project
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: Its popularity rests on language independence, zero trust, Kubernetes fit and CNCF graduation (2023). It does add overhead; eBPF in-kernel is Cilium's approach.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: Your team wants a lighter mesh with a small Rust micro-proxy, fewer features and lower overhead than Istio. Which alternative matches?
options: Linkerd
Cilium service mesh
Kiali
Consul service mesh
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: Linkerd is the simpler, lighter mesh with a Rust micro-proxy. Cilium uses eBPF plus Envoy, Consul spans Kubernetes and VMs, and Kiali is a dashboard, not a mesh.

What is Istio? What problem does it solv.q: Pods occasionally fail at startup because the app tries to call another service before its Envoy sidecar is ready. What is a recommended mitigation?
options: Add aggressive app-level retries forever so startup calls eventually get through the proxy
Hold the app until the proxy has started, or use Kubernetes native sidecars so the proxy starts first
Remove the readiness probe so the pod is marked ready before the app makes any calls
Restart istiod each time a pod starts so the sidecar receives config before the app
What is Istio? What problem does it solv.why: This is a known sidecar lifecycle issue; holding the app until the proxy is ready, or native sidecars, fix the ordering. Infinite retries just mask it and add load.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: Your product page calls a recommendations service that has started timing out. Threads in your service are piling up waiting on it, and the whole page is slowing down. What does a circuit breaker do in this situation?
options: It retries each slow call several times so that more requests eventually succeed
After failures pass a threshold it opens and stops calling the dependency for a while, failing fast or returning a fallback
It restarts the recommendations service automatically so the failing dependency recovers sooner
It queues the calls in memory and sends them all once the dependency becomes healthy again
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: A breaker protects the caller's threads and latency by not calling a failing dependency, and gives that dependency breathing room. It does not fix the dependency itself.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: Which sequence correctly describes the circuit breaker's states?
options: Closed (normal, counting results) -> Open (fail fast) -> Half-open (a few trial calls) -> Closed or back to Open
Closed (normal) -> Open (fail fast) -> Closed automatically after the wait, with full traffic
Open (normal, counting results) -> Closed (fail fast) -> Half-open (a few trial calls) -> Open
Closed (normal) -> Half-open (fail fast) -> Open (trial calls) -> Closed once trials pass
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Like an electrical breaker, closed means current flows (calls go through). After the wait it goes half-open and only a few probes decide whether it closes or reopens.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: A new service gets only a few calls a minute. Two of its first three calls to a dependency fail, and the breaker trips, then flaps open and closed all morning. What setting most directly fixes this?
options: Remove the timeout so slow calls are no longer counted as failures by the breaker
Share breaker state across instances in Redis so every instance trips together
Lower the failure-rate threshold to 10% so the breaker reacts faster to real problems
Require a minimum number of calls in the window (say 20) before the failure rate is evaluated
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: With low traffic, a couple of failures produce a high rate. A minimum number of calls stops the breaker from tripping on tiny samples; lower thresholds make flapping worse.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: Your breaker on the coupon service trips every time users enter invalid coupon codes, because the service returns 404 for unknown codes. What is the fix?
options: Raise the failure threshold to 90% so coupon 404s rarely reach the trip point
Remove the fallback so users see the real 404 and stop typing invalid codes
Configure the breaker to ignore 4xx and business errors and count only timeouts, connection errors and 5xx
Add retries for 404 responses so the second attempt usually returns a valid coupon
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: A 404 for bad input means the dependency is healthy and the request was wrong. Counting client errors trips breakers on a typo storm; raising the threshold only hides the bug.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: During checkout, the payment gateway returns "card declined" for many customers in a short burst. How should the circuit breaker treat these responses?
options: As failures, but only when more than half of the declines come from the same bank
As failures: any non-success business result should count toward tripping the breaker
As successful calls: the gateway worked correctly and the customer's bank refused the payment
As slow calls: declines take longer, so they should count only against the slow-call rate
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Business rejections are correct answers from a healthy dependency, not dependency failures. The example config lists CardDeclinedException under ignoreExceptions.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: A dependency sometimes hangs forever on a request, and your circuit breaker never opens even though users are clearly suffering. Why?
options: The failure threshold is too high, since hanging calls count only as half a failure
The breaker is in half-open state permanently, so it only lets probe calls through
Breakers only count HTTP 5xx responses, so hangs are ignored by design in all libraries
There is no timeout, so the hanging call never completes and is never recorded as a failure
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Timeouts come first: without one, the breaker cannot learn about the failure. Add a timeout and count timeouts and slow calls.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: A dependency's normal p99 latency is 300 ms. It starts returning correct results but in 5 seconds each. Error rate stays at zero. How can a circuit breaker still protect you?
options: Configure a slow-call threshold just above normal p99, so a high slow-call rate trips the breaker
It cannot: circuit breakers only react to errors, so slow successes need a bulkhead instead
Disable the timeout so the breaker waits for the full response and records its latency
Count every response under 5 seconds as a failure so the breaker treats them as errors
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Breakers can trip on slow-call rate as well as failure rate; the follow-up advice is to set the slow threshold just above the dependency's normal p99.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: After the open wait of 30 s, your breaker immediately lets all traffic through to a just-recovering gateway, which fails again under the full load. What should half-open do instead?
options: Skip half-open entirely and close the breaker after a longer wait of five minutes
Allow only a small fixed number of trial calls, close only if they succeed, and ideally ramp traffic back gradually
Stay open forever until an engineer manually resets the breaker after checking the gateway
Send all traffic but retry each failed call three times to absorb the recovering gateway's errors
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Half-open is a probe: a few calls (say 5) test recovery. Flooding a recovering dependency makes the breaker flap.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: Your pricing service exposes a fast getPrice lookup and a slow bulkExport endpoint. Bulk exports time out and trip one breaker, which then blocks all price lookups. What is the better design?
options: Remove the breaker from pricing and rely on retries with backoff for both endpoints
Use one shared breaker for the whole pricing service but raise its threshold to 80%
Share a single breaker for all dependencies of the service so state is consistent
Use separate breakers per operation, so bulkExport failures do not block getPrice
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Scope breakers per dependency and per operation (and per partner or host where it matters); a slow endpoint should not block a healthy one.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: A payment service uses two gateways, A (primary) and B (secondary). Gateway A starts returning 503s with 6-second latency during a sale. What setup gives customers the best experience?
options: No breaker, but retry each A call five times before finally trying Gateway B
A breaker on A whose fallback shows customers an error and asks them to try later
A separate breaker per gateway, with A's fallback routing the payment to Gateway B
One breaker shared by both gateways, so when A fails, B is also blocked to be safe
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Per-partner breakers let A open independently, and the fallback fails over to B in milliseconds instead of customers waiting on timeouts. Long retries on A waste the latency budget.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: Your circuit breaker to a dependency is open. A teammate's code still retries each rejected call three times with backoff. What is wrong?
options: When the breaker is open the answer is already known; retrying just wastes time and should not happen
Nothing: retries with backoff are the main way an open breaker recovers faster
The retries should go outside the breaker so they bypass it and reach the dependency
The retries should have no backoff, so they finish quickly while the breaker is open
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Retries belong inside the breaker, only for transient errors, and not while it is open. Retrying an open breaker adds latency for a known failure.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: A dependency slows down suddenly, and before the breaker has seen enough failures to trip, all 200 of your request threads are stuck waiting on it. Which pattern protects you in this window?
options: A shared breaker in Redis so all instances see the failures and trip together
A bulkhead that caps how many concurrent calls that dependency can use, for example 20
A larger failure-rate threshold so the breaker does not trip too early on the slowdown
Longer timeouts so threads wait until the dependency responds rather than failing
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: A breaker reacts after failures accumulate; a bulkhead limits resource use before that. Use both.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: Your service runs 40 instances. A teammate wants to store circuit breaker state in Redis so all instances share it. What is the usual advice?
options: Always share state, because local breakers never trip unless every instance sees failures
Keep breakers local to each instance; they each discover the failure within seconds, and sharing adds a new dependency
Share state only in half-open, since local probes would otherwise overload the dependency
Store state in the dependency itself so it can tell callers when to open their breakers
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Local breakers converge quickly and avoid a shared dependency like Redis. A service mesh can provide central behaviour if needed.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: In Istio/Envoy, one replica of the inventory service is failing while the others are healthy. Which mechanism acts like a per-host circuit breaker?
options: A bulkhead, which blocks calls to every inventory replica until the bad one is fixed
Half-open state, which keeps only the bad replica receiving trial calls forever
Outlier detection, which ejects the failing host from the load-balancing pool while healthy hosts keep serving
A fallback, which routes all inventory calls to a cache until the replica restarts
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Outlier detection is a network-layer, per-host breaker: it removes a bad replica instead of blocking the whole dependency.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: A circuit breaker opens while 50 requests to the dependency are already in flight. What happens to those 50 requests?
options: They are paused and resumed when the breaker moves to the half-open state
They are cancelled immediately and all receive the fallback response at once
They are counted again as failures, which doubles the wait duration in open state
They complete or time out normally; only new calls are rejected by the open breaker
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Opening affects new calls only; in-flight calls finish or hit their timeouts.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: A manager says, "We added circuit breakers, so the payment gateway outage is handled." What key point is missing?
options: Breakers protect callers, not the dependency; someone must still fix it, so alert on state changes
Breakers should be disabled during outages so that engineers can see the real errors
Breakers only work if the gateway also runs a breaker on its side of the connection
Nothing: an open breaker repairs the gateway by stopping traffic until it restarts itself
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Breakers do not fix the failing service. Alerting on 'breaker opened' gets humans involved early, as in the worked example.

What is a circuit breaker, and how does.q: How should you pick a failure-rate threshold for a dependency whose normal error rate is 0.5%?
options: Use the same 5% threshold for every dependency so the configuration stays consistent
Trip at something clearly abnormal, like 20-50%, with a minimum call count, then tune using chaos tests
Trip at 99%, so the breaker only opens when the dependency is completely down
Trip at 1%, just above normal, so the breaker reacts to the very first sign of trouble
What is a circuit breaker, and how does.why: Thresholds come from baselines: clearly abnormal, not just above normal (which flaps) and not so high that the breaker never helps.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: A pricing service normally handles 10,000 RPS with capacity for about 12,000. Its database slows down, callers with a 1-second timeout start timing out, and each retries up to 3 attempts in total. Why can this turn a one-minute slowdown into an outage?
options: Timeouts cancel the work on the server, so every retry restarts the database query from zero
