Retries push load towards 3x normal (about 30,000 RPS) exactly when the service is weakest, which makes it slower and causes even more retries
Retries are always sent to a different replica, so the original replica never gets a chance to recover
The callers stop sending new requests during retries, so the pricing cache goes cold and slows down
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: Failures are correlated: all callers retry together, creating a feedback loop of more load and more timeouts. Also, a timeout does not cancel server work, so the server keeps processing abandoned requests.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: The database under your pricing service recovers, but pricing stays overloaded and keeps timing out for another 20 minutes. What best explains this?
options: Autoscaling lag: the service only scales back down after 20 minutes of normal traffic
A cold cache: the database needs 20 minutes to rewarm, regardless of the traffic coming in
A metastable failure: retry traffic alone keeps the service overloaded even though the original cause is gone
A thundering herd at startup, which can only happen if the service has no load balancer
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: In a retry storm, the load itself keeps the system broken after the trigger is fixed; you may need to shed load or open circuit breakers to let it recover.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: Your mobile app, API gateway and backend service each make 3 attempts on failure. The database under the backend goes down. How many calls can one user tap generate at the database layer?
options: Up to 81, because each retry also triggers a health check at every layer
Up to 3, because each layer retries independently and only the last one reaches it
Up to 9, because only the two server-side layers count toward the database
Up to 27, because the attempts multiply: 3 x 3 x 3
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: Layered retries multiply, giving 27 calls in the worst case (64 with 4 attempts per layer). The fix is to retry at one layer only.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: Given that three layers each retrying 3 times amplifies load 27x, which layer should usually do the retrying?
options: Only the layer closest to the failing dependency, with the other layers failing fast within a shared deadline
Only the mobile app, since it is closest to the user and knows when they gave up
Only the API gateway, since it can see all traffic and balance retries centrally
Every layer, but with fewer attempts each, such as 2 attempts per layer
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: The layer nearest the failure knows best which errors are transient. 2 attempts at every layer still multiplies (2x2x2 = 8).

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: Every client in your fleet uses backoff of exactly 100, 200 and 400 ms. After a short outage, the service still sees huge spikes at 100, 300 and 700 ms. What is missing?
options: More retry attempts, so the spikes are spread across more retry rounds
A shorter timeout, so clients notice the failure and start backing off sooner
A longer cap on backoff, such as 30 seconds, so waits grow further apart
Jitter: a random wait so clients that failed together do not retry together
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: Backoff alone keeps synchronised clients in neat waves. Randomness breaks the synchronisation and lowers the peak, which is what knocks a service over.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: Using wait = min(cap, base x 2^(attempt - 1)) with base 100 ms and cap 5 s, what is the wait after the 4th failed attempt (before jitter)?
options: 800 ms
400 ms
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: 100 x 2^3 = 800 ms. 1.5 s is the total time waited so far after 4 failures (0.1 + 0.2 + 0.4 + 0.8), not the next wait.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: With base 100 ms, cap 2 s and full jitter, what range can the wait be after the 5th failed attempt?
options: Anywhere from 800 to 1,600 ms
Exactly 1,600 ms
Anywhere from 0 to 1,600 ms
Anywhere from 0 to 2,000 ms
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: Backoff is min(2000, 100 x 2^4) = 1,600 ms; full jitter picks a random value between 0 and that. 800 to 1,600 ms would be equal jitter.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: Your team wants retries spread out as much as possible, but one service must never retry instantly because it needs a guaranteed minimum pause. Which jitter style fits that service?
options: Full jitter: a random wait between zero and the full backoff value
Equal jitter: half the backoff plus a random amount up to the other half
Decorrelated retries: a random wait between zero and the request timeout
No jitter: a fixed backoff value so the minimum wait is always predictable
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: Equal jitter keeps a minimum wait (for attempt 3, 200 to 400 ms). Full jitter is the better default for spreading load but can retry almost instantly.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: A login service is down for 30 seconds while 2 lakh app users wait. Every app retries every 5 seconds. When the service comes back it immediately falls over again. What is this called and what fixes it?
options: A thundering herd caused by synchronised clients; exponential backoff with jitter spreads the retries out
A retry budget overflow; raising the budget from 10% to 50% fixes it
A metastable cache miss; pre-warming the login cache before restart fixes it
A split-brain failure; running two login clusters in different regions fixes it
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: Clients that failed together keep retrying in the same rhythm, so recovery brings 200,000 requests in one second. Backoff plus randomness breaks the rhythm.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: A dependency is badly broken. With "3 attempts per request" your callers triple its load. What does a retry budget of 10% change?
options: Each request may retry at most 10% of the time, chosen at random by the client
Retries are capped at about 10% of traffic, so extra load stays around 1.1x instead of 3x
Only 10% of clients are allowed to call the dependency until it recovers
The client waits 10% longer after each failure, which slowly spreads out the load
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: A budget is a ceiling on retries as a share of traffic; when it runs out, failures are returned instead of retried. Envoy and gRPC support this.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: A "place order" call from the app times out after 1 second. Should the client simply retry it?
options: No: write calls can never be retried, so show an error and ask the user to try again
Yes, but only after waiting the full backoff cap, so the first attempt has surely failed
Not blindly: the order may already have been created, so retry only with an idempotency key the server can de-duplicate
Yes: a timeout means the server never received the request, so a retry is always safe
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: A timeout means you stopped waiting, not that the work failed. An idempotency key lets the server return the original order instead of creating a duplicate.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: Your HTTP client retries on every non-2xx response. Which of these responses should it NOT retry?
options: 429 Too Many Requests, after honouring any Retry-After header
A timeout on a read call, because the network may have blipped
503 Service Unavailable, because the server may be temporarily overloaded
400 Bad Request, because the answer will not change on a second try
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: Retry transient errors (503, 429, timeouts). 400 and 404 are deterministic; retrying just adds load.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: The product page has an 800 ms budget. A lower service keeps retrying a request for 2 seconds after the page has already given up. What prevents this wasted work?
options: Adding a circuit breaker on the page so it waits longer before giving up on the call
Propagating a deadline down the chain so lower layers stop or skip work when the time left runs out
Giving the lower service a longer timeout than the page so its retries can finish
Increasing the page's thread pool so abandoned requests do not block new ones
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: A deadline ("finish by 10:00:00.800") lets inner layers avoid retrying when the caller is gone. In the worked example, pricing does not start work with under 50 ms left.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: During a festive sale, a hot promotion row slows the pricing database. Before the fix, the app, gateway and product page each retried 3 times with a fixed 200 ms wait, and a 2-minute hiccup became a 25-minute outage. Which set of changes kept the next sale's same hiccup to a minor blip?
options: More retries at the gateway, a longer fixed wait of 1 s, and doubling pricing pods before the sale
Retrying only at the mobile app with no backoff, so the user sees a result as fast as possible
Removing all timeouts so no call times out, and letting each layer retry until it succeeds
One retry layer, exponential backoff with full jitter, a 10% retry budget, an 800 ms deadline and a breaker with a cached-price fallback
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: With those guard rails, pricing load rose only from 40,000 to about 44,000 RPS, well under capacity. The root cause was identical; caller behaviour decided blip versus outage.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: Which statement about retries is accurate?
options: Retries always improve reliability, so more attempts at every layer is the safer configuration
Backoff alone is enough to prevent retry storms, because waits grow longer each time
Retries help with brief random failures but add load during overload, so they need backoff, jitter and a budget
Once the root cause is fixed, a system in a retry storm always recovers by itself
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: The other three are the misconceptions the answer lists: layered retries multiply, backoff without jitter keeps waves, and retry storms can be metastable.

Why can automatic retries turn a small s.q: During an incident you suspect retries are feeding the outage. What signal confirms a retry storm?
options: The ratio of retries to unique requests jumps from about 1% to 50% or more while latency climbs
The number of unique users rises sharply while total requests stay constant
Average latency stays flat while the error rate slowly drops back to normal
CPU usage on the callers falls while the callee's database load stays the same
Why can automatic retries turn a small s.why: Compare requests received with unique requests; dashboards should show retry rate separately so a storm is visible.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: Five services each pass their own load test at 2x expected traffic, but the combined product page API times out under real sale traffic. What is the most likely class of cause?
options: One of the five services has a hidden bug that only its own load test failed to exercise
The load tests used too little traffic, so simply scaling every service by 2x will fix it
The API gateway is undersized, since services that pass alone cannot fail together
Interaction effects: tail latency amplifying across the fan-out, contention on shared resources, and misaligned timeouts and retries
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: 'Fine alone, broken together' points to how the services interact. Hunting for one slow service and scaling it often misses the real bottleneck.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: Each of the 5 services in a fan-out has a 1% chance of a slow response. Roughly what share of API requests hit at least one slow call?
options: About 0.2%, since slowness must happen in all five services together
About 18%, since slow calls compound across five sequential hops
About 1%, since each service is only slow 1% of the time
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: The chance that at least one of five calls is slow is 1 - 0.99^5. 18% is the figure for 20 dependencies. So the API's p95 becomes the services' p99.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: A product page API makes five sequential calls, each with a p99 of 120 ms, behind a 500 ms gateway timeout. Catalogue, pricing, inventory, reviews and recommendations do not depend on each other. What is the simplest latency fix?
options: Call the independent services in parallel, so latency becomes the max of the five instead of the sum
Add retries to each call so slow responses are replaced by faster second attempts
Raise the gateway timeout to 1 s so the sequential chain always finishes in time
Scale each of the five services so that each one's p99 drops below 100 ms
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: Sequential tails add up towards 600 ms. Parallel fan-out turns the sum into a max. Longer timeouts just hide the problem and hold resources.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: Traces show the API waits 1.8 s to acquire an HTTP connection before calling inventory, which itself responds in 40 ms. Where is the bottleneck?
options: In the inventory database, which delays the connection handshake for 1.8 s
In the caller's shared connection pool, which a different slow dependency is holding
In the network between the API and inventory, which is dropping packets
In the inventory service, whose own metrics are under-reporting its latency
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: The time is spent waiting, not working, and happens before inventory is called. In the worked example, recommendations held 85 of 100 shared connections.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: Why should per-hop latency metrics be measured from the caller's side when hunting a cross-service bottleneck?
options: The callee only records successful requests, never errors or timeouts
The caller sees queueing time (pool waits, connection setup) that the callee's own metrics never record
Callers have more CPU available, so their timers are more accurate under load
The callee's metrics are always sampled, while caller metrics are always exact
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: A healthy-looking callee can sit behind a saturated caller pool; only the caller's view of Duration includes that wait.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: A service runs fine at 50% utilisation, but under combined load at 90% its waiting time explodes. Using Little's law (in-flight = rate x latency), why does this compound?
options: When latency doubles, the arrival rate halves, so the service becomes idle and slow to respond
When utilisation passes 90%, the law says the service must reject half of all requests
Little's law only applies to databases, so service-level queueing stays linear
When latency doubles, requests in flight double, so pools and threads run out and latency rises further
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: Near saturation queueing grows sharply (waiting can be 10x service time at 90%), and Little's law shows more in-flight work exhausts pools, feeding more latency.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: Your client timeout is 1 s, the gateway's is 2 s and the API's is 3 s, each with 3 tries. A downstream service slows to 2.5 s. What is the key problem with this setup?
options: The client timeout is too long, so users wait a full second before seeing any error
Three tries is too few, so the gateway cannot hide the slow service from users
Inner timeouts are longer than outer ones, so inner layers keep working and retrying after the user has given up, up to 27 attempts
The API timeout is too short, so it gives up before the 2.5 s service can answer
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: Timeouts must nest inside the caller's deadline, and retries should happen in one layer. Otherwise work continues for abandoned requests and load multiplies.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: You are setting timeouts for the product page, which has an 800 ms user-facing SLO. How should you derive them?
options: Subtract the API's own work, split the rest across critical calls by measured p99 plus headroom, and give optional calls a fraction with a fallback
Give every downstream call the full 800 ms so that none of them times out before the page does
Use the same 3 s default for every call, since the SLO only applies at the gateway
Set each timeout to each dependency's average latency, since p99 values are too noisy
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: A deadline budget starts from the SLO and makes each hop fit inside it. Optional calls like recommendations got 150 ms and no retries in the worked example.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: Recommendations slows to 1.5 s and eats most of a shared 100-connection pool, starving pricing and inventory. Which fix directly stops one dependency from starving the others?
options: A longer timeout for recommendations so its calls finish instead of piling up
More retries for pricing and inventory so they eventually get a connection
A larger shared pool of 500 connections so recommendations cannot fill it
Bulkheads: a separate pool or concurrency limit per dependency, e.g. recommendations capped at 15
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: A bulkhead limits how much of your resources one dependency can use. A bigger shared pool just delays exhaustion.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: A teammate says, "We have circuit breakers on every dependency, so we don't need bulkheads." Why is that risky?
options: Bulkheads replace breakers entirely, so having both just adds unnecessary configuration
Breakers trip on every slow call, so without bulkheads they open far too often
A slow but not failing dependency can exhaust shared resources before the breaker trips; the bulkhead limits how much it can use
Circuit breakers only work for databases, so HTTP dependencies need bulkheads instead
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: A breaker decides whether to call; a bulkhead decides how much of your resources a dependency may hold. A slow dependency needs the bulkhead first.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: Which classification of calls on a product page supports graceful degradation?
options: Price and stock are critical; reviews and recommendations are optional, with short timeouts and cached or empty fallbacks
All five calls are critical, so any failure should fail the whole page to stay consistent
Recommendations are critical because they drive revenue; price can fall back to empty
All calls are optional, so each one should just retry until it succeeds or times out
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: Classifying calls lets optional ones fail fast to a fallback so they never fail the page, while critical data stays protected.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: Your search API's tail latency is dominated by a few slow replicas. For idempotent reads, which technique cuts the tail at a small extra cost?
options: Send every request to all replicas at once so the fastest one is always used
Hedged requests: if no reply by the p95 time, send a second request to another replica and use the first answer
Raise the timeout to p99.9 so that slow replicas always get time to finish
Retry every request three times immediately and use whichever reply comes back last
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: Hedging only duplicates the slow ~5%, so cost is small (from Google's 'The Tail at Scale'). Sending everything to all replicas multiplies load.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: Your load tool waits for each response before sending the next request. The test shows a great p99, but production tails are much worse. What is the likely flaw?
options: The test used too many virtual users, which hides the slow tail in averages
The tool measured from the caller's side, which always exaggerates latency
The test ramped traffic gradually, so the services had time to autoscale
Coordinated omission: it under-reports tails; use open-model, constant-rate load
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: When the service slows, a closed-model tool sends fewer requests, hiding the queueing real users would see.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: In a combined ramp-up load test, recommendations shows the biggest latency, but the API's connection-pool wait time is the first metric to saturate. Which is the bottleneck?
options: The load tool, because a pool can only saturate if the test is misconfigured
The connection pool, because the first resource to saturate is the bottleneck
Recommendations, because the service with the highest latency is always the bottleneck
Neither, because bottlenecks only show up as CPU saturation on a single host
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: Ramp 10% at a time and watch which saturation metric moves first; that is the bottleneck, even if another service shows the worst latency.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: Under a sale spike, the API's in-flight requests pass the tested limit and everyone starts timing out. What protects the requests that can still succeed?
options: Load shedding: reject the excess early with 429/503, ideally with adaptive concurrency limits
Autoscaling the API, since new instances will absorb the spike within seconds
Raising every timeout so more of the queued requests finish before giving up
Retrying rejected requests at the gateway so no user sees an error response
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: Rejecting excess immediately keeps the rest fast. Autoscaling reacts in minutes while cascades happen in seconds, and can overload a shared database.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: An engineer proposes: "Find the slowest service and scale it up." Why can that fail or even make things worse?
options: Scaling resets all circuit breakers, which then let failures cascade again
Scaling is never useful for latency, because latency does not depend on capacity
The real bottleneck is often a shared pool, retry storm or timeout mismatch
The slowest service is always a database, which cannot be scaled horizontally
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: 'Fine alone, broken together' is usually interaction effects, not one undersized service.

Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.q: How can you confirm that a redesigned product page really degrades instead of collapsing when a dependency slows?
options: Wait for the next production incident and compare its p99 with the last one
Run each service's solo load test again at 3x traffic instead of 2x
Run a chaos test or game day that injects, say, 2 s of latency into one dependency and check p99 and fallbacks
Review the code for try/catch blocks around every downstream call before the sale
Your API depends on 5 microservices. Eac.why: Resilience must be proven by injecting failures; solo load tests are exactly what missed the problem originally.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: A new checkout version has a bug that fails 1 in 50 requests. It is deployed to all servers at once and takes 20 minutes to notice and redeploy. What is the core lesson from safe-rollout practice?
options: Write perfect code by adding more unit tests, so such bugs never reach production
Deploy to all servers at once but keep a faster manual redeploy script ready
Deploy only at night, when traffic is low and a 2% failure rate costs little
Limit how many users see a change before you know it is safe, and make going back cheap
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: The fix is not perfect code but a small blast radius and cheap rollback. Night deploys still hit everyone online and hide bugs that only appear under real traffic.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: Your team keeps the old version live on one full environment while deploying the new version to an identical idle environment, then switches the load balancer. What is this called, and what is its main advantage?
options: Blue-green deployment; switching traffic back to the old environment rolls back code in seconds
Canary release; only a small percentage of users see the new version at first
Feature flagging; the new code ships dark and is turned on per user later
Expand and contract; old and new versions share a backward-compatible schema
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: Blue-green keeps two environments and flips traffic, so rollback is just switching back. Its weakness is that the switch moves 100% of users at once.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: You did a blue-green switch to version 42, which also changed how order data is written. Version 41 cannot read the new format. Errors appear, and you switch traffic back to blue. What happens?
options: Rollback works, because the load balancer converts the data back to v41's format
Rollback may still fail, because both environments share the database and v41 cannot handle the data v42 wrote
Rollback is instant and safe, because blue-green duplicates the database along with the servers
Rollback is impossible, because blue-green environments cannot be switched twice
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: Blue-green gives instant rollback for code only. Shared things like databases, caches and queues do not double, so data changes must be backward compatible.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: A team runs a 1% canary but has no automated checks; they plan to 'keep an eye on dashboards'. Why is this not much safer than a full deploy?
options: Manual checks are actually safer than automated ones, but they take too long to run
Canaries only work with blue-green environments, which this team has not set up
Nobody reliably notices a problem at 1%, so the rollout continues to 100%; the safety comes from automatic comparison and rollback
A 1% canary is too small to ever reveal bugs, so canaries should start at 25% instead
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: A canary without automatic analysis is just a slow full deploy. Tools like Argo Rollouts, Flagger or Spinnaker compare canary metrics with the baseline and roll back on failure.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: Your canary analysis uses a fixed rule: 'roll back if error rate exceeds 1%'. At peak hours the old version itself runs at 1.2% errors, so every canary fails. What is the better approach?
options: Raise the fixed threshold to 5% so peak-hour canaries are no longer rolled back
Only run canaries at night, when the fixed 1% threshold is easy to meet
Compare the canary against the current version's baseline right now, e.g. canary 5xx rate <= baseline + 0.1%
Skip the error-rate check and rely only on p99 latency for canary decisions
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: Error rates vary by time of day; what matters is whether the canary is worse than the old version at the same moment.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: A checkout canary at 5% shows normal HTTP 200 rates and p99 latency, but a bug shows some users an empty cart. Which canary check would have caught it?
options: Business metrics such as orders per minute, add-to-cart and payment success rate, compared with the baseline
CPU and memory usage of the canary pods compared with the old version's pods
A stricter p99 latency threshold, such as baseline p99 times 1.01
A longer pause at 1%, so the error-rate check has more 5xx data to analyse
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: A bug can return HTTP 200 and still break the user experience; canaries should watch one or two business metrics for the service.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: Why does a canary plan pause for 10 minutes at 1% before moving to 5%?
options: Load balancers can only change traffic weights every 10 minutes
At 1%, a rare bug needs a few minutes of traffic before it shows up in the metrics
Kubernetes needs 10 minutes to schedule the canary pods at the new weight
The pause lets engineers manually approve each step before analysis begins
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: Small slices see little traffic, so each step must wait long enough for analysis to be meaningful.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: Your team merges a 'pay later' option to production two months before the sale, but it is switched off and invisible to customers. What practice is this?
options: A change freeze: holding the feature back until the sale's freeze period ends
Expand and contract: preparing the feature's data before writing its code
Blue-green deployment: keeping the new version on an idle environment until sale day
Deploying dark: separating deploy (code on servers) from release (users see it) using a feature flag
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: Feature flags let code ship dark and be released later by changing config, with a kill switch to turn it off.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: You enable a feature for 10% of users by hashing the user ID into a bucket from 0 to 99. Why hash rather than pick a random 10% of requests?
options: Hashing is cryptographically secure, so users cannot guess which group they are in
Hashing guarantees exactly 10% of revenue comes from the flag-on group
The same user always lands in the same bucket, so each user's experience stays stable
Random selection is not allowed by the app stores for mobile feature rollouts
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: Per-request randomness would flip a user between old and new flows; a stable hash keeps them consistent.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: At 10% rollout, the partner credit API behind a new pay-later feature jumps to 4 s latency and checkout p99 doubles for flag-on users. What is the fastest safe action?
options: Increase checkout pod count so the slow credit calls have more threads to wait on
Roll back the entire checkout deployment to last month's version through the canary pipeline
Ship a hotfix with a shorter timeout through a full deploy during peak traffic
Flip the feature's kill switch so all users return to the old flow within seconds, with no deploy
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: A kill switch turns the feature off in about 30 seconds. Then the team adds a timeout and fallback and resumes at a small percentage.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: Your codebase has 300 feature flags, many years old; nobody knows which paths are live and old branches are never tested. What practice prevents this?
options: Move all flags into a single config file so that they are easier to read later
Give every release flag an owner and expiry date, and delete the flag and dead path a few weeks after full rollout
Never use feature flags for releases; only use canaries and blue-green deployments
Keep all flags forever, but turn every one of them on so that only new paths run
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: Flag debt doubles code paths per flag and causes outages and confusion. Long-lived operational flags (kill switches) are fine but should be tracked and tested.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: A team renames the database column phone to mobile_number in the same deploy that ships code using the new name, and runs it as a 5% canary. What goes wrong?
options: The old version, still serving 95% of traffic, expects the old column and starts failing
Nothing, because the canary only sends 5% of traffic to the new code path
The rename is safe, but the canary analysis cannot compare across schemas
Only the canary fails, because the new code cannot find the renamed column
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: Data cannot roll back and old and new versions run side by side. Use expand and contract instead of a single rename.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: You need to rename the column phone to mobile_number safely during rolling deploys. What is the correct expand-and-contract order?
options: Add the new column, dual write, backfill, switch reads to the new column, then drop the old column last
Drop the old column, add the new one, backfill from backups, then deploy the new code
Switch reads to the new column first, then add it, then backfill and dual write
Rename the column, then dual write so old code can still read through a view
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: Every step is backward compatible, so rolling back one step leaves the previous code working. The old column is dropped only when no running version uses it.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: A new home-page widget is crashing Android app version 9.3, already installed on millions of phones. What lets you stop the damage without a new app release?
options: A canary rollback that reduces the app's store rollout percentage to zero
A blue-green switch on the backend, so 9.3 is routed to the old environment
Rolling back the app in the Play Store so installed phones return to version 9.2
A server-driven feature flag or kill switch that tells app 9.3 not to show the widget
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: Installed apps cannot be recalled. Server-driven flags work in seconds; halting a staged rollout only stops new installs.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: Which practice is specific to rolling out mobile app changes safely?
options: Canary analysis inside the app that automatically uninstalls the new version
Staged store rollouts, server-driven flags and long backward-compatible APIs
Blue-green switching of the app binary on users' phones with instant rollback
A change freeze on the backend only, since mobile apps cannot affect production
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: You control servers but not phones, so mobile teams rely on 1%/5%/20% store rollouts, remote flags, and long backward compatibility (sometimes a year or more).

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: During a festive sale, why do teams prefer flipping flags over deploying new code?
options: Flags are faster to code, so last-minute features can be written on sale day
Deploys are physically impossible during a change freeze because pipelines are locked
The code was deployed and load-tested weeks earlier, so a flag flip is a small, fast and reversible change
Flag flips do not need monitoring, so the on-call team can focus on other work
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: A fresh deploy at peak traffic adds new untested risk, which is why changes are frozen while pre-deployed features are released by flag.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: A teammate says, "We have feature flags, so we can cut testing time before release." What is the best response?
options: Flags limit the blast radius but do not find bugs; you still need tests, including for both the on and off paths
Flags actually require less testing, since the off path is never executed
Agreed, but only if the flag is enabled for 100% of users from the start
Agreed: flags let real users test the feature, so internal tests are redundant
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: Flags make a bad change easy to switch off; they do not replace testing.

How do big apps release a change to cror.q: When would you choose blue-green over a canary for a service?
options: Whenever you want to limit how many users see a bug, since blue-green exposes fewer users
Whenever the database schema changes, since blue-green duplicates the database
When you need a clean all-at-once switch with instant rollback, e.g. a version that cannot run side by side with the old one
Never, because canaries are strictly better than blue-green in every situation
How do big apps release a change to cror.why: Canary is the default because it limits exposure; blue-green suits versions that cannot coexist. Many teams combine them.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: Customers say checkout is slow, but every dashboard is green: average latency 310 ms, CPU 45%, error rate 0.2%. What is the most likely reason?
options: The customers are on slow mobile networks, so the backend cannot be the problem
CPU at 45% proves the servers are healthy, so the slowness must be in the CDN
The dashboards show averages and machine health, which hide a slow tail affecting a small slice of users
The dashboards are lagging by an hour and will turn red once they catch up
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: A slow path for a few percent of requests barely moves the average, and a server waiting on a database uses little CPU. In the worked example p99 was 6.4 s.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: Out of 1,000 checkout requests, 985 take 200 ms and 15 take 8 s. What are the average and p99, and which should you alert on?
options: Average about 317 ms, p99 200 ms; alert on the average
Average about 317 ms, p99 8 s; alert on the p99 (and p95)
Average 200 ms, p99 317 ms; alert on the p99
Average about 8 s, p99 8 s; either one works for alerting
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: (985 x 200 + 15 x 8,000) / 1,000 = 317 ms looks healthy, but 1.5% of customers wait 8 s, which the p99 reveals.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: You have p99 latency for each of 20 checkout servers. How do you get the true p99 across the whole fleet?
options: Take the highest of the 20 per-server p99 values as the fleet p99
Average the 20 per-server p99 values to get the fleet-wide p99
Take the median of the 20 per-server p99 values as the fleet p99
Store latency as histograms and compute the percentile from the combined bucket counts
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: Percentiles cannot be averaged. Histograms (counts per bucket) can be summed across servers, as in the Prometheus histogram_quantile query.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: In the observability loop, which signal answers which question?
options: Metrics say that something is wrong and how big; traces say where; logs say why
Metrics say where; traces say why; logs say how big the problem is
Traces say that something is wrong; logs say where; metrics say why
Logs say that something is wrong; metrics say where; traces say why
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: A percentile metric shows the pain, a trace of a slow request points to the slow hop, and logs from that hop (found via trace ID) explain the cause. Then metrics confirm the fix.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: A service's latency is high but its CPU is only 30%. Which metric is most likely to reveal the cause?
options: Disk utilisation, since latency without CPU load is always caused by disk I/O
A saturation metric such as connection-pool wait time or thread queue length
Requests per second, since low CPU means traffic must have dropped sharply
Memory utilisation, since high latency with low CPU always means a memory leak
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: A service waiting on a database, lock or pool uses little CPU. USE's Saturation (e.g. 200 threads queued for 20 DB connections) is the one people miss.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: You are building a standard dashboard. Which checklist pairing is correct?
options: RED and USE are the same checklist with different names for the same metrics
USE for each service or endpoint; RED for each resource such as CPU, disk and pools
RED for business KPIs only; USE for all latency and error tracking
RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) for each service or endpoint; USE (Utilisation, Saturation, Errors) for each resource
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: RED describes what users feel per service; USE describes what machines feel per resource.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: To debug per-user issues, a developer adds a user_id label to the checkout latency metric. What is the problem?
options: Nothing: metrics stores are designed to hold one series per user efficiently
It only breaks if the user ID contains special characters, so encode it first
It causes a cardinality explosion of millions of time series; per-user detail belongs in logs and trace attributes
It makes p99 inaccurate because each user's latency is averaged separately
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: Metrics are cheap because they are pre-aggregated with low-cardinality labels like route, status and region.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: Your logs say things like "Payment failed for user" in plain text, and finding the lines for one slow request across five services takes an hour. What change helps most?
options: Structured JSON logs with named fields and the same trace ID on every line from every service
Increase log level to DEBUG everywhere so more detail is available for each request
Write all services' logs into a single shared file so they are in one place
Store logs for a year instead of a week so older requests can be found
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: Named fields make logs queryable, and a shared trace ID turns a haystack into a search. DEBUG everywhere just adds cost and noise.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: In a Java service, the trace ID is put into the logging context (MDC) in a request filter. Why must it be removed in a finally block after the request?
options: Removing it triggers OpenTelemetry to export the span to the trace back end
Threads are reused, so a leftover ID would be stamped on log lines from the next, unrelated request
MDC values are sent to the client, so leaving them in would leak trace IDs to users
The trace ID expires after the request, and using it later throws an exception
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: Thread pools reuse threads; without cleanup, log lines get the wrong trace ID.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: Traces from the checkout service stop at the Kafka publish, and the consumer starts a fresh, unrelated trace. What is missing?
options: A larger span limit, since traces are cut off when they exceed 50 spans
A shared database between producer and consumer to store the trace tree
Context propagation: the producer must put traceparent into the Kafka message headers and the consumer must continue from it
Tail-based sampling, since head sampling drops the consumer half of each trace
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: Tracing only works if context propagates through HTTP, messages and thread pools; otherwise traces break into pieces.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: Which statement correctly describes a span in distributed tracing?
options: One timed step in a trace, with the trace ID, its own span ID, a parent span ID, start time, duration and attributes
A metric time series that records latency per route for one service
A log line that has been tagged with a trace ID and a severity level
A complete request across all services, identified by a unique span ID per service
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: A trace is a tree of spans for one request; the W3C traceparent header carries the trace ID and parent span ID between services.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: You use 1% head-based sampling. Checkout p99 is 6 s, yet you can barely find any slow checkout traces. Why, and what should change?
options: Head sampling drops all traces over 2 seconds by design; raising the rate to 2% fixes it
The sampling rate is too high, causing the collector to drop the largest traces
Slow traces are never exported by OpenTelemetry; you need logs to find them instead
Only about 1% of requests are slow and you keep a random 1%, so few survive; use tail-based sampling to keep all slow or failed traces
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: Tail sampling decides after the trace completes, keeping every error or slow trace plus a small share of normal ones, at the cost of collector memory.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: Your traces are sampled at 1%. Can you still trust your request-rate and error-rate numbers?
options: Only if you multiply the trace counts by 100, since metrics come from traces
No, because every signal is reduced to 1% once any sampling is turned on
Yes, if they come from metrics, because metrics count all requests even when traces are sampled
No, because tail sampling biases the metrics towards slow and failed requests
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: Metrics are recorded for every request and stay exact; sampling only affects which traces are stored.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: On sale evening, p99 for /checkout/pay-options jumps to 6.4 s. Slow traces show the promo service's 'offers DB query' taking 4.8 s. Logs for those trace IDs all show bank=XYZ and rows_scanned=2,100,000. What is the likely root cause?
options: The promo service's pods are CPU-starved, slowing every query for every customer
A new offer for bank XYZ filters on a column with no index, causing a full scan for only that bank's customers
A network partition between regions is slowing all database queries equally
The checkout gateway is misrouting bank XYZ's customers to a distant data centre
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: Only ~3% of checkouts hit the unindexed query, so averages and CPU stayed fine. Short-term fix was caching in Redis; then add the index.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: After fixing a slow checkout path, what should you do to avoid being blind to the same problem next time?
options: Add a CPU alert at 45% on all checkout pods to catch slowdowns earlier
Add an alert when average checkout latency exceeds 310 ms for five minutes
Turn on DEBUG logging permanently on the promo service in production
Add per-route p99 alerts, a per-query latency metric for the service, and a database slow-query alert
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: The original alerts were on averages and CPU, which missed the problem. Alerts should reflect what users feel, per route and per percentile.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: An interviewer asks: what is the difference between monitoring and observability?
options: Monitoring checks known failure signs set up in advance; observability lets you ask new questions you did not plan for
Monitoring is for production; observability is only for staging environments
Monitoring uses logs only; observability uses metrics only
They are the same thing; observability is just the newer marketing name
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: Rich, linked data lets you ask unplanned questions like 'which bank's customers are slow?' without shipping new code.

Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.q: You want to instrument services once and be free to send metrics, logs and traces to different back ends later. Which choice fits?
options: OpenTelemetry SDKs, agents and collector
Grafana, since its dashboards instrument the code automatically
Jaeger, since it is the standard for all three signals
Prometheus, since it collects logs and traces as well as metrics
Customers say checkout is slow, but ever.why: OpenTelemetry is the open standard for instrumentation of all three signals; Prometheus stores metrics, Grafana visualises, Jaeger stores traces.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: A product manager says, "Our 99.9% uptime target is basically perfect." Over a 30-day month, roughly how much bad time does it actually allow?
options: About 4.3 minutes
About 26 seconds
About 43 minutes
About 7.2 hours
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: 0.1% of 43,200 minutes is about 43 minutes, which can be one bad evening at peak. 4.3 minutes is 99.99%, 7.2 hours is 99%, 26 seconds is 99.999%.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: Your SLO is 99.95% over 30 days. A typical bad deploy takes 15 minutes for a human to notice and roll back. What does this imply?
options: Nothing: 99.95% allows about 4.4 hours a month, so a 15-minute rollback is a small share
The deploy is fine, since error budgets only count full outages longer than 30 minutes
You should move to 99.99%, since a stricter SLO forces teams to roll back faster
It allows only about 22 min a month, so you need automated rollback or a looser SLO
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: 99.95% is about 22 minutes per month (4.4 hours is per year). Higher nines require automation, not humans reading dashboards.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: Which correctly describes SLI, SLO and SLA?
options: SLI is the measured ratio of good events; SLO is the internal target over a window; SLA is the customer contract with penalties
SLI is the customer contract; SLO is the measured ratio; SLA is the internal target
SLO is the contract with penalties; SLA is the internal target; SLI is the error budget
SLI, SLO and SLA are the same target expressed for engineers, managers and customers
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: They build on each other: measure (SLI), aim (SLO), promise externally with consequences (SLA).

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: Your SLA with merchants promises 99.5%. What should your internal SLO be, and why?
options: Looser than the SLA, e.g. 99%, so the team has room to ship features quickly
Stricter than the SLA, e.g. 99.9%, so SLO alerts fire well before you owe anyone money
100%, so there is never any chance of breaching the SLA with merchants
Exactly 99.5%, so engineering and the contract always use the same number
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: The SLO is your early warning; keeping it tighter than the SLA protects the contract. 100% is never the right target.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: A team measures availability as the percentage of minutes their server process was running, and reports 99.99%. Yet 30% of requests failed for an hour last week. What should they change?
options: Use a request-based SLI (good requests / valid requests), measured at the load balancer or client
Exclude the failed hour as an anomaly so the SLI reflects normal operation
Measure CPU and memory health in addition to process uptime on each server
Measure server uptime every second instead of every minute for better accuracy
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: A server can be 'up' while many requests fail. Request-based SLIs measured near the user show what users actually see.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: You are defining a checkout SLI. Which definition best follows the answer's guidance?
options: % of minutes in which the checkout server process was running and passing health checks
% of checkout requests returning any status other than 4xx, including bot traffic
Average checkout latency across all servers measured inside the application every minute
% of POST /checkout requests at the load balancer returning non-5xx in under 500 ms, excluding bots and health checks
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: A good SLI is a ratio of good to valid events, with a latency threshold rather than an average, measured close to the user. 4xx are usually excluded from 'bad', not the only bad.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: At a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, you expect 10 million checkout requests. What is the error budget?
options: 43,000 bad requests
1,000 bad requests
10,000 bad requests
100,000 bad requests
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: Budget = 100% - 99.9% = 0.1% of 10 million = 10,000, roughly equal to 43 minutes of full outage.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: Over the last hour, 0.5% of requests failed. The SLO is 99.9% over 30 days. What is the burn rate?
options: 0.5, meaning only half the budget would be used by month end
5, meaning the 30-day budget would be gone in about 6 days
0.005, meaning the error rate is well inside the budget
50, meaning the budget would be gone in under a day
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: burn_rate = error_rate / (1 - SLO) = 0.005 / 0.001 = 5. At 5x the even pace, 30 days of budget lasts about 6.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: Why do SRE teams alert on burn rate instead of a simple 'error rate above 1%' threshold?
options: It ties alerts to missing the SLO: fast burns page, slow leaks open tickets
Burn rate is easier to compute because it ignores the SLO and the window length
Burn rate alerts never fire at night, so on-call engineers get more sleep
Simple thresholds cannot be computed from request-based SLIs
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: The multi-window setup (14.4 over 1 h, 6 over 6 h, 1 over 3 days) catches big outages fast and slow leaks eventually.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: In the common Google SRE workbook setup with a 30-day window, which burn rate pages someone immediately over a 1-hour window?
options: 6, which uses 5% of the budget in one hour
100, which uses the whole budget in one hour
14.4, which uses 2% of the budget in one hour
1, which uses 10% of the budget in one hour
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: 14.4 over 1 hour pages now; 6 over 6 hours pages; 1 over 3 days opens a ticket. Each also checks a short window so it stops firing soon after a fix.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: It is sale week. The checkout error budget is fully spent, and a product manager wants to launch a new feature today. What should happen?
options: Launch, but lower the SLO to 99% so the budget is no longer spent
Follow the pre-agreed error budget policy: pause the launch and fix reliability
Launch anyway: error budgets are engineering guidelines that product can override
Freeze every change including security fixes until the 30-day window resets
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: The written policy decides, so nobody argues at midnight; any exception goes to the named leader and is recorded. Security and reliability fixes still go out when the budget is spent.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: A team ends every quarter with 90% of its error budget unused and ships features slowly. What does this suggest?
options: They should tighten the SLO to 100% to reflect their excellent reliability
Their SLI must be broken, because healthy services always use their full budget
They are doing ideal SRE work, since the goal is to never use the error budget
They are probably too cautious; the budget exists to be spent on change like features, experiments and migrations
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: Like an unused data pack, unspent budget usually means unnecessary caution. They could ship faster or reconsider the target.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: Your service achieved 99.7% over the last quarter. Leadership wants to set a 99.99% SLO starting tomorrow. What is the likely result?
options: The SLA penalties will automatically drop because the SLO is now stricter
A permanent freeze, since the budget would be blown immediately; set a target you meet today and tighten over time
Engineers will naturally work harder, so reliability will rise to match the new target
Nothing changes, since SLOs are aspirational and do not affect release decisions
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: Realistic SLOs start from user needs and history; also, each extra nine costs much more.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: Checkout calls cart, pricing and payment in series, each 99.9% available independently. What is the best checkout can expect without extra protection?
options: About 99.97%, since independent failures rarely overlap
99.9%, since checkout is only as weak as its single weakest dependency
About 99.0%, since three nines across three services lose one nine
About 99.7%, roughly 130 minutes of downtime a month
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: 0.999^3 ≈ 0.997. A service cannot promise more nines than its chain of hard dependencies unless it adds caching, fallbacks or redundancy.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: Pricing's 99.9% availability means checkout cannot reliably hit its own 99.9% SLO. What did the team in the worked example do?
options: Added a cache of last known prices with 60-second validity, so a short pricing outage no longer fails checkout
Lowered the checkout SLO to 99% so pricing failures stay within the budget
Asked the pricing team to promise 100% availability for the sale period
Removed pricing from the SLI so its failures do not count against checkout
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: Removing a hard dependency's impact (cache, fallback, redundancy) is how you get more nines than the chain allows.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: Should a 'recommended for you' widget have the same SLO as payments?
options: Yes: a consistent SLO across every journey keeps the policy simple and fair
No: recommendations need a stricter SLO because they drive more page views
No: different journeys need different targets; payments deserve stricter SLOs than recommendation widgets
Yes: users judge the whole app, so every component must hit the strictest target
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: Not everything needs the same nines; each nine costs much more and slows releases.

What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.q: Why is 100% availability the wrong SLO target?
options: It forces burn-rate alerts to fire continuously even when service is healthy
It is achievable but too expensive for anyone except large banks
It means zero changes, and it is impossible anyway because users' phones, networks and ISPs fail
It makes the SLA penalties impossible to calculate for customers
What do 99.9% uptime, SLIs, SLOs and err.why: A 100% target leaves no budget for any risk, and users already see failures from their own connections.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: At 2 AM payments are failing, and a deploy went out 20 minutes ago. An engineer wants to read the diff to find the bug before acting. What should the incident commander say?
options: Write a hotfix for the most likely bug and deploy it through the normal pipeline
Wait until morning, when the original author can explain the change in the diff
Read the diff first, so the team rolls back only if the deploy is definitely the cause
Roll back first (or turn off the related flag), watch whether success rate recovers, and investigate the diff after customers are safe
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Mitigate first: a reversible action that rules out a cause is cheap compared with more minutes of failed payments.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: Which alert is the better choice to page the payments on-call engineer?
options: Payment success rate below 90% for 3 minutes (normal is about 97%)
Disk usage above 70% on any payment-service host
CPU above 80% on payment-db-3 for 3 minutes
Any single payment failure logged at ERROR level
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Page on symptoms customers feel. High CPU may hurt nobody, and paging on every error causes alert fatigue.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: Your team gets 40 pages a week, most of them for alerts that need no action. On-call engineers have started ignoring pages. What is the best fix?
options: Route all pages to email so engineers can review them in the morning
Add more alerts on CPU and memory so the real problems are caught earlier
Delete or tune noisy alerts, page on SLO-based customer symptoms, and treat repeat pages as bugs with owners
Add a second on-call engineer so the pages are split between two people
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Alert fatigue makes people ignore real pages; pages should be rare and meaningful.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: The primary on-call does not acknowledge a page within 5 minutes. What should the paging tool do?
options: Keep calling the primary every 5 minutes until they acknowledge
Escalate to a secondary on-call, and then to a manager
Send an email to the whole engineering team and wait for a volunteer
Auto-resolve the alert, since an unacknowledged page is probably a false alarm
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Tools like PagerDuty and Opsgenie escalate on missed acknowledgement so incidents are never left unattended.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: One card network's payments are failing, while UPI and other cards work. On a typical scale, which severity is this, and how often should updates go out?
options: SEV1: all hands, leadership informed, updates every 15 minutes
SEV2: dedicated responders, updates about every 30 minutes
SEV3: fix during working hours since a workaround exists
SEV4: a normal ticket, since most payments still succeed
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: The typical scale lists 'one payment method failing' as SEV2. If unsure, declare higher; you can downgrade later.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: An on-call engineer is unsure whether an issue is a SEV1 or SEV2. What is the recommended rule?
options: Declare the higher severity; you can always downgrade later
Do not declare until the root cause is known and the severity is certain
Declare the lower severity to avoid waking leadership unnecessarily
Ask leadership to decide the severity before any responders join
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Declaring should be cheap (one chat command) and erring high gets help in quickly.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: During a SEV1, the incident commander starts SSH-ing into servers to debug. Why is this a problem?
options: Only the comms lead is allowed to run commands during a SEV1 incident
Debugging by the commander will break the timeline the scribe is keeping
Commanders do not have production access, so their commands will fail anyway
Nobody is coordinating: tracking hypotheses, assigning work and deciding when to roll back or escalate
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: The IC owns the incident and big picture; if they go heads-down, the response becomes chaotic.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: During a payments SEV1, business heads keep messaging engineers "any update?", slowing the fix. Which role solves this?
options: A second incident commander who answers questions while the first one coordinates
A scribe who records the business heads' questions in the timeline for later
A communications lead who sends stakeholder updates on a fixed schedule and shields responders
The on-call engineer, who should reply to each message so nobody feels ignored
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: The comms lead writes updates for business, support, leadership and the status page, so ops engineers can focus.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: The comms lead has no new information 15 minutes after the last SEV1 update. What should they do?
options: Wait until the incident is mitigated and then send one complete summary
Send the scheduled update anyway, e.g. 'still investigating', with the next update time
Skip the update, since no news means there is nothing worth reporting
Share the team's current best guess of the root cause to show progress
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Silence creates panic. Updates go out on rhythm, and should not guess the root cause, since early guesses are often wrong.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: You are the comms lead in a payments SEV1. What should each status update to business, support and leadership contain?
options: Detailed technical metrics such as pool sizes and Kafka lag, for engineers
Only a final summary, sent once the incident is fully mitigated and resolved
Customer impact, current status, the next update time, and IC and comms names
The likely root cause and the name of the engineer whose change triggered it
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Updates are written for non-engineers on a fixed rhythm: impact, status, next update time and owners. Guessing the root cause early is often wrong, and naming people invites blame.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: Payments are failing. Payment-service v412 shipped 25 minutes ago with a new fraud check behind flag fraud_check_v2. What is the fastest sensible sequence?
options: Turn the flag off first (about 30 seconds), prepare a rollback in parallel, and roll back if recovery is incomplete
Increase payment-service replicas, since failures are usually caused by load
Roll back the database to last night's backup to undo any data changes by v412
Disable the fraud check permanently in code and deploy a hotfix within an hour
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: 'What changed?' points to v412. In the worked example, the flag only got success to 70%; the rollback to v411 brought it back to 97%.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: During an incident you roll back a deploy, and it turns out the deploy was innocent. Was the rollback a mistake?
options: No, but only because the rollback will also fix any database issues
Yes: rollbacks should only be done once the root cause is confirmed in the code
Yes: unnecessary rollbacks always cause data loss, so they must be avoided
No: a safe, reversible action that rules out a cause is cheap compared with more minutes of customer harm
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Most incidents follow a change, so rolling back is a fast, low-risk test. If it does not help, move to the next hypothesis (dependencies, overload, failover).

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: You rolled back the last deploy, but payments are still failing. What is the next step?
options: Roll back two more versions in case the bug was introduced earlier
Stop mitigation and start writing the postmortem while details are fresh
Test the next hypothesis: dependencies, overload, then failover or degrading
Downgrade the severity, since the most likely cause has been ruled out
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Mitigation continues until customers are OK: failover, load shedding or degradation, with escalation if needed.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: A postmortem concludes: "Root cause: engineer typed 10 instead of 50 for the DB pool size." What is wrong with this?
options: It should name the engineer so the team knows who needs extra training
Nothing: it is accurate and specific, which is what a good root cause should be
It is too detailed; postmortems should only state the impact and the fix
It stops at human error instead of finding the system gaps that let it through
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Human error is where investigation starts, not ends: asking why further finds no config validation, bundled config and feature changes, low-traffic staging and a short canary. The fix belongs in the system so the same mistake cannot reach production again.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: What does 'blameless' mean in a blameless postmortem?
options: Asking what in the system allowed it, while people stay accountable for fixes
Nobody is accountable for anything, so action items are optional suggestions
The postmortem is anonymous and never shared outside the affected team
Only external vendors can be named as causes, never internal systems
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Accountability shifts to fixing the system and owning action items. People who fear blame hide details; the full truth is what lets you fix the system.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: Which postmortem action item is most useful?
options: Improve monitoring across all services. Owners: whole platform team
Add validation and alerts on DB pool saturation. Owner: Meena, due in 2 weeks, tracked in the backlog
The team should be more careful with config changes in the future
Investigate whether staging could be more realistic at some point
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Good action items are specific, have exactly one owner and a due date, are tracked like normal work, and ideally prevent a class of failure.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: Six months after an incident, its postmortem document is complete but most action items are still open. What is the right view?
options: It is not done: open action items mean a repeat incident is waiting to happen
Close the items as stale, since the system has changed enough in six months
Open a new postmortem about why the old action items were not finished
It is done: the document captured the lessons, which is the main purpose
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: A postmortem is done when action items are completed and lessons shared. Review open items weekly and keep each postmortem to a few high-impact items.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: In a postmortem review, a director asks, "Who did this?" What is the likely long-term effect?
options: Postmortems get written faster because the cause is clear from the start
People become more careful, so the number of incidents drops quickly
Nothing, as long as the engineer named is not formally punished
People hide details next time and stop reporting near misses, which are the cheapest lessons
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: Leaders set the culture; asking 'what made this easy to get wrong?' encourages openness.

It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.q: Why does the incident team keep a timestamped timeline during the incident?
options: It is required to calculate the SLA refund owed to every affected customer
Memory at 3 AM is unreliable; the timeline feeds the postmortem and shows where time was lost
It replaces status updates, since stakeholders can read the timeline directly
It lets the commander replay commands automatically if the rollback fails
It's 2 AM and payments are failing. What.why: A scribe or bot records alerts, joins, hypotheses and actions; e.g. it revealed '20 minutes before anyone checked recent deploys'.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: Your EMI-reminder script runs as `0 9 * * *` cron on a single VM. One morning the VM is being redeployed at 9:00. What happens?
options: That day's reminders are skipped, since cron doesn't catch up a missed run
Cron queues the missed run and fires it as soon as the VM comes back up after the deploy
Cron hands the run to another VM in the same availability zone, so only a few minutes are lost
Only users whose rows were mid-processing are skipped; the rest go out once the VM is back
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: A single cron box is a single point of failure and cron has no catch-up for missed runs, so the whole day is lost. Cron has no built-in queueing or failover of missed runs.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: To make the reminder cron 'highly available', a teammate proposes running the same cron script on two VMs. What is the most likely result?
options: Each VM sends half the reminders, so throughput doubles
The second VM stays idle unless the first one goes down
The jobs table's primary key stops the second VM from sending anything
Every user gets two SMSes, because both boxes send all reminders
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: Plain cron has no coordination, so both boxes run the full batch and every user is messaged twice. Cron does not split work or do standby failover by itself.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: You must send 2 crore reminders within a 2-hour morning window. Roughly what send rate does that need?
options: About 116 messages per second
About 2,800 messages per second
About 280 messages per second
About 28,000 messages per second
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: 2 crore (20 million) over 7,200 seconds is about 2,800 per second. 116 per second is the average if one crore were spread evenly over a full day, which real reminder traffic never is.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: What is the core design shift that replaces 'run a script at 9 AM' in a scalable scheduler?
options: Make each reminder a durable job record with its own run time and status
Run the same script on a much bigger VM with more worker threads
Keep the script but trigger it from a message queue instead of cron
Hold all pending reminders in an in-memory timer on each app server instead
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: Per-job durable state (run time, status, attempts) is what lets work be shared, retried and audited. A bigger box or a different trigger still leaves one fragile batch with no per-user state.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: The daily planner that inserts 18 lakh reminder rows crashes at row 11 lakh and is rerun from the start. How does a good design avoid duplicate jobs?
options: A random UUID per row, so every insert is guaranteed to be unique
Delete all of today's rows first, then rerun the planner from scratch
A deterministic job_id like emi:L88:2026-10-16:D-1, so the primary key rejects repeats
Let the workers spot two rows for the same user later on and quietly skip one of them
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: A deterministic id derived from loan, date and reminder type makes the insert idempotent: the primary key rejects rows already inserted. Random UUIDs would make every rerun create fresh duplicates.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: Your scheduler query `WHERE run_at <= now() AND status='PENDING'` on one giant table is getting slow, and 9:00 AM is a hot minute. What does the answer recommend?
options: Add more read replicas and keep running the same range scan on each
Per-minute buckets split into shards, so each scheduler does cheap key lookups
Run the range scan less often, say every 10 minutes, to cut the load
Move every job into a single Redis list kept sorted by run time, polled by every scheduler
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: Buckets turn a big range scan into small key lookups, and shards (e.g. user id hash mod 64) let many scheduler instances split a hot minute. Polling less often just adds lateness.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: A worker claims a job with `UPDATE ... SET status='LEASED', lease_until=now()+2min WHERE job_id=:id AND (status='PENDING' OR (status='LEASED' AND lease_until<now()))`. The update returns 0 rows. What should the worker do?
options: Retry the same update in a tight loop until it gets 1 row
Send the SMS anyway, since the job is clearly already due
Reset the job to PENDING so that it can be claimed afresh
Skip the job, because another worker currently owns it
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: The conditional update is atomic: 1 row updated means you own it, 0 rows means someone else holds a live lease. Sending anyway or resetting the status would break single ownership.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: Worker-12 holds a lease on a reminder job and is OOM-killed. Which mechanism guarantees the user is still reminded?
options: The idempotency key forces the job back into PENDING
The lease expires and another worker can claim the job
The SMS provider retries the message on the worker's behalf
The daily planner notices the crash and reinserts the row
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: Leases are time-limited claims, so a dead worker's claim lapses and the job becomes claimable again; that is the 'never miss' half. The idempotency key prevents duplicates, it does not re-queue work.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: A worker sends the SMS, then crashes before marking the job DONE. Its lease expires and worker-30 claims the job. What prevents a second SMS?
options: The lease itself ensures only one SMS is ever sent for each job
The job's attempts counter blocks any second attempt on the job
The SMS provider always rejects a second message with exactly the same text
Worker-30 finds the idempotency key already recorded and skips the send
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: A lease alone cannot stop a duplicate because the first worker may have sent just before dying; the idempotency check at the point of the side effect does. Attempt counters only limit retries.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: An engineer says, 'We use a distributed lock around each send, so we have exactly-once delivery.' What is the flaw?
options: Locks expire, so a slow worker can finish after losing it; only an idempotency check at the send stops duplicates
Distributed locks are too slow at this scale, but the reasoning is otherwise correct
The lock should be held by the scheduler rather than by the worker for that claim to be fully true
It only holds if the lock lives in the same database as the jobs table itself
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: A lock with an expiry can be lost while the holder is still working (GC pause, slow network), so two workers can act. Duplicate prevention has to happen where the side effect happens.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: Which idempotency key best fits an EMI 'due tomorrow' reminder?
options: (user) only, so each user gets one message
(worker id, time of the send attempt)
(user, loan, due date, reminder type)
A fresh random UUID for each send attempt
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: The key must identify one logical action, so the same reminder for the same loan and due date always maps to the same key. Worker id or a fresh UUID changes on every retry and never detects duplicates.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: A worker records the idempotency key, then dies before actually calling the SMS provider. The next worker sees the key and skips. What does the answer suggest to close this gap?
options: Record the idempotency key only after the job has been marked DONE
Drop idempotency for reminders and accept occasional duplicate SMSes
Record 'attempting' then 'sent', and reconcile stuck ones against delivery reports
Make the lease much longer so that a worker can never die halfway through a send
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: Two-state recording plus a reconciler using provider delivery reports finds the stuck ones. For EMI reminders a miss can cost a late fee, so teams bias towards no misses with strong dedup.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: The SMS aggregator starts returning timeouts and 5xx errors at 09:40. What retry policy fits the answer?
options: Exponential backoff with jitter, then FAILED, with a deadline to switch channel
Retry immediately in a tight loop until the provider recovers
Retry every 30 seconds indefinitely so that no reminder is ever lost, however long it takes
Never retry at all; mark the job FAILED on the very first error
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: Backoff with jitter avoids hammering a struggling provider, and a deadline matters because a 'due tomorrow' reminder at 11 PM is pointless. Tight loops or fixed retries forever pile load onto the failing provider.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: A reminder send fails with 'user opted out'. What should the worker do?
options: Retry with exponential backoff, like any other provider error
Retry on a second SMS provider in case the first one was wrong
Re-queue it for tomorrow's run in case the user opts back in
Not retry; it's a permanent error, so mark it failed and log it
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: Permanent errors such as invalid number or opted-out will never succeed, so retrying wastes quota. Only transient errors like timeouts and 5xx deserve backoff retries.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: A product manager wants a reminder 30 days before each EMI and suggests putting the message straight onto SQS with a 30-day delay. What is the best response?
options: Fine, since SQS is durable, any delay length will work reliably
Keep long-term jobs in a database; delay queues have short limits and are hard to cancel
Use an in-memory timer wheel instead, since it is O(1) to add
Use cron on each app server to hold the 30-day timers locally and fire them when due
