How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: Delay queues suit short delays like 'retry in 2 minutes' (SQS caps at 15 minutes); long schedules belong in a durable, queryable store. Timer wheels are in memory and must sit on top of a durable store.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: Where do timer wheels fit in a scalable job scheduler?
options: As an in-memory O(1) timer layer on top of a durable store
As the main durable store for months-ahead reminders
As a replacement for leases among competing workers
As the rate limiter in front of the SMS providers
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: A timer wheel is a clock face of slots in memory, used inside Kafka and Netty; because it is in memory it would lose everything on a crash. It is not a lease or rate-limiting mechanism.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: Your scheduler stores run times in UTC and buckets on whole UTC hours. Reminders are meant for 9:00 IST. What subtle bug can appear?
options: IST's daylight-saving shift moves reminders by an hour twice a year
UTC storage makes 9:00 IST land on the previous calendar day
9:00 IST is 03:30 UTC, so whole-hour buckets can fire 30 minutes off
None, since IST is a whole-hour offset from UTC like most zones
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: IST is UTC+5:30 with no daylight saving, so the half-hour offset is the trap. India has no DST, so DST is not the issue here.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: You add users in New York. How should their '9 AM local' reminders be stored?
options: Store a fixed -05:00 offset and apply it to every occurrence
Store the zone id (America/New_York) and recompute UTC per occurrence
Store the time in IST and let the user's phone convert it to local time
Store local 9:00 as-is and compare it with server local time
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: DST shifts the offset during the year and creates skipped and repeated hours, so a fixed offset goes wrong part of the year. A zone id lets each occurrence be converted correctly; also avoid the 1-3 AM local window.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: Workers can produce 10,000 sends per second but your SMS aggregator contract allows 1,000. What is the right control?
options: Shrink the worker pool until it naturally sends about 1,000 per second
Let the provider throttle you and rely on retries to catch up with the backlog later
Batch all the messages into one big bulk call at exactly 9:00 AM
A token-bucket rate limiter per provider, plus failover across providers
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: A token bucket refills at a fixed rate and each send spends a token, keeping you within contract while workers stay busy; multiple providers add capacity and failover. Leaning on provider throttling turns into floods of errors and retries.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: Login OTPs and EMI reminders go through the same SMS provider. During the 9 AM reminder burst, OTPs start arriving late. What is the fix the answer recommends?
options: Put OTPs at the front of each reminder batch
Give OTPs a separate, higher-priority quota
Pause all reminders whenever any OTP is waiting
Raise the reminder rate limit to drain faster
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: Separate quotas keep time-critical OTPs isolated from bulk reminders. Raising the reminder limit makes contention worse, and pausing reminders entirely is unnecessary.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: Nothing errors overnight, but the scheduler pods silently stopped polling. Which monitoring signal catches this kind of silent failure?
options: Worker CPU utilisation staying below the 80% alert threshold
The count of HTTP 5xx errors returned by the SMS provider
The number of rows the daily planner inserted for the day, compared with yesterday
Schedule lag on the oldest PENDING job, plus a heartbeat dead man's switch
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: When nothing runs there are no errors to alert on, so you watch lag and a heartbeat whose absence pages someone. Provider errors and CPU stay quiet when nothing is being sent.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: At noon your reconciliation shows: expected 18,00,000; sent 17,96,100; permanent failures 3,900; stuck in PENDING 0. What does this tell you?
options: Every reminder is accounted for; the 3,900 unreached users are known and reported
About 3,900 reminders were silently lost and must be resent today
The planner over-counted, since sent should always equal expected
Workers double-sent about 3,900 messages, and those duplicates now need investigation
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: 17,96,100 sent plus 3,900 permanently failed equals 18,00,000 with zero stuck, so nothing was silently missed. Permanent failures (invalid numbers, opt-outs, DND) are known and go to the collections team.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: A user pays her EMI at 08:55, but her reminder job is already queued for 09:00. What does the answer suggest?
options: Let it send, since queued reminders can't be cancelled
Find the queued message in the Kafka topic and delete it
Mark it CANCELLED and re-check loan status just before sending
Rely on the idempotency key to drop this reminder
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: Payment may land after the job is queued, so a just-before-send status check catches it. The idempotency key only prevents duplicates of the same reminder; it knows nothing about payment.

How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.q: An interviewer asks, 'Can your reminder system guarantee exactly-once delivery?' What is the most accurate answer?
options: Yes, leases guarantee it by giving each job exactly one owner
Yes, provided Kafka's exactly-once semantics are switched on for the reminder topic
Not end to end; at-least-once plus idempotent processing is effectively once
No, so occasional duplicate SMSes must simply be accepted
How does an app send crores of \"Your EM.why: Leases recover crashed work, which means at-least-once; idempotency keys turn that into effectively once for the user. Kafka's guarantees don't cover the external SMS side effect, and giving up on dedup is unnecessary.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: Checkout reserves stock, charges payment and books delivery, each in its own service with its own database. Delivery booking fails after payment succeeded. What is the correct way to undo?
options: Issue a database ROLLBACK on the payment and inventory databases together
Leave the payment and stock as they are and keep retrying delivery forever
Delete the payment and reservation rows so it looks like they never happened
Run compensations: refund the payment, release the stock, mark the order failed
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Across services there is no shared transaction to roll back, so you undo by doing new work: compensations. Deleting rows erases audit history and doesn't return the customer's money.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: Which of these best describes a saga?
options: One distributed transaction across services, coordinated with prepare and commit phases
A chain of local transactions, each paired with a compensating action
A message queue that guarantees exactly-once delivery between services
A single database shared by all services to keep them consistent
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: A saga commits each step locally and relies on compensations for consistency. Prepare-and-commit describes two-phase commit, which sagas are used to avoid.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: An architect proposes two-phase commit (2PC) across inventory, payment and the UPI payment gateway. What is the strongest objection?
options: Gateways and courier APIs can't join 2PC, and it holds locks across the network
2PC is not supported by any mainstream relational database, so it can't be used at all
2PC only works when all the participating services are written in the same language
2PC cannot handle more than two participants, and checkout has three or more
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: You cannot 'prepare' a UPI payment, and holding stock locks across network calls kills throughput during sales. 2PC is supported by many databases and allows many participants; that isn't the problem.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: During a festive sale your team tries 2PC across services. Throughput collapses. Which 2PC property is most to blame?
options: The coordinator commits too quickly before participants are ready
Each participant must write twice to its own database log, doubling disk I/O at peak
Stock rows stay locked while waiting on network votes from other services
The prepare phase sends too many bytes over the network for each and every order
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Locks held during network round trips block other buyers of the same SKU. The coordinator being a single point of failure is another risk, but the throughput hit is from held locks.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: Under 2PC the coordinator crashes right after participants vote 'prepared'. What is the risk?
options: Participants automatically commit, causing duplicate charges
Participants can be stuck holding locks, unsure whether to commit or abort
Participants automatically roll back on a timeout, so no real harm is done
Nothing, because the prepare vote already finalised the transaction
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: After prepare, participants have promised to commit if told and must wait for the decision, so a dead coordinator leaves them blocked. That is why the coordinator is a single point of failure.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: You are ordering saga steps for checkout. Which ordering principle does the answer recommend?
options: Charge payment first so you never reserve stock for unpaid orders
Book delivery first, because it is the step most likely to fail in practice
Order does not matter as long as every step has a compensation
Cheap, easily reversed steps first; painful-to-reverse ones like charging later
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Releasing a reservation is cheap; a refund costs money and annoys the customer, so it should run only after cheaper checks. Order affects how often painful compensations run.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: In the checkout saga, delivery is booked successfully but the confirmation SMS step then fails. What should happen?
options: Cancel the delivery booking, refund the payment and release the stock
Retry the SMS until it succeeds; past the pivot you only go forward
Mark the order FAILED but keep the payment for a future retry
Ignore it, since notification failures don't matter to the saga at all
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Delivery booking is the pivot: after it, the saga goes forward, retrying remaining steps. Unwinding a confirmed order because a notification failed would be wrong.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: Delivery booking fails after stock was reserved and payment was captured. In what order do the compensations run?
options: Release stock, then refund payment, then mark the order FAILED
Mark the order FAILED, then release stock, then refund payment
Refund and release in parallel, and leave the order in PENDING for support
Refund payment, then release stock, then mark the order FAILED and notify
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Compensations run in reverse order of the completed steps: payment was last to succeed, so it is refunded first. The order is marked failed and the customer told at the end.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: A colleague says, 'Compensation is just rollback for microservices.' What is wrong with that?
options: It's a new forward action, like a refund; the charge and refund both stay recorded
A compensation is faster than a rollback but otherwise does exactly the same thing
A compensation only works if every service shares one database
Nothing is wrong; compensations erase the earlier change exactly, like a rollback
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Rollback erases changes as if they never happened; compensation is semantic undo that restores business meaning while keeping history, which also helps audits. A refund taking 3-5 days or a sent SMS shows it isn't exact undo.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: Your checkout flow has six steps and involves money, and support must answer 'what state is order OD123 in, and why?' in seconds. Which saga style fits best?
options: Choreography, because events decouple the services best of all
Two-phase commit, since flows involving money need atomicity
Orchestration, with one orchestrator holding the flow
No saga; let each service handle its own failures independently
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Orchestration keeps the flow and the saga record in one place, which makes long money flows easy to debug. Choreography spreads the flow across many logs and suits short 2-4 step reactions.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: In a choreographed saga, delivery publishes DeliveryFailed. What happens next?
options: The saga orchestrator receives it and calls refund, then release stock
Inventory and payment both ignore it until a human intervenes
Payment refunds and publishes PaymentRefunded; inventory then releases stock
The order service rolls back all three services' databases in one step
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: In choreography there is no central boss; each service reacts to events and publishes its own. An orchestrator exists only in the orchestration style.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: What is a known risk of choreography for long flows?
options: Hidden cycles and no single owner of the whole flow
The orchestrator becomes a bottleneck or 'god service'
Every service must know about every other service in the flow
Adding a new step always requires changing a central component
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Choreography's flow is scattered across services, so nobody sees the whole picture. The god-service bottleneck and central changes are orchestration's drawbacks.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: The orchestrator calls 'charge payment' and the call times out. You don't know whether the charge happened. What is the safe move?
options: Assume it failed and charge again with a brand-new request id
Assume it succeeded and move straight on to booking delivery
Compensate immediately by issuing a refund to be on the safe side
Retry with the same idempotency key, e.g. sagaId + stepName
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Retrying is the only safe move under uncertainty, and the same idempotency key makes the retry return the earlier result instead of double charging. Guessing either way risks a double charge or an unpaid order.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: Which of these operations is idempotent?
options: Add Rs 500 to the wallet balance
Set order status to PAID
Append a new row to the payments ledger
Increment the reserved-units counter by one
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Setting a value to a fixed state gives the same result however often you do it. Adding, appending or incrementing changes the result each time it is repeated.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: A RefundPayment command for PAY-77 is retried three times after timeouts. What must be true?
options: The refund is idempotent, so the customer is refunded exactly once
Each retry issues a partial refund that sums to the full amount
Retries are skipped for compensations, which are always fire-and-forget
The second and third retries are rejected as errors and alert a human
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Compensations must be idempotent just like forward steps; a repeated refund with the same key returns 'refunded'. Compensations are not fire-and-forget and duplicates should not be errors.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: A team says, 'Our client library retries automatically, so idempotency is optional.' What is the problem?
options: Retries are unsafe in sagas and should be disabled in the client library
Idempotency is only needed for read-only steps, not for payments
Retries without idempotency cause double charges and refunds
Nothing; library retries are idempotent by default
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: A retried non-idempotent charge charges twice. Retries are necessary under timeouts, but only safe when the receiving step dedups on a key.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: The payment gateway is down for an hour and the refund compensation keeps failing. What should the saga do?
options: Give up after three tries and mark the order as complete anyway
Retry with backoff from durable state, then alert a human after a threshold
Silently drop the refund since the gateway is unavailable
Re-charge the customer so that the books balance at month end
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Compensations can fail and must never be silently dropped; durable retries plus a human-in-the-loop alert handle long outages. Giving up leaves the customer charged with no order.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: The orchestrator pod restarts during a deploy while saga S-9001 is in COMPENSATING_REFUND. How does the saga resume correctly?
options: The saga state is held in the old pod's memory and copied over to the new pod
The payment service notices the restart and finishes the refund on its own
The saga restarts from step 1, re-reserving stock and recharging
The saga's state and PAY-77 are in a database; the new pod loads it and resumes
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Saga progress must live in a database, not memory, so a restart continues from the recorded step; idempotent steps make resending safe. Restarting from step 1 would charge the customer again.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: Why is the transactional outbox usually paired with stored saga state?
options: It replaces the need for idempotency keys on every saga step and compensation
It writes the state change and outgoing command in one local transaction
It lets the saga hold locks across services, much like two-phase commit does
It periodically deletes finished saga records to keep the saga table small
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Without an outbox the orchestrator could update state and crash before sending the command (or vice versa). The outbox doesn't remove the need for idempotency, since messages can still be delivered more than once.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: Right after the customer taps Pay, the saga is still running. What should the app show?
options: 'Order confirmed', since the payment step has already started
A spinner until all services finish, however long it takes
Nothing, and send an SMS later once the saga is done
'Order placed, confirming' with status PENDING, not 'Confirmed'
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Never show CONFIRMED until the saga reaches that state; honest in-between statuses handle eventual consistency. Showing confirmed early leads to broken promises if a later step fails.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: Someone claims a saga gives you ACID across services. Which property is notably missing?
options: Isolation: others can see in-between states, e.g. stock reserved, order pending
Durability: saga steps can be lost even after their local commit
Atomicity at the local level: each individual step may half-apply
Consistency: the saga can never reach a correct final state at all
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Each local step is atomic and durable, and the saga converges, but there is no isolation of intermediate states. You design for it with PENDING statuses and reservations.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: How does the answer suggest dealing with the lack of isolation in a checkout saga?
options: Wrap the whole saga in one database transaction at SERIALIZABLE isolation
Pause all other orders for the same product until the saga finishes
Semantic locks like PENDING, expiring reservations, and re-checking values like price
Hide intermediate states by caching the old values for every reader
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Semantic locks and reservations make in-between states explicit and safe without global locks. A SERIALIZABLE transaction cannot span services, and pausing all orders kills throughput.

Placing an order touches payment, invent.q: An order flow ends by sending the customer a 'your order is confirmed' email. Where should that email step go and why?
options: First, so that the customer is reassured immediately after paying
Before payment, with a follow-up 'sorry' email as its compensation
Last, once the outcome is certain, as a sent email can't be undone
Anywhere in the flow, since sending an email is idempotent anyway
Placing an order touches payment, invent.why: Non-compensatable actions belong after the pivot, once success is certain. A 'sorry' email doesn't undo the first one, so sending it early creates confusion.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: Your wallet table stores only 'balance = 750'. A customer disputes how the balance got there. What does event sourcing give you that this design lacks?
options: A faster way to read the current balance from one indexed row
Every change kept as an immutable event, so the history can be replayed
Automatic encryption of the balance column, both at rest and in transit
A hard guarantee that the wallet balance can never go negative
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Event sourcing keeps the facts (MoneyAdded, MoneySpent) rather than overwriting state, so 'how did we get here?' is answerable. A current-state row is fast to read but loses history.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: A wallet stream has events: MoneyAdded 500, MoneySpent 120, MoneyAdded 200, MoneySpent 80. On the write side of an event-sourced system, where is the balance of 500 stored?
options: Nowhere; it is computed by replaying events, perhaps from a snapshot
In a balance column that is updated alongside each appended event
In the last event's payload, which carries a running total
In the read model, which the write side queries before handling each command
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: The write side stores only events; state is derived by replay. Read models are for queries, and the write side should load the aggregate itself to check rules.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: What does CQRS mean in plain words?
options: Storing every change as an immutable event in an append-only log
Caching query results in Redis so that reads stop hitting the main database
One model for writes (commands) and separate models for reads (queries)
Splitting one database into shards keyed by customer id
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: CQRS is Command Query Responsibility Segregation: write model and read models are separate. Storing changes as events is event sourcing, a separate idea that often pairs with it.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: A teammate says, 'We can't do CQRS because we don't have an event store.' What is the best reply?
options: Correct, CQRS needs event sourcing to build any of its read projections at all
They're separate ideas; read models can be fed by triggers or CDC instead
Correct, but Kafka can simply be used as the event store instead
CQRS only needs a read replica of the main database, nothing more
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: CQRS just splits read and write models; how the read side is fed is a separate choice. They pair well because events are a natural feed, but neither requires the other. A plain read replica has the same shape as the write model, so it isn't really CQRS.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: Which naming best fits an event versus a command?
options: Event: AddItemToCart; Command: ItemAddedToCart
Both in past tense, e.g. ItemAddedToCart, for consistency
Both as imperatives, e.g. AddItemToCart, since both change state
Event: ItemAddedToCart; Command: AddItemToCart
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Events are immutable facts of what happened, so they are past tense; commands are requests that may be refused. Swapping them confuses intent with fact.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: In the Wallet aggregate, a developer adds an 'if (balance < 0) throw' check inside apply(MoneySpent). Why is that a mistake?
options: apply should check rules, but it must throw a different exception type
Past events must always replay cleanly; rules belong in spend, not apply
The check is fine, but it slows replay down and should be cached
apply should never change state at all; only spend should do that
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Past events already happened and must replay without failing, even if rules change later. Rules are checked when deciding on a new command; apply only mutates state.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: Which is the correct order of the write path for a command in event sourcing?
options: Append the event first, then check the rules, then update the read model
Update the read model, then append the event, then notify the user
Check the rules against the read model, then append without a version
Load the aggregate, check rules, emit events, append with expected version
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Load, decide, emit, append with an expected version is the standard four-step write path. Checking rules after appending or against a lagging read model can accept invalid commands.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: Two requests try to spend from the same wallet at the same moment. Both load version 4. The first appends successfully. What happens to the second?
options: Its append expecting version 4 is rejected; it reloads and re-checks
It appends at version 5, and both spends go through normally
It waits on a database row lock until the first request has fully finished
It overwrites the first request's event at version 5
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Optimistic concurrency rejects an append whose expected version is stale, preventing double spending without long locks. Events are never overwritten, and no long lock is held.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: A busy seller account has 200,000 events and every command is slow. What is the standard fix?
options: Delete old events once their effect is reflected in the balance
Merge the 200,000 events into one summary event and rewrite the stream
Snapshot state every N events (say 500) and replay only later events
Query the read model instead of loading the aggregate for commands
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Snapshots cache state at a version so loading reads the snapshot plus later events. Deleting or rewriting events would break the immutable history that is the source of truth.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: A disk cleanup accidentally deletes all snapshots. How serious is it?
options: Serious; the aggregates' current state is now permanently lost for good
Serious; every read model must now be restored from backups
Not serious; snapshots are a cache rebuilt by replaying events
Not serious, but events after the last snapshot are now gone
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Events are the truth and snapshots only speed up loading. Read models are built from events, not snapshots, so they are unaffected.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: Does a single order aggregate with 10-20 events in its whole life need snapshots?
options: No; replaying that handful of events is effectively instant
Yes; every aggregate should take a snapshot every 5 events
Yes; without snapshots the read model cannot be built at all
No, because orders should not be event-sourced in the first place
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Snapshots matter only for long streams like a busy seller account. Orders are a classic good fit for event sourcing; they just don't need snapshots.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: A customer says, 'I changed my address but the parcel went to the old one.' With event sourcing, support sees AddressChanged at 9:14 pm and OrderPacked at 9:12 pm with the old label. What does this reveal?
options: The customer is mistaken, since the change was saved
The read model lagged, so the packer saw stale data
The address event was lost and must be re-appended
A bug: packing didn't block later address changes
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: The ordered timeline shows the address changed after packing, so packing should have blocked it. With a current-state table the old address would simply have been overwritten and the story lost.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: A customer places an order and immediately opens 'My orders', but it's missing. Nothing is broken. Which fix fits the answer?
options: Run the projector inside one distributed transaction with every service
Show state from the command response, or wait for the projection's version
Drop the read model and query the event store for every order list
Tell the customer to refresh after a few minutes until it shows up
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: The projection simply hasn't processed OrderPlaced yet: eventual consistency. Read-your-own-writes techniques hide the lag without giving up the read-model design.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: Someone says, 'Eventual consistency means our data might be wrong.' What is the accurate correction?
options: Writes are consistent per aggregate; only read views lag, then converge
True, so critical systems should never rely on read models at all
True, but only when snapshots are older than about five minutes
False, because projections always update in the same transaction as events
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Lag is limited to read models, usually tens to hundreds of milliseconds; the event store is correct. Projectors run after the append, not in the same transaction.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: After a crash, a projector may reprocess a few events it had already applied. What must be true of it?
options: It must delete and rebuild its whole read model from scratch on every restart
It must skip any event that is older than one minute on restart
It must be idempotent, ideally saving its checkpoint with the update
It must lock the event store for as long as it is processing
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Saving the checkpoint atomically with the update means replays after a crash don't double-apply. Full rebuilds on every restart would be needlessly slow.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: Your 'returns by reason' report has a projector bug that miscounted for a week. What is the event-sourcing way to fix it?
options: Edit the affected ReturnRequested events so the counts come out right
Fix the projector, rebuild a new read model by replay, then switch over
Patch the report table's rows by hand with a few SQL UPDATE statements
Append a compensating event for each of the wrong counts in the report
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Source events are untouched and correct; only the derived view was wrong, so you rebuild it. Editing events breaks immutability, and compensating events are for business corrections, not view bugs.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: A support agent wrongly recorded a MoneyAdded 200 on a wallet. How do you correct it?
options: Edit the MoneyAdded event so its amount becomes 0
Delete that one event from the wallet's stream
Update the wallet's balance column directly
Append a compensating event, like a passbook reversal
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: History is never edited; corrections are new facts, just like a bank passbook reversal line. There is no balance column on the write side to update.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: Next year every MoneySpent event must include a currency, but old events don't have it. What does the answer recommend?
options: Run a one-time migration that rewrites every old event to add the currency
Add an optional field and upcast old events on load, defaulting to INR
Reject replay of any old event that has no currency field in it
Start a new event store and abandon the old events from now on
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Additive changes plus upcasting keep history intact while code sees one shape. Copy-and-transform of the whole store is expensive and risky and a rare last resort.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: A colleague plans to use Kafka as the event store for orders. What is the main concern?
options: Kafka cannot keep events for more than seven days under any setting
Kafka does not preserve the order of messages within a partition
Kafka topics cannot be read by more than one consumer group
Loading one order's events or appending with a version check is hard
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Kafka is a good transport, but event stores need per-aggregate loading and optimistic version checks; most teams keep events in a database and publish to Kafka. Kafka does preserve per-partition order and supports many consumers.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: How do you publish an event-sourced service's events to other services without a dual write?
options: A relay reads the event store in order (or CDC) and publishes to Kafka
The command handler writes to the event store, and then publishes the same events to Kafka
Use two-phase commit between the event store and Kafka
Let other services query the event store directly on demand
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Because events are already durably stored, the event store acts as the outbox and a relay publishes them in order; consumers must be idempotent. Writing to both from the handler is exactly the dual write that can lose or duplicate messages.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: A privacy law requires deleting a user's personal data, but events are immutable. What technique does the answer mention?
options: Edit the stored events to blank out the personal fields
Delete the user's whole event stream, financial history included
Keep PII out of events, or encrypt per user and discard the key
Ignore the request, since event logs are legally exempt
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Crypto-shredding makes the data unreadable without rewriting history. Editing events breaks immutability, and deleting financial history can break audit requirements.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: Your team is building an admin page to edit store opening hours, with one simple list view. Should you use event sourcing and CQRS?
options: Yes; every service in the company should use event sourcing for consistency
Yes, but only CQRS, with three separate read models for the list
Probably not; it's simple CRUD with one view and little need for history
Yes; event sourcing is required for any kind of audit log at all
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Event sourcing and CQRS pay off for orders, ledgers, payments and inventory where history and many views matter. For simple CRUD they add moving parts, lag and event-versioning pain for little gain.

What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.q: During a festive sale the seller 'orders to pack' dashboard lags 3 seconds behind. What should the team conclude?
options: Acceptable read-model lag; the write side is still correct
Orders are being lost, and the event store must be checked for gaps
Writes should block until the dashboard has caught up
The dashboard should replay all events on every refresh
What are event sourcing and CQRS, in pla.why: Read models may lag under load and then converge; correctness lives in the event store. Blocking writes on projections would throw away the point of separating them.

How does a website store your password s.q: A new engineer joins and asks to see users' passwords in the database to debug a login issue. In a well-built system, what will they find?
options: Only a salted one-way hash, from which the password can't be read
The passwords, encrypted with a key that only the security team holds
The plaintext passwords, but only in an access-controlled column
The passwords base64-encoded so they aren't directly human-readable
How does a website store your password s.why: Good systems store only a salted, slow, one-way hash, so nobody can read the password. Encryption or encoding can be reversed by whoever holds the key or knows the format.

How does a website store your password s.q: If the site doesn't store your password, how does it check it at login?
options: It decrypts the stored hash and compares it with what you typed
It sends the typed password to the email provider for verification
It hashes what you typed with the same salt and settings and compares
It compares the length and the first few characters of the typed password
How does a website store your password s.why: Same input always gives the same hash, so a match proves the right password without ever knowing it. A hash cannot be decrypted; there is no key.

How does a website store your password s.q: An interviewer asks, 'Why not just encrypt passwords instead of hashing them?' What is the best answer?
options: Encryption is too slow to handle peak login traffic on a big sale day
Whoever gets the key can decrypt every password; a hash has no key to steal
Encryption makes the stored value too long for the database column
Encryption is perfectly fine, as long as the key is rotated at least once a year
How does a website store your password s.why: Encryption is reversible by design; one stolen key exposes everything. Hashing has no key to steal. Speed and storage size are not the issue.

How does a website store your password s.q: A small site's 'Forgot password' feature emails you your current password. What does this tell you?
options: It uses a strong hash plus a pepper, which allows safe recovery
It uses bcrypt, which allows the password to be recovered
Nothing much; recovering passwords this way is normal for most sites
It stores passwords readably (plaintext or reversible): a red flag
How does a website store your password s.why: A properly hashed password can't be recovered by anyone, so emailing it proves it is stored readably. The correct design is a single-use reset link.

How does a website store your password s.q: Your team stores passwords as SHA-256 hashes. A security reviewer flags it even though SHA-256 is a secure hash. Why?
options: SHA-256 has been broken and its hashes can now be reversed directly
SHA-256 is fast, so a GPU can try billions of guesses per second
SHA-256 output is too short to stay unique across millions of users
SHA-256 can only hash passwords up to 8 characters long safely
How does a website store your password s.why: SHA-256 is fine for integrity but its speed (around 20 billion guesses per second per GPU) is terrible for passwords. It isn't reversible; the danger is fast guessing.

How does a website store your password s.q: An 8-character password of lowercase letters and digits has about 2.8 trillion possibilities. Roughly how long does one modern GPU take to try them all against unsalted MD5?
options: About a week
Several decades
Around a year
Under a minute
How does a website store your password s.why: At about 150 billion MD5 guesses per second, 2.8 trillion takes under a minute. Decades is the figure for bcrypt at cost 12, which is about a hundred million times slower.

How does a website store your password s.q: Ravi and Sethu both use the password Mango@2024. With proper per-user salts, what do their stored hashes look like?
options: Different, because each has a unique random salt mixed in
Identical, since the password and algorithm are the same
Identical except for the cost prefix at the start of the string
Different only if they signed up on different days
How does a website store your password s.why: Each user gets a fresh random salt, so identical passwords produce different hashes, which hides popular passwords and stops one crack revealing many. The cost prefix is the same for both.

How does a website store your password s.q: An attacker has a huge precomputed rainbow table of common passwords and their MD5 hashes. Which defence makes it useless?
options: Rate-limiting the login endpoint
Requiring passwords of at least 8 characters
A unique random salt per user
Enforcing HTTPS on the login page
How does a website store your password s.why: Rainbow tables precompute hash-of-password; a salt changes the input per user so lookups no longer work. Rate limiting protects the live login, not a stolen database.

How does a website store your password s.q: A developer proposes storing the salt in a separate, secret vault because 'if attackers get the salt they can crack the hash.' What is the correct view?
options: Correct, salts must be stored apart from hashes to be effective
Correct, and every user's salt should also be rotated every month
Salts aren't secret; they give uniqueness. The pepper is the secret one
The salt should be derived from the username, so it never needs to be stored
How does a website store your password s.why: Salts defeat precomputation and shared cracking even when known. A pepper is the secret kept outside the database. A username-derived salt isn't random and repeats across sites.

How does a website store your password s.q: What does a salt NOT protect against?
options: A targeted attack on one user with a weak password
Rainbow table lookups
Spotting that thousands of users share the same hash
Reusing one guess computation across all users
How does a website store your password s.why: Salt makes each hash unique but an attacker can still guess one user's weak password; slowness and strong passwords address that. The other three are exactly what salt fixes.

How does a website store your password s.q: You are choosing a password hash for a new system. Which is the usual recommendation?
options: SHA-256 with a per-user salt
MD5 applied twice in a row
AES-256 encryption with a stored key
Argon2id, tuned for time and memory
How does a website store your password s.why: Argon2id, the Password Hashing Competition winner, is slow and memory-hard with tunable parameters. Salted SHA-256 is still too fast, double MD5 is a homemade fast combination, and AES is reversible.

How does a website store your password s.q: Why are memory-hard hashes like scrypt and Argon2 especially effective against GPU cracking rigs?
options: GPUs simply cannot run hash functions that need any working memory at all, so they fail
GPUs have lots of compute but little memory per core, limiting parallel guesses
Memory-hard hashes produce longer outputs that GPUs can't store
Memory-hard hashes need an online server call to verify each guess made
How does a website store your password s.why: Requiring, say, 64 MiB per guess means a GPU can't run thousands of guesses in parallel cheaply. GPUs can run them, just much less efficiently.

How does a website store your password s.q: Your bcrypt hashes use cost 10. How much slower is cost 12?
options: Four times slower (cost is a power of two)
About twenty percent slower (12 vs 10)
Twice as slow, one doubling per step of 2
Twelve times slower, matching the cost value
How does a website store your password s.why: Cost 10 means 2^10 rounds and cost 12 means 2^12, a factor of four. The cost is an exponent, not a linear multiplier.

How does a website store your password s.q: How should you tune the work factor of your password hash?
options: As slow as the servers can bear, since slower is always safer
Leave it at the library default and never change it afterwards
So one hash takes about 100-500 ms on your servers, raised over time
So that one hash takes about 1 ms, to keep login fast even at peak traffic
How does a website store your password s.why: Around a few hundred milliseconds is unnoticeable to a user but crushing for an attacker. Too slow hurts latency and invites login floods; too fast helps attackers.

How does a website store your password s.q: You want to move bcrypt hashes from cost 10 to cost 12 without forcing everyone to reset. How?
options: Run a nightly batch job that re-hashes all stored hashes from cost 10 to 12
Use cost 12 for new hashes and rehash old ones at each successful login
Decrypt all the stored hashes and re-encrypt them at the new cost
Keep cost 10 forever since changing it breaks existing logins
How does a website store your password s.why: At login you briefly have the plaintext, so you can rehash and save the stronger version. You can't re-derive the password from a hash, so a batch rehash of the plain hash is impossible.

How does a website store your password s.q: A legacy app has millions of unsalted MD5 password hashes. What is the recommended migration?
options: Wait until each user logs in and only then replace their MD5 hash
Crack the MD5 hashes internally, then rehash all the recovered passwords with bcrypt
Email all users their passwords and ask them to log in again
Wrap now as bcrypt(md5hash), rehash on login, force resets for dormant users
How does a website store your password s.why: Wrapping removes weak hashes from disk right away instead of leaving dormant accounts on MD5 for years. Cracking your own users' passwords or emailing them is a security failure.

How does a website store your password s.q: The bcrypt string $2b$12$R9h/cIPz0gi.URNNX3kh2O... is stored for a user. How does the login code know which salt and cost to use?
options: From a separate salts table keyed by the user id
They're embedded in the string itself: algorithm, cost, salt, then hash
From the application's global configuration file at startup
They are derived afresh from the user's email address and id at each login
How does a website store your password s.why: The bcrypt format carries algorithm, cost, salt and hash together, which is why matches() can check it directly. A separate table or config isn't needed.

How does a website store your password s.q: Why should the login check compare hashes using a constant-time comparison?
options: Because ordinary string comparison is too slow for login traffic
Because hashes contain binary data that normal comparison can't handle
So that all users' logins take exactly the bcrypt cost time
So response time doesn't reveal how many characters matched
How does a website store your password s.why: A normal compare returns early at the first difference, so timing could hint at the match. Constant-time comparison takes the same time whichever character differs.

How does a website store your password s.q: What is a pepper, and how should you treat it?
options: An extra secret kept outside the database, as optional defence in depth
A second public salt, stored right next to the first one in the users table
A cheaper replacement for slow hashing when CPU is limited
The cost parameter that is embedded in the stored hash string
How does a website store your password s.why: With a pepper, an attacker who steals only the database can't even start guessing, but it is hard to rotate. It complements, never replaces, salt and slow hashing.

How does a website store your password s.q: A developer says, 'I'll make it stronger: MD5 the password, then SHA-1 the result.' What is the problem?
options: Chaining two different hashes makes later login verification impossible
It is perfectly fine as long as you also add a random per-user salt to it
Homemade combos are still fast, sometimes weaker; use a tunable algorithm
The order is wrong: SHA-1 should go first, then MD5 on top
How does a website store your password s.why: Stacking fast hashes still gives billions of guesses per second. The golden rule is never to write your own password hashing; use a reviewed library.

How does a website store your password s.q: A user has a perfectly bcrypt-hashed password on your site, yet the account is taken over. The same password leaked from a small site that used MD5. What is this attack, and the main defences?
options: A rainbow table attack on your database; defend with a longer per-user salt
Brute force on bcrypt; defend by raising the cost factor
Credential stuffing; use rate limits, breached-password checks and MFA
SQL injection on login; defend with parameterised queries
How does a website store your password s.why: Attackers crack the reused password elsewhere and try it everywhere; your strong hashing can't help. Rate limits, breached-password checks and MFA stop the reused password alone from working.

How does a website store your password s.q: Logins spike to 20,000 per second, each costing about 200 ms of CPU for Argon2id. What trade-off does this show?
options: Slow hashing costs you CPU too (~4,000 cores), so plan capacity and sessions
Argon2id should be temporarily swapped for SHA-256 during sale days
The hash cost should be lowered to 1 ms during peak traffic
No real trade-off, since the hashing actually happens on the user's own phone
How does a website store your password s.why: 20,000 x 0.2 s is about 4,000 cores of hashing, so capacity planning and long sessions matter. Weakening the hash at peak would hand attackers the advantage.

How does a website store your password s.q: What should a correct password reset flow look like?
options: Email the user their current password after verifying the email
Email a 4-digit code valid for 7 days that reveals the old password
Let the user log in with their date of birth and registered phone instead
A single-use random token (stored hashed), expiring in 15-30 minutes
How does a website store your password s.why: Since nobody can read the old password, the honest recovery is a reset. Short-lived single-use tokens limit misuse, and signing out other sessions cuts off an attacker.

How does a website store your password s.q: SMS OTP, authenticator apps and passkeys are all MFA options. Which ranking matches the answer?
options: SMS OTP strongest, since it relies on the telecom operator's network
Passkeys strongest, then authenticator apps, then SMS OTP weakest
All three are equally strong because they are all 'something you have'
Authenticator apps strongest, passkeys weakest since they skip passwords
How does a website store your password s.why: SMS OTPs are better than nothing but vulnerable to SIM swaps; authenticator apps are stronger; passkeys resist phishing because they are bound to the real site.

How does a website remember that you're.q: Why does a website need a cookie or token at all after you log in?
options: The browser forgets your password and must re-send it on every new page
TLS connections reset after every page load, wiping out your login
HTTP is stateless, so every request must carry proof of who you are
Servers drop logged-in users unless they are pinged at regular intervals
How does a website remember that you're.why: Each HTTP request stands alone, so identity has to travel with every request. That is about HTTP, not TLS, and the password should never be resent on every page.

How does a website remember that you're.q: A site keeps sessions in each web server's memory and runs 10 servers behind a round-robin load balancer. What do users experience?
options: Everything works, since the load balancer shares memory across servers
They randomly look logged out when a request hits a server without their session
Logins become noticeably slower but otherwise behave normally
Users sometimes get logged into each other's accounts by mistake
How does a website remember that you're.why: In-memory sessions exist only on the server that created them. The fix is a shared store like Redis (or, less ideally, sticky sessions).

How does a website remember that you're.q: Why is Redis a popular session store?
options: It encrypts session IDs so they can't be stolen from the browser
It stores sessions inside the browser to save server memory
It never loses data, so sessions survive any failure or restart
It's shared by all servers, sub-millisecond fast, with built-in expiry
How does a website remember that you're.why: A shared store fixes the 'logged out on another server' problem and EXPIRE handles idle timeouts. Redis doesn't encrypt session IDs or live in the browser.

How does a website remember that you're.q: What should a good session cookie actually contain?
options: The username and a hashed copy of the password, for re-checking
Only a long random session ID pointing to the server-side record
The user ID as a plain number, e.g. SID=42, to keep lookups simple
The user's full profile in JSON so the server needn't look it up
How does a website remember that you're.why: A random unguessable ID means guessing or tampering is hopeless; the data lives on the server. A plain user ID can simply be changed to someone else's.

How does a website remember that you're.q: Your session cookie is HttpOnly. A teammate says, 'So we're safe from XSS now.' What is the accurate view?
options: Correct, HttpOnly blocks all injected JavaScript from running on the page
Correct, as long as the cookie is also marked Secure and sent over HTTPS
Wrong, HttpOnly has no effect whatsoever on what an XSS attack can do
HttpOnly stops scripts stealing the cookie, but they can still act as the user
How does a website remember that you're.why: HttpOnly blocks document.cookie access, so the ID can't be exfiltrated, but an injected script can still make requests as you. You still need to prevent XSS with output escaping and CSP.

How does a website remember that you're.q: Sethu logs in on café Wi-Fi to a site whose session cookie lacks the Secure flag. What is the risk?
options: It can travel over plain HTTP and be read by others on the network
JavaScript running on the page can read the cookie value
A malicious site can trigger cross-site POSTs with the cookie
The cookie will be deleted as soon as the browser is closed
How does a website remember that you're.why: Secure restricts the cookie to HTTPS. Script access is HttpOnly's job, and cross-site POSTs are SameSite's job.

How does a website remember that you're.q: Which cookie setting blunts CSRF while still letting a user who clicks a normal link from an email land logged in?
options: SameSite=Strict
HttpOnly
SameSite=Lax
Max-Age=0
How does a website remember that you're.why: Lax withholds the cookie on cross-site POSTs and background requests but sends it on top-level link clicks. Strict also blocks CSRF but makes email links land logged out.

How does a website remember that you're.q: An attacker plants a known session ID in a victim's browser before the victim logs in. After login, the attacker uses that same ID and is in. What prevents this?
options: Marking the session cookie HttpOnly
Using a short 30-minute idle timeout
Issuing a new session ID at login
Storing the session in Redis instead of memory
How does a website remember that you're.why: This is session fixation; regenerating the ID at login makes the planted one useless. HttpOnly and timeouts don't change which ID is trusted after login.

How does a website remember that you're.q: Your security policy says users must be logged out after 30 minutes of inactivity and after 12 hours no matter what. What are these?
options: An idle timeout and an absolute timeout
A sliding timeout and a refresh-token lifetime
A cookie Max-Age and a CSRF token expiry
Two idle timeouts at different levels of the stack
How does a website remember that you're.why: The idle timeout slides forward on activity; the absolute timeout caps total session length regardless. Max-Age controls browser retention, not server session policy.

How does a website remember that you're.q: A user clicks 'Logout' and your code only clears the cookie in the browser. Why is this not enough?
options: Browsers ignore cookie deletion until the user restarts the browser
The server automatically recreates the cookie on the very next request
Clearing the cookie logs out other devices too, which is unwanted
A stolen session ID still works until the server deletes the session
How does a website remember that you're.why: A copied ID stays valid until the server forgets it, so delete the Redis key and also clear the cookie. Logout must revoke on the server.

How does a website remember that you're.q: A user taps 'Log out of all devices'. With server-side sessions, how is this usually implemented?
options: Change the cookie name so that the old cookies no longer match
Keep a per-user set of session IDs and delete them all
Restart all the web servers so that their memory is cleared
Ask each device to delete its own cookie at next launch
How does a website remember that you're.why: A per-user index lets the server kill every session at once. Asking devices to delete cookies doesn't help if a copy was stolen.

How does a website remember that you're.q: A mobile app gets a 10-minute access token and a 30-day refresh token. Why two tokens?
options: Access tokens go everywhere, so keep them short; refresh tokens go only to login
The access token is used for reads and the refresh token for writes
Using two tokens doubles the encryption strength of each API request
The refresh token is a backup in case the access token is corrupted
How does a website remember that you're.why: Short access tokens limit leak damage while the refresh token avoids forcing login every 10 minutes. Access tokens authorize all calls, not just reads.

How does a website remember that you're.q: A mobile app's access tokens last 24 hours and there is no refresh token. A phone is stolen. Why is this a poor design?
options: The app will log users out every 24 hours, which annoys them
Tokens lasting 24 hours are too large to fit in an HTTP header
The stolen token works for up to a day and is hard to revoke
The stolen phone can't use the token without the user's PIN
How does a website remember that you're.why: Signed tokens are valid until expiry, so long lifetimes stretch the damage window. Short access tokens plus a revocable server-side refresh token cut it to minutes.

How does a website remember that you're.q: With refresh token rotation, the server sees an old, already-used refresh token presented again. What should it do?
options: Accept it, since refresh tokens are meant to be long-lived anyway
Treat it as theft and revoke the whole chain, forcing a login
Issue a new access token but not a new refresh token
Ignore that request and simply wait for the next valid one to arrive
How does a website remember that you're.why: Each use issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old, so a reused old one means someone copied it. Revoking the chain kicks out both the thief and forces a fresh login.

How does a website remember that you're.q: Where should a mobile app store its refresh token?
options: In plain shared preferences so the app can read it quickly
Inside the access token's payload, so both travel together
In the query string of every API request, so servers can log it
In Android Keystore or iOS Keychain, with a revocable server record
How does a website remember that you're.why: Secure storage protects the long-lived token on the device and the server record allows revocation. URLs leak into logs, and plain storage is readable on compromised devices.

How does a website remember that you're.q: A user logs out of an app that uses signed JWT access tokens. The app deletes the refresh token record on the server. What about the current access token?
options: It is invalidated instantly because the refresh token was deleted
It works until it expires in minutes, unless APIs check a denylist
It is invalidated everywhere as soon as the app clears it locally
It keeps working until the refresh token's original 30-day expiry
How does a website remember that you're.why: Signed tokens are checked locally and stay valid until exp; deleting the refresh token only stops new ones. For emergencies, a denylist or 'tokens issued before T are invalid' check closes the gap.

How does a website remember that you're.q: What is the core trade-off between server-side sessions and signed tokens?
options: Sessions are always more secure; tokens are mainly for testing
Sessions work only on mobile apps; tokens work only on websites
Tokens are easy to revoke; sessions can never really be revoked
Sessions revoke easily but need lookups; signed tokens are the reverse
How does a website remember that you're.why: Neither is automatically safer; they trade revocability against lookup cost. Short access-token lifetimes give most of both, and many systems use both.

How does a website remember that you're.q: You are logged into your bank. In another tab a coupon page silently submits a POST to bank.com/transfer and your browser attaches the bank cookie. What is this attack?
options: CSRF: your browser is made to use your cookie for the attacker
