Yes; a TOTP code expires before the caller can use it
No; a phished TOTP code can still be used within seconds
How does OTP login work, and how is it d.why: Both SMS OTP and TOTP fall to phishing and social engineering because the code can be relayed. Only passkeys are truly phishing-resistant.

How does OTP login work, and how is it d.q: Why do passkeys resist phishing when SMS OTP and TOTP do not?
options: Passkeys are much longer codes that are harder to read aloud to a caller
A device-held key signs a challenge, and only for the real site's domain
Passkeys are delivered over an encrypted SMS channel that can't be read
Passkeys expire after 5 seconds instead of 30, too fast to relay
How does OTP login work, and how is it d.why: There is no code to type into a fake site or read to a caller, and the domain binding stops a fake site requesting a signature. Passkeys aren't codes at all.

How does OTP login work, and how is it d.q: Sethu logs in on a new phone with a correct OTP. What extra protection does the answer describe?
options: Device binding: extra checks for risky actions on a new device
Block the login entirely until she calls customer support
Send every OTP to both the old and the new phone from now on
Nothing extra, since the OTP proved her identity
How does OTP login work, and how is it d.why: Tying the account to a registered device makes a new device a risk signal; sensitive actions get extra checks for, say, 24 hours. SIM-change signals from operators can add to this.

How does OTP login work, and how is it d.q: A manager says rate limiting OTP requests is just to protect server load. What is the better view?
options: Correct; OTP servers are expensive to run at scale
It only matters for TOTP codes, not for SMS OTPs
It mainly stops guessing, OTP bombing and SMS pumping
It mainly prevents SIM swap attacks on users' numbers
How does OTP login work, and how is it d.why: Limits per number, IP, device and account curb abuse and costs, not just load. Rate limits don't stop SIM swaps.

How does OTP login work, and how is it d.q: Why do OTP SMSes in India look so uniform, like '123456 is your login OTP. Valid 5 minutes. Never share it.'?
options: Android only displays OTP messages that follow one fixed format
TRAI's DLT rules require pre-registered SMS templates
SMS gateways rewrite all messages into a standard template
The TOTP standard specifies the message wording
How does OTP login work, and how is it d.why: DLT registration fixes sender IDs and templates, and good templates say what the code is for and warn not to share it. TOTP has no message at all.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: What root cause do SQL injection and XSS share?
options: The app runs on an outdated version of HTTP
User text is allowed to be treated as code
The app stores passwords without any hashing
The app's pages aren't served over HTTPS
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Both happen when user input crosses from data into code, in the database or the browser. Password storage and HTTPS are separate issues.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: A login query is built as "... WHERE email = '" + email + "' AND password_hash = '" + hash + "'". Someone types ' OR '1'='1 as the email. What happens?
options: The database rejects the whole query because of the unmatched extra quote
The database looks for a user whose email is literally that string
The email is automatically escaped by the JDBC driver before it runs
The quote ends the string and OR '1'='1' becomes always-true SQL
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Concatenation lets the user control quotes and inject logic. Looking for the literal string is what happens with a prepared statement, not concatenation.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: What is the main fix for SQL injection?
options: Parameterised queries, so values travel separately from the SQL
Escaping single quotes in all user input before concatenating it
Validating that inputs never contain SQL keywords like SELECT or DROP
Running the database behind a firewall on a private network
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: The database parses the SQL shape first and then binds values, so data can never become SQL. Hand-escaping and keyword block-lists are fragile.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: With a prepared statement, the email field receives ' OR '1'='1. What does the database do?
options: Runs the OR condition and returns all the users in the table
Throws a syntax error because of the unmatched single quote
Looks for an email that is literally that string and finds none
Strips out the quotes first and then searches for OR 1=1
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: The query shape is locked before values arrive, so the input is just a value. No parsing of the value as SQL happens.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: A teammate says, 'We escape single quotes before building the SQL string, so we don't need prepared statements.' What is the best reply?
options: Fine, escaping single quotes covers every form of SQL injection
Also escape double quotes and backslashes, and you're fully safe
Hand-escaping is fragile; prepared statements fix the structure first
Escaping only works reliably on MySQL, so switch databases first
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Escaping rules vary and are easy to get wrong; parameters remove the problem by design. Adding more escaped characters is still the fragile approach.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: Your search page lets users sort by a column name passed in the URL. Why can't you just use a ? placeholder, and what should you do?
options: Placeholders bind only values; map the choice to an allow-list of columns
Placeholders do work for column names as long as you quote them first
Escape the column name carefully and then concatenate it into the SQL
Validate that the column name is under 20 characters and alphanumeric
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Table names, column names and ORDER BY direction can't be parameters. An allow-list in code (e.g. price_asc, price_desc, rating) keeps user text out of the SQL.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: A team says, 'We use Hibernate, so SQL injection is impossible.' When is that wrong?
options: When they use Hibernate's criteria API with bound parameters
When the database is PostgreSQL rather than MySQL
Never; using an ORM makes SQL injection impossible by design
When they build native SQL or JPQL by string concatenation
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: ORMs parameterise for you only through their parameterised APIs. Concatenated queries bring the bug straight back.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: The search service connects to the database as a user that can only SELECT from catalogue tables. What does this achieve?
options: It prevents SQL injection entirely, since writes are blocked
It limits the blast radius of a bug, but doesn't prevent injection
It encrypts all query results before they leave the database
It replaces the need for prepared statements in that service
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Least-privilege users mean an injected query can't drop tables or read payments data. Parameterised queries are still the actual fix.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: A malicious review containing a script tag is saved and later runs in every visitor's browser. What type of XSS is this?
options: Stored XSS
Reflected XSS
DOM-based XSS
SQL injection
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: The script is saved in the database and served to everyone who views it. Reflected XSS is echoed from the current request and usually needs a crafted link.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: A legacy 'No results for X' page echoes the search term from the URL without encoding. An attacker emails victims a crafted link. What type of XSS is this?
options: Stored XSS
DOM-based XSS
Reflected XSS
CSRF
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Input from the current request is echoed back in the response, so the victim must click the link. Nothing is saved, so it's not stored XSS.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: Front-end code does element.innerHTML = location.hash. What kind of bug is this?
options: Stored XSS, because the hash is saved in history
DOM-based XSS, happening purely in front-end JavaScript
SQL injection, because the hash reaches the server
No bug; the hash is never sent to the server so it's safe
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Writing untrusted data into innerHTML in the browser runs it as HTML. The fact that the hash isn't sent to the server doesn't make it safe.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: What is the primary fix for XSS?
options: A strict Content-Security-Policy header on every page
Marking all session cookies HttpOnly and Secure
Stripping angle brackets from all user input on arrival
Context-aware output encoding, e.g. auto-escaping templates
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Encoding turns < into < so the browser shows text instead of running it. CSP and HttpOnly are safety nets, and stripping input breaks legitimate text.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: Why does the answer stress 'context' in output encoding?
options: Different browsers need different encodings for the same characters
Rules differ for HTML text, attributes, JavaScript strings and URLs
Encoding is only ever needed inside HTML attributes, not body text
Context refers to the user's language and character-set settings
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Data placed in an attribute or a script needs different escaping than body text, so use a tested library like the OWASP Java Encoder. It isn't about browser vendors.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: In a code review you see a React component using dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user review text. How should you treat it?
options: Fine, because React always escapes everything it renders anyway
Fine, as long as the site also sends a Content-Security-Policy
Fine, provided the review text was validated when it was submitted
As a red flag: it bypasses escaping; render normally or sanitise
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Raw-HTML escape hatches (dangerouslySetInnerHTML, th:utext, |safe) switch off the main XSS defence. CSP and input validation are only extra layers.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: A product manager wants bold text and bullet points in customer reviews. What is the safe approach?
options: Use an HTML sanitiser allowing only tags like b, i, ul, li
Turn off auto-escaping just for the review section of the page
Allow any HTML in reviews but add a strict CSP header to the page
Ask reviewers to tick a box promising not to use script tags
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: A strict allow-list sanitiser keeps formatting while stripping scripts and other tags. Switching off escaping reintroduces stored XSS.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: Your site sends Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' 'nonce-r4nd0m'. An attacker injects an inline script tag. What happens?
options: The browser runs it because it is inline on the same origin
The browser runs it, but blocks any network requests it makes
The browser blocks it: it lacks this response's nonce
The server strips it out before sending the page to the browser
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Only our own scripts or inline scripts with the per-response random nonce may run. CSP is enforced by the browser, not the server.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: A team proposes enforcing a strict CSP on day one across the whole site. What does the answer recommend instead?
options: Enforce it immediately; legitimate scripts will adapt over time
Add 'unsafe-inline' to the policy so that nothing breaks at launch
Start in Report-Only mode and watch violations before enforcing
Skip CSP altogether, because output encoding is already enough
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Report-only reveals legitimate scripts it would break without breaking them. 'unsafe-inline' weakens CSP badly.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: Someone says, 'We have CSP, so we don't need to encode output.' Why is that wrong?
options: CSP is a backup layer that can be misconfigured or bypassed
CSP is only enforced by Chrome, so other browsers stay exposed
CSP blocks only external scripts, never inline ones
CSP slows page loads down too much to rely on it in production
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Defence-in-depth means the safety net is not the fix. CSP can block inline scripts when configured with nonces.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: Your session cookie is HttpOnly and you have a strict CSP. Are you fully protected from XSS?
options: Yes; together the two of them make XSS attacks impossible
Yes, as long as the session cookie is also marked Secure
No, because HttpOnly actually lets scripts read the cookie value
No; injected script can still act in the page, so encode output
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: HttpOnly stops the cookie being read and stolen; CSP blocks many scripts. Neither removes the root bug.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: A customer named D'Souza can't save her profile because the app rejects apostrophes 'to prevent SQL injection'. What principle was violated?
options: Apostrophes should be stripped silently instead of rejected
Validation is defence-in-depth; real data has quotes, so parameterise
Names should be stored in a separate, unvalidated table of their own
Validation should block apostrophes only in the email field
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Real data contains quotes and angle brackets; block-lists break legitimate users and still miss attacks. Validate on the way in, parameterise and encode on the way out.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: For input validation, which approach does the answer prefer?
options: Allow-lists that say what is allowed, e.g. a 6-digit PIN code
Block-lists of known dangerous words like DROP and SCRIPT
No validation at all, since encoding handles everything
Validation only in front-end JavaScript, to keep servers fast
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Allow-lists are precise; block-lists try to guess what's bad and are easy to bypass. Front-end-only validation is skipped by anyone calling the API directly.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: Where do SQL injection and XSS sit in the OWASP Top 10 (2021)?
options: SQL injection under Injection; XSS under Broken Access Control
Both under Cryptographic Failures
Both under A03: Injection
Neither; they were removed from the 2021 list
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: The 2021 edition groups both under A03: Injection. They remain among the most common web bugs.

What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.q: Which tooling pair helps catch these bugs in CI?
options: A web application firewall in front of a CDN
SAST to scan the code and DAST to probe a running test app
Unit tests on each class and load tests before release
A team password manager and MFA for every engineer
What are SQL injection and cross-site sc.why: Static analysis finds risky code patterns and dynamic scanners probe running endpoints. Safe defaults and code review still matter more than tools.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: You are designing a URL shortener and need codes that are short and guaranteed unique without checking the database for clashes. What is the standard approach?
options: Give each new link a unique numeric ID and write that number in base62
Use the product name from the long URL, trimmed to 7 characters, as the code
Generate 7 random characters and hope the space is big enough to avoid clashes
Hash the long URL with MD5 and keep the first 7 characters as the code
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: A unique ID written in base62 is unique by construction, so no collision check is needed. Truncated hashes look unique but collide surprisingly early and need a check-and-insert.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: A teammate asks why 7-character codes are typical for shorteners. Roughly how many distinct codes do 7 base62 characters give?
options: About 56.8 billion (62^6)
About 10 million (10^7)
About 3.5 trillion (62^7)
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: Each base62 place has 62 choices, so 7 places give 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208, about 3.5 trillion. 10 million is what you would get with digits only; 56.8 billion is 6 characters.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: Using the alphabet 0-9 = 0-9, a-z = 10-35, A-Z = 36-61, what does the ID 11,157 encode to in base62?
options: 2tx
2TY
2TX
XT2
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: 11,157 / 62 = 179 r 59 (X), 179 / 62 = 2 r 55 (T), then 2; reading remainders backwards gives 2TX. XT2 forgets to reverse the remainders, and lower-case letters stand for values 10-35, not 55 and 59.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: Your shortener runs on 40 app servers creating links in parallel, and a single auto-increment database is becoming a bottleneck. What is the usual fix that keeps codes short?
options: A coordinator hands each server a block of IDs (say 1,000 at a time) that it uses from memory
Each server hashes the URL plus its server name and retries on collision
Shard the auto-increment counter so every server gets its own counter starting at 1
Each server generates Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs from timestamp, machine ID and sequence
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: Range blocks give unique IDs with a network call only once per block, and the IDs stay small so codes stay short. Snowflake also avoids coordination, but its 64-bit IDs become about 11 base62 characters, which hurts shortness.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: An app server holding ID block 5,000,000-5,000,999 crashes after using 300 IDs. What happens to the remaining 700 IDs?
options: All 1,000 IDs must be invalidated because some may have been used twice
The coordinator must reclaim them and reissue them to another server to avoid gaps
They are simply never used, which is fine because codes only need to be unique, not continuous
The next server must restart from 5,000,300 so the sequence has no holes
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: The coordinator has moved on, so the leftover IDs are lost, and with trillions of codes available that costs nothing. Reissuing them would risk duplicates if the crashed server had actually used some.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: Your team decides to hash long URLs and keep the first 7 base62 characters. Around how many links before collisions become likely, and why?
options: Never in practice, because MD5 and SHA-256 do not produce collisions
About 3.5 trillion links, because collisions only happen once every code is used
About 1.9 million links, because by the birthday paradox collisions appear near the square root of the code space
About 1.75 trillion links, because collisions start once half the code space is used
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: Collisions become likely around sqrt(3.5 trillion), roughly 1.9 million, so every insert must be check-and-insert with a salted retry. The hash function being strong does not help once you truncate it to about 42 bits.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: A marketing team needs click counts by city and hour for every short link, and wants to be able to disable a link that turns malicious. Which redirect should the shortener return?
options: 301 with no cache headers, because browsers never cache permanent redirects
301, because permanent redirects are faster and still log every click
200 with the long URL in the body, so the app can decide whether to open it
302 (or 307), so the browser comes back to the shortener on every click
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: A 302 is temporary, so every click returns to your server, where it can be counted and blocked. A 301 can be remembered by browsers, which then skip your server, losing clicks and your ability to disable the link for them.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: A sale banner link on WhatsApp gets 50,000 clicks per second while most codes are rarely clicked. What keeps the database from being overwhelmed?
options: Add a database index on the long URL column so lookups get faster
Cache hot codes in Redis or each server's memory (and at the CDN edge) with LRU eviction
Use Snowflake IDs so popular links are spread evenly across shards
Switch the store from key-value to a relational database with joins
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: Clicks follow a power law, so caching the few hot codes means most clicks never reach the database; at a 95% hit rate it sees 1 click in 20. An index on the long URL does not help a lookup by code.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: Bots are hammering your shortener with thousands of made-up codes that do not exist, and each miss hits the database. What is the simplest mitigation from the design?
options: Briefly cache the "not found" answers too, so repeated fake codes are served from cache
Pre-create every possible 7-character code so nothing is ever missing
Move the link table to an in-memory database so misses are free
Return 301 for missing codes so browsers stop asking
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: Negative caching of "not found" stops repeated bogus lookups from reaching the database. Pre-creating 3.5 trillion rows is absurd, and a 301 on a miss makes no sense for a code that does not exist.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: Two marketing teams request the custom alias sho.rt/bigsale within the same second. How do you make sure exactly one of them gets it?
options: Append a random suffix to both aliases so neither team is refused
Store aliases in the same table and use an insert-only-if-the-key-is-absent write
Read the table first, and if the alias is free, write it in a second step
Let both writes succeed and keep whichever row has the later timestamp
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: An atomic insert-if-absent lets exactly one request win and the other gets "already taken". A read-then-write has a race window where both reads see the alias as free.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: A month after a festive sale, seller links expire. A product manager suggests recycling those codes for new links to save space. What is the best response?
options: Reuse them immediately, since an expired code is just a free slot in the table
Reuse them only for the same seller, so the links stay relevant
Reuse them after 24 hours, once browser caches have cleared
Do not reuse expired codes quickly; return 410 Gone or an "offer ended" page instead
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: Old SMS messages and printed QR codes still point at those codes, so quick reuse could send people somewhere unexpected; with trillions of codes there is no shortage. Waiting 24 hours does nothing about printed or saved links.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: Your shortener is used for private invoice links, and someone notices that if 2TX exists then 2TY probably does too. What is the best fix that keeps uniqueness?
options: Make all codes 11 characters long so they are harder to type
Scramble the ID with a reversible one-to-one shuffle (for example a small Feistel cipher) before base62 encoding
Switch to hashing the URL so codes look random
Encode IDs in base36 instead of base62 so patterns are less obvious
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: A bijection makes consecutive IDs produce unrelated-looking codes while still never colliding. Switching to hashing hides the pattern but brings back collisions and the check-and-retry.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: Someone creates thousands of short links to a fake "Your UPI KYC expires" page. Which set of defences does the design call for?
options: Only rate limit link creation per IP, since attackers cannot get around it
Check URLs against threat lists on creation, rate limit creation, re-scan asynchronously and be able to disable codes instantly
Only use 301 redirects so browsers handle phishing warnings themselves
Only check URLs on creation, since a page that was safe then stays safe
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: Abuse defences are layered: pages can turn bad after shortening, so asynchronous re-scans and an instant disable (helped by 302) matter as much as creation-time checks. Any single defence alone is easy to get around.

How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.q: In an interview you are asked what the genuinely hard parts of a URL shortener are. Which answer matches the design?
options: Read throughput (caching), unique ID generation and abuse, not storage
Joins between the links and users tables, which grow slow over time
Storage, because billions of links need petabytes of disk
Encoding speed, because base62 conversion is CPU-heavy at scale
How does a URL shortener turn a long lin.why: At about 500 bytes a row, a billion links is roughly 500 GB, easy to spread across machines. The challenges are serving reads fast, generating unique IDs without a bottleneck, and stopping abuse.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: A scraping bot sends 3,000 product-page requests a minute while normal shoppers send around 30. How can a rate limiter stop the bot without real users ever noticing?
options: Set the limit at 30 a minute so it matches what a normal shopper does
Slow every request down by a fixed delay so bots get less done
Set the per-user limit well above human usage, say 300 a minute, so only the bot crosses it
Block any user whose request rate is above the site-wide average
How does an app stop one user or bot fro.why: Limits sit well above normal human behaviour, so a person at 30 a minute never touches a 300 limit, while the bot is stopped at request 301. A limit equal to typical usage would block normal people having a busy minute.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: A request is over its caller's limit. What should the rate limiter send back?
options: HTTP 503 Service Unavailable with a Retry-After header
HTTP 200 with an empty body, so the client does not retry
HTTP 403 Forbidden, since the caller is not allowed
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header
How does an app stop one user or bot fro.why: 429 means this caller has sent too many requests, and Retry-After tells it how long to wait. 503 is for the whole service being overloaded, not one caller exceeding a quota.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: Your API uses a fixed-window limit of 100 requests per minute. How can a bot get nearly 200 requests through in about 2 seconds?
options: Send 100 at the end of one minute and 100 at the start of the next; each window sees only 100
Send requests faster than Redis can increment, so some are not counted
Send all 200 within one second, because windows only count completed requests
Rotate between two user agents so the counter resets halfway
How does an app stop one user or bot fro.why: This is the edge burst problem: two adjacent fixed windows each allow the limit, so almost double gets through around the boundary. A sliding window or token bucket closes the gap.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: Using a sliding window counter, the limit is 100 per minute. The previous minute had 80 requests, the current minute has 30 so far, and you are 15 seconds into it. What is the estimated count?
options: 50, so the request is allowed
30, so the request is allowed
90, so the request is allowed
110, so the request is rejected
How does an app stop one user or bot fro.why: Estimate = 30 + 80 x (1 - 0.25) = 30 + 60 = 90, under 100. Simply adding both minutes (110) ignores that most of the previous minute has already slid out of the window.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: A token bucket has capacity 20 and refills 2 tokens per second. A user has been idle for a minute. What can they do now?
options: Make 20 requests instantly, then about 2 per second after that
Make only 2 requests per second from the start, with no burst
Make 120 requests instantly, since a minute of tokens has piled up
Make 20 requests, then nothing until the bucket fully refills
How does an app stop one user or bot fro.why: The bucket cannot hold more than its capacity, so the idle user has exactly 20 tokens for a burst, then is held to the refill rate. Tokens do not accumulate past capacity, so 120 is wrong.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: You must send messages to an SMS gateway that accepts exactly 5 messages per second and fails on spikes. Which algorithm fits best?
options: Sliding window log, which rejects anything above 5 in the last second
Fixed window counter, which counts requests per calendar second
Leaky bucket, which queues requests and lets them out at a fixed, smooth rate
Token bucket, which allows a burst up to its capacity before limiting
How does an app stop one user or bot fro.why: A leaky bucket smooths output to a steady rate, which is what a spike-intolerant downstream needs, at the cost of some queueing delay. A token bucket deliberately allows bursts, which would hit the gateway in spikes.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: Your public API wants to let a user fire a quick burst of requests when they open the app, but cap their average rate. Which algorithm is the common default?
options: Sliding window log, because it tracks every request timestamp exactly
Leaky bucket, because it guarantees perfectly smooth traffic
Fixed window counter, because it is the cheapest to store
Token bucket, described by a capacity (burst size) and a refill rate (average)
How does an app stop one user or bot fro.why: A token bucket allows natural bursts up to its capacity while holding the long-run average to the refill rate. A leaky bucket smooths output and adds queueing delay instead of allowing the burst.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: Your gateway runs on 40 servers, each keeping its own in-memory counter with a limit of 10 requests per second. What goes wrong?
options: Counters drift apart, so users are randomly blocked even at low rates
Requests spread across servers, so one user could get up to 400 per second
Nothing, because the load balancer always sends a user to the same server
Each server rejects too early, so users get about 0.25 per second
How does an app stop one user or bot fro.why: With N servers counting separately, a caller can get up to N times the limit. Keep the counter in a shared store such as Redis, or knowingly give each server a share of the limit.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: Your Redis limiter runs INCR on the key and then, if the count is 1, EXPIRE key 60. What is the hidden bug?
options: Redis cannot store keys for 60 seconds, so the window is too short
EXPIRE resets the counter to zero, so the limit never triggers
INCR is not atomic, so two servers can both read the same count
If the process crashes between INCR and EXPIRE, the key never expires and the user stays blocked
How does an app stop one user or bot fro.why: The two commands are separate, so a crash in between leaves a key with no lifetime that keeps counting forever. Fix it with a Lua script that runs as one atomic unit, or SET key 0 EX 60 NX. INCR itself is atomic.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: Your OTP endpoint is limited only by IP address. Why is that risky?
options: IP addresses change every request, so the counter never builds up
Many genuine users share one IP (mobile carriers, offices), while attackers spread across many IPs
IP-based limits cannot be stored in Redis, only in the database
Per-IP limits only work for HTTP/2 and most apps use HTTP/1.1
How does an app stop one user or bot fro.why: Per-IP is easy but unfair to people behind a shared IP and weak against botnets. Layer it with per-phone-number limits, a global limit and alerts or CAPTCHA for suspicious patterns.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: Where is the main place a rate limiter usually runs, so it can apply per-user, per-API-key and per-route limits in one spot?
options: At the CDN only, because it sees requests before anything else
At the API gateway, after authentication, where every request passes through
Inside the database, as a trigger on every table
In the mobile app, which counts its own requests before sending
How does an app stop one user or bot fro.why: The gateway knows who the caller is after authentication, so it can key limits by user or API key per route. The CDN/WAF adds blunt per-IP limits, but it does not know the logged-in user.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: During a midnight sale, Redis briefly fails over. How should your rate limiter behave for product browsing versus the OTP endpoint?
options: Fail closed for browsing and fail open for OTP, since OTP is user-critical
Fail open for both, so a limiter outage never blocks anyone
Fail closed for both, since an unlimited endpoint is always dangerous
Fail open for browsing (allow and log loudly) and fail closed for OTP
How does an app stop one user or bot fro.why: Failing open for general APIs stops a limiter outage from becoming a site outage, while an unlimited OTP endpoint is costly (SMS) and dangerous (bombing, brute force). Decide this per endpoint in advance.

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: You want to introduce a new, tighter limit for a partner API without breaking them. What does the design suggest?

Enforce the hard limit immediately and let the partner fix their client
Raise the limit on the partner's side only, keeping it unpublished
Return 503 instead of 429 during the trial so partners retry

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: A colleague says, "We have autoscaling, so we don't need rate limiting." What is the best reply?
options: Rate limiting is just a cheaper form of autoscaling, so pick whichever costs less
Load shedding is the same as rate limiting, so autoscaling plus shedding is enough
Rate limiting caps each caller, autoscaling adds capacity and load shedding drops traffic when the whole system is overloaded; you need all three
Correct, autoscaling makes rate limiting unnecessary because capacity grows with demand

How does an app stop one user or bot fro.q: Clients receive 429 with Retry-After during a traffic spike. How should a well-behaved app retry?
options: Give up permanently and show an error page to the user
Wait at least Retry-After, then back off with growing gaps plus a little random jitter
Retry immediately in a tight loop until the request succeeds
Retry every exactly 1 second so all clients stay in step

The phone sends its bookmark ("after #41") and the server returns #42 to #48 in order

Global numbers cannot be stored in a relational database

Your app has real-time chat. A user lose.q: The server must assign the next sequence number to two messages saved at almost the same moment in one chat. How should it do this?

Atomically, for example by incrementing a per-conversation counter row in the same transaction that saves the message

The server locks the conversation so live pushes and sync can never overlap
The phone shows both but merges them in the UI after a few seconds

Your app has real-time chat. A user lose.q: Sethu taps send, the network drops before the server replies, and his app retries. How do you stop the server from saving two copies?

Her phone creates the message ID (for example a UUID) before the first try; the server has a unique constraint on it
The server assigns the ID, so a retry gets a new ID and the old one is discarded
The app waits 30 seconds before retrying so the first attempt can finish

Nothing breaks: the delivered tick is delayed, and the next sync still starts from the phone's own bookmark
