When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: You type "iph" and suggestions appear before you finish the word. What actually happens on the server?
options: It runs a full-text search over the product catalogue for "iph"
It asks a language model to predict the next words in real time
It walks a prefix tree to the "iph" node and returns a top-k list prepared in advance
It runs a database query like LIKE 'iph%' and sorts results by popularity
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: Suggestions are precomputed from search logs; the request just looks them up. Live catalogue search or a LIKE query scans and sorts at request time, which is too slow at tens of thousands of requests a second.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: A plain trie of 50 million queries can find the "i" node in one step, yet answering "i" is still slow. Why, and what fixes it?
options: Single letters are not indexed; requiring at least 3 letters fixes it
The trie has no cache; putting a CDN in front of it fixes it on its own
The trie is too deep; compressing it into a hash map fixes it
Listing and sorting everything under "i" is slow; storing the top-k completions at every node fixes it
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: Finding the node is fast, but without precomputed lists you would have to visit millions of queries and rank them. With top-k stored per node, the work is one step per letter plus reading a ready list.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: How long does it take to find the "iph" node in a trie?
options: Three steps, one per letter typed, whether it holds 5 queries or 50 million
A binary search over all queries, so about log2 of the total
Time proportional to the number of queries starting with "i"
Time proportional to the total number of queries in the trie
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: Walking a trie costs one step per character of the prefix, independent of how many queries are stored. That is why it suits autocomplete.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: When building the trie offline, how are the top-k lists for every node filled efficiently?
options: Fill only the leaf nodes and compute the upper nodes at request time
One bottom-up pass: each node takes the best k from its own query and its children's top-k lists
Copy the root's top-k list to every node, since popular queries are the same everywhere
For each node, scan the whole log again and sort every matching query
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: A bottom-up merge does a small amount of work per node once, offline. Re-scanning logs per node is far too expensive, and computing at request time brings back the slow-sort problem.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: Your ranking uses score = sum of searches x 0.5^(age in days / 7). What does that do?
options: It gives searches from the last 7 days half the weight of older ones
It time-decays counts so a search loses half its weight every 7 days, favouring recent popularity
It removes any query older than 7 days from the trie
It halves the score of any query that has fewer than 7 searches a day
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: This is exponential time decay with a 7-day half-life, so last week matters more than last year. It does not delete old queries; it just weights them less.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: Apple announces a new iPhone at 10 am and searches explode, but your trie is rebuilt nightly. How do suggestions catch up the same day?
options: Update the trie live on every keystroke so it is always fresh
Trigger a full trie rebuild on every new search for the launch
Wait for the nightly build, since hours-old suggestions are always fine
A streaming trending layer counts recent searches and merges hot queries into results at request time, with short CDN TTLs
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: A small trending layer fed by a stream like Kafka handles the few fast-changing queries, while the main trie stays batch-built. Updating the trie on every search would fight with reads and force constant top-k recomputation.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: Why is the main trie rebuilt in batches rather than updated on every search?
options: Batch builds are needed so personalised tries can be built for each user
Search logs are only available once a day from the analytics team
Constant writes would fight with reads and force top-k lists up the tree to be recomputed; a few hours of staleness is fine
Tries cannot be updated after they are built, by definition
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: Autocomplete is read-heavy and tolerant of slight staleness, so building versioned snapshots offline is the classic trade-off. A trie can be mutated in principle; it is just a bad fit at this scale.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: Suggestion servers need to switch from snapshot v511 to v512 without any errors. How should they do it?
options: Load v512 fully into memory while serving v511, then swap a pointer atomically
Load v512 node by node into the live trie so it updates gradually
Stop serving, delete v511, load v512, then resume serving
Send half the users to v511 and half to v512 permanently
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: Keeping the old snapshot live until the new one is fully loaded gives a clean atomic switch with no downtime. Updating the live trie bit by bit could serve a half-built mix.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: A fast typist enters "iphone" in under a second. What should the app do on the client side?
options: Wait until the user presses enter, then show suggestions
Debounce (wait about 50-150 ms after the last key) so it sends 1-2 requests instead of 6
Send a request for every key so the suggestions are always current
Send all 6 requests at once and show the one that arrives first
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: Debouncing cuts load and flicker by sending only when the user pauses. Showing whichever arrives first can display stale suggestions for a shorter prefix.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: The response for "ip" arrives after the response for "iph". What should the app do?
options: Ignore the "ip" response and show only the one for the latest text
Show the "ip" response since it arrived last and is therefore newest
Discard both and send a fresh request for "iph"
Merge both lists so the user sees more options
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: Stale responses for older prefixes must be dropped, otherwise suggestions jump backwards. Arriving last does not make a response the most relevant.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: Short prefixes like "i" and "s" are requested millions of times a day. How do you keep these from reaching your servers?
options: Add more shards for the letter "i" so it can take the load
Cache the non-personalised response per prefix at the CDN with a short TTL
Cache each user's personalised list at the CDN for 24 hours
Refuse to suggest anything until at least 3 letters are typed
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: The shared response for a prefix is the same for everyone, so a CDN can serve it near the user for a few minutes. Caching personalised lists at the CDN would not be shared and could leak one user's list to others.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: A logged-in user who browses running shoes should see "nike running shoes" higher for "nike". How is this usually done?
options: Skip the trie for logged-in users and search their order history
Add the user's searches into the shared trie so everyone sees them
Fetch a bigger shared candidate list (say top 30) and re-rank it for the user with their recent history
Build and store a separate trie for each user
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: Personalisation is a small final re-rank, so the shared trie and cache stay the same for everyone. A trie per user would be enormous.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: Your suggestion trie is too big for one server and traffic is uneven: "s" is huge, "x" is tiny. How should you shard?
options: Split randomly by query hash, so a prefix's results are spread over all shards
Keep one shard and just add more CPU to it
Split evenly by alphabet, a-f, g-m and so on, so each shard has the same letters
Split prefixes by measured traffic (for example sa-sh, si-sz) and give hot shards more replicas
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: Splitting by real load keeps every server evenly busy. An even alphabet split overloads the shard holding "s"; hashing spreads one prefix across shards, so every lookup would need to ask all of them.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: Users type "ipone" and should still see iPhone suggestions. What is the cheapest first option?
options: A spelling-correction map built from logs, where people who typed "ipone" then searched "iphone"
Asking the user to confirm their spelling before showing suggestions
Adding every possible misspelling of every query to the trie
Running edit-distance search over every node of the trie
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: A correction map learned from real behaviour is cheap and effective; limited edit distance (1 letter) over a few nearby branches is the next step. Exploring the whole trie or storing every misspelling is too costly.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: A new offensive phrase is added to the blocklist at 2 pm, but the trie was built at 4 am. How does the design make sure it is not shown?
options: It is shown until the next nightly build, which is acceptable
It is not shown because the CDN filters offensive words automatically
The blocklist is applied at serve time as well as at build time
The trie is rebuilt immediately whenever the blocklist changes
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: Filtering at build time keeps blocked terms out of the trie, and filtering again at serve time makes new blocks work immediately. Waiting for the next build would leave the brand showing unsafe text for hours.

When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.q: Bots repeatedly search a spam phrase to force it into suggestions. What defence does the design suggest?
options: Only use purchase data and ignore search logs entirely
Rebuild the trie every minute so spam does not stay long
Ignore all searches from logged-out users when building the trie
Count unique users rather than raw searches, and cap how much any one user can influence counts
When you type \"iph\" in a shopping app'.why: Counting distinct users and capping per-user influence stops a few bots inflating a phrase. Rebuilding faster would actually let manipulation show up sooner.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: You open an Instagram-like app and the feed appears in a few milliseconds. What is the main reason it is that fast?
options: The app queries every account you follow at open time and merges their posts
The phone keeps the full posts downloaded in the background all day
Most work was done in advance: a cached list of post IDs is read, then the top posts are hydrated and ranked
The server runs the ranking model over every post on the platform at open time
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: Each user has a precomputed feed list of post IDs in a cache like Redis, so opening the app is mostly a cheap read. Collecting from every followed account at open time is fan-out on read, which is the slow, expensive path.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: Riya, who has 300 followers, posts a photo. With fan-out on write, what happens?
options: Her post ID is pushed into all 300 followers' feed lists right after posting, via a queue so she does not wait
Nothing is copied; each follower's app collects her post when they next open it
The full photo and caption are copied into each of the 300 feed lists
Her post is stored only in her own profile list until it gets enough likes
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: Fan-out on write copies the post ID into every follower's list at post time, done by queue workers so her request returns quickly. Feed lists hold IDs, not full posts.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: A user with 500 followers posts once. How many feed inserts happen at post time with fan-out on write, and with fan-out on read?
options: About 500 with fan-out on write; zero with fan-out on read
Zero with fan-out on write; about 500 with fan-out on read
One with fan-out on write; about 500 with fan-out on read
About 500 with both, since every follower must eventually get it
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: Push does one insert per follower at post time (fewer if inactive followers are skipped). Pull does nothing at post time; the work happens when each follower opens the app.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: People open their feed 50-100 times more often than they post. Why does this make fan-out on write the usual default for normal accounts?
options: It moves the expensive work to the rarer side (writes), making the frequent side (reads) a single cheap lookup
It means new follows show up in the feed instantly
It makes posting faster, which is what users care about most
It uses less total memory than fan-out on read
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: With reads dominating, doing the merge at read time repeats expensive work constantly; push does it once per post. Instant visibility of new follows and no wasted work on inactive users are actually advantages of pull.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: With fan-out on read, a user who follows 400 accounts opens the app. What is the main drawback?
options: The feed list in Redis grows without limit for heavy users
About 400 lookups plus a merge on every open, and the feed is only as fast as the slowest lookup
New posts from followed accounts take hours to appear
Each post must be written 400 times when it is created
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: Pull does the costly gathering on the busy read path, and tail latency of 400 lookups hurts. Writing each post many times is the cost of push, not pull.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: A film star with 10 crore followers posts one photo. Why is pure fan-out on write a bad idea here?
options: The star's followers would see the post before the star's own profile shows it
Fan-out on write cannot handle images, only text posts
It becomes 10 crore inserts for one post, delays other fan-out jobs, and is mostly wasted on followers who will not open the app soon
Redis cannot store a post ID in more than 1 crore lists at once
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: Even at 10 lakh inserts per second, one post takes about 100 seconds and clogs the shared queue. This write amplification is the celebrity or hot key problem.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: How does the hybrid approach handle a cricketer with 8 crore followers versus a normal user?
options: Every account uses pull, but celebrity post lists are cached on the phone
Celebrities are pushed to followers first, and normal accounts are pulled at read time
Celebrity posts are pushed only to followers who liked their last post
Normal accounts are pushed to followers; accounts above a follower threshold are not, and their recent posts are pulled and merged at read time
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: Above a tuned threshold (for example 1 lakh followers), posts stay in the celebrity's own heavily cached recent-posts list. On open, your precomputed list is merged with posts from the few celebrities you follow.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: Arjun opens the app. He follows 12 celebrity accounts. What does the feed service do to build his first page?
options: Push the 12 celebrities' posts into his list first, then read it
Read only his feed list, since celebrity posts are already in it
Fetch posts from all accounts he follows, ignoring his feed list
Read his feed list, fetch the 12 celebrities' latest posts, merge, rank, take the top 20 and hydrate them
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: In the hybrid, celebrity posts never reach his list, so they are fetched (cheap cache hits) and merged at read time. Hydration then turns IDs into full posts and filters anything deleted.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: A follower of Riya has not opened the app in 2 months and was skipped during fan-out. What happens when he returns?
options: He sees his old 2-month-old feed list until he refreshes
He sees an empty feed until new posts are fanned out to him
The system finds no cached feed and does a one-time pull from the accounts he follows, then stores it as his feed list
His account is switched permanently to fan-out on read
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: Skipping inactive users during push saves wasted work; a returning user's feed is rebuilt once by pulling. After that he is back on the normal push path.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: Arjun scrolls to page 2 while 5 new posts arrive. The app uses "skip 20, take 20". What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
options: Everything shifts down by 5, so he sees repeated posts; use a cursor ("posts older than the last one I saw")
The request fails with an error; retry with the same offset later
Nothing goes wrong, because Redis sorted sets keep offsets stable
New posts are skipped forever; use a bigger page size like 50
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: On a live feed, offsets move as new items arrive, causing duplicates and gaps. A cursor based on the last score (timestamp, ties broken by post ID) continues exactly where he stopped.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: Why do feed systems often store each feed as a Redis sorted set scored by post time, rather than a plain list?
options: Sorted sets compress images better than lists
Lists in Redis cannot hold more than 20 items
Scores make cursor paging easy and keep the order correct even when inserts arrive out of order
Sorted sets automatically delete posts from people you unfollow
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: With timestamps as scores, "posts older than X" is a direct range query, and a late-arriving insert still lands in the right place. Unfollows are filtered at read time, not by the data structure.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: A post was fanned out to 2 lakh feeds and is then deleted by its author. How do you make sure nobody sees it?
options: Wait for each feed list to trim it naturally once 500 newer posts arrive
Synchronously remove the ID from all 2 lakh feed lists before confirming the delete
Leave it in feeds but blur the image so it is not readable
Mark it deleted in the post store and skip it at hydration; remove the IDs from feed lists lazily in the background
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: The feed list is a hint and the post store is the truth, so checking at hydration makes deletes, edits, unfollows and privacy changes correct immediately. Removing it from the lists is cleanup, not what correctness depends on.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: Riya edits her caption to add "What a six!" after it was fanned out. What needs to change in her followers' feed lists?
options: Every follower's list must be rewritten with the new caption
Nothing; lists hold only IDs, and the next hydration reads the new caption
The old post ID must be deleted and a new one fanned out
Only followers who already saw the post need an update
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: Because feed lists store IDs and posts are hydrated at read time, an edit is a single update in the post store. This is one reason not to store full posts in feed lists.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: Your fan-out workers fall behind during a big match and feeds are a few seconds late. How serious is this, and what do you do?
options: Critical data loss: posts in the queue are gone and must be re-posted
Acceptable eventual consistency: posts are saved, feeds are just late; monitor queue lag, add workers and prioritise active followers
Block new posts until the queue is empty so feeds stay consistent
Switch every account to fan-out on read permanently to remove the queue
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: The post itself is saved, so a lagging queue only delays feeds, which is usually fine. Blocking posting or abandoning push would be a far worse user experience.

When you open Instagram, how is your fee.q: Fan-out decides which posts you could see. What decides the order they appear in on a modern feed?
options: The number of followers each author has, highest first
The order in which fan-out workers happened to insert them
Pure reverse-time order, since ranking cannot run at feed scale
A ranking step: gather a few hundred candidates, score them with a model, then de-duplicate and add variety
When you open Instagram, how is your fee.why: Fan-out produces candidates; a model scores them on signals like closeness to the author, freshness and post type, then rules avoid five posts in a row from one author. Ranking is heavier, so it runs on a smaller candidate set.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: Your shopping app is fully closed, yet "Your order is out for delivery" appears on the lock screen. What actually received that message?
options: The app, which keeps a quiet socket open to the company's server
The app's background job, which polls the order API every minute
The mobile operator, which converts it into an SMS
The phone's OS, through its one shared always-on connection to APNs or FCM
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: A closed app is not running, so it cannot listen; the OS holds a single connection to the platform push service and shows the banner itself. Polling or a per-app socket would drain the battery and is blocked by the OS.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: Why don't iOS and Android let every app keep its own connection open to its own server?
options: Apple and Google charge per connection, so apps share one to save money
Each connection needs heartbeats that wake the radio, so many apps doing it would keep the radio awake and drain the battery
Apps cannot open network connections without being on screen
Mobile networks only allow one TCP connection per phone at a time
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: Keep-alives every few minutes wake the radio, which then stays in high power for seconds; 30 apps on their own schedules mean it almost never sleeps. So the OS suspends background apps (Doze, app standby) and shares one tuned connection.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: A user installs your app and opens it. What must happen before your server can send them a push?
options: The backend asks Apple or Google for the user's email-linked device list
The app gets a device token from the OS (after permission) and sends it to your backend, which stores it against the user
Nothing; APNs and FCM deliver to any app installed on the phone automatically
The app sends the user's phone number, which APNs and FCM use to route the push
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: The device token addresses one app install on one device and is the only way to target it. On iOS, and Android 13 and later, the user must also grant notification permission.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: Sethu has your app on his phone and his tablet. How many device tokens should your backend hold for him?
options: None, because tablets cannot receive push notifications
Two, because a token identifies one app install on one device, not the person
One, because tokens are tied to the user's account
One, because the latest device's token replaces earlier ones
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: Tokens are per app plus device, so one user can have several, and a reinstall usually gives a new one. Treating a token as the user would leave other devices without notifications.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: The order service marks an order OUT_FOR_DELIVERY. Why does it publish an event to a queue instead of calling APNs directly?
options: Queues guarantee the notification reaches the phone exactly once
The order service cannot look up device tokens for security reasons
A separate notification service handles preferences, quiet hours and sending, so the order service never slows down when Apple is slow
APNs only accepts messages that come from a Kafka topic
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: Decoupling keeps provider slowness and retries away from order processing, and centralises preference and token logic. A queue does not make push delivery guaranteed; push stays best-effort.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: You want to put the full order details, item images and invoice into the push payload so the app need not call the server. What is the problem?
options: Payloads are capped at about 4 KB and may be lost; send a short message and an ID, and let the app fetch real data
APNs encrypts large payloads, so the app cannot read them
Large payloads are fine but are always delivered with low priority
Payloads must be plain text, so JSON order details are rejected
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: Push is a small, best-effort hint, so the payload should be an order ID plus a deep link. The app fetching from the server keeps the data correct even if a push is lost.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: Three ETA updates for order OD4471 are sent while Sethu's phone has no signal. You used a collapse key per order. What does he see when he reconnects?
options: All three updates, in the order they were sent
None of them, because offline messages are always discarded
Only the first update, since later ones are dropped as duplicates
Only the latest update, because pending messages with the same collapse key replace older ones
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: A collapse key means only the newest of several waiting messages with that key is shown, which is right for a changing status like an ETA. Old ETAs would only confuse her.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: You are sending an OTP by push that becomes useless after 5 minutes. How should you set expiry (TTL) compared to an out-for-delivery update?
options: Hours for both, so the user eventually gets everything
Leave TTL unset for both, since APNs and FCM pick the right value
Zero for the delivery update and hours for the OTP
Very short or zero for the OTP, so a stale one is never shown; hours for the delivery update
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: TTL controls how long APNs or FCM keep trying while the phone is offline. A stale OTP is useless or confusing, while a delivery update is still useful a few hours later.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: A growth team wants high priority on every promotional push "to make them arrive faster". What is the best advice?
options: Use high priority only for marketing, since transactional messages are small
Keep high priority for time-sensitive messages; platforms watch usage and may downgrade apps that abuse it
Priority only affects iOS, so it does not matter on Android
Use high priority for all messages, since it has no downside
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: High priority may wake the device; if most high-priority messages produce nothing visible, Android may quietly downgrade them. Offers should use normal priority, deliveries high.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: You plan a feature that silently pushes data to the app in the background every few minutes to refresh content. What is the risk?
options: Silent pushes always show a banner, annoying users
Silent pushes are limited to 10 per day on Android and blocked on iOS
Silent/background pushes are heavily throttled on iOS, so you cannot rely on them arriving
Silent pushes require a separate device token from alert pushes
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: Data-only background pushes are best effort and throttled, so a feature built on them will fail unpredictably. Fetch data when the app opens instead.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: APNs returns 410 Unregistered for one of a user's tokens. What should your backend do?
options: Retry it with exponential backoff until it succeeds
Delete that token; the app was uninstalled or the token replaced, and resending wastes quota and slows campaigns
Delete all of that user's tokens, since the user has left
Keep it but mark the user as opted out of all notifications
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: 410 Unregistered (or FCM's UNREGISTERED) means the token is dead, so remove only that row. The user's other valid tokens still work, and retrying a dead token never helps.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: How should your app keep its device token fresh on the backend?
options: Re-send it only when the user changes their password
Send it once at install, since tokens never change
Re-send the token on every app open and update last_seen, and prune tokens not refreshed for a couple of months
Ask Apple or Google for the latest token on every send
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: The OS can rotate tokens, and tokens go stale after reinstalls, restores or long inactivity (Firebase treats about 270 days inactive as expired). Re-registering on open keeps the stored token current.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: Your API call to FCM returns success for Sethu's out-for-delivery push. What does that tell you?
options: That the app has updated the order status locally
That delivery is guaranteed within the TTL
That Sethu saw the notification on his screen
Only that FCM accepted it; the phone may be off, notifications muted or the message expired
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: Push is best effort; a 200 is acceptance, not delivery or viewing. Track opens by having the app report taps, and use a fallback such as SMS for critical messages.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: Every push could be lost. How should the order screen be designed so a missed push never shows the wrong status?
options: Show the status from the push and ask the user to refresh if it looks wrong
Store the last push payload and show that status when the app opens
When the app opens, it fetches the real order status from the server; the push is only a hint
Re-send each push three times so at least one gets through
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: The server is the source of truth, so the app always calls the order API on open. Sending pushes repeatedly still guarantees nothing and annoys users.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: A "Big sale at midnight" push must go to 10 crore devices. Which plan matches the design?
options: Queue the jobs, use many sender workers with reused HTTP/2 connections, per-provider token-bucket limits, backoff with jitter, and stagger over 15-30 minutes
Send all 10 crore at exactly midnight from one server so everyone gets it together
Loop through users and call APNs synchronously, retrying immediately on 429
Send to everyone at high priority so FCM and APNs deliver faster
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: Queues absorb provider slowdowns, rate limits respect FCM quotas, and staggering protects your own backend from everyone tapping at once. Immediate retries on 429 make the overload worse.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: A 10-crore marketing blast is running when a user requests a login OTP. How do you make sure the OTP push is not stuck behind the campaign?
options: Give transactional messages their own queue and workers, separate from marketing
Send OTPs only after the campaign finishes
Pause the campaign for a minute every time an OTP is requested
Send OTPs at high priority in the same queue so they jump ahead
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: Separate lanes mean bulk campaigns can never delay critical transactional messages. Priority on the provider side does nothing about a long backlog in your own queue.

How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.q: Users get annoyed by notifications and turn them off in OS settings. Why is this serious, and what prevents it?
options: The OS switch is beyond your reach and often permanent; respect per-category preferences, quiet hours and frequency caps
It only affects marketing, since transactional pushes bypass the OS switch
It is reversible: send a high-priority push asking them to re-enable
It is not serious, because the server can still deliver alerts silently
How does a \"Your order is out for deliv.why: Once notifications are off at the OS level, your server cannot even see it, let alone reach the user. Settings by category, quiet hours (except urgent transactional messages) and caps like three promotions a day keep users from switching off.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: A city has 3 lakh online drivers and 5,000 ride searches per second at peak. Why is scanning every driver's distance for each search a bad idea?
options: It is 1.5 billion distance calculations per second on constantly changing data, nearly all wasted on far-away drivers
Drivers' locations are stored on their phones, not the server
Haversine distance cannot be computed for moving objects
A single scan of 3 lakh drivers takes several seconds
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: One scan is only a few milliseconds, but multiplying by thousands of searches per second becomes billions of checks. A spatial index avoids reading every driver, just as a database index avoids reading every row.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: What is the core idea that lets a ride app find nearby drivers in milliseconds?
options: Ask every driver's phone over the network whether it is within 3 km
Store drivers in a SQL table with separate indexes on latitude and longitude
Divide the map into cells, keep an in-memory index of which drivers are in each cell, and look only at your cell and its neighbours
Sort all drivers by latitude and binary search for the rider's latitude
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: Grouping by cell turns 3 lakh candidates into perhaps 20-50. Two separate latitude and longitude indexes still scan a long strip of rows and cannot answer "near this point" efficiently.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: Two drivers have geohashes tdr1yk and tdr1ym, and a third has tdr4ab. What can you say?
options: The third is closest to the first two because "4" comes after "1"
The first two share a longer prefix, so they are in the same smaller box, while the third is in a different one
All three are within 150 m of each other, since they share "tdr"
Geohash prefixes say nothing about location; only the full string matters
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: A longer shared geohash prefix means the same smaller box, like PIN codes sharing digits. Note the reverse is not guaranteed: points just across a border can have very different prefixes.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: Roughly how big is a box for a 6-character geohash?
options: About 150 m x 150 m, one block
About 1.2 km x 0.6 km, a few streets
About 4.9 km x 4.9 km, a big neighbourhood
About 20 km x 20 km, a whole city
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: Length 5 is about 4.9 km square, length 6 about 1.2 km x 0.6 km, length 7 about 150 m square. Each extra character makes the box much smaller.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: You stand at the corner of your geohash box, and the nearest driver is 60 m away in the next box. Your search returns nothing near. Why, and what is the fix?
options: The driver's ping is stale; reduce the ping interval to 1 second
The geohash is too long; use a 3-character geohash for everything
GPS error put the driver in the wrong box; increase GPS accuracy
The neighbouring box can have a totally different prefix; always search your cell plus its 8 neighbours
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: This is the edge problem: nearby points across a border share no long prefix. Searching the 3x3 block (or k rings in H3) catches them; making boxes huge just floods you with far-away candidates.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: Why do many ride-hailing teams prefer H3 hexagons over square cells?
options: All 6 neighbours of a hexagon are at the same distance, so 1 or 2 rings give a nearly circular search area
Hexagons automatically split into smaller cells where drivers are dense
Hexagon IDs are shorter strings than geohashes
Hexagons tile the Earth with no gaps, while squares leave holes
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: In a square grid, side neighbours are closer than corner neighbours, making a ring search lopsided. Adapting to density is a quadtree property, not H3's.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: Google's S2 numbers cells along a Hilbert curve. What practical benefit does that give?
options: Cells resize themselves as drivers move in and out
Every cell has exactly 6 equidistant neighbours
Nearby cells mostly get nearby numbers, so an area becomes a few ranges of cell IDs that are fast to look up in a sorted store
Cell IDs can be read as plain PIN-code-like string prefixes
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: The Hilbert curve preserves locality in number order, turning a region into a few ID ranges. Equidistant neighbours describe H3; resizing describes a quadtree.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: A colleague suggests a quadtree for the live driver index. What is the main concern?
options: Quadtrees cannot handle more than 100 objects in total
Quadtrees use hexagons, which need a special library
Drivers move every few seconds, so boxes keep splitting and merging, which is awkward under heavy concurrent updates
Quadtrees cannot represent areas of different density
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: Quadtrees adapt to density (tiny boxes in Koramangala, big ones on the outskirts), which suits fairly static data like shops. For constantly moving objects, fixed grids such as geohash, H3 or S2 are simpler.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: 3 lakh drivers each send a location ping every 4 seconds. Roughly how many writes per second is that, and what keeps the write path cheap?
options: About 75,000 per second; recompute every driver's cell from scratch on each ping
About 12 lakh per second; batch all pings into one write per minute
About 7,500 per second; write each ping to a disk database with full history
About 75,000 per second; keep only the latest position in memory and move a driver between cells only when the cell changes
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: 3,00,000 / 4 = 75,000 writes per second. A bike moves only about 40 m in 4 seconds, so usually only the position updates; a queue in front absorbs bursts.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: Your team uses Redis GEO for driver locations. What does GEOSEARCH ... BYRADIUS 2 km ASC COUNT 30 do efficiently?
options: Reads only the geohash ranges covering the circle, filters by exact distance, and returns the 30 nearest, usually in under a millisecond
Returns the 30 drivers with the shortest road ETA to the rider
Scans every driver in the key and sorts all of them by distance
Automatically removes drivers whose last ping is older than 30 seconds
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: Redis stores each member with a 52-bit geohash score, so a radius search is a few range reads plus an exact distance filter. It knows nothing about roads, and members do not expire on their own.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: A rider searches her cell plus 1 ring and finds only 3 available bikes, below the target of 10. What should the matching service do?
options: Return the 3 drivers immediately, since the nearest are always best
Expand the radius step by step (2 rings, then 3) until enough drivers are found or a limit is hit
Fall back to scanning every driver in the city
Tell the rider no drivers are available and ask her to retry
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: Expanding rings keeps each step to a few dozen cell lookups; 2 rings in H3 is 19 hexagons. Scanning the whole city brings back the original problem.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: The nearest bike by straight line is 300 m away, but the app shows a bike 700 m away first. Is this a bug?
options: Yes: the 300 m bike's cell was probably not searched
Probably not: ranking is by road ETA, and the 300 m bike may face a long detour while the other is on the same road heading towards you
No: apps randomly shuffle the top drivers to be fair to them
Yes: the closest driver by haversine distance should always be first
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: Shortlist cheaply by distance, then rank by ETA from a routing service with road graph and traffic, plus heading. One-ways, dividers and missing U-turns make straight-line distance misleading.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: Why does the system call the ETA service only for a shortlist of about 30 drivers instead of all nearby ones?
options: The ETA service can only return 30 results per call by design
ETA is only accurate for drivers within 30 seconds of the rider
Road ETA with live traffic is the expensive step, so the cheap cell search narrows the set first
Drivers outside the top 30 by distance are never assigned anyway
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: The two-stage design pairs a cheap filter with an expensive ranker. Running routing for hundreds of drivers per search would be slow and costly.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: A driver entered a metro underpass and lost network 2 minutes ago, but still shows up in search results. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
options: His cell changed; recompute the geohash at a longer length
Redis GEO expired him too late; lower the key's TTL to 10 seconds
His GPS drifted; widen the search radius to compensate
His last position stayed in the index; store last-seen time, skip anyone older than about 15-30 seconds, and sweep out silent drivers
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: Redis GEO members do not expire on their own, so you need a separate timestamp set (or time-bucketed keys with a TTL) and a filter at query time. A stale driver looks nearby but cannot come.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: Two riders' requests both pick the same available driver at the same moment. How do you stop a double assignment?
options: Make assignment atomic: set status to assigned only if currently available; the loser moves to the next candidate
Let both requests through and ask the driver which rider he prefers
Search again after a random delay so the requests do not overlap
Remove the driver from the index for 5 minutes after any search returns him
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: A conditional update lets exactly one request win, and the driver is marked unavailable immediately. Random delays reduce but never eliminate the race.

When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.q: How should the driver index be sharded across servers?
options: By vehicle type only, with one shard for bikes, autos and cabs
By driver ID hash, so load is spread evenly
Not at all; one global server avoids cross-shard queries
By geography, such as per city or cell range, because every search is local
When you open Ola or Rapido, how does th.why: A Chennai search never needs Delhi's drivers, so geographic sharding keeps each query on one shard. Hashing by driver ID would scatter a single neighbourhood across all shards.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: Why can't one data centre stream an IPL final to 3 crore viewers at about 2 Mbps each?
options: That is about 60 Tbps, far beyond one site's network links, and distance would add delay to every download
Each phone can only connect to servers in its own state
Video encoding at that scale needs too much CPU for one data centre
HLS does not allow more than 1 lakh viewers per server
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: 3 crore x 2 Mbps = 60 Tbps, about 600 servers with 100 Gbps cards before headroom, and one building's links and long paths would clog. The bottleneck is network and distance, not CPU.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: Roughly how much bandwidth do 1 crore viewers at an average of 1.5 Mbps need?
options: About 150 Tbps
About 15 Tbps
About 150 Gbps
About 1.5 Tbps
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: 1 crore = 10 million; 10,000,000 x 1.5 Mbps = 15,000,000 Mbps = 15 Tbps. Off by ten in either direction is a common slip with crore and Tbps conversions.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: The live encoder produces 240p, 360p, 480p, 720p and 1080p versions of the match at different bitrates. What is this set called, and why make it?
options: A bitrate ladder of renditions, so each viewer's player can pick a quality its network can sustain
A redundant encoder pair, so one quality can fail over to another
A segment playlist, so the CDN can choose which phones get which quality
An origin shield, so the origin only serves one quality
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: Several renditions let a weak 4G phone get 360p instead of a frozen screen while fibre users get 1080p. The encoder itself also runs as two redundant pipelines, but that is a separate reliability measure.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: Why are HLS and DASH built on small segment files served over plain HTTP?
options: HTTP lets the server push each frame to the phone as soon as it is captured
HTTP is faster than any other protocol for video
Segments over HTTP give sub-second latency, unlike WebRTC
Ordinary web caches and CDNs already know how to serve HTTP files to millions, so the stream scales like a web page
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: Cacheable HTTP files are what let CDNs fan one segment out to lakhs of viewers. WebRTC is the low-latency option, but each viewer needs a live connection, which is far harder to scale.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: In live HLS, what does the media playlist (.m3u8) for a rendition look like over time?
options: A single file containing the full video, appended to as the match goes on
A sliding window listing the latest few segments; the player re-downloads it every few seconds
A list of edge server addresses the player should rotate through
A fixed list of every segment for the whole match, published before the toss
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: As each new segment is ready, it is added and the oldest entry drops off. A master playlist separately lists the available renditions.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: Who decides which video quality a viewer gets for the next segment in HLS or DASH?
options: The origin server, based on the viewer's subscription tier
The CDN edge, based on how busy it is
The mobile operator, based on the user's data plan
The player on the phone, using its measured download speed and buffer level
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: This is adaptive bitrate: the server only offers choices, and the player picks per segment. A common misconception is that the server chooses quality.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: A viewer's speed drops from 15 Mbps to 2 Mbps while watching 1080p (6 Mbps) with a 20-second buffer. What does a good ABR player do, and why doesn't the screen freeze?
options: It jumps straight back to 1080p as soon as one segment downloads quickly
It asks the server to re-encode the current segment at 2 Mbps
It notices slow downloads and a shrinking buffer and drops to a lower rendition like 480p; the buffer keeps playback going meanwhile
It keeps 1080p and waits for the network to recover, showing a spinner
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: The buffer absorbs the dip while the player switches down; at 1.2 Mbps a 4-second segment downloads in about 2.4 seconds, so the buffer refills. The spinner appears only if the buffer reaches zero.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: In the simple ABR rule, when the buffer is below 6 seconds the player picks the highest rendition below 0.5 x measured speed. Why so cautious?
options: With little buffer left, any slow download would empty it and stall, so it picks quality with plenty of headroom
Low buffers mean the CDN is overloaded, so the player helps by asking for less
Below 6 seconds the player cannot measure speed accurately, so it guesses low
The player needs to save mobile data when the buffer is low
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: The rule gets bolder as the buffer grows (0.7x, then 0.9x above 20 seconds) and never jumps up more than one step at a time. Protecting against stalls is the goal.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: In one city, 10 lakh viewers request 720p/seg_9122.ts within a few seconds. What does the edge cache do?
options: Forward each of the 10 lakh requests to the origin
Fetch the segment once upstream and serve it 10 lakh times
Re-encode it for each viewer's device
Refuse to cache it because live video is too fresh
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: Live segments cache extremely well because everyone wants the same file at nearly the same time. "Live is too fresh to cache" is a common misconception.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: 5,000 requests for a brand-new segment hit an edge before it has the file. What stops 5,000 requests going upstream?
options: Rate limiting: the edge returns 429 to all but the first 100 requests
Pre-fetching: the edge already has every segment before it is encoded
Request collapsing: the edge sends one request upstream and makes the rest wait for that single answer
Origin shield: it rejects requests that arrive too close together
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: Collapsing turns a burst of identical misses into one upstream fetch. An origin shield is a separate middle layer that reduces how many edges hit the origin.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: Why can a live segment be cached for its whole useful life but the live playlist only for about a second?
options: Segments are smaller than playlists, so they take less cache space
Segments are encrypted, so caching them longer is safer
Playlists contain user-specific data, so they cannot be shared
A segment never changes once written, but the playlist changes every few seconds as segments are added
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: Caching the playlist too long would make players miss new segments. Immutable segments are safe to keep.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: 2,000 edge servers each ask the origin for every new segment in 5 renditions. What is the purpose of an origin shield?
options: A firewall that blocks viewers in regions without broadcast rights
A middle layer of regional caches that edges ask instead, so the origin sees only a handful of requests per segment
A cache on the phone that stores segments for replay
A second origin that takes over if the main one fails
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: Without it, the origin would get about 10,000 requests every 4 seconds, plus retries. A backup origin is a separate redundancy measure.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: Your product head wants every viewer to be only 3 seconds behind live. What trade-off should you explain?
options: Lower latency means lower video quality for everyone, always capped at 480p
Lower latency is impossible with CDNs; you would need one central server
Low-latency HLS/DASH can get close, but a tiny buffer means more stalls on weak mobile networks and more small requests
There is no trade-off; low-latency HLS is strictly better and just costs more
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: Low-latency modes send parts of segments while they are written, getting delay to about 3-8 seconds, at the cost of stall risk. Many apps choose 10-20 seconds for patchy networks, because not stalling matters more.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: Why is a typical live stream 20-30 seconds behind the stadium with 6-second segments?
options: The broadcaster adds a mandatory 30-second delay for censorship
The CDN holds each segment for 20 seconds before releasing it
Each segment takes 6 seconds to travel from the origin to the phone
The player stays about three segments behind the newest (about 18 seconds) plus encoding and CDN time, so it always has a buffer

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: The IPL final is tonight. A teammate says autoscaling will handle the toss surge. What is the best response?
options: Only the video CDN needs pre-warming, since APIs are cached anyway
Disable autoscaling so the system does not flap during the match
New servers take minutes but the spike takes seconds; pre-warm CDNs and pre-scale login, entitlement and APIs before the match
Agreed; autoscaling reacts within a second for stateless services
How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.why: Spikes at the toss or a last over arrive faster than autoscaling can react. Failures often hit login, entitlement or home-page APIs, which are not cached like segments.

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: In the last over, total bandwidth nears the limit across your CDNs. What graceful degradation step does the design suggest?
options: Temporarily cap top quality at 720p, switch off non-essential features and serve a cached home page
Restart the encoders at a lower frame rate
Disconnect viewers on 240p so higher-quality viewers keep their bandwidth
Switch all viewers to low-latency HLS to reduce bandwidth

How can a streaming app show an IPL fina.q: One CDN's Kolkata region starts returning errors mid-match. How does a well-designed setup keep viewers playing?
options: Viewers are moved to the origin directly until the CDN recovers
The stream is paused for Kolkata viewers until the region is healthy
A steering service moves requests to another CDN, while players retry and keep playing from their buffer
Players drop to 240p, which the failing CDN can still serve

The engine scans every listing very quickly using many CPU cores in parallel
Every possible query result is precomputed and stored in a cache in advance
A B-tree index on the title column lets it jump to matching rows directly
How can a search engine look through cro.why: An inverted index is built once ahead of time, so a query only reads the short lists for its terms. Search engines avoid scanning; they do not just scan faster.

How can a search engine look through cro.q: Why is the structure called an 'inverted' index?
options: It stores documents in reverse order of their IDs so the newest come first
It maps each term to the documents containing it, the reverse of document to its text
It stores each word spelled backwards to speed up suffix matching
It ranks documents from least to most relevant and then reverses the list
How can a search engine look through cro.why: A normal (forward) store goes document -> words; an inverted index goes term -> list of documents. Nothing is reversed in order or spelling.

How can a search engine look through cro.q: Documents were indexed with stemming, but a user's query 'running' returns nothing although 'Running Shoes' exists. What is the most likely cause?
options: Stemming deletes words like 'running' entirely, so such words can never be searched
The refresh interval has not passed yet, so the product is not visible
Posting lists must be re-sorted after stemming before queries can match
The query was not run through the same analyzer, so it looked up 'running' instead of 'run'
How can a search engine look through cro.why: The index stores the stemmed term 'run'; an unanalysed query looks up 'running' and finds no list. This mismatch is the most common beginner bug; the same analyzer must run on documents and queries.

How can a search engine look through cro.q: Your analyzer turns 'Red Running-Shoes for Men!' into terms. With lowercasing, stop-word removal and stemming, what terms are stored?
options: red, run, shoe, men
Red, Running, Shoes, for, Men
red, running, shoes, for, men
red-running-shoes, men
How can a search engine look through cro.why: Tokenising splits the text, lowercasing makes it uniform, 'for' is dropped as a stop word and stemming reduces running->run and shoes->shoe. The second option skips stop words and stemming.

How can a search engine look through cro.q: Posting lists are kurti = [3, 8, 15, 22] and cotton = [2, 3, 9, 15, 30]. What does the AND query 'cotton kurti' return, and why is it cheap?

{3, 15}; each ID from one list is binary-searched across the whole document store
{3, 15}; two pointers walk the sorted lists once, about 9 steps regardless of collection size
{3}; only the first common ID is returned for an AND query

How can a search engine look through cro.q: An AND query has terms 'shoe' (40,000 docs) and 'red' (6 lakh docs) in one shard. Which strategy makes the intersection fastest?

Start from the shorter 'shoe' list and probe the longer one using skip pointers
Scan all documents in the shard and test each one for both words
Convert both lists to unsorted hash sets and compare every pair
How can a search engine look through cro.why: Shortest-list-first plus skip pointers lets the engine jump whole blocks of the long list. Starting from the longer list does far more work and misses nothing extra.

How can a search engine look through cro.q: A teammate proposes `WHERE title LIKE '%shoe%'` on a 1 crore row MySQL table, saying the B-tree index on title will make it fast. What is the best response?
options: It will be fast because the B-tree index can jump to any substring inside the title
It will be fast as long as the table is sharded across several database servers
It is slow only because LIKE is case sensitive; adding LOWER() makes it use the index
A B-tree only helps prefixes; a leading wildcard forces a full scan with no stemming or ranking

How can a search engine look through cro.q: Why are posting lists like 1000, 1003, 1010 usually stored as 1000, 3, 7?
options: Storing gaps keeps numbers small so they compress into a byte or less and fit in memory
Gaps make it possible to update the list in place when a document changes
Gaps are required so that BM25 can compute term frequency for scoring
Gaps hide real document IDs from users for privacy reasons

How can a search engine look through cro.q: A seller updates a product title in Elasticsearch, and a search one millisecond later still shows the old title. What explains this?

The update was lost and must be retried because the translog was full
The change lands in a new segment that becomes searchable at the next refresh, about every second
Updates only become visible after the nightly background merge of segments

How can a search engine look through cro.q: Your search cluster for 20 crore listings has 40 shards. How does a 'red shoes' query get its global top 10?
options: The coordinator sends the query to one shard chosen by hashing the words 'red shoes'
Each shard returns its local top 10 IDs and scores; a coordinator merges them, then fetches only those 10 docs
Every shard returns all its matching documents in full and the coordinator sorts them
Shards pass partial results to each other in a chain until the last one has the top 10
How can a search engine look through cro.why: This is scatter-gather with a query phase, merge and a fetch phase. Returning all full matches would waste huge network and memory.

How can a search engine look through cro.q: An engineer wants to split a 50 GB index into 500 tiny shards 'to make it faster'. What is the main risk?
options: Small shards cannot store positions, so phrase queries will stop working
Each shard can only hold one term, so multi-word queries will fail
More shards force the refresh interval to rise from 1 second to 1 minute
Every query hits every shard, so many tiny shards add overhead and worsen tail latency
How can a search engine look through cro.why: Latency is set by the slowest shard and each shard adds per-query overhead, so more shards is not always faster. Shard size depends on workload, commonly tens of GB.

How can a search engine look through cro.q: A startup wants to store orders only in Elasticsearch and drop its PostgreSQL database. What is the best advice?

Go ahead, because Elasticsearch updates its index instantly and in place
Go ahead, but disable refresh so that writes are durable immediately
Use Elasticsearch as the source of truth and rebuild PostgreSQL from it nightly

How can a search engine look through cro.q: Your product-search analyzer stems everything, and searches for SKU codes and terms like 'university' start matching wrong items. What is the best fix?
options: Turn off lowercasing, because lowercasing is what merges unrelated words
Add more stop words so that rare codes are dropped from the index
Index SKUs and similar codes in a separate unstemmed field, since stemming can over-merge words
Increase the refresh interval so the stemmer has more time to work

How can a search engine look through cro.q: Between two products matching 'red shoes', one has a short title and the other mentions the words once in a long description. With BM25, which tends to score higher and why?
options: The long-description match, because longer text contains more total words
The short-title match, because BM25 favours matches in shorter fields
Both score equally, because BM25 only checks whether a word is present
Whichever was indexed first, because BM25 uses document ID order
How can a search engine look through cro.why: BM25 rewards term frequency (with diminishing returns), rare terms (IDF) and short fields. It does not ignore length or use ID order.

How can a search engine look through cro.q: A user searches the exact phrase "running shoes". What extra information in the postings makes this possible?
options: Term frequency, which tells how many times each word appears in the document
The IDF value, which tells how rare each word is across the collection
The replica number, which tells which copy of the shard holds the document
Word positions, so the engine can check that 'run' and 'shoe' are adjacent
How can a search engine look through cro.why: Phrase queries need positions to check adjacency. Term frequency is used for scoring, not for adjacency.

How does a web search engine like Google.q: A friend says 'Google searches the live web every time I type a query'. What is the most accurate correction?
options: It searches the live web but only the top 1,000 most popular sites
It sends the query to every website's own search box and merges the answers
It looks up a pre-built inverted index, which may be minutes to weeks behind the live page
It searches a cached copy of the web that is rebuilt from scratch every second

How does a web search engine like Google.q: You are designing a web crawler. A small Indian e-commerce site complains your bot hit it hundreds of times per second. Which design best prevents this?

Use a single global FIFO queue so that URLs are fetched in the order discovered
Ignore robots.txt for small sites since they rarely have meaningful rules
Fetch all pages from a site in one burst so the crawler finishes there quickly
How does a web search engine like Google.why: Politeness comes from per-host queues with rate limits, and robots.txt must be obeyed. A global FIFO queue can send bursts to one host.

How does a web search engine like Google.q: A news homepage changes every few minutes while an old government notice never changes. How should the crawler decide how often to revisit them?
options: Revisit every page on the same fixed schedule, such as once a month
Revisit pages in alphabetical order of URL so that coverage is even
Revisit only pages that have the most outgoing links on them
Learn each page's change rate and importance, revisiting fast-changing important pages often
How does a web search engine like Google.why: Recrawl scheduling uses change rate and importance (plus sitemaps) to drive freshness. A fixed schedule wastes fetches and leaves news stale.

How does a web search engine like Google.q: The same review is syndicated on five sites with a few words changed. Which technique best groups these near-duplicates?

SimHash or shingling, so similar pages get close fingerprints or overlapping chunk sets
Comparing only the page titles character by character
PageRank, since copies always have the same inbound links

How does a web search engine like Google.q: In the PageRank example, A has only one inbound link (from C) yet scores 0.37, close to C's 0.39 with three links. Why?

A has the most outgoing links, and PageRank rewards pages that link out a lot
A was crawled first, so it starts with a higher initial score than others
The damping factor gives A an extra bonus because it links to two pages
How does a web search engine like Google.why: A vote from an important page counts more, and C has only one outlink, so A gets C's whole vote. Who links to you matters more than how many.

How does a web search engine like Google.q: In the random-surfer model with damping factor d = 0.85, what does the remaining 15% represent?

The share of each page's vote that is kept by the page itself
The chance the surfer gets bored and jumps to a random page instead of clicking a link
The fraction of the web that the crawler fails to reach
How does a web search engine like Google.why: PR has a (1-d)/N term: with probability 15% the surfer jumps randomly. That is why page D, with no inbound links, still gets a small score.

How does a web search engine like Google.q: An interviewer asks why web indexes are usually document-partitioned rather than term-partitioned. What is the best answer?

Document partitioning means each query touches only one shard, avoiding fan-out
Document partitioning removes the need for replicas because shards never fail
Each shard fully answers multi-word queries for its own pages, so only small top-k lists cross the network
How does a web search engine like Google.why: With term partitioning, multi-word queries ship big posting lists across the network. Document partitioning still fans out to every shard, but sends back only small top results.

How does a web search engine like Google.q: Your search query fans out to 1,000 shards and p99 latency is bad because a few shards are occasionally slow. Which fix fits best?
options: Reduce the number of replicas so each machine handles more load
Send hedged requests to a second replica and use per-shard deadlines with partial results
Wait for every shard to answer, however long it takes, to keep results complete
Move to a single giant shard so there is no fan-out at all
How does a web search engine like Google.why: With scatter-gather the slowest shard decides latency, so hedging, deadlines and in-memory hot data limit tail latency. One giant shard cannot hold or serve the index.

How does a web search engine like Google.q: A page repeats 'biryani' ten times but never mentions Chennai. A real review mentions 'biryani' 3 times and 'chennai' once. Why does the review win for 'chennai biryani'?

BM25 penalises any word repeated more than five times with a negative score
BM25 only counts whether each word is present, so repeats never matter
The stuffed page is shorter, and BM25 always prefers longer pages

How does a web search engine like Google.q: Which ordering correctly describes the ranking funnel for a query?
options: ML re-ranking of every page in the index, then BM25 to pick the final ten
PageRank alone sorts the entire index, then snippets are generated for the top ten
Cheap retrieval from posting lists, then BM25 plus static quality, then ML re-ranking of a few hundred
Snippets are generated first for all matches, then the best snippets are ranked
How does a web search engine like Google.why: Expensive models run only on a small candidate set; cheap scores like BM25 narrow it first. Running ML on the whole index would be far too slow.

How does a web search engine like Google.q: A user types 'dum biryani spots' and a page titled 'best places for slow-cooked rice' ranks well despite sharing no words. What made this possible?
options: Stemming, which reduces 'biryani' and 'rice' to the same root word
PageRank, which promotes any page with many inbound links
Stop-word removal, which drops every word that does not match
Neural retrieval with embeddings, where queries and pages that mean similar things are close
How does a web search engine like Google.why: Embeddings capture meaning so nearest-neighbour search can match pages with no shared words. Stemming only merges forms of the same word.

How does a web search engine like Google.q: A restaurant owner asks if buying Google ads will lift their organic ranking for 'best biryani in chennai'. What is the accurate answer?

No; ads come from a separate auction system and Google states they do not affect organic ranking
Yes, but only if the ad campaign runs for at least three months
No, because ads are never shown for local or food queries
How does a web search engine like Google.why: Ads are chosen by a separate auction and labelled Sponsored; organic ranking is independent. Ads do appear for such queries, so the last option is wrong.

How does a web search engine like Google.q: For the query 'weather chennai', the engine shows a live weather box instead of ten blue links. Which stage made this decision?
options: Query understanding, which detects intent before searching
The crawler, which fetched a weather page just before the query
Snippet generation, which decides the layout after ranking
The deduplication step, which merges all weather pages into one
How does a web search engine like Google.why: Query understanding fixes spelling, expands synonyms and detects intent (weather, navigational, local). It runs online before retrieval.

How does a web search engine like Google.q: Your team launches a new ranking model. Which evaluation approach matches how search quality is typically measured?
options: Count total clicks only, since clicks are an unbiased measure of relevance
Measure how many pages were crawled per day after the launch
Human-rater labels scored with NDCG, plus an A/B test on a small share of live traffic
Check that average query latency fell, since faster always means better quality
How does a web search engine like Google.why: NDCG rewards relevant results near the top, and A/B tests confirm on live traffic. Clicks are biased toward top positions, so they are used carefully.

How does a web search engine like Google.q: Roughly how long does a full web search take end to end, per the illustrative latency budget?
options: About 5-10 ms, because everything is served from cache
About 2-3 seconds, because every shard must be scanned fully
About 1 second, because the index refreshes once per second
About 150-300 ms, with fan-out retrieval and re-ranking the biggest middle steps
How does a web search engine like Google.why: The budget adds network, query understanding, fan-out retrieval (40-80 ms), merge and re-ranking (30-60 ms), snippets and render to roughly 150-300 ms.

How can five people type in the same Goo.why: Every replica applies the same fixed rule, so they converge and no words are lost. Clocks are unreliable and discarding text would lose edits.

How can five people type in the same Goo.q: Under OT, a delete happens earlier in the document than your concurrent insert. How must your insert's position change?
options: Shift it right by the deleted length
Shift it left by the deleted length
Leave it unchanged, since only inserts affect positions
Move it to the end of the document to be safe
How can five people type in the same Goo.why: Text removed before your position moves your target left; inserts before you shift you right. Ignoring deletes would put text in the wrong place.

How can five people type in the same Goo.q: Why do Google Docs-like OT systems rely on a central server?
options: OT cannot apply any operation locally without first asking the server
The server stores the whole document after each keystroke for safety
Only a server can generate the unique IDs that OT gives each character
Correct peer-to-peer transforms in every order are very hard; a server fixes one global order to transform against
How can five people type in the same Goo.why: Several published OT algorithms had bugs in tricky peer-to-peer cases; a server that orders ops reduces the problem to transforming against a known list. Unique character IDs are a CRDT idea.

How can five people type in the same Goo.q: A client sends an op with baseRev 41, but the server has already accepted revisions 42 and 43. What does the server do?
options: Transform the op against 42 and 43, store it as revision 44, and broadcast it
Reject the op and ask the client to reload the whole document
Apply the op unchanged as revision 44, since positions rarely matter
Store it as revision 42 and renumber the existing revisions
How can five people type in the same Goo.why: The server transforms incoming ops against everything accepted since the client's base revision, then broadcasts. Applying unchanged would put text at shifted positions.

How can five people type in the same Goo.q: How does a CRDT text editor avoid transforming positions at all?
options: It locks each paragraph so only one person edits it at a time
It sends the whole document but merges with a diff tool
Each character has a unique permanent ID, and inserts say 'put this after character X'
It orders all ops by device timestamp before applying them
How can five people type in the same Goo.why: IDs like 7@ravi never shift, so ops can be applied in any order, even twice, and replicas still converge. Device timestamps are unreliable for ordering.

How can five people type in the same Goo.q: In a CRDT editor, why is a deleted character usually kept as a tombstone instead of being removed immediately?
options: Tombstones make the document smaller by replacing text with a marker
Another person's insert may still say 'after this character', so its ID must remain until it is safe to clean up
Tombstones let the server undo deletes without version history
Tombstones are required so the OT transform function can shift positions
How can five people type in the same Goo.why: Concurrent inserts can anchor to a deleted character's ID, so it stays marked deleted until garbage collection. This adds memory, one of the CRDT costs.

How can five people type in the same Goo.q: You are building a field app where inspectors edit shared notes offline for hours, sometimes syncing peer to peer. Which approach fits best?
options: OT with a central server, since long offline edits are its strongest case
Uploading the full document on reconnect and keeping the latest copy
Locking each note while one inspector has it open offline
A CRDT library such as Yjs or Automerge, since ops merge in any order without a central server
How can five people type in the same Goo.why: CRDTs fit offline-heavy and peer-to-peer apps at the cost of extra memory per character. OT after hours offline needs many transforms and gets edge-case heavy.

How can five people type in the same Goo.q: A colleague claims CRDTs are always better than OT. What is the most balanced reply?
options: It depends: CRDTs ease offline and peer-to-peer but add per-character IDs and tombstones; OT with a server is proven at huge scale
Agree, because CRDTs need no memory beyond the plain text
Disagree, because CRDTs cannot guarantee that replicas converge
Agree, because OT cannot handle more than two editors at once
How can five people type in the same Goo.why: Mostly-online products with a strong server fit OT; offline-heavy apps fit CRDTs. CRDTs do guarantee convergence, but they cost memory.

How can five people type in the same Goo.q: Two people rewrite the same sentence differently at the same time. What do OT and CRDTs guarantee?
options: The better-written version wins automatically
The edit from the person who started typing first is kept and the other is dropped
Everyone sees the same result and each person's characters are kept, but it may read messily
The editor blocks the second person until the first finishes
How can five people type in the same Goo.why: They guarantee convergence, not meaning; both texts may survive interleaved and humans fix the sense. No technique judges which wording is better.

How can five people type in the same Goo.q: Why are live cursor positions not saved in version history, and what must still happen to them?
options: They are saved only for the document owner, and never need adjusting
They are throwaway presence data; they still must be transformed or anchored to character IDs so they do not jump
They are part of the op log, so replaying history restores everyone's cursor
They are sent once per session, so adjusting them is unnecessary
How can five people type in the same Goo.why: Cursors are frequent, throttled messages over WebSockets; a lost one is fixed by the next. Without transforming, a cursor would jump when someone types above it.

How can five people type in the same Goo.q: At 4 pm someone deletes the whole pricing table. How does version history let the team restore the 3:55 pm version efficiently?
options: Replay every op from the document's creation, since snapshots are not stored
Ask each editor's browser to upload its local copy from 3:55 pm
Roll the server's database back to 3:55 pm, discarding everyone's later edits
Load the nearest snapshot and replay ops from the op log up to 3:55 pm, then apply the restore as new ops
How can five people type in the same Goo.why: Periodic snapshots plus the ordered op log rebuild any revision quickly, and the restore is itself a new set of ops. A database rollback would wipe others' legitimate changes.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: At its core, how does Google Maps compute a driving ETA for a route?
options: Divide total distance by your phone's recent average speed
Sum the predicted traversal time of each road segment, plus turn and junction delays
Divide total distance by the speed limit of the main road on the route
Look up the average time of all past trips between the two addresses
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: The road network is a directed graph of segments; ETA adds per-segment times and junction delays. Personal speed and a single speed limit ignore traffic.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: You leave at 6 pm for a 75-minute drive. Why would using the speeds observed at 6 pm on every segment give a wrong ETA?
options: Speeds at 6 pm are not available because live data lags by an hour
Using current speeds double-counts junction delays on each segment
It would be correct, because traffic does not change during one trip
You reach later segments at 6:30 or 7:00, when traffic may be worse; each segment must be predicted for when you enter it
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: This is time-dependent routing. In the Bengaluru example, current speeds give about 64 minutes versus about 75 predicted, because the Marathahalli peak builds between 6:30 and 7:00.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: Which inputs does the ETA prediction blend?
options: Historical speed profiles, anonymised aggregated live probe data, incident reports and road attributes
Only the speed limits and number of lanes of each road
Each user's personal driving history and phone battery level
Only live speeds from the user's own phone over the last few minutes
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: History gives the baseline, live probes show current conditions, incidents adjust them and road attributes help where data is sparse. Personal history is not the basis.
