How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: For a segment you will reach in 5 minutes versus one you will reach in 50 minutes, how should the forecast weight live versus historical data?
options: Use only historical data for both, since live data is noisy
Use only live data for both, since it is the most recent information
Trust live data heavily for the near segment and lean on history plus trends for the far one
Trust history for the near segment and live data for the far one
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: Live data says what is happening now; history says what usually happens at the time you arrive. The weight on live data falls as the horizon grows.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: Two people request car directions from the same place to the same destination at the same moment. One drives much faster. What do they see?
options: Different ETAs from the start, based on each person's driving history
The same ETA at the start; during the trip the faster driver's ETA drifts earlier as it is recomputed
The same ETA for the whole trip, since it is never recomputed
The faster driver sees a later ETA to discourage speeding
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: The ETA predicts typical traffic flow, so it is essentially the same for everyone on the same route, mode and departure time. Continuous recomputation from your actual position is the implicit personal correction.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: A user wonders why their bike-taxi app ETA differs from a friend's car ETA on the same trip. Which factor explains it?
options: The two-wheeler rider's personal speed history is used at planning time
Two-wheeler ETAs ignore live traffic entirely
Car ETAs always add a fixed safety buffer of 10 minutes
Travel mode: two-wheeler, car, walking and transit use different speed models and routes
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: Mode changes the ETA a lot; in India two-wheeler mode can use narrower roads and filters through traffic differently. Personal speed barely matters at planning time.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: Why does an individual driver's speed matter little for ETA during the evening peak on Outer Ring Road?
options: In congestion the traffic flow sets everyone's speed, so careful and aggressive drivers both crawl
Google caps every driver's predicted speed at the speed limit
Phones in traffic stop sending location data, so speed is unknown
The model averages only drivers who share their personal speed
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: At 6:30 pm everyone moves at about 12 km/h regardless of style. On empty highways individual speeds vary more, and recomputation corrects for that.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: Live data shows a jam on a quiet residential lane, but it turns out one phone was parked at a tea stall. How should the system avoid this mistake?
options: Trust any single phone reading because live data is always accurate
Ignore all live data on minor roads permanently
Require enough samples before trusting a reading and filter outliers
Ask the parked user to confirm whether there is a traffic jam
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: Live probe data is noisy, so readings need a minimum sample count and outlier filtering. On sparse roads the model falls back on history, road class and neighbours.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: Why is map-matching probe data especially hard on a flyover above a service road?
options: The roads are parallel or stacked, so a GPS point could belong to either segment
Flyovers block GPS signals entirely, so no points are recorded
Service roads are not included in the road graph
Phones on flyovers report speed in different units
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: Map-matching snaps samples to the correct segment, which is difficult when roads overlap. Getting it wrong would show the flyover's speed for the service road.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: What does Google's publicly described DeepMind model add over simple per-segment averaging?
options: A rule that every segment's speed equals its speed limit minus 20%
A graph neural network over supersegments, so congestion on neighbouring roads informs each forecast up to about an hour ahead
Tracking individual users so their routes can be predicted personally
Replacing historical profiles entirely with real-time readings
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: The GNN lets each road 'see' upstream and downstream traffic, like a jam spreading back from a junction. Google describes the data as anonymised and aggregated, not tracking individuals.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: At 6:20 pm a truck breaks down on the Bellandur flyover, and segment 3 (4.5 km) is now predicted at 8.8 km/h instead of 12 km/h. Roughly how long does it take now?
options: About 18 minutes instead of 22.5
About 45 minutes instead of 22.5
About 22.5 minutes, since the plan was fixed at departure
About 31 minutes instead of 22.5
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: 4.5 / 8.8 x 60 is about 31 minutes, moving the ETA from 7:15 to about 7:23. The ETA is re-estimated continuously, not fixed at departure.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: A user complains the ETA stayed still while they crawled, then suddenly dropped by 8 minutes. Is the system broken?
options: No; ETA jumps reflect fresh data, such as clearing a predicted slow stretch or an incident ahead clearing
Yes; a correct ETA should fall smoothly by one minute every minute
Yes; it means the GPS lost signal and guessed the remaining time
No; the app randomly adjusts the ETA to keep users engaged
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: The ETA already expected the slow stretch, so it held steady and dropped once cleared. Smooth ETAs would mean ignoring fresh data.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: Which route-search approach handles costs that depend on when you enter each segment?
options: A static shortest path using each road's length only
A breadth-first search that counts the number of junctions
Time-dependent shortest path (Dijkstra, A* or contraction hierarchies) where each edge cost uses the entry time
Choosing the route with the highest average speed limit
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: The search adds travel_time(seg, arrive) at each step, so 'leave now' and 'leave in 30 minutes' can differ a lot. Length alone ignores traffic.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: Your e-commerce checkout shows 'Arrives Thursday' and the live tracker shows '12 minutes away'. Which quantile should each use?
options: The median for both, since it is the most accurate single estimate
A conservative P90-P95 for the checkout promise and the median (P50) for live tracking
P90 for live tracking and the median for the checkout promise
The fastest possible time for both to maximise conversion
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: A broken promise costs trust and support calls, so promises use a high quantile; tracking is refreshed continuously, so the median is most useful. Swapping them gives late promises and pessimistic tracking.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: A rider ETA model counts only driving time, yet deliveries to Whitefield high-rises keep arriving late. What is most likely missing?
options: The rider's personal top speed on empty roads
Turn delays at junctions, which dominate last-mile time
A conversion from km/h to m/s in the segment speed calculation
Doorstep dwell time for parking, security, lifts and OTP, learned per locality and building type
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: Dwell time can be 6-8 minutes for a high-rise versus 2 for an independent house, often bigger than driving time. Turn delays are already part of the drive estimate.

How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.q: How would you evaluate a new ETA model before full rollout?
options: Check average error only, since tails and festival days are rare
Ship it everywhere and watch social media complaints
Offline backtests on completed trips (MAPE, percent within tolerance, bias by city and slot), then a gradual A/B with guardrails
Compare predicted ETAs only against speed limits on each route
How does Google Maps calculate arrival t.why: MAPE, within-tolerance rates and bias by segment of data catch systematic errors, and checking tails and festival days matters, not just averages.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: Your checkout code reads the stock of a phone (it says 1), checks it is above zero, and then writes 0 in a separate statement. During a sale, two buyers both get confirmation for that single phone. What is the root cause?
options: The cache served a stale stock value to the second buyer
The gap between checking stock and taking it lets both requests read 1
The database did not commit the first write to disk fast enough
The second buyer's request was retried by the app after a timeout
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: This is the classic check-then-act race (lost update): both requests read 1 before either writes 0. A stale cache makes it worse, but even without a cache the read-then-write gap causes the oversell.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: You need the simplest correct fix for overselling on a normal-traffic day, using only your SQL database. Which statement do you use?
options: SELECT available, then UPDATE available = available - 1 if it was positive
BEGIN a transaction, SELECT available, then UPDATE inside the same transaction
UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 1 WHERE sku_id = ? AND available >= 1, and check rows affected
UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 1, and fix negatives in a nightly job
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: The conditional update does the check and the decrement as one atomic statement; 1 row affected means you got the unit, 0 means sold out. Wrapping a read and write in a default-isolation transaction still lets two transactions both read 1.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: A teammate says, "Just wrap the read and the write in a transaction and we can't oversell." The database runs at READ COMMITTED. What is the best response?
options: Agreed, any transaction makes the read and write atomic together
Agreed, as long as the transaction is committed within 100 ms
Disagree, transactions are never safe for inventory and should be avoided
Disagree, at READ COMMITTED both transactions can read qty = 1; use a conditional update or row lock
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: A transaction at the default isolation level does not stop two transactions from both reading 1. You need a conditional update, a row lock, or stricter isolation, and the conditional update is the cheapest. Transactions are not useless, they just don't close this gap by themselves.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: A flash sale puts 1,000 units of one phone on sale and 20k checkouts per second hit that SKU. Your conditional SQL update is correct but checkout latency explodes. Why?
options: Every buyer of that SKU queues on one hot row, which handles only hundreds to low thousands of updates per second
The conditional update is not atomic under heavy load, so the database retries it
Row locks are released only at the end of the day, blocking later buyers
SQL databases cannot run conditional updates on indexed columns at scale
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: The conditional update is correct, but all buyers serialise on one row, which tops out at a few hundred to low thousands of updates per second. That is why the hot path moves to an in-memory counter like Redis for flash sales.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: For a flash sale you move the stock counter into Redis. Which approach gives an atomic check, decrement and record-of-holder?
options: GET the stock key, check it in the app, then DECR it if positive
A Lua script that checks the hold, checks stock, decrements and writes the holder in one run
A Redis distributed lock with a fixed expiry around the app's read-modify-write
Optimistic WATCH on the key with unlimited client retries on conflict
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: Redis runs a Lua script atomically, so nothing else on that shard runs between the check, the decrement and recording the holder. GET-then-DECR from the app reintroduces the check-then-act gap.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: You use optimistic concurrency (read qty and version, then UPDATE ... WHERE version = :v) for a hot SKU during a sale. What happens near the tail?
options: It works perfectly, because version checks remove all contention
It oversells, because version numbers are not checked atomically
Almost every attempt collides and retries pile up, so it is the wrong tool at peak
It deadlocks, because two versions lock each other's rows
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: Optimistic concurrency is correct and great at low contention, but on a hot SKU nearly every attempt fails the version check and retries, wasting work. It does not oversell; it just collapses throughput.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: Product wants to decrement stock when a user adds the phone to their cart, "so nobody loses it." What is the best advice?
options: Agree, because reserving earlier reduces payment failures
Agree, but give cart holds a 24-hour TTL so carts eventually clear
Disagree, and instead never hold stock until payment succeeds
Disagree, reserve at checkout with a short TTL, because idle carts would lock up the tail
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: Carts are wish lists; holding stock for them lets idle carts hold the last units hostage. Reserving at checkout with a short TTL keeps units available. Never holding at all brings back the race at payment time.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: A user taps Buy Now, the stock is reserved, and then their bank OTP times out. What should happen to the unit?
options: The release path returns it to stock and deletes the hold, so it is sellable again
It stays reserved for that user until they retry payment later in the day
It is marked sold and refunded later if no payment arrives
It is removed from stock until the nightly reconciliation runs
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: On payment failure or timeout the release path increments the stock and deletes the hold immediately; the TTL sweeper is the backstop for holds nobody releases. Keeping it reserved for hours would starve the tail.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: How long should the reservation TTL be?
options: As short as possible, such as 10 seconds, to free stock quickly
Slightly longer than the 95th-percentile payment time, typically 5-10 minutes
Exactly equal to the average payment time
Until the end of the sale event, so paying users never lose their unit
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: The TTL should cover nearly all genuine payments, so slightly above p95 payment time, typically 5-10 minutes. Too short and real payers lose their unit; too long and abandoned holds starve the tail.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: A user double-taps Buy Now, and the app also retries after a network blip. How do you stop them taking two units?
options: Rate-limit each user to one request per minute at the load balancer
Check in the app whether the user has any order today before calling Redis
Pass the same idempotency key (order id) to the reserve script, which returns the existing hold
Let both succeed and cancel the duplicate order in reconciliation
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: The Lua script first checks whether this order id already holds a unit and returns it instead of decrementing again. An app-side check before Redis is another read-then-act gap.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: To beat the one-key-one-core limit, you split 1,000 units into 32 Redis buckets. Near the end, buyers see "sold out" while 6 units remain. What is the best fix?
options: Add more buckets so each bucket holds fewer units
Show 'sold out' only after reconciliation confirms zero stock in the database
Move the whole sale back to the conditional SQL update
Retry other buckets on an empty one, and collapse to a single bucket below a stock threshold
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: Buyers routed to empty buckets see a false sold-out while other buckets still hold units. Retrying other buckets and collapsing to one exact counter for the tail fixes it; more buckets makes the problem worse.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: Two million users will tap Buy Now for 1,000 phones at midnight. Why put a virtual waiting room in front of checkout?
options: It admits users at the rate the reservation path can serve, protecting latency, payments and the rest of the site
It is what prevents overselling, since the atomic counter alone cannot handle that load
It lets you skip the database guard because fewer users reach checkout
It guarantees every waiting user eventually gets a unit
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: The atomic counter stays correct either way; the waiting room is admission control that keeps load at a rate the system can handle. It does not replace correctness or the database guard.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: Mid-sale, the Redis primary fails over to a replica, and the counter jumps up by a few units because the last decrements weren't replicated. Which combination best protects you?
options: Make Redis replication synchronous for the sale and trust Redis as the source of truth
Load slightly less than real stock into Redis, keep the database guard on confirm, and run reconciliation
Switch every reservation to a distributed lock while the failover completes
Stop the sale and restart it from the beginning with fresh counters
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: Redis replication is asynchronous, so a small held-back buffer, a database conditional update that rejects confirms beyond real stock, and frequent reconciliation keep the count trustworthy. Redis is the fast gate, not the truth.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: An engineer proposes a Redis lock around read-modify-write instead of an atomic decrement. What is the main risk?
options: Redis locks cannot be acquired by more than one service
Locks make the stock counter go negative
A lock can expire while its holder is paused, letting two holders proceed unless you use fencing tokens
Locks work only with SQL databases, not with in-memory stores
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: A GC pause or network stall can outlast the lock's expiry, so two processes both think they hold it; fencing tokens are needed. An atomic decrement avoids the problem and is faster.

How does an e-commerce website make sure.q: Despite all safeguards, an alert fires that sold count exceeds physical stock by one. What is the planned business response?
options: Ship the order late once the supplier restocks, without telling the customer
Ignore it, since one unit is within normal tolerance
Cancel the oldest order, because it had the most time to pay
Auto-cancel the newest order, refund it and apologise with a coupon
How does an e-commerce website make sure.why: The answer recommends having a ready process: detect with an alert on sold > physical_stock, auto-cancel the newest order, refund and apologise with a coupon. Silently delaying or ignoring it hurts trust.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: In a BBD interview you described a Redis atomic decrement plus a TTL hold before payment. The follow-up: "What if 10,000 people hit Buy in the same second and payment takes 30 seconds?" What is the best way to open your reply?
options: Apologise and redesign around a distributed lock to handle the concurrency
Say Redis cannot take 10,000 requests a second, so you'd shard it first
Say the design does not oversell: exactly 50 get holds, and 9,950 get 'sold out' within milliseconds
Say you'd move payment before the decrement so holds never wait 30 seconds
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: The follow-up probes whether you understand why the design holds under a stampede. Reframe with confidence: the atomic gate admits exactly the stock and answers losers instantly. Moving payment before the decrement would bring back overselling.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: 10,000 users tap Buy for 50 units in the same second, and each payment takes about 30 seconds. How many users actually wait 30 seconds?
options: Only the 50 holders, each for their own payment, because the decrement happens before payment
All 10,000, because they queue behind the payment gateway
About 9,950, because the losers wait until holds expire
None, because payment runs asynchronously after the order is confirmed
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: The atomic decrement runs before payment, so the 9,950 losers are told 'sold out' within milliseconds. Only the 50 holders wait, and only for their own payment.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: Why is a single Redis key able to absorb 10,000 Buy taps in one second for this 50-unit deal?
options: Redis spreads each key across all cluster shards automatically
Redis runs commands one at a time on a single thread and handles roughly 100k+ simple ops per second
Redis batches the requests and processes only the first 50
Redis uses row locks like a database but keeps them in memory
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: Redis executes commands serially on one thread, so 10,000 requests become 10,000 tiny queued operations, tens of milliseconds of work. A key lives on one shard; it is not spread across shards.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: You use plain DECR on the stock key. After the stampede the counter reads -9,950. Besides looking wrong, what is the deeper problem?
options: DECR is not atomic, so two clients can still get the same unit
Negative values crash Redis and force a failover
DECR is slower than a Lua script for every request
It cannot enforce a per-user cap or idempotency, and compensating INCRs can drift if a client dies
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: DECR is atomic but goes negative, needs a compensating INCR that can be lost if the client dies, and can't check per-user caps or duplicate holds. A Lua script does check, decrement, cap and hold write in one atomic step.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: Your Lua script touches stock:{sku42}, holds:{sku42} and usercnt:{sku42} on a Redis Cluster. Why the {sku42} braces?
options: They mark the keys as hot so Redis replicates them faster
They make the keys expire together when the sale ends
They are a hash tag that puts all three keys on the same shard, which a multi-key script requires
They encrypt the SKU id so scalpers can't guess the key name
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: In Redis Cluster, every key a script touches must live on the same shard; the hash tag makes the cluster hash only the part in braces, so all three land together.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: Your design uses a 30-second hold TTL. Buyer A starts a UPI payment, the bank is slow, the hold expires, Buyer B reserves the same unit, and A's payment succeeds at 70 seconds. What is the real trap here?
options: The TTL expired while payment was in flight, so the unit was resold and A's success becomes an oversell or refund
Redis lost A's hold during a failover, so B could reserve it
B bypassed the atomic gate because the hold key had already been deleted
UPI does not send success callbacks for payments longer than 30 seconds
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: A 'short TTL' that is shorter than the real payment window lets a unit be released and resold while the first payment is still pending. UPI collects, OTPs and bank redirects often exceed 30 seconds.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: To fix the TTL-versus-slow-payment problem, which design does the answer recommend?
options: A single fixed 60-second TTL for every hold, with no extensions
No TTL at all, so holds never expire until the user cancels
Releasing holds only during nightly reconciliation
A HELD to PAYMENT_PENDING to CONFIRMED/RELEASED state machine, extending the TTL to the gateway window once payment starts
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: Holds get a few minutes in HELD and are extended (for example to 10-15 minutes, matching the gateway's expiry) once payment starts, with heartbeats while 'pending'. No TTL at all would let abandoned holds starve stock.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: The release job and a late payment-success callback both act on the same hold at the same moment. How do you make sure only one wins?
options: Run the release job only once a day so collisions are rare
Make each transition a compare-and-set UPDATE that only succeeds from the expected state
Let both run and fix the result in reconciliation
Have the payment callback delete the hold row before confirming
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: Release updates only WHERE state IN ('HELD','PAYMENT_PENDING') AND expired; confirm updates only WHERE state is still held or pending. Whichever runs first changes the state, so the other updates zero rows.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: The confirm CAS for a payment success updates 0 rows because the hold was already released. What should the service do?
options: Confirm the order anyway, since the customer has paid
Leave the payment as pending and ask the customer to retry
Try to claim spare stock atomically; if none exists, auto-refund and tell the user immediately
Cancel another customer's confirmed order to free a unit
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: The policy is explicit: honour the late success if spare stock exists, otherwise refund automatically and notify the user at once. Confirming anyway would oversell.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: Before the release job frees a hold in PAYMENT_PENDING, what should it do?
options: Ask the gateway for the final payment status, using webhooks plus polling
Release it immediately, since webhooks always arrive on time
Wait until the next reconciliation before doing anything
Extend the hold indefinitely until the user contacts support
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: Webhooks can be late or lost, so the job checks the final status with the gateway. Also set the gateway's own payment timeout shorter than the hold TTL, so it never reports success for a payment you have given up on.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: Twelve of the 50 holders abandon payment. A teammate suggests simply adding the 12 units back to the Redis counter. What is the better approach?
options: Add them back immediately, since the gate is atomic and fair
Keep them out of sale to avoid any risk of overselling
Give them to the 12 users who tapped Buy fastest after the sale started
Send them to a FIFO waitlist, giving each person a short claim window
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: Putting units back into the public counter triggers a fresh stampede that bots win. A FIFO waitlist with claim windows (for example 5 minutes) is fairer and keeps load predictable.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: Your manager worries the payment gateway will be overwhelmed because 10,000 people tapped Buy on a 50-unit deal. What is the sharpest reply?
options: Payment load is bounded by stock: only about 50 payment sessions can ever open for this SKU
We will scale the payment gateway to 10,000 concurrent sessions
We will queue all 10,000 payments and process them in order
We will let only the waiting room talk to the gateway
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: Because the gate runs before payment, only holders (plus waitlist re-offers) start payment, so roughly 50 sessions exist whatever the traffic. The cheap layers (CDN, waiting room, Redis) absorb the stampede.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: Once the deal sells out, users keep refreshing the product page. What front-door measure keeps that traffic off your services?
options: Increasing the hold TTL so fewer units return to stock
A sold-out flag served from the CDN once stock hits zero
Adding more Redis buckets for the sold-out SKU
Disabling the idempotency key so refreshes are faster
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: A CDN-served sold-out flag answers refreshes at the edge. The answer lists it with the waiting room, rate limits, bot checks and per-user caps as front-door protection.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: Redis runs with a replica and AOF everysec. During a failover it may lose about a second of decrements. What guarantees the last units are still not oversold?
options: AOF everysec guarantees zero data loss, so no extra guard is needed
The replica rejects writes until it is fully caught up
A database conditional update as the final commit, plus reconciliation from confirmed orders and active holds
A distributed lock held across the failover window
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: Redis is the gate, not the ledger. Only the ~50 Redis winners reach the database's conditional UPDATE, which gives a hard guarantee at tiny load, and reconciliation rewrites the counter.

Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.q: The interviewer asks how this changes for a 50,000-unit deal at 500,000 taps per second. Which answer fits best?
options: Replace Redis with the database conditional update for every request
Increase the hold TTL so fewer requests hit the gate
Use a single bigger Redis instance with more memory
Stock bucketing across shards, local admission tokens on app nodes, a waiting room, and per-warehouse pre-allocation
Big Billion Days interview: 50 units lef.why: At that scale the hot key matters, so you spread stock across shards, reject excess traffic early with local tokens, admit at checkout capacity and split pools by fulfilment node. For 50 units these levers are overkill, and you should say so.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: At 9 PM, 2 lakh people have Maggi in their cart at a dark store with 340 packets, and all of them see "In stock". Why is that even possible?
options: The app over-reserved stock because add-to-cart locks were not atomic
A cart is only a note of interest; no packet leaves the shelf until someone pays and a picker packs it
The dark store's shelf count was out of date by several hours
Each cart reserves a packet, but reservations are released every minute
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: Adding to cart takes nothing from the shelf; it is like writing Maggi on a shopping list. The app shows 'In stock' to everyone because its only check is 'shelf count > 0'.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: What is the core flaw in the app's current stock check?
options: It reads the shelf count from the database instead of Redis
It refreshes the stock count too often, slowing the cart
It asks 'is the shelf count above zero?' instead of 'is there enough for people likely to buy soon?'
It shows the label after checkout instead of on the product page
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: With 340 packets, 'count > 0' says yes to all 2 lakh people, so the bad news only arrives at checkout. The better question compares stock with likely buyers in the next few minutes and warns early.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: A product manager proposes reserving a Maggi packet the moment someone taps Add to cart. What is the best objection?
options: The first 340 tappers would block everyone though most never pay, and every tap becomes a slow locked write
Reservations are illegal for grocery items under consumer law
Redis cannot store more than 340 reservations per store
It would make the payment step slower for the customers who do pay
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: Locking at add-to-cart lets idle carts hold all the stock and turns a cheap read into a contended write for 2 lakh taps. The only lock should be the atomic hold at payment.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: The shelf shows 340 Maggi packets. 60 are ordered and waiting to be packed, 30 are held for people paying right now, and you keep 10 as a safety margin. How many can you honestly promise?
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: Available to promise = 340 - 60 - 30 - 10 = 240. The 60 are still physically on the shelf but already belong to someone.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: Why are the 60 already-paid packets subtracted from available-to-promise even though they are still physically on the shelf?
options: Because they belong to customers who paid; the picker simply hasn't reached them yet
Because they might be damaged, so they count as safety margin
Because they are reserved for the next delivery wave tomorrow
Because Redis counts them twice unless they are removed
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: Those packets are spoken for by paid orders awaiting picking. Promising them to new customers would create orders the store cannot fill.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: You want a reasonable estimate of how many of the 2 lakh carts will actually pay in the next few minutes. Which set of signals does the answer recommend?
options: Each user's past total spend, their city tier and app version
Historical buy rate at this hour, where each cart is in the funnel, and the current selling speed
The exact shelf count and the number of pickers on shift
A survey asking cart holders whether they intend to buy
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: Like cooking for a wedding, you estimate the crowd, not individuals: past buying rate on similar days, per-cart likelihood (payment screen vs abandoned an hour ago), corrected by current sales speed to catch surprises like a viral post.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: 100 people have Maggi in their cart, the store has 10 packets, and about 1 in 10 carts pays in the next few minutes. Then the cart count jumps to 500. Which label should the app show now?
options: In stock, because 10 packets are still on the shelf
Out of stock, because there are more carts than packets
Selling fast, may run out, because about 50 likely buyers exceed 10 packets
Exactly '10 left', updated on every tap
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: 500 carts at 1 in 10 means about 50 likely buyers for 10 packets, so warn early with 'Selling fast'. 'Out of stock' is shown only when available reaches zero.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: The stock label keeps flickering between "In stock" and "Selling fast" as estimates wobble around the threshold. What is the recommended fix?
options: Recompute the label on every add-to-cart tap for accuracy
Show the exact remaining count instead of a label
Remove the 'Selling fast' label and keep only In stock and Out of stock
Use hysteresis: switch to Selling fast above about 80% and back only below about 60%
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: Two different thresholds stop the label from bouncing on small changes. Showing an exact count is worse, because it changes hundreds of times a minute in a rush.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: 2 lakh people tap Add to cart at once. How do you keep the tap fast while still showing an honest label?
options: Run the likely-buyers calculation on each tap with a read replica
A background job computes the label every few seconds and saves it in Redis; the tap only reads it
Lock the product row briefly on each tap so the count is exact
Cache the shelf count in the app and refresh it once an hour
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: None of the maths happens on the tap. The tap is a millisecond Redis read with no lock and no database access, so it stays fast at peak.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: Two customers tap Pay for what is, at that instant, the last promisable Maggi packet. What guarantees only one gets it?
options: An atomic check-and-decrement in Redis (one script), so the second caller sees zero
The background job, which recomputes available every few seconds
The 'Selling fast' label, which discourages the second customer
The picker, who rejects the second order when packing
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: The hold at payment is the only lock, and it must be atomic: check and subtract happen together, so one caller always reaches the counter first. The label job is only a warning, never the correctness guarantee.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: A customer gets a hold at payment but closes the app without paying. What happens to the packet?
options: It stays held until the end of the day
It is marked sold and refunded by support
The hold expires after about 5 minutes and the packet returns to the available count
It is moved to the safety margin permanently
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: The payment hold lasts a few minutes (say 5, the time allowed to pay). If payment fails or the customer leaves, it expires and the packet goes back to available.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: Your likely-buyers estimate turns out too low during a viral surge. What is the consequence?
options: Customers may be charged for packets that do not exist
The store may accept more orders than it can fill
The cart becomes slow because the job runs more often
Only the warning is late; the atomic payment hold still prevents unfillable orders
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: The guess affects only the label, never correctness. Guessing too high shows 'Selling fast' a bit early, which costs little; guessing too low is caught by the atomic hold at payment.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: Someone suggests showing an exact "27 left" count instead of a label. Why does the answer prefer the label?
options: Exact counts are illegal to display in Indian e-commerce
In a rush the count changes hundreds of times a minute and ignores how many others are trying to buy
Exact counts require locking stock on every page view
Labels can be cached on the CDN but numbers cannot
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: The number is often wrong by the time it's read and says nothing about competing demand. A label based on likely buyers versus available is more honest.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: Maggi is selling fast and most of the 2 lakh people won't get it. Which set of actions best handles the people who miss out?
options: Let them reach checkout and show 'sold out' after payment fails
Hide Maggi from search so nobody adds it anymore
Warn in the cart, offer substitutes or a nearby dark store, cap 2-3 packets per person, and alert open carts at zero
Raise the price until demand matches the 240 available packets
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: The goal is that people find out early and leave with something: early warnings, substitutes, nearby stores, back-in-stock alerts, per-person limits, and telling open carts as soon as the count hits zero.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: Redis, which stores the labels and payment holds, goes down at peak. What is the recommended fallback?
options: Fall back to a simple rule read from the database and keep the payment hold there: slower but still correct
Show 'In stock' for everything until Redis recovers
Block all add-to-cart taps until Redis is back
Skip the payment hold and let pickers resolve conflicts
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: Correctness must survive: the database can serve a simpler label rule and hold the atomic payment check, at the cost of speed. Showing 'In stock' everywhere brings back the original problem.

Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.q: How would you measure whether this redesign worked?
options: Total number of add-to-cart taps during the rush
Number of Redis keys written per minute
Average shelf count across dark stores
Fewer sold-out-at-checkout errors and cancellations, more substitute uptake, flat add-to-cart latency
Quick commerce at 9 PM: 2 lakh people ad.why: Success means bad news arrives earlier (fewer checkout failures and cancellations), more people accept alternatives, and the cart stays fast at peak.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: A restaurant marks Butter Chicken out of stock. Your menu cache TTL is 60 s and the search index refreshes every 30 s, built from that cache. Why can search keep showing the dish for about 90 s?
options: The two windows run in parallel, and the worst case is the larger of them plus network delay
The indexer copies the still-stale cache just before it expires, so the stale flag lives another full refresh: 60 + 30
The database takes 90 s to commit the tablet's write under load
Elasticsearch queues writes for three refresh cycles before applying them
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: Staleness stacks in series when one cached layer is built from another. If the indexer runs at t=59 from the stale cache, its next run at t=89 is the first to see the fix.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: You change the search indexer to read from the DB primary instead of the menu cache, keeping the 60 s TTL and 30 s refresh. What happens?
options: Search staleness drops to at most 30 s, but the restaurant page and checkout can still be 60 s stale
All staleness disappears because the database is the source of truth
Search staleness stays at 90 s because the TTL still applies to the index
Search becomes stale for 60 s and the cache for 30 s
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: With the indexer reading the database, the windows no longer stack, so search's worst case is 30 s. But the menu page and checkout still read the 60 s cache, so orders can still go through until checkout validates against the source of truth.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: Besides the cache TTL and index refresh, which delays can push the stale window even further?
options: Kafka partition rebalancing and JVM warm-up time
DNS propagation and TLS handshake time
Tablet sync over poor Wi-Fi, read-replica lag, CDN caching, and the menu already open on the user's phone
Payment gateway latency and delivery partner assignment
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: The answer lists tablet sync, replica lag, CDN or gateway caches and the menu already loaded on screen as adders; the last one can last until the user refreshes.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: Why did 2,000 people manage to place orders for a dish that was already out of stock?
options: The restaurant's tablet failed to save the change to the database
Users placed orders from an old version of the app
Payment success was confirmed before the menu loaded
The order path validated against the same stale cached menu as the browse path
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: Cart and checkout trusted the stale copy, so orders were created and rejected by the restaurant minutes later. Browse may be stale; money paths must not be.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: You can make only one change this sprint to cut bad Butter Chicken orders from 2,000 to near zero. Which is it?
options: Lower the menu cache TTL from 60 s to 5 s
Check availability at checkout against a Redis key written synchronously with the DB, with a primary-key fallback
Push menu changes to open apps over WebSocket
Set the Elasticsearch refresh interval to 1 s
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: Correctness comes from an authoritative check on the write path; then a stale menu can only show a wrong badge, not create a bad order. The other options improve freshness but checkout would still trust a copy.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: A teammate proposes cutting the menu cache TTL from 60 s to 5 s as the main fix. What are the two strongest objections?
options: It breaks Redis eviction and violates the cache's memory limit
It makes the menu look different on Android and iOS
It multiplies DB rebuild reads about 12x for every hot menu, and checkout still trusts a copy, so correctness isn't guaranteed
It forces the search index to be rebuilt from scratch every 5 s
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: Lowering the TTL re-reads every hot menu whether it changed or not, raising stampede risk at peak, and it leaves search and client staleness with no correctness guarantee at checkout.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: At checkout, the cart has three items from one restaurant, and the Redis availability hash has missed one of them. How should the service read availability without stampeding the database?
options: Fall back to a primary-key read with single-flight, so one query per restaurant serves all waiting requests
Query a read replica per item without coordination, since replicas are cheap
Reject the checkout until the cache is repopulated by the next TTL refresh
Assume the item is in stock and let the restaurant reject it later
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: Checkout does one batched HMGET; on a miss, single-flight lets one request load from the primary while others wait. Replica reads can be stale, and assuming in-stock brings back bad orders.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: To replace TTL polling, the answer publishes availability changes reliably. Which pipeline does it use?
options: The menu service writes directly to Redis, Elasticsearch and push servers in one request
A cron job scans the menu table every 10 s for changes
The tablet sends events straight to every consumer over HTTP
An outbox row committed with the item row, published by Debezium CDC to a Kafka topic keyed by item_id
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: The outbox makes the change durable once in the same transaction, CDC publishes it, and each consumer (cache, search, push) retries independently. Writing directly to every system is a dual write with no retry on failure.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: Why is the Kafka topic item_availability_changed keyed by item_id?
options: So that all changes for one item land on one partition and stay in order
So that consumers can skip items they don't recognise
So that Kafka compresses messages for popular items better
So that each restaurant gets its own consumer group
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: Keying by item keeps one item's changes ordered on a single partition. Versions on each event then handle replays and redeliveries.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: Butter Chicken flips out of stock (version 42) and back in (version 43) a second later. The cache consumer receives 43, then a redelivered 42. What should happen?
options: Apply 42, because the latest message received always wins
Ignore 42, because it is older than the stored version 43
Delete the cache key so the next reader refills from the database
Pause the consumer and alert on-call to resolve the conflict
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: Events carry a monotonically increasing version, and consumers apply only newer versions with an idempotent overwrite. Applying 42 would wrongly mark the dish out of stock.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: Reader A misses the cache and reads the old value from a lagging replica. Meanwhile the invalidation deletes the key. Then A writes the old value back for a full TTL. What fixes this race?
options: Shorten the TTL so the stale value expires sooner
Add more read replicas to reduce lag
Versioned compare-and-set (set only if newer), refilling from the primary, or delayed double delete
Disable caching for the menu entirely
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: This is the stale-refill race; 'delete on change' alone isn't consistent. Version-checked writes, primary refills or a delayed second delete stop the old value being written back.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: Your menu is one 40 KB blob per restaurant containing names, photos, prices and availability. Why split it?
options: Redis cannot store values larger than 32 KB
Search engines cannot index nested JSON blobs
Prices must be stored in a separate PCI-compliant store
Volatile fields change many times an hour; one blob means every toggle invalidates static data and one TTL fits neither
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: Keep static menu data in a long-TTL versioned, CDN-cacheable key, and availability in a tiny Redis hash overlaid at read time with one batched read for the 20-50 restaurants on the page.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: If availability is overlaid at read time from Redis instead of being indexed, what happens to the search refresh lag problem?
options: It stops mattering, because the index never knows about stock
It gets worse, because the index now refreshes less often
It moves to Redis, which now needs a 30 s refresh
It is unchanged, because search still returns the dish
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: Search returns candidates and the API greys out unavailable items with a 1-2 ms pipelined Redis read, so a search from t=0.7 s already shows the dish as unavailable.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: You now have event-driven invalidation. Should you remove the cache TTL entirely?
options: Yes, events make TTLs redundant and only add load
No, keep a longer TTL (5-10 minutes) plus a reconciler as a safety net for lost or delayed events
No, keep the original 60 s TTL exactly as it was
Yes, but only after moving the cache to the CDN
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: Outbox plus CDC is at-least-once and consumers can be down, so a longer TTL heals any missed event. It is a backstop, not the freshness mechanism.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: Your manager worries that event-driven invalidation will increase database load at dinner peak. What is the best answer?
options: It does increase load, so add read replicas before rolling it out
It increases load only on the search cluster, not the database
Work scales with the few keys that change, not with every hot key expiring on a timer, so DB load drops
Load stays the same, because the TTL still forces periodic re-reads
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: A few hundred toggles a minute each touch one small key, whereas TTL polling re-reads every hot menu every period. In the worked example the change cost one write, one outbox row and a few fallback reads.

Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.q: With the redesign, how quickly is checkout correct after the manager taps 'Out of stock', and how long until every view agrees?
options: Both within about 0.5 s
Checkout in about 5 s, views in about 30 s
Checkout and views both in about 2-4 s
Checkout in about 0.5 s; all views in about 2.5-4 s
Swiggy SDE-3 system design: A restaurant.why: Checkout reads the synchronously written Redis key, so it is right within about half a second. Browse views follow via CDC, consumers, index updates and push, adding up to roughly 2.5-4 s.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: A UPI payment request from your checkout times out after 30 seconds. What should your system record?
options: Failed, and show a Retry button so the customer can pay again
Pending (unknown), because the debit and credit may already have happened
Success, because most UPI payments eventually go through
Cancelled, and release the order back to the cart
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: A timeout says nothing about whether the work was done; only the reply may have been lost. Marking it Failed and allowing a new payment can charge the customer twice.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: A UPI request can break before the debit, after the debit but before the credit, or after everything with only the reply lost. How do these three look from the customer's phone?
options: Each shows a different error code, so the app can tell them apart
The first shows 'failed'; the other two show 'pending'
All three look the same: a spinner, then silence
Only the last one times out; the others fail fast
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: From the phone, all three cases are indistinguishable, which is exactly why a timeout must be stored as Pending and resolved later rather than guessed.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: Your payment service calls the gateway first and saves the payment record only after the gateway replies. The service crashes mid-call. What is the problem?
options: Money may move with no record on your side, so you can't check its status or reconcile it
The gateway will automatically refund any payment without a merchant record
The customer will see a duplicate SMS from their bank
Nothing, because the gateway's callback will recreate the record
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: Save first (state Initiated with a unique key), then call the bank. Then every payment, even one interrupted by a crash, can be found and resolved.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: A customer taps Pay again while the first payment is still pending. Your app generates a fresh transaction reference for the retry. What is the risk?
options: None, because the bank de-duplicates by the customer's phone number
The retry will be slower because the gateway rate-limits new keys
The first payment will be cancelled automatically
A new key looks like a new payment, so the customer can be charged twice
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: Idempotency only works if retries reuse the same key; every layer de-duplicates on it. Generating a new key on retry is exactly how double charges happen.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: Two retries for the same order hit two different app servers at the same instant, each trying to create the payment. What ensures only one payment is created?
options: A unique constraint on the idempotency key: one insert wins, the other reads the winner's record
The load balancer's sticky sessions, which route both to one server
A check in application code that looks up the key before inserting
The gateway's fraud check, which blocks the second request
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: The database's unique index makes the race safe: the losing insert hits a duplicate-key error and returns the existing result. A lookup-then-insert in app code alone is a check-then-act race.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: Your webhook handler receives the same Success callback three times for one payment. What should happen?
options: Confirm the order three times and let fulfilment de-duplicate
Only the first changes state and confirms the order; the others see a final Success and do nothing
Reject all three, since duplicates suggest a spoofing attack
Mark the payment Pending again and re-run a status check
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: Callbacks can be lost, delayed or repeated, so the handler must be idempotent: 'if already Success, ignore'.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: Your team relies only on gateway webhooks to resolve pending payments. Some orders stay pending forever. What is missing?
options: A shorter gateway timeout so fewer payments go pending
A second webhook URL for redundancy
A status-check job with backoff for lost callbacks, plus reconciliation as the final check
A rule to mark payments Failed after 60 seconds without a callback
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: Callbacks give speed but get lost. Polling covers lost callbacks, and reconciliation against settlement files is the final judge. Auto-failing after 60 s would treat unknown as failed.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: Your status-check job polls pending payments. Why does it use backoff instead of asking every second?
options: Because the status API returns cached answers for the first few minutes
Because backoff makes payments complete faster
Because UPI transactions cannot change state after the first minute
Because NPCI limits how soon and how often apps may call status, since millions of anxious retries would overload banks
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: Checks are spaced out (for example 90 seconds, then a few minutes, then later), and after a cutoff the payment is left Pending for reconciliation.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: Which source is the final source of truth for whether a UPI payment really happened?
options: The settlement files from NPCI and the banks listing money that actually settled
The status-check API response from the gateway
The latest webhook received by the merchant
The customer's bank SMS saying the amount was debited
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: Status APIs are a fast guess and can be wrong or unavailable; a debit SMS doesn't prove the payee was credited. Settled money in the official files is the truth that reconciliation matches against.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: Nightly reconciliation finds a payment marked Pending internally but listed as Settled in the NPCI file. The order is still open. What do you do?
options: Leave it Pending until the customer contacts support
Mark it Success and confirm the order
Mark it Failed and refund, since it timed out earlier
Ask the gateway's status API and trust that over the file
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: Settled money is the source of truth, so the payment is Success and the order is completed. If the order had already been cancelled, you would refund instead and log it.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: Reconciliation finds 12 payments marked Failed internally that appear as Settled in the settlement file. What is the correct handling?
options: Silently flip them to Success in the database
Ignore them, since final states never change
Send them to the exceptions queue so the team either fulfils the order or refunds the customer
Wait for the next settlement cycle to see whether they disappear
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: Final states never silently flip; a contradiction means money moved, so it raises an alert and goes to an exceptions queue for a deliberate fulfil-or-refund decision.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: A customer's bank debited ₹500, but the payment truly failed because the payee bank couldn't credit it. How does the customer get the money back?
options: The merchant must manually transfer ₹500 back via NEFT
The customer must file a chargeback with NPCI within 30 days
The gateway retries the credit until the payee bank accepts it
The payer bank auto-reverses the debit, typically by T+1, through its reconciliation with NPCI
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: RBI turnaround rules require failed UPI debits to be reversed, typically by the next working day, with compensation for delay. The reversal is triggered by the bank, not by the customer asking.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: What should the app show the customer while a payment is pending?
options: 'Payment pending. Do not pay again.' with the UPI reference, the Pay button blocked, and a notification on resolution
'Payment failed. Please try again.' so they can complete the order quickly
A spinner that continues until the payment resolves, however long that takes
'Payment successful' to avoid panic, correcting it later if needed
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: Good apps say exactly what they know. Showing the reference and blocking Pay for that order prevents most panic retries.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: Hours after a payment was marked Failed, a late Success callback arrives. What should the system do?
options: Ignore it, because Failed is final
Raise an alert, then deliberately fulfil the order or refund, and record why
Flip the state to Success automatically and ship the order
Flip the state to Pending and wait for reconciliation
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: Final states don't silently flip. A contradicting late message is surfaced to humans, who resolve it explicitly; ignoring it could leave the customer charged with no order.

You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.q: A teammate says, "Idempotency is the bank's problem; our backend doesn't need it." What is the best response?
options: Agree, because NPCI guarantees exactly-once delivery
Agree, as long as the app disables the Pay button after one tap
Disagree, every layer needs it: app, merchant backend, gateway, webhook handler and bank
Disagree, but only the webhook handler needs to be idempotent
You pay ₹500 by UPI, the app spins and s.why: Duplicates can enter at any layer, from double taps to repeated webhooks to server retries, so each must de-duplicate on the same transaction reference.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: Your wallet service stores each user's money as one balance column and runs UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 349. A user claims they were charged twice. What is the core problem with this design?
options: The UPDATE is too slow for wallet traffic at peak
Integer columns cannot store rupee amounts accurately
The old value is overwritten, so there is no history to prove what happened
Balance columns cannot be indexed for fast lookups
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: A single overwritten number loses history, invites lost updates and can't be reconciled line by line. A ledger keeps the movements; the balance becomes a cache.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: Two requests read a wallet balance of ₹500, each subtracts ₹349 in application code and writes back ₹151. What has happened?
options: A lost update: ₹349 has been given away
A correct result, since both writes produce the same value
A deadlock that the database will resolve by rolling one back
A rounding error from floating-point arithmetic
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: Read-modify-write in application code lets both requests act on the same stale ₹500, so two purchases debit only one ₹349.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: In a double-entry ledger using signed amounts (debit positive, credit negative), what invariant must every transaction satisfy?
options: The debit entry must always be larger than the credit entry
Each transaction must touch exactly two accounts
The wallet entry must always be negative
All entries of the transaction must sum to zero
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: Money is never created or destroyed inside the system, so each transaction's entries sum to zero, and therefore the whole ledger always sums to zero. Transactions can have more than two entries, like a purchase with merchant and commission credits.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: A user tops up ₹500 by UPI and the money lands in the company's escrow bank account. Which entries does the ledger post (in paise)?
options: wallet:42 +50000 and bank:escrow -50000
bank:escrow +50000 (debit) and wallet:42 -50000 (credit)
wallet:42 +50000 only, since the bank already recorded its side
bank:escrow +50000 and revenue:topup -50000
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: Escrow is an asset (increases are debits) and the wallet is a liability the company owes the user (increases are credits). The two entries sum to zero.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: User 42 (wallet ₹500) buys a ₹349 order, and the platform keeps 5% commission. Which posting is correct?
options: wallet:42 +34900, merchant:7 payable -33155, revenue:commission -1745
wallet:42 -34900, merchant:7 payable +34900
wallet:42 +34900, bank:escrow -34900
wallet:42 +34900, merchant:7 payable -34900, revenue:commission -1745
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: The wallet is debited ₹349, the merchant is owed ₹331.55 and commission earns ₹17.45, summing to zero. No money leaves the bank yet; only who it belongs to changes. The last option doesn't sum to zero.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: A support agent finds a top-up posted as ₹5,000 instead of ₹500. How should it be fixed?
options: UPDATE the entry's amount to 50000 and add a note in the reason column
DELETE the wrong transaction and post the correct one
Post a reversal transaction with opposite signs referencing the original, then post the correct ₹500
Adjust the cached balance to ₹500 and leave the entries as they are
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: Entries are append-only; editing destroys the audit trail and breaks past reconciliation. Many teams even revoke UPDATE and DELETE for the app's database user.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: Why do many teams revoke UPDATE and DELETE permissions on ledger tables for the application's database user?
options: To make inserts faster by avoiding row locks
Because regulators forbid SELECT queries on ledger tables
So that only the DBA can post new transactions
So that even a bug cannot rewrite money history
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: Application code should only INSERT. Removing the permissions enforces append-only at the database level, protecting the audit trail.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: Summing millions of entries every time a user opens the app is too slow. How should you keep a fast balance?
options: A cached balance row updated in the same DB transaction as the entries, with a row lock, and periodically recomputed from entries
A balance stored in Redis, updated asynchronously after each posting
A nightly batch job that recomputes all balances
Store the balance as the source of truth and derive entries from it
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: The cache can never disagree after commit if it changes in the same transaction. The row lock decides 'enough balance?', and periodic recomputation catches bugs, where the entries win.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: Two ₹349 purchases arrive at the same moment for a wallet holding ₹500. What stops both from succeeding?
options: A check in application code that reads the balance first
Locking the wallet's cached balance row (SELECT FOR UPDATE or a version check) inside the posting transaction
The zero-sum check, which rejects the second transaction
The idempotency key, since both purchases come from the same user
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: The row lock serialises the two postings, so the second waits, sees ₹151 and is rejected. The idempotency key wouldn't help because these are two different business events with different keys.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: A developer stores amounts as double and plans to round at the end. Why is that wrong?
options: Doubles cannot hold amounts larger than ₹1 lakh
Doubles are slower to add than integers in Java
Most decimal fractions aren't exact in binary, so errors accumulate before rounding and services round differently
Doubles are not supported by PostgreSQL bigint columns
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004; across millions of transactions balances drift by paise. Store whole paise in a 64-bit integer and round once, deliberately.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: You need to split ₹100 equally among three accounts. How should the ledger record it?
options: 33.33 rupees each, stored as doubles
3333 paise each, with the leftover paisa dropped
3333.33 paise each, rounded at month end
3333 + 3333 + 3334 paise, handling the remainder explicitly
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: Integer paise force you to place the remainder deliberately so the total still equals 10000 paise and the posting still sums to zero.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: A client sends "debit ₹349 for order OD991", times out without seeing the reply, and retries. Which key design prevents a double charge?
options: An idempotency key derived from the business event, like purchase:OD991, with a database unique constraint
A fresh UUID generated by the client on each attempt
A timestamp-based key so the ledger can spot near-simultaneous requests
A client-side check that queries the ledger before retrying
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: The retry hits the unique key and gets back the first result. A fresh key per attempt protects nothing, and a client-side check is a check-then-act race.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: The ledger sums to zero, yet the escrow account in the ledger shows ₹2,000 more than the bank statement. What most likely happened, and what catches it?
options: A floating-point error; recompute balances from entries
A top-up was marked successful but the bank never settled it; bank reconciliation catches it
A missing reversal entry; the zero-sum check catches it
A race condition on the cached balance; the row lock catches it
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: Zero-sum proves internal consistency only. A balanced but wrong ledger is found by matching escrow entries against bank statement lines, for example by UTR.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: Reconciliation finds ₹500 that arrived in the bank but has no ledger entry, because the payment callback was lost. What should happen?
options: Credit it to the company's revenue account until someone complains
Ignore it, because the ledger is the source of truth
Park it in a suspense account, then post the top-up properly (or refund) once identified
Credit it to the most recent user who attempted a top-up
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: The suspense account holds money you can't yet explain. Its balance should trend to zero; a growing suspense balance is a red flag.

How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.q: One large merchant account receives thousands of credits per second, and its balance row has become a hot spot. What is a recommended fix?
options: Remove the row lock for merchant accounts
Store the merchant balance as a double for faster updates
Post to the merchant only at month end
Split it into several sub-accounts and sum them for the balance, or post in batches
How do wallets and payment apps keep mon.why: Sharding a hot account into sub-accounts spreads the locking, and batching reduces postings. User wallets are naturally spread out, so they rarely need this.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: A marketplace has crores of listings and a 100-200 ms budget per search. Why does it split search into retrieval and ranking instead of scoring every product with its best model?
options: Because ranking models can only read text, not numbers
Because a heavy model over crores of items won't fit the budget, so cheap retrieval finds candidates and expensive ranking orders a few hundred
Because retrieval is more accurate than ranking for popular queries
Because the search index can store only a few thousand products
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: Retrieval is fast and rough and aims for recall; ranking is expensive and aims for precision on a small set. One big model over everything is simply too slow.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: A user types "red nike running shoes size 9". What should query understanding do with "red", "nike" and "size 9"?
options: Drop them as stop words so retrieval is faster
Match them only as plain words in the product description
Extract them as attributes (colour, brand, size) and use them as filters
Send them to the ads system to choose sponsored results
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: Attribute extraction turns them into colour = red, brand = Nike, size = 9, which become filters, not just words to match. Query understanding also fixes typos, adds synonyms and predicts the category.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: For the query "running shoes", a "running shoes" phone cover keeps appearing near the top. Which query-understanding step should push it down?
options: Category prediction, which classifies the query as Footwear > Sports Shoes
Spelling correction based on edit distance
Synonym expansion to 'sneakers' and 'trainers'
BM25 length normalisation
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: A small classifier predicts the query's category (say 92% Sports Shoes), and products from other categories are pushed down or dropped.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: A shopper searches "jogging trainers", but the best product's title says "Running Shoes" and shares no word with the query. Which retrieval method finds it?
options: Keyword retrieval from an inverted index
Exact-match filtering on the title field
BM25 with a higher k1 value
Semantic retrieval with embeddings, where similar meanings sit close together
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: Embeddings turn queries and products into vectors where meaning, not shared words, decides closeness. An inverted index needs the words to overlap.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: In a 1,000-product catalogue, "shoes" appears in 200 products and "running" in 50. Under IDF, which word tells you more when it matches?
options: 'running', because rarer words carry more information (ln 20 = 3.0 vs ln 5 = 1.6)
'shoes', because it appears in more products
Both equally, since both are in the query
'shoes', because it is the product type
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: IDF is roughly log(total products / products containing the word), so rarer words get a higher weight.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: A seller's title is "Shoes Shoes Shoes Formal Shoes". With plain TF-IDF it outscores "Nike Running Shoes for Men" for the query "running shoes" (6.4 vs 4.6). What fixes this?
options: Removing the word 'shoes' from the index
BM25 saturation, where repeats add less and less, so the stuffed title drops to about 2.7
Boosting products with longer titles
Sorting candidates by price before scoring
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: BM25's term weight tf x (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1) gives only 1.69 for four repeats with k1 = 1.2, so keyword stuffing can't catch up with a title matching both words. BM25 also slightly penalises long titles.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: Two Nike running shoes have almost identical text relevance for the query. What mostly decides which ranks first?
options: Which one was listed in the catalogue earlier
Which one has the longer description
Behaviour and business signals: query-level conversion, ratings with review count, stock, delivery speed, price
Which seller paid more for the listing
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: Text match only gets products into the candidate set; the final order is decided mostly by behaviour, quality, availability and personal signals.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: Product A has 5.0 stars from 3 reviews; product B has 4.4 stars from 20,000. How should ranking treat them?
options: Rank A higher, since its rating is higher
Ignore ratings entirely, since they can be faked
Average the two ratings and treat both the same
Trust B more: smooth ratings toward the category average by review count, or give the model the count as a feature
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: A rating from 3 reviews is weak evidence. Smoothing (or letting the model learn from the review count) captures that 4.4 from 20,000 is more reliable.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: A new ranking model raises CTR by 5% but conversion falls. What has most likely happened?
options: It promotes items that attract clicks but don't sell, like very cheap or flashy listings
The A/B test was run for too long
The model improved relevance but users need time to adjust
The search index lost some products during the rollout
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: CTR alone can be gamed by clickbait images and fake discounts. Optimise for purchases as the main label, with returns and cancellations as guardrails.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: Your team trains a learning-to-rank model on click logs, and it mostly reproduces the old ranking. Why?
options: Gradient-boosted trees cannot learn from click data
The logs are position-biased: top items got clicks partly because they were shown at the top
The model has too few features to learn anything new
Click logs are deleted after one day, so there is too little data
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: Item 1 gets clicked partly because it is at position 1. Teams correct this with position as a training-only feature, a little randomisation, or click models.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: When building learning-to-rank training data from logs, which labelling scheme does the answer describe?
options: Shown = 3, clicked = 2, added to cart = 1, bought = 0
Clicked = 1, everything else = 0
Bought = 3, added to cart = 2, clicked = 1, shown but ignored = 0
Labels assigned by human raters only, never from logs
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: Graded labels from behaviour let the model learn to put purchased items above clicked ones and clicked ones above ignored ones; models like LambdaMART then learn the ordering.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: Your main LTR model is too slow to score 3,200 candidates in time. What is the standard approach?
options: Score only the first 100 candidates returned by the index
Replace the model with a hand-tuned weighted formula
Skip ranking for popular queries and sort by sales
A ranking cascade: a cheap first-pass model trims to a few hundred, and the heavy model scores those
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: In the worked example, a light model using BM25, category match and sales keeps the top 400, and the LTR model scores those 400.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: Two people search "running shoes". One usually buys Asics around Rs 3,000 in men's UK 9. How does personalisation affect their results?
options: Brand, price, size and location affinities enter the ranking model as features, so matching items rise
The query is rewritten to 'Asics running shoes size 9' for that user
Products that don't match the user's history are removed from retrieval
Personalised results are shown only in sponsored slots
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: Personalisation adds features like brand affinity = 0.8. It should stay light for very specific queries or new users, and respect privacy settings.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: A seller with an irrelevant product bids very high to appear for "running shoes". How should a good ad system handle this?
options: Show it in the top slot, since ads are ranked by bid
Rank ads by bid x predicted click probability x relevance, with a relevance floor, so it can't simply outbid everyone
Show it only to users who have bought from that seller
Mix it into organic results without a 'Sponsored' label
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: Irrelevant ads earn nothing and harm trust. Ads go in fixed, labelled slots, must pass a relevance floor, and you measure total conversion, not just ad clicks.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: Your ranking puts items with relevance grades [0, 3, 2] in positions 1-3. The ideal order [3, 2, 0] has DCG 4.26, and yours has DCG 2.89. What is the NDCG, and what does it mean?
options: 1.47; the ranking is better than ideal
0.32; most relevant items are missing from the results
0.68; the good items are present but not in the best order
0.68; the ranking is correct but the grades are too low
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: NDCG = 2.89 / 4.26 = 0.68, with 1.0 being perfect. Here the most relevant item sits at position 2 instead of 1.

You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.q: A new ranking model lifts offline NDCG from 0.71 to 0.74. Should you ship it?
options: Not yet: offline metrics pick candidates, and an A/B test on conversion, with guardrails like returns, decides
