Yes, a higher NDCG always means more purchases
Yes, but only if CTR in the logs also went up
No, NDCG improvements below 0.05 are never meaningful
You search \"running shoes\" on a shoppi.why: Offline NDCG is computed on saved data; real users decide. In the worked example the model went to 10% of users for a week and shipped after conversion rose 1.8% with no rise in returns.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: You toss a coin 10 times and get 6 heads, then 1,000 times and get 600 heads. Why are the two results so different in what they tell you?
options: The second has a higher ratio of heads
The first was done too quickly to count
With more tosses, luck has less room to hide, so the same 60% is far more convincing
Coins become biased after many tosses
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: A fair coin gives 6+ heads in 10 tosses about 38% of the time, but 600 in 1,000 less than once in a billion tries. Sample size decides how much a ratio means, which is the core idea of A/B testing.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: You showed the new Buy now button to everyone this week and saw 3% more clicks than last week. Why can't you credit the button?
options: Weekly comparisons always underestimate the effect
Salary day, a cricket final or a new campaign may also have changed this week; that is confounding
Clicks are not a valid metric for any button test
The button needs at least a month before any comparison
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: Comparing different periods mixes the button's effect with everything else that changed. A random split in the same period exposes both groups to the same events.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: In an A/B test, why does random assignment of users to control and treatment matter?
options: It balances everything else (week events, platform, city, user tenure), so the only systematic difference is the change
It guarantees the treatment group will perform better
It removes the need to calculate a sample size
It lets you choose which users see the new design
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: Randomisation balances even the factors you didn't think of, so any gap is either the change or chance, and statistics measures the chance part.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: A user sees the green button on Monday and the orange one on Tuesday because your test assigns by session cookie. What is the recommended fix?
options: Assign users randomly on every page view
Store each user's group in a cookie that expires daily
Show both buttons and let users pick
Hash a stable user ID together with the experiment name and take it modulo 100
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: Hashing a logged-in user ID is deterministic, so a user always lands in the same bucket without storing anything. Including the experiment name keeps different experiments' splits independent.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: Why include the experiment name in the hash, rather than hashing only the user ID?
options: So different experiments get independent splits and the same users aren't always together in group B
Because MD5 needs at least two inputs
So the experiment can be renamed without reassigning users
To make the hash harder for users to reverse
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: Without the experiment name, every experiment would split users identically, so one group would always get every treatment and effects would interfere.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: You're testing a brighter Buy now button. Which primary metric should you pre-declare?
options: Clicks on Buy now, since that's what the button changes
Time spent on the product page
Orders per exposed user, with guardrails like page load, cart abandonment and returns
The number of metrics that improve
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: Clicks are easy to move and easy to fool; a bright button can draw curious clicks that abandon the cart. Pick a metric close to business value and write it down before the test starts.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: Your baseline click rate is 4% and you want to detect a 3% relative lift (0.12 points) at 5% significance and 80% power. Using n ~ 16 x p x (1-p) / d^2, roughly how many users do you need per group?
options: About 4,300
About 50,000
About 120,000
About 427,000
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: 16 x 0.04 x 0.96 / 0.0012^2 is about 427,000 per group. A one-week test with 50,000 per group simply cannot see a 3% lift reliably.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: Your PM now wants to detect a lift half as large as originally planned. What happens to the required sample size?
options: It doubles
It roughly quadruples
It stays the same, since only power matters
It halves
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: Noise shrinks only with the square root of the sample, so halving the minimum detectable effect needs about four times the users.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: After a week with 50,000 users per group, control converts at 4.00% and treatment at 4.12%. The standard error is about 0.00125, so z is about 0.96 and p about 0.34. What is the right conclusion?
options: The 3% lift is real, ship it
The green button is worse than orange
Not significant: the gap is within noise and the CI (roughly -3% to +9% relative) includes zero
The test proves the button has no effect
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: A gap smaller than one standard error is what luck produces about one week in three. 'Not significant' means the test couldn't tell, not that there is no effect.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: A test returns p = 0.03. Your manager says, "So there's a 97% chance the button works." What is the correct interpretation?
options: If the button did nothing, a gap this big would appear about 3% of the time
There is a 3% chance the button is harmful
The button's true lift is 97% of the observed lift
Yes, that is exactly what p = 0.03 means
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: The p-value assumes the change does nothing and asks how surprising the data is. It is not the probability that your idea is right.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: The 95% confidence interval for the lift is -1.2% to +9.1%. What does this tell you?
options: The change definitely improves the metric by about 4%
The test was invalid and must be discarded
The change definitely does nothing
The interval crosses zero, so you can't rule out no effect or even harm
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: The CI is the range of plausible true effects. One like +0.1% to +5.9% says probably positive but possibly tiny; one crossing zero leaves 'no effect' on the table.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: A teammate checks the dashboard daily and wants to stop the test the first day p drops below 0.05. Why is that a problem?
options: Daily dashboards use a different formula for p-values
Each look is another chance for noise to cross the line, raising false positives from 5% to roughly 20-30%
Tests must always run exactly 30 days
Stopping early reduces the effect size
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: This is peeking. Fix the sample size and look once at the end, or use sequential testing methods designed for continuous monitoring.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: You hit your planned sample size on day 3 of the test. What should you do?
options: Stop now, since the sample size is reached
Restart the test with a larger sample
Keep running to complete whole weeks (at least 1, usually 2), because behaviour follows a weekly cycle
Extend it into the upcoming sale for extra traffic
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: Weekend shoppers differ from weekday office browsers, so partial weeks bias the result. Also avoid starting or ending inside a big sale, whose traffic is atypical.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: A new button shows +8% on days 1-2 and +1% by day 10. What is likely happening, and how do you check?
options: Sample ratio mismatch; rerun the chi-square test
Multiple testing; apply a Bonferroni correction
Seasonality; compare with last year's data
A novelty effect; plot lift by day and compare new users with returning users
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: Users click because the design is new, and the lift fades. If it fades for returning users, expect the long-run lift to be the smaller number.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: You tracked 15 metrics and one shows p = 0.04. The others show nothing. Is that a win?
options: Probably not: with 15 metrics at 5%, at least one false positive is likely (about 54%); treat it as a hypothesis or apply Bonferroni
Yes, p below 0.05 on any metric counts as significant
Yes, because the other 14 metrics didn't get worse
No, because only metrics with p below 0.01 are ever valid
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: Testing many metrics or slices inflates false positives. One pre-declared primary metric decides; secondary 'wins' become new tests, or tighten the threshold to about 0.05/15.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: Your 50/50 test shows 51,000 users in control and 49,000 in treatment. What should you do before looking at the metrics?
options: Nothing, a 2% imbalance is normal random variation
Treat it as sample ratio mismatch, distrust all metrics, and find the bug (crashes, redirects, bot filters, logging gaps)
Reweight the groups so they are equal and read the results
Drop the extra 2,000 control users and continue
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: A fair split almost never produces this imbalance at this scale; it signals broken assignment or logging that can bias every metric. Reweighting hides the bug rather than fixing it.

A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.q: After two full weeks, clicks are up about 3% early on but settle near +2%, orders per user are up 1.8% with guardrails flat, and the SRM check passes. What is the best decision?
options: Ship green and report the +3% click lift from week one as the expected gain
Don't ship, because the lift faded over time
Rerun the test for another month before deciding anything
Ship green expecting about +2% orders, and keep a small holdout on orange to confirm the effect lasts
A new \"Buy now\" button colour gets 3%.why: The result is significant on the primary metric with healthy guardrails, but the novelty effect means the realistic gain is the settled number, not the early spike. A small holdout verifies it persists.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: During checkout, your fraud check needs "orders placed by this device in the last 10 minutes". The order database is huge and the fraud check has about 100 ms. What is the best way to get this number?
options: Use the count from last night's batch job, since it is already computed and cheap to read
Have a streaming job keep per-device windowed counters and read them from an online feature store in a few ms
Ask the payment gateway to return the device's recent order count with its auth response
Run a COUNT query on the orders table for that device inside the checkout request
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: Window counts are kept up to date by streaming jobs (Flink/Kafka Streams) and stored in a low-latency store like Redis, so a lookup takes 1 to 5 ms. A live database query is too slow for the latency budget, and a nightly count misses the burst happening right now.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: A 4-year-old account suddenly logs in from a brand-new Android phone in another city, changes the address to a new pincode and orders a 95,000-rupee phone. The model scores it 0.61. What is the best action?
options: Allow it, because a 4-year-old account with clean history is very unlikely to be fraud
Challenge it: ask for an OTP on the registered mobile, which the real owner passes and an attacker cannot
Hold it for manual review for a day so an analyst can call the customer before dispatch
Block the order and lock the account, since new device plus high value is classic takeover
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: A medium score calls for a cheap challenge: the genuine owner clears it in seconds while an attacker with only the password cannot. Blocking is the most expensive mistake if the customer is real.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: The risk service starts timing out during a big sale. What should checkout do?
options: Keep retrying the risk service until it answers, even if checkout then takes several seconds
Follow a pre-agreed fallback: allow low-value orders from trusted users, challenge or queue risky ones, and score skipped orders later
Block every order until the risk service recovers, because unchecked orders are too dangerous
Allow every order without exception and skip scoring them, since sale revenue matters most
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: A timeout with a fallback agreed in advance (fail open for low-value trusted orders, fail safe for risky ones) keeps checkout alive without leaving everything unchecked. Blocking all orders turns an outage into lost sales for every customer.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: A team proudly reports that their new fraud model is 99% accurate on orders where under 1% are fraud. What is the right response?
options: Check only the ROC curve, because accuracy and ROC-AUC always tell the same story
Ship it, because 99% accuracy means only 1 in 100 decisions will ever be wrong
Ask for precision, recall and money saved versus good sales lost, since "never fraud" alone scores about 99%
Ask them to push accuracy to 99.9% first, since fraud needs extra-high accuracy
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: With fraud this rare, a model that approves everything is already about 99% accurate and catches nothing. Precision, recall and rupee impact show whether it actually helps.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: A rule blocks any device with more than 5 failed card attempts in 10 minutes. Fraudsters now stop at 4 attempts per device and spread across many devices. What is the best response?
options: Drop all rules and rely only on the ML model, so there is no threshold to learn
Show users the exact block reason so genuine customers know how to avoid it
Combine the rule with the ML model and graph features linking shared devices, cards and addresses
Lower the threshold to 1 failed attempt so nobody can stay under it any more
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: Fraudsters learn rule thresholds, so you mix rules with a model that is hard to reverse-engineer and graph links that expose rings even below the threshold. A threshold of 1 would block huge numbers of genuine users who mistype a card.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: Your fraud model only learns from orders that were let through, because blocked orders never get a true label. How do you get unbiased labels for borderline cases?
options: Treat every blocked order as confirmed fraud and add it to the training labels
Retrain only on manual review outcomes, since reviewers see exactly the borderline cases
Wait for chargebacks on blocked orders, since banks still report them after a block
Let a tiny random sample of borderline orders through as a control group and see how they turn out
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: A blocked order never shows whether it was really fraud, so a small random control group gives honest labels for retraining and threshold tuning. Labelling every block as fraud just teaches the model its own past decisions.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: A fraud model looked excellent offline, but live scores are strange. You find the training data computed "orders in last 24h" with a nightly SQL job, while live traffic uses a streaming counter with different rules. What is this problem and the fix?
options: Overfitting; reduce the number of trees so the model generalises better
Training-serving skew; use the same feature definitions to feed both the offline training store and the online store
Concept drift; retrain the model weekly on fresh data and the scores will settle
Latency trouble; move the model closer to the feature store to speed it up
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: When the numbers a model trains on differ from the numbers it sees live, it quietly breaks: that is training-serving skew. Retraining does not help if the two pipelines still compute the feature differently.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: In the last hour, 40 new accounts were created that share two devices and one address, each ordering the 1-rupee speaker deal. What is the best decision?
options: Block the new orders and flag the accounts, since velocity and shared-address graph signals clearly mark a ring
Put all 40 orders into manual review so analysts can judge each account separately
Send an OTP challenge to each account, because each one alone looks like a normal new user
Allow them, because every account is new and has no bad history on its own
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: Accounts per device hitting 20 and 40 accounts on one address is a clear ring caught by velocity rules and graph features, so blocking is justified. An OTP challenge is weak here because the fraudsters control the phones they registered with.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: Your team wants to retrain the fraud model weekly but uses only chargebacks as labels. What is the main problem?
options: Chargebacks arrive 30 to 90 days late, so add fast labels like review outcomes, complaints and failed deliveries
Chargebacks only cover COD orders, so card fraud never gets labelled this way
Chargebacks are too noisy to use at all and should be dropped from training completely
Weekly retraining is too frequent; fraud models should be retrained only once a year
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: Chargebacks are strong labels but come weeks late, so a weekly model trained only on them misses recent patterns. Combining them with faster labels keeps the model current.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: A 3-month-old account with mixed history orders a 30,000-rupee laptop on cash on delivery to a new address. Score is 0.45. What is a sensible action?
options: Block it, since COD to a new address is always a fake order that will be refused
Allow COD as normal, since a score below 0.5 means the order is safe
Cancel the order and ask the customer to place it again after 24 hours
Offer prepaid only or confirm by OTP, so a genuine buyer can still complete the order
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: COD abuse costs shipping both ways, so limiting COD or confirming by OTP is a cheap challenge that keeps the real customer. 0.5 is not a magic safety line; thresholds are business choices.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: A teammate wants to call a third-party device-reputation API that takes about 300 ms at p99, inside the fraud check that has a 100 ms p99 budget. What is the better design?
options: Call it anyway and raise the checkout timeout, since better data always beats speed
Call it sequentially before the feature store so the model gets the freshest value
Call it after the payment gateway, then cancel the order if it comes back bad
Keep slow third-party calls out of the main path; fetch features in parallel from fast stores and precompute what you can
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: The fraud check must fit a strict latency budget because slow checkout loses real customers. Slow external calls belong off the main path, with results cached or scored asynchronously.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: A marketplace does 10 lakh orders a day, and its fraud model wrongly blocks 1 in 1,000 genuine orders. Why does this worry the business?
options: That turns away about 1,000 real buyers every day, and lost good sales can cost more than the fraud stopped
It means about 10,000 real buyers are blocked daily, which breaks the latency budget
It shows the model has low recall, so more fraud is slipping through than expected
It does not; 0.1% is a tiny error rate that customers will never notice
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: 10 lakh x 1/1,000 = 1,000 genuine buyers a day. That is why teams track the false decline rate alongside the fraud rate.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: Your marketplace sees customers returning used items or a cheap fake in place of a high-value phone ("box swapping"). Which response fits?
options: Remove the return option for all electronics so no customer can ever abuse it
Ignore it in the fraud system, since only stolen cards and hijacked accounts count as fraud
Use open-box delivery, serial-number checks at pickup and limited returns for risky users
Raise the card-payment fraud threshold, since returns abuse is a payment fraud problem
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: Returns abuse is a real fraud problem in e-commerce, handled with signals like return rate and serial mismatches plus actions like serial checks. Removing returns for everyone hurts all honest buyers.

How does a payment or shopping app spot.q: A new attack pattern appears at 9 pm on sale night. Why do fraud teams still keep a rules engine next to the ML model?
options: Rules are needed only to generate labels for the model, not to make decisions
Models cannot run in real time, so rules are the only thing that fits the latency budget
Rules can be written and changed in minutes during an attack, and they enforce clear hard policies
Rules are more accurate than models at spotting subtle combinations of weak signals
How does a payment or shopping app spot.why: Rules are fast to change, easy to explain and right for hard policy, while the model catches combinations no analyst would write. Models are the ones better at subtle combinations, not rules.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: It starts raining at 6 pm and your cab fare shows 1.8x. What is the real reason?
options: The app learned you are likely to pay more in the rain and priced your account higher
The app applies a fixed 1.8x rain surcharge whenever weather data shows rain
Fuel and toll costs rise in the rain, so the base fare is recalculated for the evening
In your cell, demand jumped and free supply fell, so the demand-to-supply ratio maps to 1.8x on the pricing curve
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: Rain only changes the inputs: more people open the app while fewer drivers are free and trips take longer. The multiplier comes from the ratio in your cell at that minute, not a fixed rain charge.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: Two friends standing 2 km apart check fares at the same moment. One sees 1.0x, the other 1.7x. Why?
options: One quote was cached from earlier in the day while the other is live
Surge is computed per small cell, and the two cells have different demand-to-supply ratios
Surge is city-wide, so one app must have a bug showing the wrong multiplier
One friend has a newer phone, and premium devices are shown higher prices
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: Prices are set per zone because conditions differ street to street: one cell may have many free drivers, the other many requests. Standard surge is per zone and time, not per person.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: A zone's multiplier shows 1.0x, then 2.0x, then 1.1x in three consecutive minutes and riders feel cheated. What should you add?
options: EMA smoothing, a cap on change per minute and a locked quote once shown to the rider
Recalculation every second so the price always matches the latest ratio
A higher cap so the curve has more room and stops hitting its limit
Smaller cells so each one reacts faster to local demand and supply
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: A moving average plus a step limit (say +0.2x per minute) makes the price climb and fall gradually, and a locked quote protects the rider while they decide. Smaller cells would make the ratio even noisier.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: Why should the surge system count app opens and fare checks, not only actual ride requests?
options: Requests are often fake, so app opens are a more honest measure of demand
App opens are cheaper to log than requests, so they reduce load on Kafka
Many people see a high price and leave without requesting, so counting only requests hides real demand
Regulators require platforms to price on app opens rather than completed requests
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: When prices are high, many riders check and close the app. Counting only requests would make the gap look smaller than it is, and the system would under-price.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: Your team uses tiny 100 m cells. Each cell holds 2 riders and 1 driver, and multipliers jump wildly. What is the best fix?
options: Ignore supply and price only on demand, since driver counts are too small
Switch from hexagons to rectangles, since geohash removes the noise
Use larger cells or blend in drivers from neighbouring cells, since tiny cells make the ratio noisy
Make cells even smaller so each price fits its street more exactly
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: Cell size trades accuracy against noise: too small and a couple of events swing the ratio. Bigger cells, or counting neighbours as partial supply, steady it.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: Sethu accepts a quote of Rs 396 (1.8x). One minute later the zone drops to 1.3x before the driver arrives. What does he pay?
options: Rs 396, because the quote was shown upfront and locked for a few minutes
Whatever the multiplier is when the trip ends, since surge applies per minute
The lower 1.3x fare, because the final price is recomputed at pickup
An average of the two multipliers, to be fair to both rider and driver
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: The fare is quoted upfront and locked: even if the zone's multiplier changes while you decide or wait, the accepted price is what you pay. This prevents riders feeling cheated by flicker.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: Using the textbook curve (ratio up to 1.2 gives 1.0x, rising to the cap at 3.0), a cell at 5:55 pm has demand 29 and supply 26. What is the raw multiplier?
options: About 1.1x, because the multiplier simply equals the ratio
The cap, because any ratio above 1.0 means demand exceeds supply
About 1.5x, because the curve starts rising as soon as demand passes supply
1.0x, because the ratio is about 1.1, inside the no-surge slack
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: 29 / 26 is about 1.1, which is below 1.2, so the curve stays flat at 1.0x. The curve deliberately allows some slack so small gaps do not trigger surge.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: A city-wide flood hits Bengaluru. Surge is at its cap, but very few extra drivers appear. Why?
options: The streaming job stops in rain, so the multiplier never reaches drivers
Higher fares only pull supply if drivers can reach zones in time; in a city-wide flood price mostly rations rides
Drivers never see the surge, because heatmaps are shown only to riders
The cap is too low; raising it would always bring in enough drivers
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: More price brings more drivers only if they get enough of it and can physically move in. In a city-wide disaster supply cannot grow much, and many platforms limit surge in emergencies.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: You notice that in one zone, many drivers go offline together just before peak, then come back once surge kicks in. What should the system do?
options: Flag unusual supply drops as possible gaming and treat them carefully in pricing
Raise the cap in that zone so surge rewards the drivers who stay online
Switch the zone to a fixed price permanently so surge can never be triggered
Nothing; drivers logging off is normal supply, so surge should rise as usual
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: Coordinated log-offs to trigger surge are a known gaming pattern, so systems watch for unusual supply drops. Raising the cap would reward the very behaviour you want to stop.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: A food-delivery app sees orders double during rain but cannot add delivery partners quickly. Which set of levers fits best?
options: Cancelling all orders above a certain distance until the rain stops
Raising restaurant menu prices so fewer people order during rain
A flat rain fee, rainy-hour partner bonuses, and wider ETAs or a smaller delivery radius
A multiplier on the whole bill, applied to food and taxes alike
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: Food delivery runs the same control loop with different levers: a flat fee, incentives to pull partners online, and throttling demand with longer ETAs or a smaller radius. A multiplier on the whole bill is not how these apps usually price.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: A product manager asks you to set a 4x surge cap for autos in a state. What should you check first?
options: Nothing; the cap is purely a company decision and can be any value
The Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines and that state's current rules, which cap surge as a multiple of base fare
The driver union's preference, since only they can approve surge caps
Only what competitors charge in that city, since the market sets the cap
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: In India, aggregator guidelines and state rules cap surge relative to the base fare and also set a floor; the exact numbers vary by state and year, so check the current notification.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: A big cricket match ends at 10 pm near a stadium every week, and surge always kicks in only after long queues form. What would help prices react earlier?
options: Lower the cap near the stadium so riders are not shocked by high prices
Make the smoothing heavier so the multiplier changes more slowly
Add a forecast model using past weeks, weather and events, so prices rise before the queue builds
Count only completed trips, since they are the most reliable demand signal
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: Many systems add a forecast on top of live counts so supply is pulled in before the rush. Heavier smoothing would make the response even later.

Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.q: Your team changed the pricing curve. How should you judge if the change worked?
options: Measure only revenue per ride, since a higher multiplier means pricing works better
Check that the multiplier stays at the cap more often than before
Count how many riders complained on social media in the first week
Measure fulfilment rate, pickup ETA, rider conversion and driver earnings, with experiments by city or time slice
Why does a cab ride cost 1.8x when it ra.why: Surge's job is to balance the market, so you track whether riders get rides quickly and drivers earn well, and test curve changes with experiments. Revenue per ride alone ignores whether people actually got a cab.

When you order food, how does the app de.q: Rider A is 2 min from Restaurant 1 and 3 min from Restaurant 2. Rider B is 4 min from Restaurant 1 and 10 min from Restaurant 2. Orders for 1 then 2 arrive seconds apart. What does batch matching do?
options: Gives Restaurant 1 to A and Restaurant 2 to B, for 12 minutes of total travel
Gives Restaurant 1 to B and Restaurant 2 to A, for 7 minutes of total travel
Gives both orders to A, since A is closest to both restaurants
Waits for a third rider, since no pairing is better than greedy here
When you order food, how does the app de.why: Seeing both orders together, the solver minimises total cost: 4 + 3 = 7 minutes. Greedy locked A into Order 1 before Order 2 arrived, leaving B with a 10-minute trip (12 total).

When you order food, how does the app de.q: Prep time is 18 minutes, the chosen rider is 5 minutes away and the buffer is 2 minutes. Roughly when should the rider be dispatched?
options: Immediately, because assigning instantly is always fastest for the customer
About 13 minutes after the order, so the rider arrives exactly at ready time
About 18 minutes after the order, once the restaurant marks the food ready
About 11 minutes after the order, so the rider arrives just as the food is ready
When you order food, how does the app de.why: dispatch = order time + prep - travel - buffer = 18 - 5 - 2 = 11 minutes. Sending right away would make the rider wait about 13 minutes at the restaurant instead of doing other work.

When you order food, how does the app de.q: It is raining at dinner peak and riders are scarce. When might the engine assign a rider earlier than the timing formula says?
options: Never, because the formula always gives the best dispatch time
Only if the customer pays extra for priority delivery
Only after the restaurant presses the food-ready button
Now, because waiting risks losing nearby riders to other orders and getting only a far one later
When you order food, how does the app de.why: Holding an order makes sense when riders are plentiful. When supply is tight, engines lock in a rider earlier rather than risk ending up with a distant one.

When you order food, how does the app de.q: Two riders' apps both tap "accept" on the same order at the same instant. How do you ensure only one gets it?
options: A conditional update like UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'UNASSIGNED'; the second sees zero rows changed
Read the order status first, then write the rider if it is still unassigned
Assign it to whichever rider's request has the earlier phone timestamp
Let both accept and ask the customer to choose which rider to keep
When you order food, how does the app de.why: A conditional update is atomic, so only the first write changes the row and the other is told the order is taken. A separate read then write leaves a gap where both can see "unassigned".

When you order food, how does the app de.q: A rider's 20-second offer timer runs out because their phone was in their pocket. What should happen to the order?
options: It is cancelled and the customer is asked to reorder
It goes back into the next matching window, usually with higher priority because time was lost
It is sent to the nearest restaurant staff member for delivery
It waits for the same rider to come back, since they were the best match
When you order food, how does the app de.why: Rejections and timeouts return the order to the pool for the next window, boosted in priority. Waiting for the same rider wastes the time the customer has already lost.

When you order food, how does the app de.q: Two orders come from restaurants 300 m apart and go to nearby streets. When should the engine consider giving both to one rider?
options: Only during quiet hours, since batching slows everyone at peak
Only when both customers order from the same restaurant
When ready times are similar, drops are on one route, and the second customer's extra delay stays within a limit
Always, because one rider for two orders halves cost no matter what
When you order food, how does the app de.why: Order batching needs close pickups, similar ready times, drops along one route, and a cap on the second customer's delay (for example 5 to 8 minutes). It helps most at peak, when riders are short.

When you order food, how does the app de.q: Pure lowest-cost assignment keeps giving every order to riders parked near one busy restaurant while others wait an hour. Why fix this, and how?
options: Idle riders log off and supply shrinks; add a penalty for many recent orders and a bonus for long-idle riders
It needs no fix, because lowest cost is always best for customers and the business
Ban riders from waiting near busy restaurants so they spread across the city
Assign orders at random so every rider gets the same number regardless of distance
When you order food, how does the app de.why: Riders are paid per order, so unfairness hits income and drives them off the app, which slows deliveries for everyone. A fairness term in the cost trades a little speed for healthier supply.

When you order food, how does the app de.q: A rider is 1 km from the restaurant in a straight line, but a river lies between them. How should the engine estimate their travel time?
options: Use the restaurant's average delivery time across all its past orders
Use a road-network routing service, which may show 15 minutes instead of 3
Use straight-line distance divided by average bike speed, as it is quick to compute
Ask the rider to type their own estimate each time they get an offer
When you order food, how does the app de.why: Assignment needs real travel ETAs on the road network; straight-line distance ignores rivers, one-ways and flyovers.

When you order food, how does the app de.q: You want to test a new cost-function weight. Why should you split the A/B test by zone or time slot instead of by user?
options: Per-user splits cannot measure delivery time, only conversion
Zones have fewer users, so the experiment finishes faster
Per-user splits are illegal for delivery apps under data protection rules
Riders are shared across users, so a per-user split leaks: both versions compete for the same riders
When you order food, how does the app de.why: Riders serve everyone in an area, so control and treatment orders would influence each other. Splitting by zone or time slot keeps the two worlds separate.

When you order food, how does the app de.q: A restaurant's prep model says 15 minutes, but on Friday nights it regularly takes 25 and riders wait. What should the system do?
options: Learn per-restaurant corrections from the food-ready button and actual rider waits, and re-plan live
Remove the restaurant from the app on Friday nights
Ignore it, since prep times average out over the week
Always dispatch riders immediately for that restaurant to be safe
When you order food, how does the app de.why: Prep estimates are noisy, so systems keep correcting them per restaurant and watch live signals, delaying or swapping riders if the kitchen runs late. Dispatching immediately just makes riders wait longer.

When you order food, how does the app de.q: A product manager says, "Assign the nearest rider the moment the customer pays; it is always fastest." What is the flaw?
options: Instant assignment breaks the conditional update and causes double assignment
Nothing is wrong; nearest-first is what large platforms actually use at scale
Delivery time is the same because food is not ready, but rider time is wasted, slowing other orders at peak
Instant assignment is slower because the matching solver takes several minutes
When you order food, how does the app de.why: If food needs 20 minutes, a rider sent now waits at the counter and the customer gets the food at the same time anyway. That idle capacity is what makes other customers wait at peak.

When you order food, how does the app de.q: How does an assignment engine scale matching to a whole city with thousands of orders a minute?
options: Run one global Hungarian algorithm over every rider and order every second
Give each restaurant its own fixed riders so no matching is needed
Split the city into zones such as a hex grid, match each zone in parallel, and let border riders be seen by neighbours
Send every order to all riders and let the first one to accept win
When you order food, how does the app de.why: Exact solvers work for small tables; at city scale platforms use zones (and faster approximate solvers), solved in parallel, with riders near borders visible to neighbouring zones.

When you order food, how does the app de.q: Why is it acceptable for batch matching to hold orders for a window of 5 to 30 seconds?
options: Riders need that time to finish reading the previous offer
Customers cannot see the delay because the app hides assignment status
The window is needed to wait for payment confirmation from the bank
The food takes 10 to 20 minutes to cook anyway, so a short wait costs little and gives far better matches
When you order food, how does the app de.why: The cost of batching is at most one window of delay, which is tiny compared with prep time, while solving all orders together improves the whole city's assignments.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: Marketing needs a "Rs 100 off on orders above Rs 999 for first-time users" offer live tomorrow. What should happen?
options: Create it as configuration in the offer console, get it approved and schedule it, with no code change
Add a new offer type to the engine, since every new offer needs its own type
Ask engineers to add a new if-condition for first-time users in the cart service
Hard-code the discount in the checkout page for one day and remove it after
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: This is a standard cart-level offer with a user-segment condition, so it is just data. Code is needed only for genuinely new offer types.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: A bank offer's Rs 2 crore budget ended up overspent by Rs 40 lakh during the sale. What most likely went wrong?
options: Budget was checked with a read and a separate write, so many checkouts saw money left at once; reserve atomically instead
The product page cache showed the offer too long, which spent the extra money
The bank changed the budget mid-sale without telling the platform
Too many offers were indexed, so the engine evaluated this one twice per cart
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: Under sale-day load, read-then-write oversells. Atomic reservation (a Redis Lua script or conditional update), release on payment failure, and reconciliation with the ledger fix it.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: The product page showed Rs 21,299, but checkout asks Rs 22,799. Which is a legitimate reason, and what should the system do?
options: The product page is always right, so checkout must have a bug and should charge Rs 21,299
The bank offer's budget ran out or the card's BIN does not match; recalculate and show the new breakdown before payment
The offer engine randomly picks offers, so the price can change between pages
Prices rise at checkout to cover delivery, so no explanation is needed
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: The product page uses cached offers and can be seconds out of date; checkout recalculates from the source of truth with the actual payment method and must show the updated price clearly.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: The platform has 10,000 live offers. How does the offer engine avoid checking all of them for every cart?
options: Show only the 50 newest offers, since older ones are rarely used
Let the customer type the offer name so the engine knows which one to check
Evaluate all 10,000 in parallel on many servers so the cost is spread out
Index offers by SKU, category, brand, seller and payment method, cache the index, and evaluate only the matching candidates
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: An indexer builds lookup tables like category:mobiles to offer ids, cached in Redis and in-process, so each request evaluates tens of candidates instead of thousands.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: During testing, a phone gets a seller deal, a coupon, a bank offer and a brand discount all at once, ending up 85% off. What prevents this "stacking accident"?
options: Allow only one offer per order in all cases, regardless of who funds it
Let the customer service team cancel such orders manually after they are placed
Stack groups, exclusivity and priority rules, plus caps and a maximum combined discount per order
Apply every matching offer, since customers deserve the biggest saving available
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: Combination rules decide which offers can stack, and a maximum combined discount (for example never more than 70% or below cost) is a hard guardrail. Allowing only one offer ever would block legitimate seller plus bank combinations.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: A phone shows Rs 26,999 after a seller deal. The customer adds an exchange worth Rs 4,200 and pays with an X Bank card (10% off, max Rs 1,500). A Rs 500 coupon is exclusive with the bank offer. What is the final price?
options: Rs 20,799, applying both the bank offer and the coupon on top
Rs 22,299, applying the coupon because it is simpler to redeem
Rs 20,519, applying the full 10% of 22,799 without the cap
Rs 21,299, since 10% of 22,799 is capped at Rs 1,500, which beats the Rs 500 coupon
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: 26,999 - 4,200 = 22,799; 10% is 2,280, capped to 1,500, giving 21,299. The coupon is exclusive with the bank offer and worth less, so the engine picks the bank offer.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: A customer's checkout request times out and the app retries it. You find the offer's per-user count was used twice. What is the fix?
options: Use the order ID as an idempotency key so a retried checkout does not consume the offer again
Increase the per-user limit to 2 so retries never block anyone
Disable retries on checkout so a timeout always fails the order
Check the per-user count only on the product page, not at checkout
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: An idempotency key tied to the order ID makes the reservation happen once no matter how many times the call is retried.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: A wrongly configured 90%-off offer goes live at midnight on sale day. What should stop it fastest?
options: Waiting for the offer's end date to pass in the configuration
Asking customers via push notification not to use the offer
A code deployment that removes the offer from the engine
A per-offer kill switch that takes effect everywhere within seconds through cache invalidation events
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: Each offer needs a kill switch that propagates fast via OfferChanged events. A deployment takes far too long during a live sale.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: Someone wants to change the discount on a live offer directly in the database to save time. Why is that a bad idea?
options: It is fine, since the cache will notice the change on its own within a day
Live offers should never be edited in place; an approved change is a new version that publishes an OfferChanged event
Databases cannot store discounts, so the change would be lost on restart
Edits are allowed only on the product page, not in the offer store
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: Versioning, maker-checker approval and change events give an audit trail and refresh caches correctly. An in-place edit skips approval and leaves stale caches.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: At "Pay", the system reserves the bank offer's budget and the user's limit, but the card payment then fails. What should happen?
options: Cancel the offer for this user permanently to prevent abuse
Release the reservation so the budget and the user's offer use are available again
Keep the reservation, since the customer already chose the offer once
Write it to the offer ledger as used, and reverse it at month end
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: Reservations are confirmed into the ledger only on order confirmation; on payment failure or cancellation they are released.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: A customer returns a phone bought with a seller deal and a bank-funded instant discount. What does the offer ledger make possible?
options: Reversing each benefit proportionally and settling with the bank and seller by their recorded funding split
Nothing, since discounts are only shown on the page and never stored
Charging the full discount back to the customer's card as a penalty
Keeping the bank discount with the platform as compensation for the return
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: The ledger records each discount and who funded it (bank 100%, seller 60% / platform 40% and so on), so settlement, reconciliation and reversals on returns are accurate.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: Before a new festive offer goes live, finance asks how much it will cost. What is the best way to estimate it?
options: Guess from the discount percentage and the number of products it covers
Ask the bank or seller funding it to estimate the cost for you
Simulate it over yesterday's carts or run it in shadow mode, computing the discount without applying it
Launch it for everyone and check the ledger at the end of the first day
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: Simulation over historical carts and a shadow mode show cost and surprises before real money is spent. Launching first is exactly how stacking accidents happen.

How are offers configured in an e-commer.q: How does checkout confirm that a card really qualifies for an "X Bank credit card" offer?
options: It trusts the customer's choice from the payment method dropdown
It checks the card's expiry date against the offer dates
It checks the card's BIN, the first digits of the card number, against the offer's issuer and card type
It asks the customer to upload a photo of the card
How are offers configured in an e-commer.why: Bank offers depend on verifying the payment instrument; the BIN identifies issuer and card type, which is why the bank offer is re-evaluated at checkout with the actual card.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: One sponsored slot. Seller X bids ₹15 with predicted CTR 1%. Seller Y bids ₹6 with predicted CTR 3%. Who wins, and roughly what does the winner pay per click?
options: Y wins and pays its full ₹6 bid, since it bid less than X
X wins because it bid the most, and pays its full ₹15 bid
Y wins (score 0.18 vs 0.15) and pays about ₹5, just enough to beat X
X wins and pays about ₹6, just enough to beat Y's bid
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: Ranking uses bid x pCTR: 6 x 0.03 = 0.18 beats 15 x 0.01 = 0.15. In a second-price-style auction Y pays 0.15 / 0.03 = ₹5 (plus a paisa), below its bid.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: A seller bids ₹20 per click to show a formal leather shoe on the search "running shoes" but loses to an ₹8 bid. Why?
options: The seller's daily budget was too small to cover a ₹20 click
The platform always prefers lower bids to keep ads affordable for sellers
Its predicted CTR is so low that bid x pCTR is smaller; irrelevant ads earn less and annoy shoppers
Formal shoes are banned from running-shoe searches by policy
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: Paid per click, an ad nobody clicks earns the platform little. Relevance and revenue point the same way, so a relevant product with a lower bid often wins.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: A seller bid ₹8 per click and won the top slot. The next ad would have needed them to score 0.24 with their pCTR of 3.5%. What do they pay?
options: Exactly ₹8, because you always pay what you bid
About ₹12, the bid of the next ad below them
About ₹6.87, the minimum needed to keep the position, not the full ₹8
₹3, the reserve price, since the winner pays the floor
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: Generalized second price: 0.24 / 0.035 is about ₹6.86, plus a paisa. You pay just enough to beat the next ad, above the reserve price.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: A seller's ₹2,000 daily budget is always gone by noon, and evening shoppers never see the ad. What is wrong?
options: The attribution window is too short, so later clicks are not counted
Spend is not paced; a pacer should enter fewer auctions or shade bids when ahead of the day's plan
The bid is too low, so the ad wins only cheap morning auctions
The ad has too few keywords, so it shows only in the morning
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: Traffic peaks in the evening, but without pacing the ad wins every morning auction. Pacing compares spend so far with expected spend by that hour and adjusts participation or bids.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: A campaign spent ₹20,000 and shows ₹80,000 of attributed sales. Which statement is correct?
options: ROAS is 4 and ACoS is 25%, but that alone does not prove the ads were profitable
ROAS is 4 and ACoS is 25%, which proves a ₹60,000 profit from the ads
ROAS is 0.25 and ACoS is 400%, so the ads should be stopped
ROAS is 25% and ACoS is 4, so the campaign lost money
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: ROAS = 80,000 / 20,000 = 4; ACoS = 20,000 / 80,000 = 25%. Profit needs product cost subtracted and incrementality checked, since some buyers would have bought anyway.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: A seller spent ₹10,000 for ₹50,000 of attributed sales (ROAS 5) at a 25% margin. Tests suggest 60% of those buyers would have bought anyway. What is the real picture?
options: Incrementality does not matter, since all attributed sales count as caused by ads
ROAS of 5 means a ₹40,000 profit, so the seller should double the budget
Incremental gross profit is about ₹5,000 against ₹10,000 spend, so the ads lose money
Gross profit is ₹12,500 minus ₹10,000, so ₹2,500 profit is the true number
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: Margin gives ₹12,500 gross profit on ₹50,000, but only 40% is incremental: ₹5,000 versus ₹10,000 spend, a loss. ₹2,500 ignores that most buyers would have bought anyway.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: A brand asks, "Would these shoppers have bought anyway?" What is the best way to answer?
options: Extend the attribution window to 30 days to capture more sales
Run a holdout test: keep a random group from seeing the ad and compare their purchases with the exposed group
Look at ROAS; a high ROAS shows the ads caused the sales
Count how many shoppers clicked the ad more than once
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: Incrementality is measured by comparing exposed and unexposed random groups, the A/B testing idea applied to ads. Attributed sales and ROAS do not tell you what would have happened without the ad.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: Why can a marketplace report ad results more directly than a typical news-site banner?
options: Marketplaces charge per impression, which makes counting easier
Marketplace shoppers are more likely to click ads than news readers
News sites are not allowed to track clicks under data protection law
It owns both the ad and the checkout, so it joins clicks to actual orders within an attribution window
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: This closed loop is the retail media advantage: the platform sees the purchase. A news site rarely knows whether an ad led to a sale.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: The search page must respond in about 200 ms. On a heavy-load evening the ads service misses its deadline. What should happen?
options: Delay the search page until the ads are ready, since ads earn high margin
Show the ads from the shopper's previous search instead
Return an error so the client retries the search
Render the page without ads rather than making the shopper wait
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: Ads run in parallel with organic search within a strict budget; if they are late, the page renders without them. Slowing search would hurt every shopper.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: Logs show 300 clicks on one ad within a minute from a few data-center IP addresses, and some click events were sent twice by app retries. What should billing do?
options: Bill every logged click, since the seller agreed to pay per click
Filter the invalid traffic and deduplicate by click ID before charging the seller
Bill the clicks but refund them later if the seller complains
Stop the seller's campaign, since bots clicking means the ad is fraudulent
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: Invalid traffic (bots, click farms, rapid repeats) is filtered and not billed, and click IDs prevent retries from double-charging.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: A small seller runs an auto campaign for a week. Some search terms convert well; "kids" and "spikes" waste money. What is the best next step?
options: Delete the auto campaign and bid on broad match for every term
Keep everything on auto, since the platform always picks the best keywords
Raise bids on all terms equally so the good ones get more clicks
Move converting terms into manual exact-match with their own bids, and add the poor terms as negative keywords
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: This is keyword harvesting: auto discovers terms, manual exact scales the proven ones, and negatives block irrelevant searches.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: A seller spends ₹10,000 on ads. Ad-attributed sales are ₹50,000 and total sales (ads plus organic) are ₹1,25,000. What is TACoS and what does it show?
options: 12.5, showing return on total spend across channels
8%, showing how dependent the whole business is on ad spend
20%, showing the ads paid for themselves five times over
40%, showing that most sales came from ads
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: TACoS = ad spend / total sales = 10,000 / 1,25,000 = 8%. ACoS would be 20% (ad spend / attributed sales).

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: A platform wants to rank a CPC sponsored-product ad against a CPM display ad for the same slot. What makes this comparison fair?
options: eCPM, the expected earnings per 1,000 impressions, roughly bid x predicted CTR x 1,000 for CPC ads
Compare the raw bids, since both are in rupees
Always prefer CPC ads, since clicks prove the shopper was interested
Always prefer CPM ads, since they pay even when nobody clicks
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: eCPM converts both pricing models into expected money per 1,000 impressions so they can be ranked together.

How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.q: Leadership wants to double ad revenue by filling every search row with sponsored tiles. What is the main risk, and how do platforms manage it?
options: Shopper trust and conversion fall over time; platforms cap ad load, keep a relevance bar and label ads "Sponsored"
Only a latency risk, solved by adding more ad servers
Only a legal risk, solved by moving ads to the bottom of the page
No real risk, since sponsored tiles look the same as organic ones
How do ads work on e-commerce sites like.why: Every ad slot replaces an organic result, so too many or irrelevant ads hurt long-term sales. Ad-load caps, relevance thresholds and clear labels balance revenue with trust.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: Your one-weight delivery model has w = 1, the gradient is -149 and the learning rate is 0.01. What is the new w?
options: About 1.0149; the gradient only nudges w by a tiny fixed amount
About 2.49; the gradient is negative, so increasing w lowers the loss
About 150; you add the full gradient to the weight each step
About -0.49; you subtract the gradient, so w must go down
How does a neural network actually learn.why: new w = 1 - 0.01 x (-149) = 2.49. A negative gradient means the loss falls as w rises, so the update moves w up.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: A few hundred steps into training, your loss suddenly becomes NaN. What is the most likely cause and first fix?
options: The dataset is too small; collect more data before training again
The learning rate is too high, so weights overshoot and blow up; lower it by about 10x
The model has too few layers; add more hidden layers and retrain
The learning rate is too low, so the model is stuck; raise it by 10x
How does a neural network actually learn.why: Steps that are too big overshoot the valley, land higher each time and explode. A too-low rate gives slow progress, not NaN.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: A friend says, "Backpropagation is what updates the weights." What is the accurate correction?
options: Backprop updates the weights, and gradient descent only measures the loss
Backprop picks the learning rate, and gradient descent picks the loss function
Correct; backprop and gradient descent are two names for the same step
Backprop computes each weight's gradient; gradient descent or Adam uses those gradients to change the weights
How does a neural network actually learn.why: Backprop measures (who gets how much blame); the optimiser moves the weights. Two different jobs.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: You have 1 million training examples and a batch size of 1,000. How many weight updates happen in one epoch?
options: 1,000 updates, each using the averaged gradient of one mini-batch
1 million updates, one per training example
1 update, since an epoch means one pass over all the data
1,000 x 1,000 updates, one per example in every batch
How does a neural network actually learn.why: 1,000,000 / 1,000 = 1,000 steps. Mini-batches give many cheap, good-enough steps instead of one slow full-data step that may not fit in memory.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: A teammate removes the activation functions to make the network faster. Why is that a problem?
options: Without activations the network trains faster and gives the same results
Without activations backprop cannot run, so the weights never change
Without activations, any stack of layers collapses into one straight-line formula and cannot fit curved patterns
Without activations the loss function cannot be computed at all
How does a neural network actually learn.why: The non-linear bend (ReLU, sigmoid) is what lets a deep network fit messy patterns. Without it, all layers are equivalent to a single linear layer.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: With a learning rate of 0.0001, after 30 steps w has only moved from 1 to 1.41 (the right answer is 5). What is happening?
options: The gradient is pointing the wrong way, so w will never reach 5
The model is overshooting and will explode if training continues
The steps are in the right direction but far too small, so training is painfully slow
The model has found the global minimum and cannot improve further
How does a neural network actually learn.why: A tiny learning rate crawls downhill. Too big overshoots; too small takes forever. Teams try a few values and often lower the rate over time with a schedule.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: After epoch 12, training error keeps falling but validation error starts rising. What should you do?
options: Stop and keep the weights from the best validation point (early stopping), since the model is overfitting
Keep training, since falling training error means the model is still improving
Merge the validation set into training so both errors fall together
Raise the learning rate so the model escapes the rising validation error
How does a neural network actually learn.why: Rising validation loss with falling training loss means the model is memorising. Early stopping saves the version that generalises best.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: Why do GPUs train neural networks much faster than CPUs?
options: GPUs store the training data permanently, so no disk reads are needed
GPUs skip backpropagation and estimate the gradients directly
GPUs have a few very powerful cores that handle complex branching logic faster
Training is billions of independent multiply-adds in matrices, and GPUs have thousands of simple cores doing them at once
How does a neural network actually learn.why: Forward and backward passes are huge parallel matrix multiplications. CPUs have a handful of strong cores for step-by-step logic, which fits this work poorly.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: Your ETA model was trained on 10 million orders from big cities. A new city has only 50,000 orders. What is the sensible approach?
options: Use the big-city model as is, since delivery times are the same everywhere
Start from the big-city model and fine-tune it on the new city's data (transfer learning)
Train a new model from random weights using only the 50,000 orders
Wait until the new city has 10 million orders before building a model
How does a neural network actually learn.why: Transfer learning starts from good pretrained weights and adapts them with the same gradient descent and backprop, needing far less data than training from scratch.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: With w = 1 the predictions are off by -8, -16 and -24 minutes. Using mean squared error, what is the loss, and why square?
options: 16; the loss is the plain average of the absolute errors
About 896; the loss is the sum of squared errors, not the mean
About 299; squaring makes big mistakes count much more than small ones
-16; the loss is the average error, which keeps its sign
How does a neural network actually learn.why: (64 + 256 + 576) / 3 is about 299. Squaring removes the sign and punishes large errors more heavily.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: Does gradient descent always find the best possible weights?
options: Yes, as long as the learning rate is large enough to skip small dips
No; it only works for one-weight models and fails on real networks
No; it finds a low point, not necessarily the lowest, though for big networks that is usually good enough
Yes; following the slope always ends at the single lowest point
How does a neural network actually learn.why: Walking downhill in fog reaches a valley, but there may be lower ones elsewhere. In practice, the low points found for large networks work well, with no guarantee.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: A neuron gets distance = 3 km and raining = 1, with weights 4 and 6 and a bias of 5, then applies ReLU. What does it output?
options: 23, because 3x4 + 1x6 + 5 = 23 and ReLU keeps positive values
18, because the bias is applied only after ReLU
1, because ReLU squashes every output to between 0 and 1
0, because ReLU turns any value above 1 into 0
How does a neural network actually learn.why: Weighted sum plus bias is 12 + 6 + 5 = 23. ReLU keeps positives and turns negatives into 0; squashing to 0..1 is what sigmoid does.

How does a neural network actually learn.q: In backprop, the hidden neuron H was almost silent (output near zero) on an example where the prediction was 6 minutes too high. How much blame does the weight from H to the output get?
options: Exactly half, because blame is split equally between every weight
The most, because the weights closest to the output always take the full blame
None of it ever, because hidden-layer weights are not updated by backprop
Very little, because blame for that weight is proportional to how active H was
How does a neural network actually learn.why: Using the chain rule, a weight's gradient depends on how much its input contributed. A quiet H barely affected the output, so its outgoing weight gets little blame.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: Your model has 98% training accuracy and 71% validation accuracy. What is the likely problem and a good fix?
options: Distribution shift; the validation data comes from a different country
Underfitting (high bias); use a bigger model and train for longer
Data leakage; the validation set must have been copied from training
Overfitting (high variance); add data, regularisation or early stopping, or use a simpler model
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: A big gap between low training error and much higher validation error is the clearest overfitting signal. A bigger model would widen the gap further.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: A model scores 62% on training data and 60% on validation. What is going on and what would you try?
options: Underfitting; try a more flexible model, better features, less regularisation or longer training
A perfect fit, since training and validation scores are close
Overfitting; add dropout and stop training earlier
Leakage; remove the strongest feature and retrain
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: Both errors high and close together means the model is too simple to capture even the real pattern (high bias). Close scores alone do not mean a good fit.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: A demand-forecasting model was evaluated with a random 80/20 split of two years of daily sales and looked excellent, but it fails in production. What went wrong?
options: The test set was too small; a 50/50 random split would have caught it
The model was underfitting; a deeper model would have generalised
Random splitting let it train on days after the ones it was tested on; use a time-based split instead
Daily sales need no split at all, since every day is different
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: Shuffling time-ordered data lets the model see the future. Train on the past, validate on the next period and test on the one after.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: Why can't you report your validation score as the final number for your model?
options: The validation set contains training rows, so it measures memorisation
The validation set is always smaller than the test set, so its score is too noisy
Validation scores are computed differently from test scores in most libraries
You looked at it many times while choosing models and settings, so your choices partly fit it and the score is optimistic
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: The validation set is for making decisions; the untouched test set gives the one honest final measurement.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: A fraud model uses the feature "chargebacks filed on this account" and scores 99%. What is the problem?
options: Leakage: chargebacks are filed weeks after the order, so this value does not exist when the decision is made
Underfitting: one strong feature makes the model too simple
Overfitting: the model has too many trees and memorised the chargebacks
No problem: chargebacks are the most reliable fraud signal available
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: Ask of every feature: would I know this value at the exact moment of prediction? Future information makes a fake 99% that collapses live.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: In a churn dataset, the same customers appear in both the training and test sets, and the model scores very high. What split should you use?
options: A stratified split, so each set has the same churn rate
No change; seeing a customer twice helps the model learn them
A bigger random split with more data in the test set
A group split, so each customer's rows sit in only one of training, validation or test
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: When the same entity is on both sides, the model learns that person instead of the pattern. Group splits keep each customer on one side.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: A teammate fills missing values and scales features using the mean of the whole dataset, then splits into train and test. What is wrong?
options: The split should happen after training, not before preprocessing
Test statistics leak into training; fit preprocessing on the training data only, then apply it to the others
Nothing; using more rows gives a more accurate mean for everyone
Scaling is unnecessary for most models, so the step should be removed
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: Preprocessing on all data first lets test information shape training. Fit it inside each training run, on training rows only.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: A fraud model performed well for six months, then its catch rate fell with no code change. What is the likely cause and response?
options: Overfitting that appeared slowly; add dropout and keep the old data
A hardware fault; move the model to a new server
Data leakage introduced later; re-split the original data randomly
Concept drift as fraudsters changed tactics; monitor, retrain on recent labelled data and keep fallback rules
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: Even an honest model decays when the world changes. Monitoring inputs and outcomes against a baseline and retraining are the defence.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: You have only 5,000 labelled orders, of which 1% are fraud, and one validation split gives very different scores each run. What is a better way to compare models?
options: Use plain random 5-fold folds, since class balance does not matter here
Stratified k-fold cross-validation, which averages several folds while keeping the fraud rate in each
Train on all 5,000 rows and report the training score
Use the test set to compare models, since it is the most honest data
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: Cross-validation gives a steadier estimate on small data, and stratified folds keep the rare class in every fold. Using the test set for choices turns it into another validation set.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: What does dropout do when training a neural network?
options: Removes the least important features permanently from the dataset
Drops the training examples with the highest error from each batch
Randomly switches off parts of the network during training so it cannot rely on any single path
Stops training early when validation loss starts rising
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: Dropout is a regularisation method that reduces overfitting. Stopping when validation loss rises is early stopping, a different fix.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: Retrain a model on a slightly different sample of the same data, and you get a very different model each time. What does this describe?
options: High variance: the model is too sensitive to the exact training data, which leads to overfitting
Data leakage: the samples must share test rows
High bias: the model is too rigid to bend to the truth
Concept drift: the real-world relationship has changed
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: Variance is error from sensitivity to the training sample; bias is error from being too simple. Making a model more flexible usually lowers bias and raises variance.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: Your team tuned settings repeatedly while checking scores on the test set, and the final test score looks great. What has happened?
options: The model is now underfitting because it was tuned too much
The test set has effectively become a validation set, so its score is optimistic; you need a fresh held-out set
Nothing; checking the test set often just confirms the model is good
The training set must be leaking into the test set
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: Tuning after seeing the test set fits your choices to it. A test set should be used once, at the end.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: Training and validation errors are both low and close, but the model performs badly in production. What should you check?
options: Underfitting: add more layers until production improves
Nothing in the data; production failures are always infrastructure bugs
Leakage or shift: audit the split and features, and compare live data with training data
Overfitting: the gap is too small, so add regularisation
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: A good offline score that collapses live points to a dishonest split or the world differing from training data.

A model scores 99% in testing but fails.q: A "will this order be returned?" model scores 99% accuracy, and about 8% of orders are returned. What is the first reality check?
options: Always predicting "not returned" already scores 92%, so check precision and recall on returns instead
The model needs more training, since 99% is below the 100% target
99% is far above 8%, so the model is clearly excellent
Returns are too rare to model, so the project should stop
A model scores 99% in testing but fails.why: Compare with the majority-class baseline first. On rare events, accuracy hides whether the model catches the cases you care about.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: A disease affects 2 in 1,000 people. A test says "healthy" for everyone. What are its accuracy and recall?
options: Accuracy 99.8% and recall 0%, since it catches none of the sick people
Accuracy 99.8% and recall 99.8%, since both measure correct answers
Accuracy 0.2% and recall 100%, since it never raises a false alarm
Accuracy 50% and recall 0%, since it is no better than a coin toss
A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: 998 of 1,000 are correct, but recall = TP / all sick = 0 / 2. Accuracy hides the failure; recall exposes it.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: A model flags 500 orders; 300 are real fraud. There were 1,200 fraud orders in total. What are precision and recall?
options: Precision 60% and recall 25%, giving F1 of about 0.35
Precision 60% and recall 60%, giving F1 of 0.60
Precision 42% and recall 25%, giving F1 of about 0.31
Precision 25% and recall 60%, giving F1 of about 0.35

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: Your fraud model has ROC-AUC 0.96, yet the review team says most flagged orders are good customers. How can both be true?
options: They cannot both be true; a ROC-AUC of 0.96 guarantees high precision
ROC-AUC measures recall only, so precision is never affected
The review team is wrong, since ROC-AUC already counts their flags
ROC uses the false positive rate over a huge number of genuine orders, so thousands of false alarms look small; check precision or PR-AUC
A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: With 1% fraud, FPR divides by about 99% of all orders, so the curve looks great while most flags are wrong. PR-AUC exposes that.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: You are building an SMS spam filter that might accidentally hide bank OTPs. Which metric should you protect, and why?
options: Recall, because catching every spam message matters most
Precision, because hiding a real OTP (a false positive) is worse than letting some spam through
ROC-AUC, because it removes the need to choose a threshold
Accuracy, because spam is common enough that accuracy works well
A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: Only filter when very confident, with an easy "not spam" button. Fraud and medical screening lean to recall; spam leans to precision.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: A screening test for a serious illness will be followed by a second, more precise test for anyone flagged. What should the first test favour?
options: The highest accuracy, since the illness is rare
Very high recall, so few sick patients are missed; the second test cleans up false alarms
Very high precision, so nobody is ever sent for a second test wrongly
An F1 score of exactly 0.5, to balance both mistakes
A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: Missing a sick patient is the worse mistake, so the first test casts a wide net and the second improves precision.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: You lower your fraud model's threshold from 0.7 to 0.3. What happens?
options: Fewer orders are flagged: recall goes down and precision goes up
Both precision and recall go up, since the model sees more fraud
More orders are flagged: recall goes up and precision goes down
Nothing changes, since the threshold does not affect the model's scores
A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: In the example, recall rises from 60% to 90% while precision falls from 60% to 20%. Same model, different behaviour.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: A missed fraud costs ₹5,000 and a false alarm costs ₹200. F1 peaks at threshold 0.7, but total cost is lowest at 0.3 to 0.5. Which should the business choose, and why?
options: 0.1, because it has the highest recall and catches the most fraud
0.9, because it has the highest precision and the fewest angry customers
0.3 to 0.5, because F1 treats both mistakes as equal while here a miss costs 25 times more
0.7, because F1 is the best single measure of model quality
