A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: Cost per threshold = FN x ₹5,000 + FP x ₹200, which is lowest around 0.3 to 0.5 (₹12.2 to 12.4 lakh). F1 ignores unequal costs.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: Your fraud model, on data with 1% fraud, has a PR-AUC of 0.45. A colleague says "0.45 is poor". Is that right?
options: Yes; any AUC below 0.5 is worse than a coin toss
Yes; PR-AUC must be above 0.9 to be useful for fraud
No; PR-AUC is always about twice the ROC-AUC, so it is fine
No; a random model scores about the positive rate, 0.01, so 0.45 is a big lift over random
A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: PR-AUC's baseline is the positive rate, not 0.5. The 0.5 coin-toss baseline belongs to ROC-AUC.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: What does a ROC-AUC of 0.85 mean in plain words?
options: The model catches 85% of all fraud at the default threshold
85% of all predictions are correct at the best threshold
85% of the model's flagged orders are real fraud
There is an 85% chance a random fraud order gets a higher score than a random genuine order
A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: ROC-AUC measures ranking across all thresholds. Share of flags that are right is precision, and share of fraud caught is recall.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: Threshold 0.3 minimises cost but flags 4,500 orders a day, while the review team can check only 3,000. What is the practical design?
options: Use score bands: auto-cancel or ask for prepaid above 0.7, review or OTP for 0.3 to 0.7, pass below 0.3
Drop manual review and auto-block every order above 0.3
Use 0.3 anyway and let the review queue grow each day
Switch to 0.9 so the review team is never busy
A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: A threshold that flags more than the team can check is useless. Bands send only the uncertain middle to humans and handle clear cases automatically.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: Your ETA model misses by 2, 4 and 12 minutes. What are MAE and RMSE, and when would you prefer RMSE?
options: MAE 18 and RMSE about 12.8; prefer MAE when big misses matter more
MAE 6 and RMSE about 7.4; prefer RMSE when big misses are much worse than small ones
MAE 6 and RMSE 6; they are always equal for small datasets
MAE about 7.4 and RMSE 6; prefer RMSE when all minutes count equally
A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: MAE = (2 + 4 + 12) / 3 = 6. RMSE = sqrt((4 + 16 + 144) / 3), about 7.4. Squaring punishes the 12-minute miss more.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: A model has 100% precision and 1% recall. What is its F1, roughly?
options: 1.0, because perfect precision means a perfect F1
About 0.10, the square root of the recall
About 0.02, because the harmonic mean is dragged down by the smaller number
About 0.50, the simple average of precision and recall
A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: F1 = 2 x 1 x 0.01 / 1.01, about 0.02. You cannot game F1 by maxing one side, unlike a simple average.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: You only see outcomes for orders you flagged. How can you estimate recall in production?
options: Use precision as a stand-in, since the two always move together
Use delayed labels like chargebacks and complaints, plus a small random sample of unflagged orders reviewed by humans
Assume every unflagged order is genuine, since nobody complained
Recall cannot be measured in production, so use the offline test number forever
A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: Missed fraud surfaces later as chargebacks and complaints, and reviewing a random sample of unflagged orders estimates what slipped through.

A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.q: Finance says a missed fraud is far more costly than a false alarm and asks for one summary metric. Which fits better than F1?
options: F2, which weighs recall more than precision, or better still a direct rupee cost function
F0.5, which weighs precision more, since false alarms annoy customers
Accuracy, since it counts both kinds of mistake together
ROC-AUC, since it avoids the cost question by covering all thresholds
A fraud model is 99% accurate but useles.why: F-beta lets you weight recall (F2) or precision (F0.5); here misses cost more, so F2 or an explicit cost function picks a better threshold.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: An intern says, "RNNs fail on long reviews because they read the review one word at a time and carry a small memory forward." Which pair of problems does that design actually cause?
options: The model cannot handle words it has never seen, and it needs a hand-written label for every word
The model uses too much GPU memory per word, and it cannot be fine-tuned once training is finished
Early information fades over long distances, and training cannot run in parallel within a sequence
The model loses all sense of word order, and it can only ever be trained on very short sentences
Why did transformers replace older model.why: RNNs carry a fixed-size, fading hidden state and step t needs step t-1, so memory fades and training is sequential. Losing word order is a transformer issue (fixed by positional encodings), not an RNN one.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: Your team trains an LSTM on 2,000-token support transcripts. A manager offers eight more GPUs to make training on each single transcript faster. What is the honest reply?
options: They let you run more transcripts side by side, but steps within one must still run in order
They will make each transcript about eight times faster, because the 2,000 steps are split evenly
They will sit idle, because LSTMs cannot run on GPUs at all and must be trained on CPUs instead
They will help only after switching the LSTM to a GRU, since GRUs remove the sequential loop
Why did transformers replace older model.why: Each RNN/LSTM step needs the previous hidden state, so steps within one sequence cannot be split. GRUs are a simpler gated RNN and are still sequential.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: During backpropagation through a long RNN, the gradient is multiplied by about 0.9 at each step. Roughly how much signal reaches a token 100 steps back, and what is this called?
options: About 0.9 of the original signal; this is the exploding gradient problem
About 0.005 of the original signal; this is the exploding gradient problem
About 0.1 of the original signal; this is the quadratic attention problem
About 0.00003 of the original signal; this is the vanishing gradient problem
Why did transformers replace older model.why: 0.9 multiplied 100 times is about 0.00003, so early tokens get almost no learning signal: vanishing gradients. About 0.005 is the 50-step figure, and exploding gradients happen when factors are above 1.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: A colleague claims LSTMs "completely solved" vanishing gradients. What is the most accurate correction?
options: LSTMs made the problem worse, which is why GRUs were invented in 1997 to replace them entirely
Gates and a cell state reduced it, but long-range links stayed hard and training stayed sequential
LSTMs solved it fully, and they were abandoned only because they needed too many parameters
LSTMs solved it by clipping gradients, which is the same method that transformers use today
Why did transformers replace older model.why: The LSTM's gated cell state is a conveyor belt that helps gradients survive longer, but it is a patch, not a cure. Clipping handles exploding gradients, not vanishing ones.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: Attention was already being used with RNNs for translation around 2014-2015. So what was genuinely new in "Attention Is All You Need" (2017)?
options: It invented the attention mechanism for the first time, using it to replace word embeddings
It dropped recurrence entirely, building the model from attention, positions and feed-forward layers
It added a second LSTM layer so that attention could look both backwards and forwards in text
It introduced the KV cache so that a model could generate its whole answer in a single step
Why did transformers replace older model.why: The paper's contribution was showing the recurrence could be dropped, giving direct links and fully parallel training. Attention itself predated it, which is the common misconception.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: In self-attention, the token "colour" needs to find which earlier token tells it the product's colour. Which description of the mechanism is correct?
options: Its key is compared only with the previous token's value, and the top score replaces the hidden state
Its value is copied from the nearest noun, and its query is used only later during text generation
Its query is passed step by step through each earlier token in turn until a matching one is found
Its query is scored against every token's key, softmax turns scores into weights, and values are mixed
Why did transformers replace older model.why: Each token compares its query with all keys, softmax makes weights summing to 1, and the output is a weighted mix of values. Passing step by step is the RNN chain attention removed.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: You remove the positional encodings from a transformer as an experiment. What problem do you expect?
options: It loses word order, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look the same to it
It can no longer train in parallel, so it falls back to processing tokens one by one
Its attention cost drops from quadratic to linear, so long inputs get cheaper but worse
It forgets which attention head handles grammar, since heads are assigned by position
Why did transformers replace older model.why: With no recurrence, order information comes only from positional encodings added to embeddings. Parallel training and quadratic cost do not depend on them.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: You are choosing a model family for a product-search re-ranker that mainly needs to understand text, versus a chat assistant that must generate replies. Which mapping matches the answer?
options: Decoder-only (GPT-style) for search and understanding; encoder-only (BERT-style) for chat generation
Encoder-decoder for both, since the original paper showed the other two designs were always inferior
Encoder-only (BERT-style) for search and understanding; decoder-only (GPT-style) for chat generation
RNN encoders for search, since transformers cannot produce the embeddings that ranking needs
Why did transformers replace older model.why: Later models split the original encoder-decoder: BERT-style encoders for understanding and search, GPT-style decoders for generation. Most chat LLMs today are decoder-only.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: A PM says, "Transformers process everything in parallel, so our chatbot's 800-token answers should take the same time as 80-token answers." What is the best response?
options: That is right, because the causal mask lets the model emit all of its output tokens at once
That is right for decoder-only models; only encoder-decoder models generate token by token
Generation is parallel, but the UI adds streaming artificially so that replies look natural
Training is parallel, but generation is still one token at a time, so longer answers take longer
Why did transformers replace older model.why: Parallelism is mainly a training advantage; generation is autoregressive. The KV cache makes each new token cheap, but output length still drives latency.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: Your support bot's prompt grows from 4,000 to 16,000 tokens to include more history. Roughly how does attention work change, and what is the best response?
options: About 4 times more work; attention is linear, so just add GPUs in the same proportion
About 16 times more work; retrieve only relevant history, summarise old turns, track tokens
No change at all, because FlashAttention makes attention cost independent of length
About 16 times more work; switch to an LSTM, which handles long context more cheaply
Why did transformers replace older model.why: Attention scales with length squared, so 4x length gives about 16x work; the fix is trimming and retrieving context. FlashAttention speeds things up and saves memory but computes the same quadratic result.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: Why did transformers, and not RNNs, benefit from the scaling laws published around 2020?
options: Scaling laws apply only to attention layers, and RNN error never falls as the model grows
RNNs had already reached the largest size their architecture allows, so there was no room left
They trained efficiently on thousands of GPUs, so labs could grow data, compute and size together
Transformers need far less data than RNNs, which is exactly what the Chinchilla result showed
Why did transformers replace older model.why: Scaling laws show error falling predictably as data, compute and parameters grow together; RNNs never rode that curve mainly because they could not be trained efficiently at scale. Chinchilla said data and model size should grow together, not that transformers need less data.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: A blog post claims, "State-space models like Mamba have already replaced transformers." What is the most accurate view?
options: They are promising for long inputs and used in some hybrids, but transformers remain the default
It is correct; transformers are no longer used in any new frontier model released recently
It is wrong; state-space models are plain RNNs, so they cannot be trained in parallel at all
It is wrong; state-space models have quadratic cost, which makes them worse than attention
Why did transformers replace older model.why: State-space models use a recurrence designed to train in parallel with roughly linear cost, and they are promising, but they have not displaced transformers. Saying they are plain sequential RNNs is the tempting but wrong distractor.

Why did transformers replace older model.q: In a Flipkart-like assistant, a customer mentions "blue 6 GB variant" at token 12 and asks "same colour?" at token 600. Why does a transformer handle this better than a 2016 LSTM system?
options: Attention links "colour" to "blue" in one hop; the LSTM must carry it through ~588 updates
The transformer stores every product's colour in its weights, so it never needs the context
The LSTM cannot read 600 tokens at all, because its hidden state is capped at 512 tokens
The transformer reads the chat backwards, so the latest tokens are always processed first
Why did transformers replace older model.why: In the transformer, the path between any two tokens is one hop; in an LSTM, "blue" must survive hundreds of hidden-state updates. LSTMs have no hard 512-token cap; the problem is fading memory.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: You are explaining reinforcement learning to a new hire using a delivery rider who learns city routes. What makes RL different from supervised learning?
options: The rider is shown the perfect route for each order and learns to copy it exactly
The rider groups similar orders together without any feedback on whether routes worked
No correct answer is given per step; the agent gets reward feedback and adjusts its policy
The rider memorises a fixed table of routes that never changes once training is over
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: RL learns from rewards rather than labelled answers. Copying a given correct route is supervised learning, and grouping without feedback is unsupervised.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: A rider keeps taking the familiar main road but occasionally tries an untested back lane at 6 pm that might be faster. Which RL concept is this?
options: Exploration versus exploitation
Credit assignment versus discounting
On-policy versus off-policy evaluation
Value-based versus policy-gradient learning
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: Trying the new lane is exploration and taking the known road is exploitation; this is the central RL trade-off. Credit assignment is about which earlier action earned a delayed reward.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: A customer rates a delivery an hour after it happened. The system must decide which of the rider's 50 earlier actions deserve the credit. What is this problem called?
options: The exploration problem
The Markov property
The reward hacking problem
The credit assignment problem
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: When reward arrives late, attributing it to the right earlier actions is credit assignment. The Markov property is about the current state containing everything needed to decide.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: A team wants to use Q-learning to train an LLM where each action is "write a 500-token paragraph". Why is this a poor fit?
options: Q-learning needs a discount factor of exactly 1, which LLM training cannot support
Q-learning needs a max over actions, and you cannot max over every possible paragraph
Q-learning only works with human preference pairs, which are too costly to collect
Q-learning cannot use neural networks, so it cannot represent language in any form
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: Q-learning suits small, discrete action sets because it needs a max over actions. DQN shows Q-learning can use neural networks, so that distractor is false.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: In a REINFORCE-style policy gradient, an action led to a return of 8 while the critic's baseline expected 10. What happens to that action's probability, and why use a baseline?
options: It goes up, since the return is positive; the baseline exists only to speed up training
It goes down, since the advantage is negative; the baseline cuts noise from lucky episodes
It stays the same, since the baseline cancels the return and replaces the reward signal
It goes up, since critics favour recent actions; the baseline sets the learning rate
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: Advantage = return minus baseline = -2, so the loss lowers that action's probability. Without a baseline, any positive return would raise probability even in a merely lucky episode.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: Why did PPO become the default RL algorithm for LLM training?
options: It removes the need for a reward signal by learning only from human-written demonstrations
It removes the critic network by comparing each sampled answer with its group's average
It computes the optimal policy in closed form, so no sampling or rollouts are ever needed
It clips each update so action probabilities cannot jump too far, trading speed for stability
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: PPO's clipping (around 20 percent) prevents the large jumps that collapse training. Dropping the critic via group averages is GRPO, and the closed-form trick is DPO.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: During a festive sale you must pick one of 12 banners for the hero slot per impression, using user segment, device and hour. Which framing fits best?
options: A contextual bandit: one-step choices with independent rewards, personalised by context
A full MDP with Q-learning, since each banner shown changes the user's long-term state
RLHF with PPO, since human raters must compare every possible pair of banners first
A fixed A/B test only, since bandit algorithms cannot make use of user features at all
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: Single-slot banner choice is a contextual bandit, the workhorse of e-commerce RL. Full RL is for when today's action changes tomorrow's state, at much higher complexity.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: Your banner bandit's reward is "click". After a week a clickbait banner with a misleading discount dominates, yet orders are flat. What is the best diagnosis and fix?
options: Too little exploration; raise epsilon to 50 percent so other banners get traffic
A broken Markov property; add full user history to the state and use Q-learning
Reward hacking; reward orders within a time window, guard creatives, monitor orders
Delayed reward; update the posteriors every 5 seconds instead of every 5 minutes
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: The policy optimised the proxy (clicks) rather than the goal (orders), which is reward hacking per Goodhart's law. More exploration would not fix a wrong reward.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: A growth team asks whether a Thompson-sampling bandit can replace all their A/B tests. What is the best advice?
options: Yes, bandits give cleaner statistics than A/B tests, so they should replace them entirely
No, bandits always lose more revenue than A/B tests because they explore completely at random
Yes, but only with epsilon-greedy, since Thompson sampling results cannot be measured at all
Bandits for ongoing optimisation with low regret; A/B tests for decisions needing clean causal proof
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: Bandits shift traffic to winners while learning, cutting regret, but their statistics are messier. Thompson sampling explores using posterior uncertainty, not blindly at random.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: Before launching a new banner policy, the team wants to estimate its performance on yesterday's logged traffic without risking live users. What makes this possible?
options: Logging only the clicked banners, then retraining the current bandit on them overnight
Logged propensities per chosen arm, enabling off-policy evaluation such as IPS
Running the new policy live behind a 70 percent traffic cap and a manual kill switch
Training a reward model on human banner preferences and scoring the policy with PPO
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: Propensities let you reweight logged outcomes to estimate a different policy offline. Traffic caps and kill switches are live guardrails, not offline evaluation.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: In PPO-based RLHF, the reward is RM_score minus beta times KL(policy || SFT model). What does the KL term protect against?
options: The reward model overfitting to the raters during its own training phase
The SFT model forgetting its demonstrations while PPO updates the reward
The policy drifting into odd outputs that fool the imperfect reward model
The policy exploring too slowly, by adding a bonus for unusual outputs
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: The reward model is a learned proxy; the KL penalty keeps the policy near the trusted SFT model so it cannot exploit RM blind spots. It penalises drift rather than rewarding unusual outputs.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: A small team wants preference tuning for their support assistant but cannot afford four models in memory (policy, reference, reward model, critic). What is the best option?
options: DPO, training directly on chosen-versus-rejected pairs with no reward model or RL loop
PPO with a smaller critic, since the critic is the only expensive model in the setup
GRPO with a learned reward model, since GRPO needs no reference model in memory
Q-learning over answer tokens, since it needs only a single model to be trained
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: DPO looks like ordinary fine-tuning: no reward model, no sampling, no critic, so it is cheaper and stabler. Its trade-off is learning only from the fixed offline dataset.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: Your team wants to train an LLM to write SQL for internal analytics. Which reward setup fits best?
options: A verifiable reward: execute the SQL on a test database and check the result, with hidden tests
A learned reward model trained on raters' preferences for neatly formatted SQL queries
A click-based reward from analysts' usage, updated continuously through a contextual bandit
No reward at all, since supervised fine-tuning on SQL examples gives exactly the same effect
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: Executing SQL is a cheap, hard-to-fool programmatic check, which supports long RL runs (for example with GRPO). Hidden tests guard against the model special-casing visible test queries.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: What is GRPO's main advantage over PPO in RL from verifiable rewards?
options: It drops the reward function, learning directly from chosen-versus-rejected pairs
It drops the KL penalty, so the model is free to move further from the reference
It drops the critic, using each answer's reward relative to its sampled group's average
It drops sampling entirely, so training uses only a fixed offline preference dataset
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: GRPO samples a group (say 8) per prompt and normalises rewards within the group as the advantage, saving a whole model's memory. Training straight on preference pairs is DPO.

How does reinforcement learning work, an.q: Someone says, "RLHF is how the model learns new facts." What is the more accurate statement?
options: RLHF is the main source of facts, since pre-training only teaches grammar and syntax
RLHF mostly shapes behaviour and style using knowledge already learnt in pre-training
RLHF adds facts through the reward model, which stores a knowledge base of answers
RLHF and pre-training teach exactly the same things, only using different datasets
How does reinforcement learning work, an.why: RLHF tunes helpfulness, format and refusal boundaries; RLVR on reasoning is the stronger case for new capability. The reward model is an imperfect proxy for preferences, not a store of ground truth.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: You are building a model that tags support tickets by intent. In this setup, what is a "label"?
options: The raw text of each ticket after its PII has been masked out
The written rulebook that labellers follow when tagging tickets
The correct answer attached to each example, such as "refund status"
The model's predicted probability for each possible intent class
Where does training data for an AI model.why: A label is the right answer paired with an input in supervised learning. The rulebook is the labelling guideline, a separate thing.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: A team trains a search-ranking model only on click logs. Over time it keeps promoting the same products the old system already showed. What is happening?
options: Feedback-loop bias: logs reflect what was shown, so the model repeats the old system's habits
Model collapse: the model is being trained repeatedly on text generated by earlier models
Label noise: labellers rushed and misclicked while tagging the search results by hand
Concept drift: the meaning of a click has changed permanently since the festive sale
Where does training data for an AI model.why: Clicks are implicit labels biased by what was displayed, so models trained only on logs reproduce current behaviour. Model collapse concerns training on synthetic model output.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: Your team debates whether "Where is my refund?" is a refund-status or order-status intent. Who should settle this, and how?
options: Let each labeller decide case by case, and the model will average their views
Let the model decide after training, since it will find the natural clusters
Drop such tickets from the dataset, since ambiguous examples only add noise
Treat it as a product decision: agree a ruling and write it into the guideline
Where does training data for an AI model.why: Defining labels is a product decision that must be written down, or labellers and the model stay confused. Dropping hard cases removes exactly the boundaries the model needs to learn.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: Two labellers agree on 85% of tickets, yet Cohen's kappa is only 0.4. What is the best explanation?
options: Kappa is always about half of raw agreement, so 0.4 is actually a strong score for this task
One label dominates, so much agreement is chance; kappa removes it, exposing weak rare-label rules
The labellers are careless, so they should be replaced before any further labelling continues
Kappa measures agreement only on the test set, so it does not apply to the training labels
Where does training data for an AI model.why: Cohen's kappa corrects for chance agreement, which is high when one label dominates. Below about 0.6 usually means an unclear guideline, not careless people.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: Pilot labelling gives kappa 0.62, with disagreements clustered on refund status versus return request. What is the best next step?
options: Accept 0.62 as final, since any kappa above 0.5 already counts as strong agreement
Add a guideline ruling for that boundary, then re-measure agreement on a fresh batch
Merge every intent into fewer, broader labels so that agreement rises automatically
Switch to a new labelling vendor, since low agreement means the labellers are poor
Where does training data for an AI model.why: Low agreement on one label pair tells you exactly which definition to fix (for example, already picked up means refund status). In the example this took kappa from 0.62 to 0.81.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: One vendor labeller always marks "cancel order" tickets as "refund". Why is this worse than a few percent of random mistakes, and how do you catch it?
options: It is harmless, because the model averages it out with the other labellers' work
It only hurts the training set; the test set is never affected by labeller mistakes
It can only be caught after deployment, by watching for drops in live accuracy
It is systematic noise the model learns as a rule; hidden gold questions expose it
Where does training data for an AI model.why: A few percent of random noise is often tolerable, but consistent errors teach the model the mistake. Gold questions, multiple labels and model-assisted review catch it early.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: You have 2 lakh unlabelled tickets and budget for 3,000 labels. Why not just pick 3,000 at random?
options: Random picks are mostly easy cases; label where the model is least sure, plus some random
Random is better, because any selection made by the model biases the dataset completely
Random is fine, but only if every single example is labelled by three different people
Random wastes money, because rare classes should be labelled only by an LLM instead
Where does training data for an AI model.why: Labelling uncertain, boundary examples teaches the model most per label. A small random share is still mixed in so the data keeps looking like real traffic.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: You need a fast first intent model but have almost no labels. Experts can write rules like "otp|login|password means account access". Which approach fits?
options: Active learning: let the rules pick which examples humans should label next, one batch at a time
Synthetic data: have the rules generate brand-new tickets and train the model only on those
Weak supervision: rules vote, a combiner weighs them into probabilistic labels; keep a clean test set
Data versioning: store each rule as its own dataset version and train on all of them together
Where does training data for an AI model.why: Weak supervision turns noisy, partial rules into probabilistic labels at scale in hours. It gives a quick first version, but you still need hand-labelled test data to know if it works.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: The "seller complaint" intent has only 120 real examples. A teammate proposes generating 5,000 with an LLM and evaluating on a synthetic test set too. What is the best plan?
options: Generate all 5,000 and test on synthetic data, since LLM text is cleaner and reliable
Skip synthetic data entirely, since it always lowers accuracy on rare classes like this
Generate the data and let the same LLM label the real test set to save labelling time
Generate to fill the gap, keep reviewed examples, cap the share, test on real chats only
Where does training data for an AI model.why: Synthetic data is great for rare classes but is cleaner and more uniform than real text and can carry the generator's errors. Never evaluate only on synthetic data; real data stays the anchor.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: Researchers warn about "model collapse". In terms of training data, what does it mean?
options: A model's accuracy collapses once the labellers' kappa score drops below about 0.6 on a task
Training repeatedly on earlier models' output makes rare real patterns fade and outputs blander
A model trained only on clicks stops recommending anything new to users over time
Too many labelling functions disagree with each other and the combining step fails
Where does training data for an AI model.why: Model collapse is the loss of diversity from training generation after generation on synthetic text. The defence is to keep real human data as the anchor and track the synthetic share.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: Your intent model scored 95% on its test set but only 70% in production. Which pair of data causes is most likely?
options: The model code has a bug, or the GPU used for training was simply too slow
Too many labels were collected, or the guideline included too many examples
The test set is synthetic or too clean, or the data has drifted since labelling
Active learning was used, or the test set was double-labelled by reviewers
Where does training data for an AI model.why: A gap like this usually traces to a test set that does not match real traffic, or to new products, policies or sale patterns since labelling. Double-labelling the test set is a good practice, not a cause.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: A customer asks for their data to be deleted. Why does dataset versioning matter here?
options: It shows which datasets, and so which models, held their data, so you can remove and retrain
It lets you restore the customer's data later on if they ever change their mind about it
It automatically masks the customer's PII inside every model that was trained in the past
It does not matter here, since deletion requests only apply to the production database
Where does training data for an AI model.why: Recording dataset, guideline and labeller versions per training run lets you trace a person's data to models. Versioning does not mask anything by itself.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: Before sending support chats to an external labelling vendor, which step is most important for privacy?
options: Mask PII like phones, emails and UPI IDs, send only needed fields, spot-check
Send full chats but have the vendor sign an NDA, which removes any need to mask
Send full chats but delete them from your own systems right after the export
Encrypt the chats so the vendor can label them without reading any of the text
Where does training data for an AI model.why: Masking and minimisation reduce exposure before anyone outside sees the data; India's DPDP Act also expects a lawful basis and purpose. Labellers must read the text, so encryption alone does not work.

Where does training data for an AI model.q: A leader says, "We'll just get the latest algorithm; data is a commodity." Which statement best reflects the answer?
options: Algorithms are the real moat, since labelled data can now be bought cheaply from any vendor
Data and algorithms matter exactly equally, so the budget should be split fifty-fifty
Algorithms are shared and open; good task-specific labels are slow and costly, so they are the moat
Once enough click logs exist, hand-labelled data is no longer needed for any model at all
Where does training data for an AI model.why: Garbage in, garbage out: label quality caps model quality. In the worked example the code took two days and the data work six weeks, and the data work moved accuracy.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: A data scientist's Jupyter notebook model looks great on a CSV export. Why can't it simply go live for lakhs of users as-is?
options: Notebooks cannot run Python models, so it must first be rewritten in Java
It can go live as-is, provided the laptop stays on and connected to production
It is a one-off experiment; it must become a repeatable, monitored pipeline
It only needs a faster GPU, since the notebook itself is production-ready
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: A notebook worked once, on one laptop, on one data copy. MLOps turns it into a pipeline of data, features, training, evaluation, registry, deployment and monitoring.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: A model performs worse live than offline from day one. Investigation shows "orders in last 30 days" is computed differently in the training SQL and the serving code. What is this, and the standard prevention?
options: Training-serving skew; share one feature definition, such as a feature store
Concept drift; retrain the model every week on a rolling window of fresh data
Data drift; compute PSI on each feature and retrain once it crosses 0.25
Overfitting; add more regularisation and hold out a larger validation set
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: Features computed two ways give the live model different numbers, a common silent bug; also log served features and compare them with training. Drift is about the world changing, not a code mismatch.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: You need a nightly "customers likely to churn" list and a fraud score at checkout. Which serving choice fits each?
options: Real-time API for both, since batch jobs cannot write their results to a table
Batch for both, since real-time APIs cannot meet a 100 ms latency budget at scale
Real-time for churn, since it matters more; batch for fraud, since it is much rarer
Batch for churn, since hours-old is fine; real-time API for fraud, which depends on now
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: Rule of thumb: use batch unless the prediction depends on something that just happened. Real-time also needs autoscaling and a fallback.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: Your checkout return-risk API must answer within 30 ms. What should be in place if the model service is slow or down?
options: Block checkout until the model service recovers, to avoid any unscored orders
A fallback, like a simple rule or a cached category score, so checkout keeps working
Retry the model call until it finally responds, however long that happens to take
Switch the model into batch mode automatically for the remainder of the day
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: Real-time serving needs a fallback so the business flow continues. Blocking or endless retries would hurt users far more than a slightly less accurate score.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: An auditor asks you to rebuild exactly the model that made a decision three months ago. What must you have versioned?
options: Only the model file, since it already contains everything needed to rebuild it
Data, code and config: data snapshot, git commit, registry version, seed and settings
Only the training code, since the data can be re-queried from the live warehouse
Only the evaluation metrics, since they prove that the model was approved at the time
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: A model is the product of data plus code plus configuration. Re-querying live data will not give the same snapshot, so data must be versioned too.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: You want to check a new model's latency and predictions on real traffic without affecting any user. Which release step is this?
options: Canary deployment: it serves 1% of users while you watch the metrics closely
A/B test: it serves half of all users for weeks to measure business impact
Rollback: it is kept loaded and warm beside the old model in case of failure
Shadow deployment: it gets live traffic, but its predictions are only logged
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: In shadow, users are never affected. In canary, the new model's answers are actually used for a small share of real users.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: After shadow testing, the new return-risk model goes to 2%, then 10%, then 50% of users while business and model metrics are watched. What is this called?
options: A canary deployment
A shadow deployment
A batch deployment
A blue-green training run
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: Gradually serving a small, growing share of real users with the option to pull back is a canary release. Shadow does not use the predictions at all.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: A fraud model's precision drops, but the distribution of its input features looks the same as in training. What is the most likely cause?
options: Data drift: the inputs have shifted, so the model now sees unfamiliar values
Prediction drift: the share of predicted fraud moved, which lowers precision
Concept drift: the same inputs now map to different answers, as fraudsters adapt
Training-serving skew: features are computed differently in the serving code
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: Unchanged inputs with worse outcomes points to the input-to-answer relationship changing. Data drift would show up as changed input distributions.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: During a festive sale, lakhs of first-time buyers arrive and order values jump. PSI on these features goes above 0.3. What kind of drift is this?
options: Concept drift: the meaning of a first-time buyer has changed permanently
Label drift: returns now take two weeks to arrive instead of only one
No drift at all: a PSI above 0.25 indicates the feature is fully stable
Data drift: the inputs changed, even if the input-to-answer rule did not
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: Data drift (covariate shift) means the model sees inputs it rarely saw in training. As a rough convention PSI under 0.1 is stable and above 0.25 deserves a look.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: Drift alarms fire on day one of a planned Diwali sale. A junior engineer wants to retrain immediately on today's data. What is the best response?
options: Retrain immediately and auto-promote, since any drift at all means the model is broken
Check if outcomes are hurt; the drift was expected, and sale-only retraining can backfire
Turn off monitoring for the whole sale, since the alarms during a sale are only noise
Roll back to the very first model version, which was trained before any sales happened
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: Some drift is expected for known events; the model should already have seen past sales and carry features like "days to sale". Guardrails and a release freeze are better than panicked retraining.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: Returns take two weeks to confirm, so outcome metrics lag. How do you know today whether the return-risk model is degrading?
options: You cannot know; wait two weeks for the real labels before looking at anything
Check that the API returns no errors, since models rarely fail without errors
Watch input drift, prediction shifts and fast proxy outcomes, then confirm later
Retrain the model daily so any degradation is fixed before it can be measured
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: Outcomes are the truth but delayed, so input and prediction monitoring are early warnings. Models fail silently, returning confident numbers even when wrong.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: Your team sets up automatic retraining whenever drift crosses a threshold. What rule must still apply?
options: Every retrained model passes the same evaluation gate and staged release
Retrained models may skip evaluation, since their data is fresher than before
Retrained models must always replace the old version within one hour
Retraining should be continuous for every model, since schedules are outdated
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: Automatic retraining must not mean automatic, unchecked promotion. Continuous retraining suits fast-changing areas like fraud or ads but is more complex and risky.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: Version 7 of a model shows a feature-pipeline bug on one category soon after promotion. How should recovery work?
options: Point serving back to the warm version 6 in the registry: a config change
Rebuild version 6 from scratch on the latest data, then redeploy it
Keep version 7 live and patch its bad predictions by hand for now
Delete version 7 from the registry and wait for the weekly retrain
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: Because the registry keeps old versions, rollback is a stage change rather than a rebuild, with a pre-agreed owner and signals. Rebuilding on new data would not give you the same proven model.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: A new model beats production on overall AUC. Before it enters the registry, what else should the evaluation gate check?
options: That it trains faster than the current production model does
That it uses more input features than the current production model
That it is not worse on key slices like new users or small cities
That it was built in the same notebook as the current model
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: The gate compares against production on held-out data, including key slices such as low-end phones. A better overall number can hide harm to a smaller group.

How does a machine learning model go fro.q: A team spends weeks debating MLflow versus Vertex AI. According to the answer, what matters more?
options: Picking a managed cloud, since open-source tools lack model registries
Habits like versioning, gates, staged release and monitoring, not the tool
Picking Kubeflow, since only Kubernetes-based tools can monitor drift
Picking the newest tool, since older ones cannot do real-time serving
How does a machine learning model go fro.why: MLflow, Kubeflow, SageMaker and Vertex AI all help, but the practices are what make the pipeline reliable. MLflow is open source and includes a registry.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: Nobody on the team wrote any rule to treat a group worse, yet the COD model denies one region far more often. What is the basic explanation?
options: A programmer must have hard-coded a region rule, since models cannot be biased alone
The model is randomly unfair, so retraining with a new random seed removes the gap
It learned from past data, copying unfair history, skewed samples, bad labels or proxies
The model is biased only because overall accuracy is low, so raising it fixes this
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: Models learn from data, so historical, sampling, label and proxy bias pass straight into them. Bias is systematic, not random, and high overall accuracy can hide it.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: A loan model is trained on whether past customers repaid. But outcomes exist only for people the old process approved. What is this problem called?
options: Selection bias: the visible data was filtered by the old decision process
Label noise: some of the repayment records were typed in wrongly by staff
Sampling bias: the training set simply has too few rows overall to learn
Concept drift: repayment behaviour has changed since the data was collected
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: Even training on outcomes instead of decisions, you only see outcomes for those approved, so the old filter shapes the data. This is a form of historical bias.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: 92% of training rows come from metro users and 8% from tier-3 towns. Overall accuracy is 94%. What risk should you check first?
options: Label bias: the tier-3 labels must be wrong, simply because the sample is smaller
Proxy bias: the metro flag is standing in for income, so it must be removed first
No real risk: 94% overall accuracy means every group is comfortably above 90%
Sampling bias: the model fits the majority, so the small group may sit near 80%
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: Optimising overall accuracy spends effort on the majority, and the average hides the thin group. Slice testing reveals it.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: In COD data, "customer refused the parcel" is often recorded when the courier could not find an informal address. What harm does this cause?
options: Sampling bias: those areas simply place fewer orders, so the model learns to ignore them
Label bias: the model learns those areas refuse parcels, punishing a region for a recording error
Historical bias: those areas were denied COD before, so the refusal label is accurate anyway
No harm: refusals and failed deliveries cost the same, so the label is fine to keep as is
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: The label is a measurement, not the truth, and the error is more common in some areas. The fix in the example is relabelling by refusal reason.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: A team says, "We dropped gender and religion columns, so our model is fair." What is the best response?
options: That is correct; without the sensitive columns the model cannot treat groups differently
That is fairness through unawareness; proxies rebuild the signal, so measure outcomes per group
That is correct only if pin code is kept, since it balances out the other features' effects
That is wrong only for deep learning; tree-based models are unable to make use of proxies
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: Removing a column does not remove correlated features such as first name, device or categories; a pattern-hunting model rebuilds the signal if it helps predict the label.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: How can you quickly test whether your features leak a sensitive attribute you removed?
options: Check the feature importance chart; if the attribute is not listed, nothing leaks
Compare overall accuracy with and without the column; if equal, nothing leaks
Ask labellers whether any of the feature names look sensitive to them
Train a small model to predict that attribute from your features and see if it succeeds
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: This proxy test directly measures how much sensitive information the features carry. Importance charts cannot show a column that is not in the model.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: Group A and group B both truly contain reliable customers. Among those reliable customers, A is approved 95% of the time and B 80%. Which fairness metric is violated?
options: Equal opportunity: deserving people in B are wrongly denied 20% vs 5% in A
Demographic parity: the overall approval rates of the two groups differ
Calibration: a score of 0.8 means a different risk level in each group
Four-fifths rule: B's approval rate falls below 80% of A's approval rate
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: Equal opportunity compares true positive rates among the truly deserving. Demographic parity compares overall approval rates regardless of who deserves it.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: A compliance analyst asks, "Do both pin-code clusters get COD approved at the same rate overall?" Which metric is she asking about?
options: Equal opportunity
Equalised odds
Demographic parity
Calibration
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: Demographic parity checks equal approval rates across groups. Equal opportunity checks equal approval only among the truly deserving.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: After fixes, TPRs are 94% and 90%, but approval rates are 88% and 79%, because the true reliable share differs (90% vs 85%). Why might the team accept the approval gap?
options: Because fairness metrics never conflict with each other, so a small approval gap is just noise
Because demographic parity applies only to hiring decisions, never to e-commerce decisions
Because the four-fifths rule is a binding legal standard that the 79% rate already passes
Equal approval would mean approving risky or denying reliable people; they chose equal opportunity
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: When base rates differ, the metrics cannot all be satisfied at once, so teams pick based on the main harm and document why. For a benefit like COD, wrongly denying a deserving person is usually the harm to minimise.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: Your slice report shows a 12-point TPR gap for "women in tier-3 towns", based on 40 people. What is the right reading?
options: Act at once; any gap above 5 points is significant whatever the slice size is
Check slice size; a gap on 40 may be noise, so gather more data before concluding
Ignore it; intersections of groups should never be tested as separate slices
Drop the slice from the report, since small slices distort the overall average
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: Slice testing should include intersections and always print n; a gap on 10,000 people is real. Small slices are noisy, but they should be watched, not dropped.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: Pin code is the model's strongest feature and pushes whole towns' scores. A teammate wants to delete it outright. What is the better approach?
options: Delete it immediately, since any location-based feature is always discriminatory by nature
Keep it unchanged, since a very strong feature must always reflect genuine underlying risk
Check what it carries; swap it for the customer's own history plus area delivery-success rate
Apply separate pin-code thresholds for each community, without involving legal review
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: Pin code also carries real delivery cost and courier coverage, so removing it blindly loses legitimate signal. Replacing coarse proxies with individual, fair signals often improves both fairness and accuracy.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: Pin codes denied COD last year have almost no fresh data, so they stay denied. How do you break this feedback loop?
options: Run small, capped exploration, such as COD for a random 2% of denied low-value orders
Retrain more often on the same data, so that the model eventually corrects itself
Remove those pin codes from the training data entirely so they stop skewing results
Lower the threshold for everyone so that every single order becomes eligible for COD
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: Denied people never generate outcome data, so the loop feeds itself. Deliberate, limited exploration collects unbiased data with controlled risk, which you then retrain on.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: You don't store gender or caste for privacy reasons, but need to audit fairness. What is the recommended approach?
options: Use a consented, governed audit sample or coarse region, only for evaluation
Infer gender from first names and add it to the model as a new input feature
Skip fairness audits, since you cannot measure groups that you do not store
Collect sensitive attributes from all users without consent, just for the audit
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: Governed audit samples let you measure outcomes without feeding sensitive data to the model. DPDP-style rules require consent and purpose limits.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: The COD model ships to production. What should accompany it so reviewers and auditors can check it?
options: Only the training code, since auditors can simply rerun it themselves if needed
Only the overall accuracy number, since per-slice details are kept confidential
A model card: purpose, limits, data sources, per-slice results and fairness checks
A press release describing the model's business impact during the festive sale
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: Model cards (and datasheets for datasets) make reviews possible. Laws such as the EU AI Act expect documentation for high-risk uses like credit scoring.

How can an AI model end up treating some.q: A manager says, "Fixing fairness will always cost us a lot of accuracy." What does the worked example suggest?
options: Yes; every fairness fix trades away accuracy one-for-one, so gains must be weighed
Often not; better labels and individual history improved both, since the bias was an error
Yes; the only fair model has equal approval rates, which is always far less accurate
No; fairness fixes always raise accuracy, so there is never any trade-off at all
How can an AI model end up treating some.why: Mislabelled refusals and coarse proxies were errors as well as unfairness, so correcting them helped both. Trade-offs can exist, but they are not automatic.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: A fraud model blocks a seller during the sale. Who needs an explanation of the decision, and why?
options: Only engineers, since sellers and support cannot understand model outputs
Only regulators, since sellers have no right to be given any reason at all
Sellers to appeal, support to reply, engineers to debug, compliance for rules
No one, as long as the model's overall accuracy on the test set is high
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: Explanations serve trust, appeals, debugging and regulation. "The model said so" is not enough for any of these groups.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: For a high-stakes seller-blocking decision, which modelling approach does the answer recommend?
options: Start interpretable (logistic regression, small tree); go black-box only if clearly better
Always start with a deep neural network, since it is most accurate on tabular data
Always use gradient-boosted trees, since SHAP makes them exactly as readable as a tree
Let an LLM make the decision directly, since it can explain its own choice in words
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: On tabular seller data, interpretable models are often close in accuracy and easier to defend. Black boxes need extra explanation tools.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: Permutation importance ranks "complaints" as the top feature. Can you tell a blocked seller, "you were blocked because of complaints"?
options: Yes; the top global feature is always the main reason for every individual decision
Yes, but only if complaints also ranks highest in the built-in tree importance chart
No; permutation importance only works with logistic regression, not other models
Not from that alone; it is global, so you need a local method like SHAP for that seller
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: Global importance describes the model overall; this seller's complaints might have been low. SHAP or LIME explain one prediction.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: How does permutation importance measure how much a model relies on a feature?
options: Count how many times, and how usefully, the trees split on that feature
Shuffle that feature across the test set and measure the accuracy drop
Remove the feature, retrain the model, and compare the training losses
Average that feature's raw values across all of the model's predictions
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: Shuffling turns the column into noise; a big accuracy drop means reliance. Counting splits is built-in tree importance, which is biased toward features with many distinct values.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: With two features, scores are: none 0.10, return rate only 0.40, account age only 0.20, both 0.70. What is return rate's SHAP value?
options: 0.30, the amount it adds when it is the first feature to join
0.40, the average of 0.30 (added first) and 0.50 (added second)
0.50, the amount it adds when it is the second feature to join
0.60, the full gap between the baseline and the final score
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: SHAP averages a feature's marginal contribution over all join orders: (0.30 + 0.50) / 2 = 0.40. Account age gets 0.20, and 0.10 + 0.40 + 0.20 = 0.70.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: A model's baseline is 0.10 and its prediction for a seller is 0.70. SHAP gives return rate +0.40. What is the total SHAP value of all other features?
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: SHAP values add up: baseline plus all SHAP values equals the prediction, so 0.70 - 0.10 - 0.40 = 0.20.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: Your risk model is a LightGBM ensemble with 20 features. You need exact, fast SHAP values per seller. Which tool fits?
options: TreeSHAP, which gives exact values for tree models quickly
KernelSHAP, the only exact SHAP method for tree models
LIME, which returns exact Shapley values for any model
Built-in tree importance, which gives per-seller values
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: With many features you cannot enumerate every order, so libraries approximate, but TreeSHAP is exact and fast for trees. KernelSHAP works on any model but is slower.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: A teammate bolts on LIME to explain one seller's score. What does LIME actually do, and what is its main weakness?
options: Averages contributions over all feature orders; it works only for tree-based models
Shuffles each feature across the test set; it can give only a global importance ranking
Fits a simple linear model to perturbed copies of that seller; results can vary between runs
Searches for the smallest change that flips the decision; it ignores whether it is actionable
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: LIME fits a local linear surrogate and is model-agnostic, but less stable than SHAP. The last option describes counterfactuals.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: A blocked seller asks, "What would I need to change?" Which kind of explanation answers this best?
options: A global feature-importance chart computed across all of the sellers
The full list of model weights and every exact threshold the model uses
The step-by-step reasoning text produced by an LLM about the decision
A counterfactual, like "with returns below 8%, you would not be blocked"
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: Counterfactuals give the smallest realistic change that flips the decision. Exposing exact thresholds and all features could also help fraudsters.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: Which counterfactual is most appropriate to show a seller?
options: "If your account had been two years older, you would not have been blocked"
"With under 1 complaint per 100 orders, your risk would fall below the threshold"
"If you had been registered in a different state, you would not have been blocked"
"If your pin code had been in a metro city, you would not have been blocked"
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: Good counterfactuals change actionable features. Account age cannot be acted on, and location-based ones are unfair and possibly discriminatory.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: SHAP shows a fashion seller's high return rate added +0.35 to fraud risk. An analyst writes, "Returns caused this fraud." What is the flaw?
options: SHAP values are always negative for fraud cases, so +0.35 must be a calculation error
SHAP reveals causes only when the baseline is above 0.5, and here the baseline is lower
SHAP shows how the model used the feature, not a real cause; sizing can explain returns
There is no flaw here; a large positive SHAP value proves the causal link directly
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: Explanations describe what the model relied on, correlation not cause. Real causes need investigation, which is why human review exists.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: "Returns" and "refund amount" move together. After a retrain, SHAP credit shifts from one to the other and the explanation story changes. Why?
options: Correlated features split credit unstably, so it can land on either after a retrain
The model has concept drift, so SHAP values must be recomputed every single hour
TreeSHAP is random by design, so its values always differ from one run to the next
The baseline changed, and a baseline change always flips the sign of SHAP values
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: With correlated inputs, attribution between them is unstable. Explanations can also be gamed or plausible but unfaithful, so treat them as evidence, not proof.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: An LLM support bot explains its refund decision with neat step-by-step reasoning. How much should you trust that as an explanation?
options: With caution; reasoning text may not match what drove it, so prefer citations and tool logs
Fully; the reasoning text is a direct recording of the model's internal computation steps
Fully, provided the reasoning is longer than five steps and cites at least one policy
Not at all; LLM outputs can never be audited or traced in any way whatsoever
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: Research shows reasoning traces are not always faithful. Grounding citations and tool logs give a more trustworthy audit trail.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: You are designing a seller-blocking system that uses an LLM somewhere. What is the sensible split of roles?
options: The LLM makes the block decision, and SHAP is then used to explain the LLM's choice
The LLM decides, and its reasoning text is sent straight to the seller as the reason
An explainable risk model decides; the LLM at most drafts the message from its output
Both models vote, and the seller sees whichever explanation sounds more convincing
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: High-stakes actions need an explainable, auditable decision maker; the LLM can word a message from the SHAP and counterfactual output. It is useful for wording, not for deciding.

A model blocked a seller's account. How.q: Over a week, 40 blocked sellers appeal, all after the same bank merger forced new IFSC codes. Global SHAP shows "bank change count" jumped in importance. What is the best fix?
options: Lower the block threshold so that fewer sellers are flagged across the board
Unblock verified cases, add a "bank change from known merger" feature, retrain
Remove all bank features permanently, since bank data is always unreliable
Keep the model and reject the appeals, since every score was above 0.6
A model blocked a seller's account. How.why: Explanations plus human review exposed a legitimate cause the model could not distinguish. Adding the merger feature fixes the root cause without discarding a useful fraud signal.

You take a photo of a friend's sneakers.q: A junior engineer asks what a 224x224 colour photo looks like to a vision model. What is the best answer?
options: A list of object names the camera detected when the photo was taken
A short compressed text caption describing the main object shown
A grid of about 150,000 numbers: red, green and blue values per pixel
A single number summarising the overall brightness of the image
You take a photo of a friend's sneakers.why: 224 x 224 x 3 is about 150,000 numbers; the model only ever sees this block. That is why a shadow, which changes thousands of numbers, matters so much.

You take a photo of a friend's sneakers.q: A 3x3 filter with -1, 0, +1 in each row slides over a photo. Where does it give a large output?
options: Where a dark sole meets a white floor, since one side is much brighter
Over a flat white area, since all nine pixels share the same high value
Only at the image centre, since filters are applied once in the middle
Wherever the colour is red, since the weights select the red channel
You take a photo of a friend's sneakers.why: Over flat areas the left and right columns cancel to near 0; across a vertical brightness change they do not. Sliding the filter everywhere gives a feature map of vertical edges.

You take a photo of a friend's sneakers.q: A colleague says, "Our engineers hand-wrote the edge and stripe detectors in our CNN." What is the correction?
options: Correct; all filters are hand-designed and only the classifier is learned
Correct for early layers; only deep layers learn, since edges never change
Filters are copied directly from pixel values of the training images

Read the same replies faster so that long lists finish inside the latency budget
Show the full text reply on screen and play a short beep instead of any speech
Keep replies short and speakable, with no URLs or markdown, and confirm risky actions
How does a voice assistant understand \".why: Lists, links and long paragraphs sound terrible when spoken. Voice needs short, speakable answers, and risky actions like cancellation need spoken confirmation.

How does a voice assistant understand \".q: A TTS voice reads '₹1,299 by 5 Oct' as 'rupee symbol one comma two nine nine'. Which TTS stage is at fault?
options: The vocoder, which converts the predicted spectrogram back into a waveform
Text normalisation, which turns symbols, numbers and dates into speakable words
The acoustic model, which predicts rhythm, stress and intonation for the sentence
The endpointer, which decides when the user's sentence has actually finished
How does a voice assistant understand \".why: Text normalisation turns '₹1,299 by 5 Oct' into natural words before the acoustic model and vocoder run. Prosody and waveform generation come after and do not fix symbol reading.

How does a voice assistant understand \".q: Your LLM takes several seconds to write a full answer, but users expect a reply in about a second. What is the most effective design?
options: Wait for the full LLM answer, then use a faster TTS model so playback ends sooner
Lengthen the endpointing silence so the LLM gets a head start during user pauses
Stream every stage, sending each finished LLM sentence straight to streaming TTS
Remove the STT step and pass raw audio directly into the text-only LLM instead
How does a voice assistant understand \".why: Overlapping stages is the secret: speech starts after the first sentence while later ones are generated. A faster TTS alone cannot hide multi-second LLM generation, and longer endpointing adds delay.

How does a voice assistant understand \".q: Using the illustrative latency budget, roughly how long from 'user stops talking' to 'first sound plays' should a well-built pipeline target?
options: About 0.8 to 1.6 seconds, since above about 1.5 seconds the bot starts to feel broken
About 50 to 150 milliseconds, the same as a single network round trip
About 3 to 5 seconds, since users expect a pause while the bot looks things up
About 30 seconds, matching the chunk length of Whisper-style models
How does a voice assistant understand \".why: Adding endpointing, STT, LLM first tokens, TTS first chunk and network gives about 0.8-1.6 s to first audio. People normally reply within a few hundred milliseconds, so multi-second pauses feel broken.

How does a voice assistant understand \".q: A user interrupts mid-reply with 'No, not that one, the shoes', but the bot keeps talking and later 'remembers' saying things she never heard. What does proper barge-in need?
options: Echo cancellation, fast VAD to stop TTS in about 200 ms, and history of what she heard
A louder TTS voice so the interruption is drowned out and the full reply completes
A longer endpointing threshold so interruptions are ignored until the reply ends
Muting the microphone during playback so the bot can never hear its own voice
How does a voice assistant understand \".why: Barge-in needs echo cancellation so the bot does not hear itself, fast voice detection to stop playback, and honest history. Muting the mic during playback makes interruption impossible.

How does a voice assistant understand \".q: A product manager wants to replace the STT-LLM-TTS pipeline with a single speech-to-speech model for refund support. What is the best balanced response?
options: It makes the pipeline obsolete, being cheaper and better on every Indian language
It is not possible, since no model can take audio in and produce audio out directly
Lower latency and better tone, but harder to audit and guardrail than a pipeline
It only changes voice quality, so latency and auditability stay exactly the same
How does a voice assistant understand \".why: Speech-to-speech models skip text steps, giving lower latency and better tone, but they are harder to audit, often pricier and weaker on some Indian languages today. Teams keep pipelines where auditable transcripts and reliable tool calls matter.

How does a voice assistant understand \".q: A team wants customers to approve refunds by saying 'yes, I confirm', verified by voiceprint alone. What is the right call?
options: Approve it, because a voiceprint is unique and cannot be imitated by any software
Use voice for intent, but confirm with an OTP or in-app tap, since voices can be cloned
Approve it only if the phrase is spoken in English, which is far harder to clone
Store raw audio forever so any disputed refund can be replayed later as evidence
How does a voice assistant understand \".why: Voice cloning can imitate someone from a short sample, so voice should not be the only authentication. Keeping raw audio forever also conflicts with data minimisation.

How does a voice assistant understand \".q: Which logging policy best fits the privacy guidance for a voice shopping assistant in India?
options: Keep raw audio for all users by default so models can be retrained on it later
Keep nothing at all, not even transcripts, so no data can ever be misused
Keep raw audio but encrypt it, which removes the need for consent under DPDP
Keep transcripts briefly, not raw audio unless agreed, and redact OTPs and addresses
How does a voice assistant understand \".why: Data minimisation, short retention, redaction and consent are recommended; the DPDP Act expects purpose-limited consented use. Encryption alone does not replace consent.

Run the query on the offline store instead, since it already holds full history
Precompute it and read it from the online store with a single key lookup
Cache the query result in the browser so repeat checkouts skip the database

options: Offline: timestamped history for training; online: latest value for fast lookups
Offline: latest value for live models; online: full timestamped history for training
Offline: features from batch jobs only; online: features from streaming jobs only
Offline: raw Kafka events for replay; online: model weights for the serving service

options: Data leakage: training used future fraud labels, so offline accuracy was inflated
Concept drift: customers genuinely started ordering more, so the model is outdated
Overfitting: the model memorised training users and cannot generalise to new ones
Training-serving skew: production counts differ from what the model learned on

Log serving-time features and compare their distributions with the training data
Re-run offline evaluation on the training set, since skew lowers offline accuracy
Increase the model size, since skew mainly affects small models with few features

A model needs \"how many orders has this.q: A data scientist builds training data by joining each labelled March order with the user's feature values as of today. Offline accuracy is amazing. What is wrong and what is the fix?
options: Nothing is wrong; the freshest values always give the most accurate training set
It leaks the future; use a point-in-time join as of each order's timestamp
The features are stale; recompute them with a streaming job before the join
The labels are too old; drop March orders and train only on this week's data

A model needs \"how many orders has this.q: Which feature most clearly needs a real-time streaming pipeline rather than a nightly batch?
options: user_avg_order_value_90d, since averages are the most important fraud input overall
product_return_rate_30d, since return rates change many times every single second
pincode_cod_share_30d, since the COD share must always be exact to the second
user_failed_payments_1h, since a burst of recent failures is a strong fraud signal

A model needs \"how many orders has this.q: How does a stream job keep a sliding 7-day order count fresh per user without rescanning all orders on every event?
options: Keep 168 hourly buckets per user, sum them, and drop the oldest as time moves
Re-run the full 7-day SQL query every second and overwrite the online value
Keep only the latest order timestamp per user and estimate the count from it
Store the count once a week and interpolate between the weekly snapshots
A model needs \"how many orders has this.why: Hourly buckets let the processor update a running count as events arrive and expire old buckets, then write the result to the online store within seconds. Rescanning every second would be very expensive.

A model needs \"how many orders has this.q: Your manager asks to make every one of the 300 fraud features real-time 'to be safe'. What is the best response?
options: Agree, since streaming is cheaper per value than nightly batch once it is set up
Agree, since real-time features remove training-serving skew from the system
Choose freshness per feature; stream only where recent behaviour really matters
Refuse, since online stores are unable to hold features written by stream jobs
A model needs \"how many orders has this.why: Streaming jobs run all day, write constantly and need support; most features are fine at daily freshness. Real-time does not remove skew, which comes from inconsistent definitions.

A model needs \"how many orders has this.q: In training, missing 'device_accounts_24h' values were filled with 0. In serving, they are sent as -1. Why is this a problem?
options: It is harmless, since most models ignore negative input values automatically

It is data leakage, since -1 reveals that the user is likely a fraudster
It is training-serving skew: the model gets a value it never learned to read

A model needs \"how many orders has this.q: Fraud, recommendations and delivery-promise teams each built their own 'user orders in 7 days' with slightly different definitions. What feature store capability addresses this, and what governance rule matters?
options: A larger online store so each team can keep its own private copy of the feature
A shared registry with owners for reuse; meaning changes get a new version
A vector database so that similar feature definitions are merged automatically
A nightly job that averages the three teams' values into a single shared number

A model needs \"how many orders has this.q: During a festive sale the online store starts timing out on feature lookups at checkout. What should the checkout service do?
options: Block the order until the feature store recovers, since scoring without features is unsafe
Switch to querying the offline store, which has the same data with full history
Use timeouts with safe defaults and fall back to a simpler rule-based check, never blocking checkout
Compute all features on the fly from the orders database until the store recovers
